R E P O R T
General Background
 
1.         Science and Technology has had a long and rich tradition in India. Even in ancient times, India is known to have
 made pioneering contributions in the areas like mathematics, astronomy and chemistry. Iron-pillar situated near Qutab
 Minar is an eloquent testimony to the great advances made in the field of metallurgy in ancient India. From towards the
 end of the last century and during the first half of the present century, science in India witnessed a period of renaissance
 when India produced renowned scientists like J.C.Bose, S. Ramanujan, C.V. Raman, S.N. Bose, Meghnad Saha, P.C.
 Mahalanobis, Birbal Sahni, H.J. Bhabha, S.Chandrasekhar and others who are known for their path-breaking
 contributions in the areas of basic research.
 
2.         Spectacular achievements made in the field of science and technology during the last century brought about
 unprecedented economic growth and social transformation in the industrialised countries. This led to the creation of a
 favourable climate for science and technology being made a part of the national endeavour in developing countries as
 well. Governments in developing countries started paying increasing attention to science and technology on the
 assumption that an indigenous scientific and technological base would bring faster economic development and social
 transformation.
 
3.         After Independence, India also decided to use science and technology as a key instrument in the process of
 nation-building particularly through the vision and initiative of Jawaharlat Nehru. At the time of Independence, the
 scientific and technological base in India was neither properly organised nor capable enough to take on major national
 challenge. It was, therefore, decided to give special attention to create the necessary infrastructure for the development
 o4 science and technology in India. Various institutions and a network of laboratories for conducting research in
 specialised areas were established. Ministry of Scientific Research and Natural Resources was created by the
 Government of India in 1951 for organising and directing scientific research for national development.
 
4.         A symbol of the Government's forward-looking thinking in promoting science in the country was the adoption of
 the Scientific Policy Resolution in 1958 which aimed at securing for the people of the country all the benefits that can
 accrue from the acquisition and application of scientific knowledge. The Resolution aimed at producing research
 scientists of the highest quality in the country and introducing programmes for training scientific and technical
 personnel on a scale adequate to fulfil the country's need in areas like Health Education, Agriculture, Industry, Defence,
 etc.
 
5.         The Department of Science and Technology (DST) was, therefore, set up in 1971 with a view to providing a
 "nodal department for organising, coordinating and promoting science and technology (S&T) activities in which a
 number of institutions and Departments have interests and capabilities". This, of course, does not cover the specific
 programmes in fields such as atomic energy and space for which Government has specially set up Departments and
 Commissions. Major roles assigned to DST involve promoting new areas of science and technology and formulating
 policy statements and guidelines on S&T. The Department has since undertaken various projects and programmes for
 this purpose, such as providing support to basic and applied research; critical technology programmes; socially oriented
 S&T activities for
rural areas and weaker sections; and entrepreneurship development with a view to creating self-employment
 opportunities.

6.         In order to assess whether the DST is fulfilling its mandate effectively and efficiently, the Committee decided to
 study the various aspects of the functioning of the Department by analysing its Annual Report for the year 1992-93.
 
7.         The Committee was informed about various programmes and activities undertaken by DST for development of
 S&T and coordination of multi-institutional and inter-disciplinary activities at the national level. The Department also
 undertakes various societal programmes to help people in rural areas and weaker sections of society. It is also rendering
 scientific services such as collection and supply of meteorological .and seismic data to different user agencies and
 departments of the Government. Besides, these, the Department is also looking after various autonomous high quality
 research institutions and professional bodies throughout the country. The Department is promoting scientific research in
 frontline and priority areas of Research and Development (R&D) in various disciplines of science and technology by
 funding those through the mechanism of science and Engineering Research Council (SERC). SERC supports and
 monitors R&D efforts in new and inter-disciplinary areas by providing financial assistance, setting up of core groups
 and establishing national facilities required for promoting a given discipline of S&T. During the year 1992-93, SERC
 approved 155 projects costing Rs.22.96 crores in different areas of S&T. The Committee was informed about the
 'Young Scientists Scheme' meant for providing opportunities for pursuing exciting and innovative ideas 'by young
 scientists.
 
8.         The Committee was also given an idea about the multi-disciplinary activities of the National Centre for Medium
 Range Weather Forecasting and Development of Agro-meteorological Advisory Services which aim at the
 development of the capability of issuing medium range (3-10 days in advance) weather forecasting mainly for
 preparation of the weather based advisories for the farming community and dissemination of the same to the users.
 
9. The Committee was also informed about the support and facilities provided by the Department for science promotion
 through the initiation of several schemes such as the Regional Sophisticated Instrumentation Centres (RSICs),
 Sophisticated Instrumentation Facilities (SI Fs), National Coordination of Testing and Calibration Facilities (NCTC),
 support to State S&T Councils to professional bodies for various S&T activities. One Department also provides
 assistance for international travel to participate in scientific seminars and symposia.
 
10.       In the area of technology development, DST has evolved certain schemes intended to accelerate growth of
 indigenous capability such as Instrument Development programme, Robitics and Automation, Biomedical engineering,
 Cryogenics, Ceramics, etc. "Critical Technology Programme" is a new initiative to support selected activities conducive
 to strengthening technological capabilities of the country. The Technology Information Forecasting & Assessment
 Council (TIFAC) generates Technology Forecast and Technology Assessment documents in various areas. 'A number
 of technology forecasting, technology assessment and techno-market survey studies were conducted by the TIFAC in
 prioritised areas. DST has also set up a Science & Technology Advisory Committee (STAC) with a view to formulating
 long term S&T plans/ programmes relevant to concerned sectors.
 
11.       As regards the programmes involving international cooperation in scientific and technological fields the
 Committee was informed that DST has the nodal responsibility of coordinating international collaborations. Such
 programmes are in operation at bilateral, regional and multilateral levels. Agreement for cooperation in S&T has been
 signed with Hungary, Ukraine, Uzbekistan, Poland, Italy, Mangolia and Israel during the year 1992-93. Multilateral
 programmes on S&T including regional cooperation programmes and those involving UN and other international
 agencies are also being looked after by DST.
 
12.       Application of science and technologyfor the benefit of society is one of the important concerns of DST. Several
 experimental projects were undertaken by the Department in the past with a view to demonstrating the changes that
 could be brought about by S&T in improving the living conditions of the rural people and those of the women and other
 weaker sections of society.
 
13.       Activities connected with science communications and popularisation and National Science and Technology
 Entrepreneurship Development were also promoted by the
 Department. The Bharat Jan Gyan Vigyan Jatha (BJGVJ-92) communication event, which could directly address a
 large number of people in various parts of the country touching nearly a fourth of the population . The programme
 informed on some of the basic problems like water, nutrition; health, environment and literacy. The 144 - part radio

 serial on "Manav ka Vikas' being broadcast simultaneously in 18 Indian languages, is the largest science serial ever
 produced in the world. A scheme called Mass Employment Generation through Science and Technology (MEGST) has
 been launched for providing avenues for self-employment to unemployed science and engineering graduates, mainly

 14.       Besides, DST provides operational services in the field of meteorology and surveys
 through India Meteorological Department (IMD), Survey of India (SOI) and National Atlas
 and Thematic Mapping Organisation (NATMO). These services are being modernised through
 the introduction of sophisticated equipments. With the help of widely distributed INSAT-based
 disaster warning receivers, it has been made possible to forecast and issue tropical cyclone
 advisories. These services are offered to departments dealing with Agriculture, Aviation, etc.
 Survey of India (SOI), the country's principal agency for surveying and mapping has been
 actively engaged in the production of various types of topographical and geographical maps
 for defence mid developmental purposes. It has been carrying out geodetic and geophysical
 surveys, viz., tidal gravity and geomagnetic observations for tunnel alignments and crustal
 movement studies etc. The National Atlas and Thematic Mapping Organisation (NATMO)
 provides valuable services in the preparation of thematic maps. The Department also supports
 a number of autonomous research and academic institutions which are working in areas like
 medical science, plasma physics, palaeobotany, astronomy, astrophysics, geo-magnetism,
 Himalayan geology and climatology, etc.
 
Role of DST
 15.       When asked about the role and overall impact of DST in the promotion of S&T
 activities, the representative of the Department informed the Committee that DST was supposed to promote scientific
 research and development technology-related programmes and that it was also mandated to constitute the S&T inputs
 into society-related programmes. He informed the Committee that there was no single agency in the Government which
 was solely responsible for implementing society-related programmes. There are many departments/ agencies involved
 in it. In this regard Secretary, DST observed:
 
If we have to have the impact of demonstrations what is important is to make DST more effective in
 participating in the programmes of other departments .... there are large number of programmes. If coordination
 can be ensured, if effectiveness can be ensured whether it is the Ministry of Welfare or the Ministry of Rural
 Development, then we can make the impact.
 
In view of the observations made by the Secretary, DST, the Committee feels that the DST should dovetail its
 efforts not only with scientific departments but also with such Ministries/Departments like Railways, Defence,
 Communications, Commerce, Industry, etc. The Department should also coordinate its activities with the other socio-
economic Ministries. Whilst this is being attempted, the real success of S&T for national development will come about
 when this coordination can be made most effective.
 
Allocation of Funds :
 
16.       The Committee noticed that while the Annual Plans allocation for the DST during 1990-92 was Rs.274.20
 crores, actuals for the period were Rs.240.06 crores only. In other words, actuals were Rs.34.14 crores less than the
 allocation for this period. Attention of the Committee was drawn towards the fact that the allocation to the Department
 constituted just 0.2% of the total Central Sector outlay during the Sixth Plan. It went slightly up to 0.36% in the
 Seventh Plan. This share has further come down in the Eighth Plan. The Secretary, DST, also informed the Committee
 that of the total allocation made to the Department, a lion's share is being spent on the India Meteorological Department
 and Survey of India. Besides, DST is also required to support 13 autonomous research institutions like Raman Research
 Institute, Indian Institute of Astrophysics, etc. Thus, the remaining funds are not sufficient to fulfil the mandate
 assigned to it. The Committee, therefore, realises that the DST is working under severe financial constraints, and that
 with present level of allocation, it was difficult for the Department to promote effectively the mandate assigned to it.
 The Committee took particular notice of the financial paucity for carrying out R&D activities and various society-

related programmes. The Committee was told that any of the society-related programmes did not have more than Rs.4
 crores. Since these programmes are committed to supporting a large number of core groups, this amount is not
 sufficient. The Committee feels that there is need to spend more in the field of S&T. The Government should,
 therefore, make a realistic assessment of the financial requirements of the DST keeping in view the obligations which it
 has to fulfil and make suitable allocation to the Department.
 
17.       Survey of India and India Meteorological Department are huge organisations employing 17042 and 8307
 persons, respectively. This is needed in their cases as they are all India service organisations with considerable
 technical and field work. DST has a sanctioned strength of 757. The staff strength of DST, since it includes the
 personnel of IMD and SOI naturally conveys the impression that the Department is organised like any other
 administrative department of the Government rather than a scientific department which normally is expected to be very
 compact and highly scientific and officer-oriented. The Committee, however, is of the view that the ministerial strength
 of DST is also large for the role it has to play. The Committee, therefore, recommends that DST should organise itself
 in such a manner as may facilitate it to devote the bulk of its funds on scientific and research activities.
 
Technology Fee :
 
18.       The Committee is also of the view that a part of the fund could be raised from various beneficiaries of the
 technologies developed by DST. When asked about collecting something like development cess as was being done in
 the case of sugar and coal, the Secretary, DST had this to say :
 
"Fortunately for us we have what is known as technology fee which is being levied. Every import of
 technology requires a fee to be paid .... commodity cess is usually used by the corresponding socio-
economic Ministries more for the purpose of expansion of their activities. So, if we use the amount for
 the promotion of technology development and the DST has to perform that role, it will be very good.
 This is one cess to which we would like to have access. This is now being levied as part of the
 technology growth in the country. Industries are importing technology and in the liberalised
 environment, more and more imports will take place and there is a five per cent cess which is being paid
 towards those imports of technology. If we can have access to this, then we really don't have to trouble
 or burden the Planning Commission."
 
In view of the above, Committee feels that the Government may examine the feasibility of implementing the
 suggestion of allowing DST to have access to the technology fee; but there would have to be careful monitoring of the
 use to which funds' are put.
 
Research and Development (R&D) :
 
19.       Research and Development in various disciplines of S&T forms one of the important activities of the DST. Basic
 objectives of the R&D activities cover integrated research programmes in inter-disciplinary fields, frontier areas in
 science and engineering, encouraging brilliant young scientists and promoting general research capabilities in relevant
 areas of S&T. National R&D programmes are supported by DST involving a number of academic and research
 institutions, professional bodies and other socio-economic departments of the Government. Industrial R&D forms an
 important component of overall R&D activities in the country in which both the Public and the Private Sectors are
 involved. As regards the state of Industry-related R&D in India, the Committee was informed that of the total national
 R&D expenditure (Rs.4186.43 crores) during 1990-91, 68.9% came from Central Government, 7.9% from State
 Governments, 10.6% was contributed by public sector industries and 12.6% by the private sector industries. The major
 share of national expenditure on R&D was thus met from government sources (87.4%) and the rest 12,6% came from
 the private industries.
 
The Committee notices that this ratio is just the reverse in the developed economies such as Korea and Japan. In
 Korea, for example, in 1988, government share in the expenditure on R&D was just 18.1°/o and that of the private
 sector was 81.9%. Similarly, in Japan, this ratio was 20% and 80% respectively during the same year. The Committee
 feels that the share of private sector industries in R&D activities in India is far more less, particularly when the various
 incentives have been given to them. There is a need to raise standard of industrial research with a view to meeting the

 changing economic situation and to see that the country competes with others. Achieving this would certainly require
 substantial financial input which, as things stand today, is not possible, unless the private sector industries which are
 making use of expertise and technology developed by DST and its various centres, gives part of its cost back to the
 nation. The Committee, therefore, suggests that efforts should be made to motivate private industries to put more
 money into industry-related R&D activities. The Committee feels that by doing so a close linkage between Science-
industry-university can also be established.
 
Technology Information, Forecasting & Assessment Council:
 
20.       Technology Information, Forecasting & Assessment Council (TIFAC) has the primary mandate to generate
 Technology Forecasting (TF) and Technology Assessment (TA) documents in various technology areas and establish
 an on-line nationally accessible technology information system. The Committee noted the fact that according to the
 Department TA/TF studies have been completed in some areas like sugarcane and sugar production technologies,
 biotechnology, electronic technologies, aviation, etc., the tempo in implementing various programmes relating to
 TA/FF on an overall basis has not caught up; and even in the areas where work has been taken up, the depth is not
 adequate. The Committee is of the view that further major initiatives are required to be taken by the TIFAC to create an
 impact in this regard.
 
International Cooperation :
 
21.       On the question of international cooperation in the areas of science and technology, particularly at the bilateral
 level, the Committee was informed that such cooperation could play a prominent role in R&D activities at a relatively
 low cost. A great impetus can, therefore, be provided to S&T activities by seeking cooperation of the advanced
 countries. In this connection the representative of the Department gave the example of India's cooperation with Israel
 under which there would be a 3 million dollar Joint fund contributed equally by both the governments. It has been
 proposed that the projects to be taken up under this scheme should be decided by experts not by government officials.
 Similarly, a research centre has been set up in Hyderabad in cooperation with Bylorussia, where coating of blades of
 aircrafts has been started. This used to be earlier got done in England which involved a considerable amount of foreign
 exchange. In view of the benefits accruing from the international cooperation the Committee emphasises the need for
 building broad based R&D infrastructure even with foreign help and cooperation which would be advantageous to the
 country to make use of its comparatively inexpensive scientific manpower.
 
Brain Drain :
 
22.       Most of our young scientists and engineers who go abroad for higher study do not come back even after
 completing their studies. When Committee enquired about their number and employment profile, etc. it was informed
 that no such data was available with the Government. Department of Science & Technology, however, had sponsored
 some pilot-studies at IIT, Delhi and AIIMS, New Delhi yielding some estimates in this regard. For example, it was
 found that about 30% of the graduates from IIT had migrated abroad where most of them worked as practising research
 engineers and scientists. Similarly, the overall brain drain from AIIMS for the period 1956 to 1980 was 50% with a
 decreasing trend from 1971 onwards. The magnitude varied from 3% in 1980 to 89% in 1967. The field of work of
 those settled abroad had shown that 84% were in clinical practice, 30% in teaching and 19% in research, etc. The
 Committee feels that a poor country like India can ill-afford the drain of trained engineers, scientists and doctors,
 particularly when the country spends scarce money on training them. The Committee desires that the government
 should study the phenomenon of brain drain and evolve effective strategies to convince and motivate our scientists and
 engineers to come back after completing their studies abroad and furthermore, devise measures whereby we can make
 use of our scientists located abroad who desire to help in development of science and technology in our country and
 thereby contribute to the development.
 
Bharat Jan Gyan Vigyan Jatha (BJGVJ) :
 
23.       When asked about BJGVJ and post-Jatha activities, the Committee was informed in a written reply that during
 the Jatha period, over 400 Jathas in 375 districts touching nearly one-fourth of the population of the country were
 organised. Each district had its own Jatha covering 100 villages. Some 2500 volutarty agencies and other government

 activities and identifying local problems and mobilisation of people for the possible solution of the same. Thereafter, a
 Mass Action For National Regeneration would be launched. Programme planned for this might include, inter alia, basic
 surveys of the village/gram panchayat on themes such as literacy and elementary education, traditional methods of
 communication, organisation of competitions among local students/youth on making posters/slogans, village gram
 panchayat/ block level competitions on best farmer, best craftsman, etc. The Committee appreciates the steps taken and
 proposed to be taken by the Department in strengthening S&T communication/ popularisation. The Committee is of the
 opinion that such steps would go a long way in inculcating scientific temper and rational thinking among villagers. The
 BJGVJ programme should also be utilised for the purpose of taking science and technology from laboratories and
 universities to the people,
 
Appropriate Technology:
 
24.       S&T has to be utilised as a key instrument in taking care of problems faced by weaker sections, particularly
 those living in rural areas. Scientific researches and technology development efforts, no doubt, aim at devising
 technologies appropriate to the local needs and conditions but much more needs to be done in this regard. For example,
 particle board which is being manufactured from the rice-husk which can replace natural wood can also be
 manufactured from other materials such as Sugarcane skin or coir waste. In rural areas, poor people live in thatched
 houses made of locally available material which lasts only a year or two. If a chemical treatment could be worked out
 as could prevent or delay the decay of these leaves, etc. which would make them last longer, it would immensely
 benefit poor people. CSIR has already developed many packages for the poor people, particularly those living in rural
 and remote areas. For example, fire-proofing of thatched roofs is a technology which has already been developed by
 CSIR. But unfortunately such technologies have not reached the target-groups. In this regard Committee is aware of the
 limitations of the scientific departments. The scientific departments can promote socially-beneficial technologies but
 they are not always in a position to deliver such technologies to the people because the extension mechanism requires
 not only additional funding but extra efforts for which these departments are not particularly trained. Moreover, the
 emphasis of these departments is on the developing of socially-beneficial technologies. The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that in order to ensue that the socially beneficial technologies reach the target groups, DST should make
 efforts to enlist the support of socio-economic Ministries/Departments of the Central and State Governments which
 should help in promoting extension activities and coordinate its activities with CSIR in this regard.
 
State Councils for S&T:
 
25.       About the nature of activities of S&T Councils in various .States and Union territories and their sources of
 finance, the Committee was informed that State S&T Councils were set up for "promoting and fostering the application
 of science and technology for socio-economic development of States and Union territories . Some of the programmes
 being undertaken by  them are in the area of popularisation of science, entrepreneurship development, remote
 sensing, rural development, R&D support for location specific needbased projects,
 demonstration and field trials, etc. As regards funding of the State S&T Councils, the
 representative of DST told the Committee that while DST provides funding towards the
 secretarial staff in the State S&T Councils, the funds for the activities/programmes are
 provided as a part of the State Annual Plans, based on discussions in the Planning
 Commission in which Department of Science and Technology also participated. When asked
 about the existence of control or monitoring mechanism, if any, the Committee was informed
 that it was very difficult for DST to perform a controlling role because the States are
 autonomous. Generally, they would not accept a controlling role of DST and, therefore, it
 only plays a promotional role. Monitoring of the activities of the State S&T Councils,
 however, is done through an annual all-India review meeting on specific S&T themes with
 heads of S&T Secretariat of Council in which Union Minister of State (S&T) is also present.
 Regional level meetings are also held to review the existing S&T structure at the State level
 and to identify areas of mutual cooperation between the States and Union territories in the
 respective regions. Executive Committees of all the State Councils meet 3 or 4 times a year
 to consider new activities as well as to review on-going programmes. A DST officer
 participates in all these meetings. Besides, DST participates while State S&T Annual Plans

Natural Vagaries:
 
26.       India Meteorological Department (IMD) which provides meteorological services is the principal institution in all
 matters relating to meteorology, and allied subjects. IMD has developed various techniques by which it can now very
 accurately locate and monitor cyclones as they develop and move over time and space and issue warnings about
 magnitude, point of impact, time of impact, etc. While the Committee appreciates the progress made by IMD in its
 cyclone-forecasting, as a result of which disaster prevention and mitigation in this area has attained world standard, it
 expresses its serious concern over the fact that not enough work has been done in the field of seismology. The
 Committee discussed various aspects of seismology including the possibility of earthquake prediction and warning and
 noted the fact that a separate study on the subject is being conducted by the Rao Committee appointed in the aftermath
 of the earthquake in the Marathwada region.
 
27.       With regard to other natural vagaries, the Committee notices that the entire Himalayan region faces problems
 generated by natural vagaries such as rivers changing their course, landslides, etc. These often result in loss of life and
 property. The Committee, therefore, feels that the Department should address itself to taking care of the problems faced
 by the people inhabiting these areas. Basic problems like these should be studied by our scientists and effective
 measures should be evolved with a view to protecting people from such natural disasters.
 
Format of the Annual Report:
 
28.       The Committee observes that the Annual Report of the DST provides only a narration of the on-going
 programmes and activities but it does not give meaningful information which may help in reviewing the progress of
 various programme. In the absence of such information, it becomes very difficult to take stock of and assess the
 performance of the Department. The Committee, is therefore, of the opinion that DST should provide inter alia, either
 in the Annual Report as Annexure or in some other form, such vital information with regard to various on­going
 programmes as the year when a programme was sanctioned the money which has already been spent on the
 programme, the progress made in the execution of that programme and so on. The Committee feels that the Department
 should clearly evaluate its strength and weaknesses and should in clear terms, inform through its Annual Report as to
 what are its areas of strength and where lies the weakness. Unless strengths are identified the Department cannot
 assume the leadership in the development of S&T in the country. Likewise, identification of weak areas is also essential
 as this would naturally lead the Department to initiate necessary corrective measures to improve its working.
 
29.       The Committee notes that at present there is no adequate audit of various programme/ projects undertaken and
 sponsored by the DST. An audit mechanism which should also go into the social benefits that would be accruing
 through a programme undertaken by the Department should also be instituted. The Committee has particularly found
 that in many areas the monitoring mechanism in the Department needs to be revamped.
 
30.       The Committee noted with satisfaction that DST, besides promoting scientific research and technology
 development, is also promoting society-related programmes which are of immense value. In such a situation, the
 Committee feels that DST has to associate with it persons from different areas of life who would function as a
 'thinktank' of the Department. Such a thinktank would be responsible for identifying areas to be emphasised and for
 chalking out an integrated strategy for achieving the desired results more efficiently.

NEW DELHI; 
December 18, 1998 
S.R. BOMMAI, 
Chairman, 
Committee on Science&: Technology,

REPORT \ 
The Report of the Committee deals ·with the Action Taken by the Department of 
Biotechnology on the recommendations contained in the Fifty-fourth Report of the 
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Envi­
ronment and Forests on the Demands for Grants (1998-99) of the Department of 
Biotechnology which was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 7th July, 1998. There are seven 
recommendations contained in the Fifty-fourth Report of the Committee. Action Taken 
notes on the recommendations of the Committee were received from the Department on 
20th August , 1998. 
On scrutiny pf the Action Taken Report as received from the Department of 
Biotechnology, the Committee finds that all the seven recommendations have been fully 
implemented . 
The· Committee's recommendations, action tuken thereon and comments of the 
Committee on the action taken by the Department of Biotechnology are given in the 
succeeding paragraphs:-
RECOMMENDATION 
While the Committee expresses its satisfaction over various basic and produc~oriented 
R&D activities of the Department, the Committee does feel that much of the work done by the 
Department particularly which aims at benefiting farmers, weaker sections of society and 
backward regions in the country lacks publicity. The Department should try to give wide 
publicity to its work by using all modern methods of mass communication including print and 
electronic media. 
(Para 9) 
The Committee observes that the monitoring mechanism which exist today is quite lax 
because the benefit of biotechnology based programmes is not reaching a large section of our 
population, though the Committ~e is aware of the fact that the Department of Biotechnology 
can only demonstrate the technology and it is ultimately for the concerned Ministries and 
Departments to do the needed extension work to make the technology acceptable by the 
concerned sections of the society. There is a strong need to have an effective coordinating 
mechanism between the Department, socio-economic Ministries/Departments and the State 
Governments/Bodies in order to make the biotechnology based programmes reach the people. 
(Para 17) 
Action Taken by the Department: 
Department of Biotechnology can only demonstrate the technology and it is ultimately 
for the concerned Ministries/ Departments to do the extension work to make the technology 
acceptable by the concerned sections of the society. The Department has made concerted 
effort s in popularising the technologies developed through (i) exhibitions, national and 
international level, (ii) field demonstrations in farmers' fields through State Departments and 
Universities, (iii) technology transfer to industries, (iv) by involving the user ministries both 
technically and financially in its programmes to launch joint projects and (v) convening Inter­
Ministrial Steering Committees on specific aspects of nation al needs. 

During the year 1997-98 the Department has participated in about 10 exhibitions, 
assisted 85 seminars/conferences and 6 series of 18 popular lectures in various institutions. 
Ten popular monograms in English and Hindi have been published. Representatives of 
concerned user ministries have been included as members in all the programmes, having 
impact on society specially women, weaker sections of people and rural population, Several 
projects/programmes jointly funded by Central Silk Board, Central Coffee Board, Spices 
Board, ICAR, ICMR, CSIR and State Governments have been launched involving 
concerned user ministries to ensure application of specific biotechnoiogies relevant to 
different needs. Discussions are held with State S&T Councils for developing specific 
programmes. More than 20 technologies have been transferred for commercial production of 
vaccines, diagnostics in health care, nearing 40 lakhs Tissue Culture Plantlets have been 
supplied to Forest Depart111ent and 100 demonstrations in farmers' fields to popularise use of 
biopesticides, biofertilizers, allied tissue culture plants, vermicomposting etc. have been 
undertaken. Special Inter-Ministerial Steering Committees are convened to promote applica­
tion of biotechnologies in various sectors from time to time. 
Comments: 
The Committee is satisfied with the efforts being made by the Department of 
Biotechnology for popularising the research leads made and technologies developed among the 
users. The Committee, however, recommends that the Department should keep up the tempo 
of its activities. 
RECOMMENDATION 
The Committee is of the view that in order to reduce the dependence of farmers on 
pesticides and insecticides, a vigorous research is required to be pursued for the development 
of pheromones which could control the damage caused to crops by harmful insects and pests. 
The laboratory scale technology developed by the Department in this area requires upscaling 
and further test should be conducted through pilot projects so that the efficacy of the 
technology is fully demonstrated. 
(Para 13) 
Action Taken by the Department: 
The Department of Biotechnology has initiated several research projects to reduce the 
dependence of farmers on pesticides and insecticides. Four areas have been identified for 
this purpose viz. (i) Development and production of biocontrol agents for management of 
pests, diseases and weeds, (ii) Use of natural pesticides from plant sources, (iii) Develop­
ment of pheromones, and (iv) Studies on pesticides degradation as well as monitoring 
pesticides residues in the environment. 
Eight new bio-pesticides have been developed and two pilot plants are producing bio­
control agents for use of the farmers, catering to the needs of about 0.224 million ha. An 
area of 55000 ha. have been covered in various field crops for demonstrating the use of bio­
control agents. About 20,000 farmers benefited by attending the on-site training programmes 
and extension activities. The technologies for mass production of candidate biocontrol 
agents-baculovirus, parasites, predators, antagonistics, fungi and bacteria for economically 
important crops have been transferred to industries. 
About 12 potential plant species are being investigated for their insecticidal properties at 
various centres. The research includes extraction, isolation and formulation of Botanical 
pesticides for development of safe, bio-degradable and efficient insect control agents. 

The projects on various development aspects of pheromones include synthesis of 
pheromones, formulations , preparation of luresldispensors and optimization parameters for 
field trials. Pheromone s are being used the overall Integrated Pest Management package for 
monitoring the i>ests incidence in the field with a view to decide the time and rate of release 
of biocontrol agents. Pheromones of various insects have been synthesisted and field 
evaluated in number of crops e.g. cotton, gram, potato, sorghum, maize, red gram, tomato, 
cabbage, mango and other fruits. Laboratory scale process has been developed and 
optimized for their preparation. Milligram quantities are required in the field. Various 
dispensers were developed using different support materials to have slow release rate of the 
pheromone s. A technology package for INB (Inter Node Borer) - using pheromones has 
been developed . The pheromone technology is being validated in terms of its synthesis and 
bioefficacy in various fields. The up-scaling of the process for large scale synthesis of 
pheromones through pilot projects will be undertaken by the department. 
Towards studies on pesticides degradation and monitoriing of pests residues, lhe 
Department of Biotechnology has supported projects on research for food safety. Simple 
detection kits and sophisti~ated sensitive diagnostics and biosensors have been developed to 
detect the residual levels of insecticides and fungicides Consortia of microbes have also been 
developed in the form of a biofilm which could be used for process development and for 
decontamination of pesticides/xenobiotics contaminated effluents. 
Comments: 
The Committee notes with satisfaction the progress made in the field of bio-pesticides an.d 
bio-control agents and- hopes that this will help reduce the dependence of farmers on harmful 
chemicals being used as pesticides and insectic~. 
RECOMMENDATION 
The Committee recommends that if the proposed programme for the generation of 
emplo)'Dlent opportunities for women proves successful, it could be replicated in other parts of 
the country and more rural woll)en should be associated with the programme . 
(Para 19) 
Action Takeo by the Department: 
The foundation stone for the first "Golden Jubilee Women's Biotechnology Park" at 
Chennai was formally laid by His Excellency the President" of India on 29th July 1998 at 
Chennai. The Department is pursuing the project implementation. 
Comments: 
The CommiUee recommends that the implementation of project should be pursu ed 
vigorously to ensure its completion as per schedule and without any escalation of costs. 
RECOMMENDATION 
The Committee expresses its satisfaction over the fact that BIBCOL has supplied 330 lakh 
doses of OPV to National Immunization Programme upto March, 98. The Committee is of the 
view that the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare may purchase the required number of 
doses of OPV from the BIBCOL which is a public sector company. The Committee fails to 
understand as to why after signing a rate contract for procuring 120 million doses of OPV in 
June, 1997, the Ministry purchased from the BIBCOL only 27.9 million doses. 
(Para 22) 
The Committee also stresses the need for the Department to make vigorous efforts to 
produce new and improved vaccines and immunodiagnostics such as rabies, measles 
recombinent Hepatitis 'B' vaccine, etc. as has been planned under the Product Diversification 
Plan for the BIBCOL. 
(Para 23)

The EFC memo of revised cost estimates and product diversification plan of BIBCOL 
was circulated among concerned Ministries/Departments for their comments in order to 
produce BCG, Measles, T T vaccines in addition to oral ._ polio vaccine and other 
immunobiologicals to generate additional revenue to sustain its activities. Further BIBCOL 
has planned to produce rabies and Hepatitis 'B' vaccine and Immunodiagnostics in second 
phase of its diversification plan. The Department has taken up the matter with the 
Department of Family Welfare to give supply order to procure OPV from BIBCOL during 
the current financial year (1998-99) to National Immunization Programme. 
Comments: 
Reply furnished by the Department is evasive and incomplete. The Committee bad asked 
a pointed question. After signing the rate contract for procurement of 120 million doses of 
OPV in June, 1997, why only 27.9 million doses were purchased. The ·committee would like 
to have a detailed reply ,on this specific question. 
RECOMMENDATION 
The Committee wanted to know how best the assets of the Company IVCOL are being 
utilised by the Department to minimise the losses. 
(Para 24) 
Action Taken by the Department: 
The Department .has prepared a proposal for optimum utilization of assets of IVCOL, 
for the establishment of National Brain Research Centre and also to establish Biotechnology 
Integrated Complex and other new activities and projects and the same is under 
consideration at the highest level. 
Comments: 
The Committee notes the reply.

Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and 
Technology, Environment and Forests on the Demands for Grants (1998-99) of the 
Department of Scientific and Industrial Research which was presented to the Rajya Sabha

New DELHI; 
December 18, 1998 
S.R. BOMMA1, 
Chairman, 
Committee on Science and Technology,

REPORT 
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of 
Scientific and Industrial Res earch on the recommendtltions contained in the Fifty-sixth 
Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and 
Technology, Environment and Forests on the De munds for Grants (1998-99) of the 
Department of Scientific and Industrial Research which was presented to the Rajya Sabha 
on lOth July, 1998. There are ten recommendations contained in the Fifty-sixth Report of 
the Committee. Action Taken notes on the recommendations of the Committee, were 
received from the Department on 22nd September, 1998. 
On scrutiny of the Action Taken Report as received from the Department of Scientific 
and Industrial Research, the Committee finds that all the ten recommendations have been 
fully implemented . 
The Committee's recommendation, action taken thereon and comments of the Commit­
tee on the action taken by the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research are given in 
the succeeding paragraphs:-
RECOMMENDATION 
The Committee observes that it is not a happy situation. Funds which could have been 
utilised for R&D work were used for meeting inescapable commitment towards payme nt of 
salaries, pensions and other related administrative expenditure. Something need urgently be 
done to remedy the situation. The CSIR should pursue the matter with the Ministry of 
Finance for higher allocation at the Revised Estimates stage to enable it to meet its liability 
under the Central Management Head. As regards th~ diversion of Plan funds to uon-Pian 
sector, the Committee would like to reiterate its earlier views as contained in its Thirteenth, 
Twenty-fourth, Thirty-sixth and Fifty-second Reports in which this Committee had recom­
mended in unambiguous terms that sufficient pro\'ision be made in the non-plan outlay of 
DSIR to meet its committed liability. Despite a clear recommendation of the Committee, in 
the budget estimates of 1998-99, thete is still a wide gap between the allocations made and 
expected liability of the Department. The plan funds should be utilised for plan activities only 
as per the accepted budgetary norms. 
(Para 6) 
Action Taken by the Department: 
The CSIR has take.n up with the Ministry of Finance for enhancement of its non-plan 
allocation, so as to be able to meet the committed expenditure without encroaching upon the 
Plan funds. The Ministry of Finance is considering the CSIR request. It is expected that the 
requisite funds would be provided for at the RE stage. 
Comments: 
The Committee notes the action taken by the Department of Scientific and Industrial 
Research and observes that this has been going on for quite some time. The Committee 
therefore would like the Ministry of Finance (Department of Expenditure) to help DSIR 
come out of the -situation once for all. 

RECOMMENDATION 
The Committee observes that most of the laboratories functioning under the administra­
tive control of DSIR are equipped either with the ageing equipment and facilities or with the 
obsolete equipment· and communication and networking system. Most of the laboratories 
require urgent upgradation and replacement to make them globally competitive. The 
Secretary, DSIR informed that the Government, keeping in view the recommendations of this 
Committee in its Thirty-sixth and Fifty-second reports has committed to provide a 
modernisation grant of Rs. 250 crores to DSJR during the Ninth Plan period. But the 
Committee would like the Department to generate internal resources also for modernising the 
CSIR laboratories. DSIR should also make concerted efforts to bring down the non-Plan 
expenditure of the laboratories coming under the CSIR system. 
(Para 8) 
Action Taken by the Department: 
The allocation of Rs. 250 crore for modernisation during IX Plan is to meet only a part 
of the overall requirement . CSJR is already meeting a major part of the modernisation 
expenditure from its internal and ottier resources. 
CSIR is seized of the matter aud has issued instructions for economy in expenditure 
pertaining to consumables, travel, contingencies etc. 
Comments: 
While the Committee notes th.e instructions issued by DSIR for economy in expenditure 
on travel etc .• nothing has been indicated about the modernisation of the laboratories . The 
Committee reiterates its recomm,endation and would like the Department of Scientific and 
Industrial Research laboratories to come up to the expectations of its users by providing 
better standard of services an<f other requirements . 
RECOMMENDATION 
. The Committee is of the view that the industry-related laboratories of the CSIR should 
abn at havina better interface with the industry so that the technologies developed by them 
are eventually commercialiseft. Th~ would bring self-reliance and confidence within the CSIR 
system providing further impetus of R&D activities of these laboratories. 
(Para 12) 
Action Taken by the Dep~rtment: 
CSIR is seized of the matter and infact its Vision 2001 document has outlined CSIR's 
technology strategy, which inter alia lays emphasis on partnering Indian industry to emerge as 
a significant global player and assist the nation in derivin& enhanced and sustainable value 
from . endogenous resources. This would be relentlessly pursuad . 
Comments: 
The Committee notes the reply. 
RECOMMENDATiON 
The Committee is of the yiew that in order to attract talent to take up S&T as a career, 
and retain them, housing and other amenities be provided to the scientists. Possibilities may 
also be explored for providing campus-housing facilities to the scientists working in CSIR 
laboratories. 
(Para 15) . 
Action Taken by the Department: 
CSIR within the confines of the budgetary allocations, is endeav.ouring to provide 
campus-housing facilities for its scientists. 

Comments: 
The Committee is of the view that in order to check the brain drain it is necessary to 
have higher budgetary allocations so that exodus of scientists to foreign countries is checked. 
Likewise those willing to return from abroad be provided sufficient amenities particularly 
housing so that they do not miss their comforts and surroundings which they had during 
their stay abroad . 
RECOMMENDATION 
The Committee is of the view that since we have got the highest cattle population in the 
country and, therefore, raw material is available in abundance, if the eco-friendly and cost 
effective technologies and techniques are utilised for leather processing, it would be possible 
for us to compete at the international level and increase our exports. For this there has to be 
a greater interaction between tanneries and the concerned laboratories of the CSIR. 
(Para 19) 
Action Taken by the Department: 
CSIR has infact mounted a mission mode programme that seeks to dovetail the oraanised 
and informal sectors of leather lodustry for sustainable and symbiotic development and to 
achieve a 10% share of the World Leather exports. 
Comments: 
While the Committee notes the reply it would like sustained effort to achieve the 
targets. 
RECOMMENDATION 
The Committee is of the view that plant-based drugs and herbal drup are becoming 
popular all over the world. This can become our area of strength and the traditional 
knowledge about plants and herbs which exist in this country is required to be probed 
sclentifacally for its medicinal use and further validation. The Committee would Uke the CSIR 
to work in this area with appropriate thrust. 
(Para 22) 
Action Taken by the Department: 
Recoanisina the Indian core strengths in traditional system of medicine using .plaats and 
herbs, CSIR has already initiated a high priority co-ordinated programme on develo~nt 
and commercialisation of bio-actlve molecules during the Ninth Plan. 
Comments: 
The Committee notes the reply. However it would like to point out that the traditional 
knowledge about plant based and herbal drugs is fast disappearing ~n the commercialisation 
of new remedies through ads. It is necessary that the knowledge aoout traditional herbal 
drugs and home made remedies appearing in language newspapers and other journals from 
time to time is collected. As a first step in that direction it is necessary to collect information 
about these nearly forgotten remedies through whatever source one can lay hands on and 
document them before drug formulations based on them are prepared and tested . The 
Committee is ~oubtful whether sufficient administrative machinery for the purpose is 
available in DSIR. 
RECOMMENDATION 
Tile Committee is of the c:onsidered opinion that the Food Processin& sector in our 
cowatry offen tnmeadous scope for application of teChniques and technologies for redudJI&. 

post harvest losses and for generating wealth and · employment in the rural sector. The 
Committee would like that cheap and simple processing technologies for value addition, 
minimising post-harvest losses and employment generation be developed which could be easily 
learnt by the people living in rural areas . 
(Pam 24) 
Action Taken by the Department: 
CFTRI, Mysore of CSIR is developing and disseminating knowledge, techniques and 
devices for minimising post-harvest losses and enhancing employment generation amongst the 
rural population. 
Comments: 
The Committee observes that it should have been apprised of the results, if any, of the 
steps taken, in concrete terms. 
RECOMMENDATION 
The Committee recommends that innovative work of generating new technologies for 
rural road should continue and the State and concerned agencies may be informed of the low 
cost road construction technologies available with the CRRI through publicity folders , 
brochures and by producing literature on the subject. 
(Pnrn 26) 
Action Taken by the Department: 
CSIR welcomes the suggestions of the Committee. CRRI would take steps to widely 
disseminate the required information and knowledge. 
Comments: 
The Committee observes that there is vust potential in improving the technology with a 
view to have better roads. If the CRRI possesses the technology it should use it first in the 
roads connecting villages to cities, within the cities and then on St<Jte and National 
Highways. 
RECOMMENDATION 
The Committee is happy over the fact that in 1997 DSIR and NRDC had organised over 
fifteen patents and IPR-related workshops for the schmCific community with expert resource 
persons drawn from India and abroad and these initiatives are being further enlarged. The 
Committee would like the Department to prol•ide wide publicity to its scheme being 
administered by NRDC under which assistance is provided to Indian scientists and inventors 
to secure patents for their products and process<'s through engaging of patent attorneys. 
(Para 29) 
Action Taken by the Department: · 
The suggestions of the Committee is well received and NRDC would endeavour to provide 
wide publicity on IPR related matters. 
Comments: 
The Committee notes the reply. 
RECOMMENDATION 
The Committee is of the view that on the front of providing drinking water to all the 
villages in the country not much work has been done. The dream of Rajiv Gandhi, the former 
Prime Minister of India, who launched the National Drinking Water Mission, still remains to 
be fulfilled. Despite the technical inputs provided by CSIR Laboratories to the Mission by way 

of quality testing of water, removal of arsenic from drinking water, etc. what is needed today 
is to develop technologies for water conservation and water harvesting. The water table 
everywhet·e is going down. Traditional sources of water are drying up. Water is the necessity 
of life. The Committee would like the Department to co-ordinate its activities with the 
Ministries of Water Resource , Rural Development and the State Governments for transferring 
technologies in the area of purifying water to make it potable. At the same time the scientists 
working in the area may also think of devising new and cheaper methods of water harvesting 
and water conservation. 
(Para 32) 
Action Taken by the Department: 
CSIR welcomes the suggestions of the Committee. It is further enhancing its earlier 
initiatives in this regard . 
Comments:· 
While the Committee notes the reply , it would like a not e on the s ubject listing the 
steps taken in the direction and the result s, if any, achieved by the time the Committee 
take:; up consideration of Demand for Grants next time.

Commillee on Science and Technology, 
Environment and Forests. 

REPORT 
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of 
Electronics on the recommendations contained in the Fifty-Eighth Report of the Depart­
ment-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment 
and Forests on the Demands for Grants (1998-99) of the Department of Electronics which 
was presented to the Rajya Sabha on lOth July, 1998. There are 7 recommendations 
contained in the Fifty-Fourth Report of the Committee. Action Taken notes on the 
recommendations of the Committee, were received from the Department on 19th 
November, 1998. 
On scrutiny of the Action Taken Report as received from the Department of 
Electronics, the Committee finds that all the 7 recommendations have been fully im­
plemented. 
The Committee's recommendation, action taken thereon and comments of the Commit­
tee on the acti'on taken by the Department of Electronics are given in the succeeding 
paragraphs:-
RECOMMENDATION 
Apart from many sources for the funding of the Technology Development Council 
Projects, the Committee learnt that the Central Government Departments have also been 
advised by the Planning Commi ssion to allocate 2 to 3 per cent of their outlay to promote 
Information Technology. The Committee recommends that the Department should con­
stantly interact with various MinistrieS'Departments of the Government to monitor that the 
allocation made by them to promote information technology is being used in the right 
direction. The. Committee feels that in the absence of such a monitoring agency no checks 
can be imposed on the diversification of these funds for other purposes. 
(Para 13) 
Action Taken by the Department: 
. 
As a sequel to the advice of the Planning Commission to all MinistrieS'Departments to 
allocate 2-3% of their Budget to promote Information Technology, Department of 
Electronics has written to all Ministries/Departments to make a separate subhead for IT. 
DOE has nominated its senior officers to function as Nodal officers to assist Ministries/ 
Departments in identifying applications of IT in their sector. The Government has also 
constituted a High Powered Committee under the Chairmanship of Cabinet Secretary for 
improving administrative efficiency by using IT. 
Comments: 
The Committee notes the . reply. 
RECOMMENDATION 
The Committee notes with satisfaction that due to the efforts of the Department, Indian 
software export has made a tremendous progress and has jumped to a level of. US$ 1.6 billion 
in 1997-98. The Committee is, however, constrained to observe that the Department has 
made relatively less progress in the hardware sector and recommends that definite plans/ 
schemes be chalked out for steady promotion and integrated development or' hardware in 
the country for domestic as well as export market. 
(Para 1)) 

Action Taken by the Department: 
DOE has prepared a document titled-Indian IT Vision 2010: Action Plan, which 
elucidates plans/schemes for steady promotion and integrated development of hardware in 
the country for domestic as well as export market. This document covers important areas of 
Infrastructure, Skill Development, and Education, Finance and Marketing, Promotion and 
Application Development, Technology, R&D, Policy Support and Indigenous Manufacture 
for self reliance. The National Task Force on IT and Software Development set up by the 
Prime Minister's office vide Gazette Notification No. F. 360/31/C/10/98 ES. II dated 
22.5.98 has made 108 recommendations on the Information Technology Action Plan vide 
Resolution No. IT-TF/5/98 dated 25th July, 1998. The said Task Force has also set up a 
panel on Development, Manufacture and Export of Information Technology Hardware. The 
panel has prepared a report emphasising the need for local manufacturing of Hardware for 
domestic as well as for export market. With the implementation of recommendations of the 
Task Force, the production of Electronics hardware will substantially increase. 
Comments: 
The Committee notes the reply and would like the recommendations of the Task Force to 
be expeditiously implemented. 
RECOMMENDATION 
The Committee observes that the manpower development for software export should be 
considered a priority area. Everything possible must be done to launch comprehensive 
programmes for updating the technological skills and knowledge of our software profession­
als so that India could compete in international software market with other world leaders in 
the area. 
(Para 17) 
Action Taken by the Department: 
The Department of Electronics has set software export target of US$10 billion for terminal 
year (2001-02) of the Ninth Plan. In order to achieve this target, National Software 
Capability Enhancement Programme (Soft-Cap) has been approved by the Committee of 
Secretaries for implementation by the DOE and M/o HRD. 
2. The Soft-Cap programme broadly covers increasing of intake capacity for computer 
courses at leading institutions, starting of bridge computer course for students from other 
disciplines, training of teachers, conducting specialised courses in Software Engineering, 
Project Management, International Marketing etc., Strengthening of STP Infrastructure, 
ERNET Project, Distance Learning and Quality Assurance aspects in Software develop­
ment. 
3. Further, the following measures have also been initiated towards development for 
Human Resource Development for Software Exports:-
Programme on Quality Assurance through Standardisation Testing and Quality Certifi­
cation (STQC). 
Part-funding to State initiated projects sponsored Institutes for setting up of STPs and 
development of Information Technology to meet growing requirements of computer 
professionals in the country. 
Comments: 
The Committee would like to know the yearly targets set to achieve US $10 billion mark 
by the end of the Ninth Five Year Plan. 

RECOMMENDATION 
The Committee recommends that all out efforts be made by the Department to see that 
the outlay earmarked for ruraVsocial sector during the current year for programme 
implementation of watershed development projects is fully utilised and the benefits of the 
schemes percolate down to a large segment of rural population . 
(Para 21) 
Action Taken by the Department: 
The above recommendations of the Committee have been noted for implementation . 
Comments: 
The Committee notes the reply. The Committee would like to know as to how the lfunds 
are to be spent during the year? How much amount has been spent as on 31st October, 1998 
with corresponding figures for the previous year? 
RECOMMENDATION 
The Committee recommends that Department should make concrete efforts for the 
utilisation of funds allocated for various schemes like Health, Electronics , Hi-tech Power 
Electronics , IPR Promotion Programme and Environmental Management in Electronks fully 
during the year 1998-99. 
(Para 22) 
Action Taken by the Department: 
The above recommendation of the Committee have been noted for implementation. 
Comments: 
The Committee notes the reply and would like to be kept informed about the full 
utilisation of the funds allocated for the purpose giving full details as to how fund s, scheme­
wise are to be spent and actual expenditure incurred so far . 
RECOMMENDATION 
Since the 'India IT Vision 2010: Action Plan' covers a wide range of activities which aim 
at making India a world leader in the software market and making India self-reliant in the 
field of Information Technology , the Committee would like the Plan to be implemented with 
focussed attention of the Department . The Department may, therefore , consider appointing 
a high level Committee which should periodically review the progress of the projects 
initiated and targets achieved under the Plan. 
(Para 27) 
Action Taken by the Department: 
The National Task Force on Information Technology and Software Development was set 
up by the PM's office vide Notification No. F. 360131/cll0/98 -ES. II dated 22.5.98 to 
formulate the draft of a National Informatic Policy to enable India to emerge as an 
Information Technology Superpower within the next 10 years. The Task Force has in its first 
report , submitted in July, 1998, made 108 recommendations on the Information Technology 
Action Plan for removing bottlenecks in the existing policy and procedures fo1r achieving a 
pre-eminent status for India. The Task Force has taken into consideration man·y of the issues 
included in the document INDIA IT VISION 2010. 
The Task Force has not yet suggested any institutional framework for implementation of 
the IT Action Plan. However DOE as the Nodal Department for development and 
promotion of IT and Electronics in the country, has initiated action for implementation of 
recommendations of the Task Force. All concerned Ministries/Department have been 
requested to take action on related points and also nominate a Nodal Officer of the level of 
Joint Secretary for implementation of the IT Action Plan and preparing : Action Taken 
Report. 
Comments: 
The Committee notes the reply. The Committee would however like to impress on the 
Department of Electronics for expeditious implementation of the recomnnendations. 

RECOMMENDATION 
The Committee would like the Department to finalise its future programme with regard to­
the ET&T. Either this venture be closed down as recommended by the Disinvestment 
Commission or a well thought out diversification plan should be prepared for the revival of 
the company. Uncertainty with regard to its future would prove costly to the public 
exchequer. 
(Para 36) 
Action Taken by the Department: 
The Capital Restructuring proposal has been consideted by the Disinvestment Commis­
sion, which has recommended that the ET&T Corporation Ltd. should discontinue all its 
operations with immediate effect. The recommendations of Disinvestment Commission have 
b-een considered by Core Committee of Secretaries under the Chairmanship of Cabinet 
Secretary and it has decided that ET&T should be wound-up with the approval of the 
Cabinet. Further action is being taken accordingly. 
Comments: 
The Committee would like that necessary action be completed within a given time frame 
to wind up ET&T after taking the approval of the Cabinet.

INTRODUCTION 
I, the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & 
Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the report on its behalf, 
present this Report, on aspects related to Food Preservation and safety aspects. 
2. Keeping in view the vast potential for expansion of Food Processing Industries a Sub­
Committee under the Convenorship of Prof. Radhika Ranjan Pramanik, Member of Lok 
Sabha, was appointed to examine the aspects related to Food Technology and related 
aspects. 
3. The Committee places on record its appreciation of highly commendable work done 
by the Sub-Committee comprising of Prof. Radhika Ranjan Pramanik- Convenor, Dr.D . 
Masthan, Dr. (Mrs.) Beatrix D'Souza, Dr. Charan Das Mahant , Smt. Vijaya Raje Scindia, 
S/Shri Rahasbihari Barik, Ram Chandra Khuntia, B.P. Singhal, Prakanta Warisa, Ranjib 
Biswal, Olengara Surendran, George Eden, Rupchand Murmu, S. Vijaya Rama Raju, 
Inderjit Singh Rao , Maheshwar Singh, Virendra Singh & Mukul Wasnik. 
4. The Sub-Committee, (of the Parliamentary Stauding Committee on Science & 
Technology, Environment & Forests) on Food Technology and related aspects made an in­
depth examination of various aspects related to Food Technology und Preservation. The 
Sub-Committee visited Industrial Toxicology Research Institute (Lucknow) on 22nd and 23rd 
October, 1998 to examine the safety aspects related to food. The Sub-Committee also visited 
Central Agricultural Research Institute (CARl), Port Blair and Indian Institute of Chemical 
Biology (IICB), Calcutta from 23rd November to 27th November, 1998. 
5. The Sub-Committee had the benefit of notes and other documents supplied by the 
Department of $cientific and Industrial Research and other constituent bodies like CFTRI 
and ITRC . 
6. In the meetings of the Committee held on 24th September, 1998 and Sub-Committee 
held on 9th November, 1998, the Secretary and other Officers of the Department of 
Scientific & Industrial Research, and Directors CFTRI and ITRC gave an overview of the 
major R & .D efforts being pursued and achievements made in regard to Food Technology & 
related aspects. 
7. The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the Officers and representatives of the 
Department of Scientific and Industrial Research and CFTRI and ITRC for their co­
operation and answering the queries raised by Members on the food technology and related 
aspects. 
8. The Sub-Committee considered and adopted the Report of the Sub-Committee on 
the 22nd December., 1998. 
9. The Committee in _its meeting held on 22nd December , 1998 considered and adopted 
the Report of the Sub-Committee.
