REPORT 
Throughout the three or four million years that man has been on earth, his principal 
concern has been quest for food. He has often sought more food, and always, for food more 
to his liking. Man has had a series of sources of food, each affording some advantages over 
the preceding source. Throughout the past ten thousand or so years agriculture has been a 
reasonably satisfactory source of food for most people. 
2. From the beginning of man on the earth human population has tended to increase 
upto the limit of food supply. Crisis have arisen, but there has usually been time in which a 
transition to a new, larger, and more favourable food supply has been effected. 
3. In India, one-third of the food consumed by the people goes to the body and two­
thirds go to the doctors. This is because the value addition to food-production is a mere 7% 
in India, compared to as much as 23% in China and 45% in Philipines. Food with food 
value is food and food without food value is not food at all. People in our country have yet 
to develop scientific food habits based on food values and not on the taste of tongue. Habit 
is to be decided first and then the taste will follow because taste is developed by habits. 
People have adopted old traditional food habits. Indian diet consists almost extensively of 
cereals, and 'what we lose from them on account of refinement is not made good from other 
sources as it happens to be in more developed countries. The poor people of this country, 
who form the vast majority, suffer to a far greater extent than the wealthy minority, who can 
afford a richer, more varied diet, on account of the both qualitative and quantitative losses 
in case of cereals. 
4. Food, thus remains one of the most complex economic, political and moral problem 
Qf our times. In India, the future of hundreds of millions poor, hungry, malnourished people 
depend largely on.our willingness and ability to take up challenge of providing them with an 
adequate supply of good and cheap food. 
5. Thus, in us lies the responsibility to build capability to increase and improve food 
supplies, raise knowledge of human nutrition and simultaneously contribute to the reduction 
of poverty, malnourishment and other related diseases. To meet the challenge of providing 
people with adequate good quality food at all the times and abo e~t cheap rates we have to 
rely on food processing. Apart from the fact that our people gl'l the right food, we must 
create awareness among them what is the right food and what is the right manner of 
preparing and partaking it. 
6. Recently, changes i!l food consumption patterns have hcen occurring world-wide, 
including India. In urban India, protein consumption has increased by a quarter between 
1970 and 1990 on the basis of total expenditure on food, while cereal consumption has 
dropped more than a third of all expenditure to just a quarter. The shift is to da iry products 
and meat. The change in food habits in rural India has been more dramatic. Cereals which 
accounted for more than half of all food expenditure in 1970 in rural India, dropped to a 
little over third in 1990. Protein consumption, however , increased by more than half, in 
addition to more than a third increase in case of fruits and vegetables. 
7. Food processing is primarily done to improve and safeguard the agricultural 
productivity; reducing wastage of perishable food items like fruits and vegetables and for 
improving food availability for domestic markets and for exports and finally to ensure an 
adequate food supply during non-agriculturall~ productive periods . 
8. Today, the Indian food processing industry ranks fifth in its contribution to value 

addition but tops in terms of employment; employing about 20 per cent of the country's 
industrial labour force. Though food industries account for annually 5.2% of the total 
industrial investment, yet contribute around 18% to the ODP. The food processing 
industries in India are broadly classified into three categories, l'iz. primary sector, infQrmal 
and cottage scale sector and large scale sector. The primary sector predominantly comprises 
of about 90,000 rice hullers, 26,000 flour chakkies, 1,20,000 dhall mills, 2,20,000 oil ghanis, 
besides myriads of homescale dehydration and processing units in rural as well as semi urban 
areas. ln the informal sector, there are around 54,000 bakeries, over 5,000 paste goods units, 
15,000 traditional food units, 2,000 poha making units and 5,000 fruit vegetable and spice 
processing units. The organised sector accounts for over 800 large flour mills, 450 modern 
rice mills, 400 fish processing units, 5,000 fruit and vegetable processing units, 130 meat 
processing units, 650 sweetened and aerated water (soft drinks) units, 100 milk products 
units, 650 sugar mills and 800 solvent extraction (oil) units. 
9. The challenges before food processing sector in India are to extend the period during 
which food remains wholesome i.e. shelf life by preservation techniques which inhibit 
microbiological or biochemical changes and thus allow time for distribution and home 
storage; to increase the variety in diet through enhanced range of attractive (and safe) 
flavours, colours, aromas and textures in foods (to enhance the eating, sensory and 
organolleptic quality); to change the form of the food to allow further processing (e.g. the 
milling of grains to flour); to improve the nutritional quality of food and to ensure the food 
safety at manufacture and at consumption levels. However, the major basic problems faced 
by the Indian food processing industry are; Seasonal availability of raw materials; fluctuating 
and high raw material cost; uncontrolled material quality (for inputs); general consumer 
indifference to quality and hence poor returns on investment on quality; meager 
infrastructure for refrigeration storage and refrigerated transport. High cost of waste 
treatment without any monetary return. 
10. DSIR, through its various institutions, is working to pursue these challenges before 
the food processing industry. It has created a sound technological base to assist the food 
processing industries, mostly in the cottage, small and medium scale sectors, through 
appropriate technology and services in food preservation, studying and analysing food 
toxicity and safety and certification. Besides, it generates appropriate techniques, 
technologies and equipment for processing food produce suited to our socio-cultural needs. 
The Central Food Technological Research Institute (CFTRI) of DSIR is solely devoted to 
R&D in Food and Food Processing, besides the Regional Research Laboratories at Jammu 
and Thiruvananthapuram and the Institute of Himalayan Bioresource Technology (IHBT), 
Palampur have some R&D pertaining to food processing, whilst the Industrial 
Toxilogicology Research Centre (ITRC) at Lucknow undertakes R&D pertaining to food 
safety especially adulterants and their toxicity. These CSIR laboratories over the years have 
developed around 350 knowhow comprising about 300 processes and 50 designs, most of 
which are suited to the resource endowments of the informal sector even in rural areas. 
11. Another vitally inter-linked and integral part of the food problem is the related 
safety aspects. Use of various food additives added for technological purposes has become 
inevitable with the growth of food processing industry. Moreover, some <ldulterants are 
deliberately added for earning undue profits. The recent incident of outbreak of dropsy 
disease due to consumption of adulterated mustard oil is cause for concern. ITRC does a 
regular monitoring of food stuffs to check the nature of food adulterants/contaminants. It 
has devised lot of simple techniques for checking the adulteration in common household 
food stuffs. These techniques are simple and practicable. 

ROLE OF CFTRI 
12. The major R & D programmes of the Central Food Technological Research 
Institute (CFTRI) are related to development of food products and processes for optimal 
utilization of the country's agricultural produce, technology packages for vulnerable and 
ready-to-eat foods, low cost nutritive foods for vulnerable population, processes for value 
added products from plantation produce, protocols for post-harvest handling and 
transportation of fruits and vegetables for export and inland shipments, methods of 
packaging of food, packaging of food materials and processed food products for extended 
shelf life, techniques for crop and grain protection, technologies for eliminating or reducing 
post-harvest losses of perishables and durables, and modernisation of the primary food 
processing, industry through development of energy-efficient, machinery and equipment. 
Besides, basic research is also carried out on food additives, preservatives, micronutrients, 
food toxicity and safety, food microbiology and bioactive substances . 
13. The Committee is of the view that our villagers and cultivators are still ignorant of 
the useful technologies developed for increasing the yield, and knowledge ab~ut the proper 
usage of .pesticides, fertilizers etc. and recommends that knowhow developed by the 
departments in these fields should be made available to the persons working at the grassroot 
through the State Govt~·nments, and there must he a mechanism for feedback on the 
application of the technology. The correct slogan should be .. From Lab to the Land and From 
Land to the Lab". 
14. The Committee recommends that food processing and vnluc addition should be done 
in a way as not to harm the natural and traditional tastes of food items. Hence, the 
department should aim at good quality, hygienic and nutritious food with the original 
motherly touch. 
CFTRI has done pioneering work as regard various food products which can be 
summarised as follows:-
FRUITS & VEGETABALES 
15. India though is a producer of wide variety of fruit both tropical and temperat e yet 
its share in the world trade of processed fruits and vegetables is still less than one per cent. 
The annual production is about 30 million tonnes of fruit and 70 million tonnes for 
vegetables, however over 30% of the produce is wasted due to lack of proper processing and 
infrastructural facilities. Even the industries working in this sector are not working to their 
installed capacity. Other. major hurdle in this sector is that the processing industry is highly 
decentralised as a large number of units except for a few large corporate players including 
multinationals are in the informal sector. Many new items have been added to hitherto 
exported fruits and vegetables items and thus the scope of vcrti\·al expansion of the industry 
to more value adde~ and sophisticated products has been considerably increased. 
16. CFTRI has done pioneering R&D work in this sector in the field of curt ailment of 
lihortages, improvement of quality and extension of storage life of various fruits and 
vegetables. The contribution of the CFTRI to aspects of food preservation and safety can be 
summarised as follows; 
(a) Modified Atmosphere Storage: 
17. CFTRI has developed an standardised modified atmosphere storage methods to 
extend the storage life of selected fruits and vegetables both under ambient as well as low 
temperature conditions. The technique helps in extending the shelf-life as the modified 

atmosphere inside the system produce more carbon dioxide and consequently suppresses 
normaly occurring respiration in open environment. This technique is very advantageous as 
it is very simple, inexpensive and provides a number of benefits such as maintenance of 
freshness and quality, extension of storage life by 3-5 folds and is suitable for operation at 
home, cottage, small scale and large scale industrial levels, besides it also does not require 
much infrastructural facility. The technique is being scaled up at CFfRI for commercial 
application. This has been successfully used for bananas and mangoes. The techniques are 
also expected to be equally successful with several other tropical fruits of India. 
(b) Anti-Fungal Paste: 
18. CFfRI has developed anti-fungal paste for treating cut portions of banana bunches. 
The paste prevents fungal infection during storage and transportation. It has made possible 
to sh'ip bananas to distant countries, involving extended period of transportation. 
(c) Wax Emulsion Treatment: 
19. CFfRI has developed formulations of wax emulsion which form microscopic coating 
on the surface to extend the storage life of fruits and vegetables by 100% thus reducing 
physiological losses in weight, shrivelling, rate of respiration an1.l impart glossiness and eye 
appeal to the fruits thereby improving the marketability. There is no undesirable odour or 
flavour and no hazard to health. 
(d) Technologies for Fresh Fruit Exports: 
20. Using a combination of the above technique CFfRI has successfully devised specific 
technology packages for export of alphonso and banganapalli varieties of mango and 
cavendish variety of banana, by ship reefer containers. The package of technologies include 
pre-harvest treatments to control spoilages; harvesting procedures; desapping; treatments to 
control post-harvest spoilages; pre-cooling' suitable CFB boxes; modified atmosphere 
packaging; low temperature storage in containers and ripening protocols. The techniques are 
being deployed for export of alphonso and banganapalli mangoes. 
21. The Committee expresses its concern over the fact that India has its share as low as 
less than one· per cent in the world market of processed fruits and vegetables and recommends 
that vigorous efforts be made to achieve higher share in the global market. The Committee 
also recommends that techniqiles developed for preservation of fruits and vegetables should be 
commercialised for application. 
22. During tl)e visit to Central Research Institute of Chemical Biology in Calcutta on 
27th November, 1998 the Sub-Committee was informed by the Scientists of the Institute 
about the toxicity in the vegetables grown on the Calcutta Corporation garbage in Dhapa 
and Mathpukur near Calcutta. Most of the people of Calcutta ronsumc these vegetables 
throughout the year. The Scientists were asked to consider the feasibility of conducting a 
research on toxic effect of the vegetables grown on garbage and ascertain whether these 
vegetables are. fit for human consumption. Likewise they were asked to find out whether the 
sewage water discharged by the Calcutta Corporation is safe for pisciculture, because fish 
cultured in this water is consumed by Calcuttans. 
23. The Committee thus recommends that Government should pursue these Research 
Projects and report the findings thereof. 
FOOD GRAINS 
24. India is the second largest producer of rice and the fourth largest producer of wheat. 

It produces nearly 200 million tonnes of food grains per year of which colossa l 20 million 
tonnes are lost due to damage and waste. 
Wheat: 
25. Around 800 flour mills involved in commercial milling operations are working in the 
organised sector. The output consists of white flour, semolina, whole meal flour and bran. 
About 80-85% of the output is directly consumed by the household sector and 15-18% is 
consumed by the confectionery products. A mini wheat mill comprising a system which 
cleans and grinds the grains, in addition to sieving of atta has been deve loped by CITRI. 
The mini wheat mill developed by CITRI uses indigenously available low cost machinery 
like destoner (developed by CFTRI) aspirator, huller, metallic chakki and sifter. Its capacity 
is 100 kg/hr. and investment required is about Rs. 6 lakh wjth grinding cost of Rs. 0.50/kg. 
wheat grain is adaptable in rural as well as urban areas. A variety of pesticidal formulations 
and application packages right from the storage at farmers end to bulk storage in 
warehouses, to bagged grains to household storage have also been developed. 
Rice: 
26. In rice milling modern rice mills are steadily replacing traditional milling in hullers/ 
shellers. The hullers developed by CFTRI for .rice milling and used in rural areas are not 
effective for milling of rice, as the yield of rice b very poor (60-04%.) and broken content is 
very high (25-40%). The byproducts, viz. bran and husk get powdered and are obtained as a 
pulverized mix which has almost no economic value. Cl~TRI has developed a series of 
system to enhance their efficiency. CFTRI has also been propogating the use of improved 
hullers and modernisation of rice milling industry under the uctivities of The Regional 
Extension Service Centre established by the Ministry of Food Processing Industries, 
Government of India for the last ten years. CITRI has published several booklets and has 
conducted a number of workshops, seminars, demonstrations, in the rice producing States 
and other parts of the country. 
COARSE GRAINS 
27. The coarse grains like Bajra, jowar, maize etc. account for 20% of the total food 
grain products. Their poor acceptance is due to the presence of outer husk or bran which 
makes them coarse in feature. CFTRI has developed techniques to improve the acceptability 
and enhance the value of coarse grains. The technique of removing both the bran and germ 
of maize greatly increases the shelf life of helished maize grits which becomes acceptable for 
preparing conventional foods. 
DHAL MILLING 
28. CFTRI has concentrated its effort on improvement of the traditional Dhal Mill to 
enhance product yield and quality and for making process more economical. The improved 
machinery developed are Hand operator range Dehusker , Dhal Mill and versatile Dhal Mill. 
29. The Committee observes that over the years we h:tvc failt. .. t un the food front precisely 
because we have focussed our attention, almost exclusively to lht! ctuantitative aspects and not 
to improve quality of our food. The Sub-Committee recommcmls that vigorous efforts be 
takE'n for value addition in the food to fight the problem of malnutrition. 
30. The Committee recommends that the techniques developed by CFTRI for value 
addition in food grains should be popularised by taking help of vnrlous source~ of media viz. 
local newspapers, All India Radio and Doordarsban so that benefits of these technologies 
could percolate to the rural masses. The Sub-Committee also ·feels .that 

something urgently needs to be done to reduce losses of food grains due to damage and waste. 
The Sub-Committee recommends that unwarranted refinement of food grains, which result in 
loss of quality protein, fats, minerals and vitamins should be checked. 
MILK AND MILK J.>RODUCTS 
31. "India is perhaps the largest milk producing country in the world with the current 
annual production of over 70 million tonnes . The consumption of liquid milk is around 46% 
and the remaining 54% is utilized for conversion to milk products CITRI pioneered the use 
of buffalo milk, to make baby food powder leading to the establishment of vast baby food 
industry. CITRI is working with NDDB for manufacture of baby food and at present 
working on technology for low-cost protein foods." 
MEAT AND POULTRY 
32. India has the world's largest cattle population but consumption of meat is quite low. 
There is good demand for ready to cat and semi-processed meat products in the domestic 
market as well as for export. To improve and enhance the production of value-added 
products based on meat, it is necessary to employ modern technologies, appropriate 
machinery and modern packaging systems. Most of the CFI'RI proccssess are worked out at 
laboratory/bench scale and their scale-up can lead to modern tcl·hnologies. 
33. The Committee expresses its concern over the low contribution of our country in meat 
export although it has world's largest animal population and recommends that all out efforts 
be made to improve meat exports and for producing value added products based on meat. 
The Sub-Committee also recommends that to meet international standards proper hygenic 
measures and economically viable packaging materials be developed. 
PLANTATION PRODUCE 
34. CITRI has also worked on cardamom, spice and oleoresins, white pepper, 
Dehydrated green pepper and chemical free spices. 
ACmEVEMENTS OF CFTRI 
35. Over the years, CITRI has transferred many major technologies to industry. The 
notable among the technologies transferred are (i) flavour concentrates and soft drink 
manufacturing technology for cola beverages, lemon and orange drinks; (ii) total technology 
for dehulling and extraction of superior quality oil from sesame, mustard and sunflower; (iii) 
improved designs for grain milling machinery for increased yields of milled products; rice, 
maize, wheat and pulses; (iv) total technology for manufacture of Spirulina platensis, the 
fresh water glue green alga, which has emerged world-over as a much sought after health 
food; (v) infant food from buffalo milk; (vi) total technology for manufacture of pickles in 
large scale; and (vii) viable small-scale technologies for produrtion of oyster mushroom, 
culture preparation, spawn production, mushroom growing and dehydration. 
ROLE OF INDUSTRIAL TOXICOLOGY RESEARCH CENTRE (ITRC) 
Safety of Food Materials: 
36. The fast growth of food processing industry has led to the increased use of various 
food additives added for technological purposes. The safety of chemical additives appearing 
in food stuffs has been a matter of continued concern both for consumers and regulatory 
authorities. The common adulterants causing concern are the ones deliberately added for the 
purpose of disguising inferior commodities and/or earning undue profits. The other group of 

non-intentional contaminants however, creep up during field production or processing, 
packaging and storage. Industrial Toxicology Research Centre (ITRC) does a regular 
monitoring of foodstuffs to find out the extent and nature of food adulterants, and conducts 
detailed safety evaluation studies to assess the health risk implications. 
Adulteration with Non-permitted Colours: 
37. Because of comparatively low cost and easy availability, a number of non-permitted 
toxic colours are frequently used in food products and thus constitute a hazard to health. 
ITRC has been engaged in both monitoring and safety evaluation of various permitted and 
non-permitted colours. 
Adulterants in edible oils: 
38. Edible oils have been a commodity that has attracted maximum scope and variety of 
adulterants. Argemone oils is used as an adulterant in mustard due to its low cost and 
complete mixibility with mustard oil. Consumption of argemone contaminated mustard oil, 
even at low levels for a short duration, is known to cause injurious health effects. The 
disease is commonly referred to as epidemic Dropsy. lTRC hus developed a fluorescene 
based prototype kit to rapidly (approximately in 30 minutes) st.:rccn Argemone oil in 
mustard oil with a sensitivity of 0.01 %. 
39. Besides ITRC has succesfully developed technologies for detection of Butter Yellow, 
Tricresly Phosphate Adulteration, Levels of Nickel. 
40. Edible oils have attracted maximum scope and variety of adulteran ts. The recent 
incident of outbreak of drop sy disease due to consumption of adulterated mustard oil clearly 
proves this. The Sub-Committee recommends that concrete steps be taken by the Council for 
generating public awareness in regard to the methods developed for detecting the level of 
adulterat ion. A mechanism should be evolved for regular interactions with the DSIR and State 
Governments for effective implementation of the required technologies and for proper 
awareness of the concerned people. 
Pesticide Residues: 
41. The use of pesticides is an important contributing factor to the agricultural 
revolution resulting in an increased quantity of food grain. Some pesticides persist even after 
they have served their purpo se. Monitorin g of pesticide residues at national level has been 
proposed with ITRC as a Nodal Laboratory. The laboratory coordinates the pesticide 
residue analysis at national level. 
42. The Committee recommends that the dependence of ugrkulfure on chemical fertilizers 
and pesticides be reduced by developing biofertilizers and biupt!sticidcs as serious health 
hazards are caused due to percolating of chemical pesticides and ht!avy metals into the food 
chain. The Committee recommends that awareness among ~he fnrmers and cultivators be 
created for the proper, scientific and right use of pesticides. 
MYCOTOXIN REFERENCE CENTRE 
43. In India, food raw materials and processed food products are highly susceptible to 
mycotoxin formation, necessitating toxin inactivating steps in food processing . This also 
needs highly reliable and sensitive methods of toxin estimation in food. CFTRI has been 
working on its own on aflatoxin in foods since its inception and is recognised throughout the 
world as a pioneer. CFTRI is actively engaged at present in the R&D efforts on 

biotechnological aproach for analysis and reduction of anatoxin in food materials. A 
combined project on food safety which also involves setting up of the Mycotoxin Reference 
Centre has been recently submitted to the Ministry of Food Processing Industries, New 
Delhi. 
44. The Committee recommends that setting up of the proposed Mycotoxin Reference 
Centre be expedited. 
FOOD IRRADIATION CENTRE 
45. Food irradiation help to decontaminate food from bacteria, parasites and insects. 
The process of irradiation involves exposing food material to ionizing radiations i.e. X-rays 
or gamma rays, It's a cold process and has advantage of treating the produce even in the 
final packaged form, thus packaged and forzen foods can also bl' taeateu without any change 
in the form of nutritional value. The irradiation centres pre!.ently operating at Mumbai and 
Delhi are mainly utilised for pharmaceutical prodm:ts and nwdil:al devices. Thus DSIR 
proposes to set up a model food irradi<.tion centre at CFI'Rl. Tht: ~entre would be primarily 
involved in development of expertise, products, technologies anu evaluation of irradiated 
food focussing on fruits, vegetables, spices, herbs, meat, fish and poultry products. 
46. The Committee recommends that the technique of low dose irradiation technology for 
preservation of various food items if found useful and cost effective be upscaled for 
commerical purposes. 
47. To edt adequately is one of the fundamental needs of every living being. The history 
of man has been the history of the fight for food, and the greater part of his activity has 
been aimed to achieve this objective. The fight was a difficult one and hunger, 
undernutrition and misery were always his usual companions. It is only during the last 
epochs and due to enormous amount of knowledge accumulated by man, that the availability 
of food has increased. Contemporary science and technology is being increasingly applied to 
meet the world's current and future needs. The scope of these developments imply an urgent 
need for safety and nutritional quality of new products. 
48. In the emerging scertario, we should hope for enough food and correct food to 
enable every child that is born to realize his full potential, the maximum physical, mental 
and emotional development of which he is capable. The Germans anJ Japanese are pioneer 
on this issue. After the first world war Japanese increased thl'ir national average height by 
two inches by changing their food habits. The Germans have devdoped their food habits on 
food values and not on taste. 
49. Food Processing Industry has vast potential for growth. Food Preservation and 
related safety aspects shall continue to be a major concern in lnuia, for which there are no 
easy solutions or short cuts. The returns from this sector could be maximised by the 
continued support and inputs from science and technology and thereby ensuring food quality 
and safety to people.

of promoting new areas of Science and Technology and act as a nodal department for 
organizing, coordinating and promoting S & T activities in the country with mandate which 
includes inter alia the following:-
• Formulation of policy statements and guidelines on S & T 
• Promotion of new areas of scientific research 
• Coordin ation of inter-departmental S & T efforts 
• Support bas1c and applied research in universities and other institutions 
• International S & T cooperation 
• Support high quality research in autonomous bodies 
• Catalyz ing S & T interaction in societal programmes, entrepreneurship development 
• Science popularisation, communication and S & T Management Information System 
• Promotion of commerc ialisation of home grown technology 
• Support to technology development programmes, technolo gy information and 
asses!.ment. 
• Providing services in areas of ' 
(a) Surveying and Mapping :(SOl & NATMO) 
(b) Me teoro logy (IMD, NCMRWF) 
(c) Techno h>~Y Development and Applications (TDB) 
Apart from the abm e the Department has recently taken initiatives m the areas 
which include: 
• Creation of Technology Development Board to accelerate technology development

programmes aimed at ensuring higher degree of precision in weather forecast by IMD.

cyclone detection network and indigenous fabrication of one doppler radar was in the 
process of being completed in collaboration with ISRO. Besides, RTH computer would be 
installed at New Delhi to enhance the capacity to handle more weather data. Old and 
obsolete skograph at Mumbai and Calcutta would be replaced. HWSR for 10 coastal stations 
would be procured. Automatic computing system at 35 RS/ RW stations would be upgraded 
and augmentation of National Data Centre at Pune to be completed. Modernisation/ 
Augmentation for Air Pollution Lab at Pune would be undertaken. 
62. Upgradation of Meteorological Ground Segment of INSAT-ll and Earth Station for 
reception of meteorological data from INSAT-2E series is expected to be completed and 
replacement of 100 CDWS receivers is programmed. Deployment fo 50 Strong Motion 
Accelerograph in field station under WB seismo project is scheduled. 

63. Adion for establishment of Mountain Meteorological Centre would be taken up at 
Srinagar. Besides, 3 Upper Air Stations under Joint Project "Development of Mountain 
Meteorology in Himalayas" in collaboration with Defence would be undertaken. Digitisation 
of analysed weather charts and seismo charts is to be completed. 3 Nos. Doppler Radars 
would be procured under WB Project "Andhra Pradesh hazard mitigation and emergency 
cyclone tecovery". The work on the project under World Bank Scheme to improve the 
quality and services of Hydrometeorology data in 8 selected States will be continued on large 
scale with full complement manp,~wer. 
64. Th6 Committee has been given to understand that India Meteorological Department 
placed an order on a foreign firm in February, 1994 for supply of '25 Alden Model 9315 
TRT-128' compact facsimile recorders in which customs duty was assessed at rates higher 
than the prescribed rate resulting in excess payment of Customs Duty of Rs. 16.95 lakhs. 
The Committee was informed that the matter was taken up with the Assistant Commissioner 
of Customs, IGI Airport, New Delhi 'for claiming the refund of custom duty paid to them 
alongwith all the relevant documents required to facilitate the refund. In the absence of any 
reply from the Assistant Commissioner of Customs, a meeting was arranged with the higher 
authorities to get back the excess amount of custom duty paid to them. The outcome was 
still awaited. All steps have, however, been taken to avoid recurrence of such things in 
future. 
65. The Committee recommends that efforts be made to get back the excess payment of 
Custom duty without any furtbet delay. 
SOCIETAL PROGRAMMES 
66. The Committee was informed that the Department aims at evolving and 
implementing specific programmes to promote application of Science and Technology in 
order to improve the quality of life especially for the disadvantaged sections of the 
population. Some of the tangible benefits of such programmes have been the generation of 
appropriate tural technologies, reducing drudgery, generating employment, improving health 
and conserving environment. A large number of field based R & D laboratories are involved 
in the programme. Many successful projects have resulted in viable technology packages and 
systems, which are then standardised after elaborate field trials for large scale replication. 
The target groups include, T{ibals, Women, Rural poor and Scheduled castes . 
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY FOR WOMEN 
67. The programme aims at developing technology for women belonging to the 
economically weaker section of the Society. During the year 1998-99 as many as 30 projects 
have been initiated in the priority sectors such as Post harvest technologies, land-based 
activities, women's health, income generation activities and Drudgery removal and also 
preservation of horticulture produce. 
68. All India Coordinated Programme on low cost is underway in seven different 
agroclimatic locations of the country. In this programme efforts are being made that the 
women are able to handle the quality control aspect all by themselves. 
69. The Committee was infomed that a Programme on Development of Training-cum­
service facilities for women on electrical, electronic, computer and information technology 
applicaHon is scheduled to be launched in 13 remote locations of the country. All the 
Centres would benefit women belonging to be weaker sections and run by them, whereas a 
program me on cultivation, processing and market ing of high value medicinal plants involving 

women has been started in different agroclimatic Zones and women are being given training 
in low cost agrotechnologies for cultivation, semi-processing, storage and marketing of 
medicinal plants. 
WOMEN'S TECHNOLOGY PARK 
70. Two technology parks exclusively for women one each in the Mountain Region 
Dehradun and at Manipal for the West Coastal Region are being set up with following 
objectives: 
To establish inter linkages with R&D institutes for promotion of technology 
relevant to women; 
To highlight women's technology need; 
Upgradation of indigenous technologies; 
Income generation programmes for women; and 
To access women's health. 
71. The Committee was further informed that third Technology Park for the arid zone is 
likely to be launched shortly. 
72. The Committee feels that the scheme aimed at developing Women's TechnoiQgy Parks 
should be so oriented that it should benefit women belonging to different parts of the country. 
PROGRAMME ON WOMEN'S HEALTH 
73. Three projects h;Lve alre ady been launched to look into the needs of the women's 
health. Some of the project s launched include : (i) Developing a reproductive health 
diagnostic kit for use o f ~emi-literate village health workers, (ii) Building an effective 
sust ainable health activist s force using S&T inputs and programme design, (iii) Intervening 
he alth hazards faced by women engaged in ston e crushers and quarries being implemented 
by Institute of Small Mine s, and (iv) Women wor kers a nd occupational hazard s in the 
min ing sector of So~th Rajasthan. 
74. While the Committee appreciates the work being done hy the Department for the 
improvement of the health of the women, it feels much more needs to be done. 
SPECIAL COMPETENT PLAN FOR DEVELOPMENT OF SCHEDULED CASTE 
75. The Committee was mformed that the Department has taken up S&T intervention 
projects for the socio-economic uplift of SCs and scavengers, in order to promote research, 
development and adaptation of technology and to promote scientists and technologists to 
apply their knowledge and expertise to the needs of SC community especially in rural areas. 
76. The SC population has been mobilised in Western U.P. to use easily available 
biomass for the manufacture of smokeless agrobased cakes. The technology was 
demonstrated to make them capable to generate income and employment. Similar efforts 
have also been made in other parts of country such as Yidarbha, Maharashtra etc. 
77. The Committee wa~ further informed that training of agncultural labourers on the 
use of modern agricultural applications for improved agricultural productivity has been 
started so as to check rural urban migration of SCs and about 300 SC youths have been 
trained in the use :md service of agricultur-<tl appliances. 
78. In Maharashtra, a programme on cultivation of disease free sugarcane for 

unemployed SC youth has been given shape whereby a large number of SC youth have 
started nurseries for producing sugarcane seedling in plastic bags, using single nod cuttings of 
virus free sugarcane. 
79. The Committee commends the work done for training and skill upgradation by the 
Department for training and skill upgradation for harnessing and displaying age old 
craftsmanship and developing the livelihood of SC youths. Marginal farmers and landless 
agricultural workers have increased production with the use of new technology for valued 
addition. The areas covered are computer training and repair and maintenance, training cum 
production of wooden toys and decorative items; electrical mechanism, minor automobile 
repairs, carpentry, plumbing, training in jute product diversification, artisanal leather 
footwear etc. 
80. The Committee is happy to note that few projects including the organisation of a 
workshop for the benefit of scavengers in the areas of waste utilisation and income generation 
have been started. The Committee, however, feels that much more needs to be done towards 
improving the lot of vulnerable sections of the Society. 
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY POLICY 
81. On a question on the revision of the Scientific Policy Resolution of 1958, the 
Committee was informed that the Scientific Policy Resolution does not require any major 
changes and is still valid. The Technology Policy Statement, however, requires some 
modifications keeping in view the changed scenario both at global and national level and the 
modifications required are under consideration. 
82. The Committee observes that the Government should have a comprehensive review of 
the Technt)JogicaJ· Policy Statement with a view to decide whether to have a consolidated 
technological policy or different Policies-~>ne for promotion of Science and the other for 
Technology. 
SCIENCE AND ·ENGINEERING RESEARCR COUNCIL (SERC) 
83. The Council ' was constituted with the primary objectives: 
(i) To promote research in newly emerging and front ier areas of science and 
engineer~ng including multidisciplinary fields. 
(ii) To selectively promote th~ genera~ resea rch capab ility in relevant areas of 
science a~d engineering taking int<> account. capab ility of the host institute. 
(iii) To 'enco~rage .y.oung scie~tists · to . take up challenging R&D activitie·s. 
·(iv) To give special encouragement ·.· to project s from less endowed university 
departments. 
(v) To encourage patenting facilities to scientists and technologies in the country 
for Indian and foreign patents on a sustained basis. 
84. The Science & Engineering Research Council is an apex body consisting of eminent 
Scientists from Universities, National laboratory and industry. 
... \ 
85. The Science and Engineering Research Council (S,eRC) continued to support 
research projects in challenging fields of Science and Eng ineering and encouraged Young 
Scientists .to take up research as a career. The programmes supported under SERC are 

distinctly different from those that are supported by specialised agencies. During the year 
under report, some of the important initiatives taken to promote R&D programmes are as 
fo11ows: 
• "SERC Students Fellowships" 
• "SERC Chairs" in key fields of Science and Engineering in Academic Sectors. 
Enhancement of Research Fellowships of JRF/SRFIRA 
• Funds for Improvement of Infrastructure in Universities and other Academic Sectors 
(FIST) 
• Kishore Vigyanik Protsahan Yojana 
86. The DST could spend Rs. 57.58 crores (Rs. 56.28 Plan and Rs. 1.30 crores Non­
Plan) in the year 1997-98. The allocation enhanced to Rs. 58.32 at BE stage (Plan Rs. 57.00 
crores and Non-Plan Rs. 1.32 crores) of the year 1998-99 with further enhancement to Rs. 
58.13 crores (Plan Rs. 56.94 crores and Non-Plan Rs. 1.19 crores) in RE of 1998-99. The 
Department has asked for an outlay of Rs. 70.54 crores (Rs. 69.25 crores Plan and Rs. 1.29 
crores Non-Plan) for the said programme for the year 1999-2000. 
87. The Committee notes that despite the increase in allocation for Science and 
Engineering Rese~rch Council (SERC) the number of projects supported by it has come 
down by about one third. The Department has explained this due to the change in rupee­
dollar parity increasing the cost of equipments and also due to increase in the fellowship­
amount and travel costs etc. 
88. The Committee feels that there is a need for quantum increase in funding for the 
SERC related activities to maintain the momentum in fundamental research. 
89. After considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Science and 
Technology and assessing the progress of various important programmes and projects 
administered by it, the Committee recommends that the Demands for Grants of Rs. 654.63 
crores, as sought by the Department of Science and Technology, for the year 1999-2000 
under Demand No. 73, may be approved.

INTRODUCfiON 
1, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and 
Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, 
present this Sixty-fifth Report of the Committee. This Report deals with the detailed 
Demands for Grants (1999-2000) of the Department of Ocean Development (Demand 
No. 92). 
2. In the meeting of the Committee held on the P' April, 1999 the Secretary and other 
Officers of the Department of Ocean Development gave an overview of the various activities 
of the Department. The Committee sought clarifications on various aspects of the 
performance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants. 
3. The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Department replying to the 
darifications sought by the Members and placing before it the required material to enable it 
to scrutinise the Demands for Grants- of the Department of Ocean Development. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on April 20, 
1999: 
New DeLHI; 
April 20, 1999. 
S.R. BOMMAI, 
Chairman, 
Committee on Science & Technology,

REPORT 
The Department of Ocean Development, since its inception in July, 1981, has directed its 
programmes towards development and use of science and technology for the sustainable and 
environment friendly exploration and exploitation of marine resources for the socio­
economic benefit of the country. Its technology development programmes are for future 
application~ with strategic, industrial and economic significance. 
2. The Department of Ocean Development is a nodal Department for orgamzmg, 
coordinating and promoting ocean development activities in the country. The national level 
R&D laboratories, educational institutions and industries assist the Department in carrying 
out its multi-disciplinary and multi-institutional plans and programmes of national 
importance. Further, marine research and capacity building is one of the key areas of the 
Department to promote basic research in marine science for self-reliance. 
3. The programmes of the Department which have been reoriented and revamped during 
the Ninth Five Yeur Plan period cover Polar (Antarctic) Science, Marine Living Resources, 
Marine Non-Living Resources, Ocean Observation & Information Services, Marine and 
Coastal Area Management, Marine Research and Capacity Building, Coastal Community 
Programmes, Ocean Awareness and International Cooperation. It has been stated that while 
formulating the research and development programmes, stress is laid on accelerated 
development of applied technology so that benefits continue to accrue to the society. 
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
4. The Department proposed an outlay of Rs. 656 crore for the Eighth Five Year Plan 
period. But the Planning Commission allocated Rs. l30 crore only as indicative outlay. 
Later, based on the requirement!i of various programmes, a sum of Rs. 224 crore was 
provided against which the expenditure was about Rs. 200 crore. During the Eighth Five 
Year Plan, the strategic areas such as Antarctic Research, Polymetallic Nodules Programmes 
and International Cooperation Programmes received priority in terms of fund allocation 
amounting to a total of 66 per cent, followed by Societal Programmes 21 per cent, Scien:ific 
and Technological Development Programmes 8 per cent and Basic Research 5 per cent. 
5. The Secretary, DOD informed the Committee that the Ninth Five Year Plan has since 
been approved by the National Development Council (NDC). The Planning Commission, 
however, has informed that the Cabinet has approved an outlay of Rs. 510.62 crore in 
respect of the Department's Plan schemes for the Ninth Plan period. The break up of the 
outlay is given in Annexure-!. 
6. The Plan outlay for 1999-2000 is Rs. 90.00 crore and a Non-Plan outlay of Rs. 20.88 
crore. The Department would thus have a total outlay of Rs. 110.88 crore against the 
Rs. 107.41 crore (Plan as well as Non-Plan) allocated at RE stzge for 1998-99. Thus there is 
a marginal increase of Rs. 3.47 crore as compared to the anticipated expenditure for 
1998-99. The comparative figures in terms of actual expenditures for various programmes of 
the Department for 1996-97, 1997-98 and 1998-99 are given in Annexure- II and the financial 
allocations earmarked for 1999-2000 have been brought out in Annexure-III.

7. The Department projected an outlay of Rs. 140 crore which was reduced to Rs. 90 
crore by the Planning Commission, due to the resource crunch. Accordingly, the 
Department has revised the budget estimates by differing/scaling down some of the 
programmes/projects. The programmes likely to be affected are Antarctic Research, 
Metallurgy component of Polymetallic Nodules and Ocean Energy Mission of National 
Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT) and on Delineation of the outer limits of Continental 
Shelf. Thus, an additional outlay of Rs. 35.92 crore is required at revised estimates (RE) 
stage of the current financial year-Rs. 5.42 crore for Antarctic Research, Rs. 10 crore for 
Metallurgy Pilot Plant, Rs. 1.00 crore for Drugs from Sea, Rs. 5.00 crore for Ocean Energy 
Mission and Rs. 14.50 crore for Delineation of Continental Shelf. 
NON-PLAN EXPENDITURE 
8. The Non-Plan expenditure broadly falls under four heads, namely (i) ORY Sagar 
Kanya; (ii) FORV Sagar Sampada; (iii) Secretariat and Economic Services; and 
(iv) Administrative infrastructure. The major increase in the Non-Plan expenditure is against 
ORV Sagar Kanya which was acquired in 1984. It is a sophisticated research vessel which 
has been carrying out survey and exploration of marine non-living resources particularly in 
the field of physical and chemical oceanography, marine biology, meteorology, marine 
geophysics, marine geology, etc. It provides a common platform to the National Institute/ 
Laboratories in the field of Oceanographic research. 
9. The Committee was informed that during 1998-99 the ORY Sagar Kan ya conducted 
13 scientific cruises both in the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal. The scientific investigations/ 
research carried out by ORY Sagar Kanya during 1998-99 include data collected from sea 
for validating satellite derived oceanic parameters; deployment, retrieval and servicing of the 
shallow and deep water data buoys in the Arabian Sea under the National Data Buoy 
Programme; bathymetric data collection in Arabian Sea for delineation of outer limits of 
continental shelf; multidisciplinary experiments under the INDOEX programme; BOBMEX 
pilot project in the Bay of Bengal for Monsoon Experimental studies; trial testing of various 
sub-systems of the crawler at shallow depth; and Lar}d Ocean Interaction in Coastal Zone 
(LOICZ) studies for comprehending climate change induced reactions in the coastal regions. 
10. The Secretary, DOD, informed the Committee that an enhanced budget provision in 
the Non-Plan sector would be required for operation and maintenance of ORV Sagar Kanya 
and FORV Sagar Sampada which were about 15 years old necessitating replacement of both 
the deck machinery and other essential equipment/instruments. The allocation of Rs. 9.48 
crore and Rs. 7.50 crore made for operation and management of ORV Sagar Kanya and 
FORV Sagar Sampada respectively during 1999-2000 is the barest minimum as against the 
required amount of Rs. 43.00 crore. This has resulted in accumulation of huge amounts of 
payments over the years to be made to Shipping Corporation of India, which run s the 
vessels. 
11. Th~ task of survey is to locate and map the resource potential of living and non-living 
resources by ORV Sagar Kanya and FORV Sagar Sampada. This will have to he continued 
for collection of enormous oceanographic data and information and exploration activity which 
are essential in or~er to understand various oceanographic phenomena. The Committee feels 
that an extra budgetary support is necessary for the programme to ensure continuity of the 
survey programme and avoid men and machinery being rendered idle. 

ANT ARCTIC RESEARCH PROGRAMME 
12. Tht: Indian Antarctic Programme and its scientific expeditions are held on annual basis 
with the launching of the first expedition to Antarctic in 1981. The first Indian research 
station , Dakshin Gangotri was commissioned in 1983 and replaced by the indigenously 
designed second Indian permanent station 'Maitri' in the Schirmacher Oasis in 1988. The 
Station 'Maitri' has adequate infra-structural facilities for conducting multi-faceted scientific 
research in Polar (Antarctic) Science::. While using An~m:tic a!\ a platform for conducting 
scientific experiments, India has always recognised the importance of preserving the pristine 
naturo.: of thi!\ remote and unique continent. In order to uphold thi!> commitment, India, an 
origin;tl 'otary of the Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty, has 
ratified thl.! Pn..Howl in April. 1996. 
13. The Committee was informed that so far 20 scientific expeditions have been 
launched on a regular basis whkh have carried research work in the thrust areas of polar 
sciem:t:, including an expedition to the weedell Sea and one for assessment of Antarctic 
Krill. During the year under reference the broad scientific and logistic activities planned to 
be undertaken are in continuation of studies on ozone, trace gases and aerosols of the 
Antarctic atmosphere using various state-of-the-art equipment; archival of meteorological 
parameters that can be employed for climatic modeling and prediction; experiments on solat 
terrestrial phenomenon like optical aurora and geo-magnetic perturbations; studies on 
adaptation techniques of human beings in adverse conditions; application and utiliz<ltioh of 
dean energy sources like wind and sun in Antarctica; experiments in Antarctic ice moss in 
relation to snowdrift patterns and snow albedo; up-gradation of communication facilities with 
special emphasis on real time picture transmission; and reorientation of waste discharge and 
handling facilities. Towards the end of 1999, the Nineteenth Indian Antarctic Expedition 
would be launched for carrying out contemporary research in the fields of atmospheric, 
geological, biological, environmental, medical sciences, engineering and commuRication. 
During the year 1999-2000, in order to continue the scientific activities, it would be 
necessary to continue the chartering of the ice-breaker along with other logistics in the 
research station. 
14. The Department proposed an outlay of Rs. 25.42 crore towards the annual 
expedition to Antarctica, scientific pro~rmnmes and strengthening the facilities at research 
station in Antarctica - "Muitri" and for facility augmentation and operation of the 
Antarctic Study Centre at Goa. Due w paucity of reso~rces outlay has been reduced to 
Rs. 20.00 crore by deferring some of the scientific programmes and phasing out some of the 
R&D facilities. The Committee was given to understand that an upward revision by Rs. 5.42 
crore at RE stage would help in promoting the interaction of our scientists with the scientific 
community abroad and in undertaking joint cooperative programmes. 
15. Antarctic Study Centre (ASC) at Goa, which had an attached office of the 
Department of Ocean Development, has been transformed into an autonomous institute 
from September, 1998. The Centre is responsible for in-house R & D activities in polar 
sciences and for coordinating expedition activities to Antarctic. Besides , the Centre is 
responsible for developing expertise in the field of polar sciences and logistics through 
activities such as coordination and execution of the entire scientific and logistic activities of 
the Antarctic expeditions, establish and maintain a research base in Antarctic and provide all 
operational and logistic support and encourage cooperative research both at national and 
international levels specially in the area of Global Change. 

16. A S rega rds in-hou se R&D activities, the Centre is conducting research on clima te 
modelin g, sea- ice-ocea n-atmosphere c oupling , monit oring all issues a rising o ut of the 
Environmental Protocol, develop ing a complete data base invento ry a nd rep osito ry for 
An tarctic a nd Arctic science and logistics, generatin g s pecialised manpowe r for polar science 
and logistics and cruise plann ing and management of,the Oceanograp hic resea rch vessels. 
17. Over the years the Antarctic Programme has generated valuable data w hich would be 
useful in future . Besides, the programm e has gained internation al importance in as much as it 
has provided internation al interaction among countri es to shar e their experience s in an 
atmo sphere of mutual friend ship. The Committee , therefore , feels that this programm e s hould 
not be allowed to suffer for wan t of funds. 
DRUGS FROM THE SEA 
18. The Na tional Project on "Drugs from the Sea" initiate d during 1990-91 is a multi­
institution al proje ct on devel opment of p oten tial dru gs and chemicals from marine organisms 
which was funded under R & D prog ramme till the end of Phase- 11 (1995-96). The 
Comm ittee was informe d tha t during the period 1998-99, 15 new marine flora and .53 fauna 
were collected for general biologica l s creening. I n order to confi rm biological activity and 
follow-up stud ies, repeat collect ion of 7 6 flora and 40 fauna was made which has yielded 
valuab le clues for develop ing potent dru gs. 
19. T he Depa rtment propose d an outlay of Rs. 3.00 crore for 1999-2000, it was reduced 
to Rs.1.60 crore due to financial crunch. The project has completed Phase-I II . It will enter 
the crucial Phase- IV from 1999-2000 onwards. In Phase-III, the resea rch activ ities have led 
to ide ntification of five marine organisms having potent ial properties as anti-d iabetic, anti­
viral, anti-anxiety, anti-cholesterol and larvicidal agents for develop ing new drugs du ring the 
Ninth Plan period. In Phase -IV, steps would be taken to investigate further and release new 
drugs developed from marine flora and fauna under Phase- Ill. Chemical trials are expected 
to be complete for anti-diabetic (CDR -134) drug. It has now been observed that the same 
lead has antidiabetic as well as anti-diarrhoeal propert ies. The Drug is as good as the 
standard antidiabetic drug like Phonformin and better than Tolbutamide. Also commercial 
work for patenting anti-cholesterol lead would be initiated. 
20. While the Committee appreciates the work being done by the Department in 
developing the drugs from Sea, it observes that a large number of multinational as well as 
Indian companies are engaged in researc h in this field in different systems of medicines. 
Medicines coming to market from these companies have largely a profit motive at th~ir back. 
The Committee therefore feels that a mere addition of a drug in the market would not serve 
the purpose. The country has a large potential of resources, be they in the form of herbs 
grown in forests or in other forms of natural deposits in the vast sea bed. A large number of 
diseases should be curable once for all. It should also be possible ~0 prevent the diseases by 
either preserving the natural force in the body or by restoring it with the help of medicines, 
as Hahneman, the founder of Homoeopathy put it. Our belief in Hahneman's principle of 
Similia Similibus Curenter (i.e. likes are treated by likes) is further strengthened because of 
the vast amount of natural resources available in our country. The Committee, therefore, 
observes that whatever number of drugs are taken up for research and development they 
should aim at excellence by curing the diseases once for all. The programme on research for 
these medicines should be time bound, well-knit to avoid delays and should not he allowed to 
suffer for want of funds otherwise it may lose its significance in the fast changing world. 

POLYMETALLIC NODULES PROGRAMME (PNP) 
21. In 1987, India was accorded the status of Registered Pioneer Investor and started 
the Polymetallic Nodules Programme (PNP). Considerable progress has since been made in 
the country in resource identification and evaluation, technology and manpower 
development towards exploitation of these resources. However, presently, this programme 
has been expanded to develop technologies for deep-sea mining and metallurgy for recovery 
of metals, etc . 
22. The major activities proposed to be undertaken during the current financial year are 
Survey & Exploration in the Central Indian Ocean Basin (CIOB) for spot sampling of 
nodules using grab sampler and updating of geo-statistical resource evaluation in the pioneer 
areas, ·Benthic disturbance and impact assessment studies in the Indian Pioneer Area', 
prepared on baseline benthic conditions. Besides, under Technology Development (Mining) 
programme activities would be undertaken for demonstrating shallow bed mining system 
along the coast. Also the work relating to development of manipulator for underwater 
operation and testing of materials for deep-sea operation would be undertaken including 
initiating a joint programme between NlOT and Russian Academy of Science, Moscow for 
design, development and testing of unmanned submersibles operational unto 6000 meter 
depth. An outlay of Rs.8.35 crore has been provided for this programme. 
23. Also initiatives will be made under Technology Development (Metallurgy) for 
carrying out demonstration campaigns to validate the data obtained from earlier campaigns 
and designing and development of semi-continuous demonstration pilot plant of 500 kg/day 
capacity at Hindustan Zinc Ltd. (Udaipur). Due to resource limitation, financial outlay for 
the Pilot Plant is kept at Rs.5.15 crore with a request to HZ Ltd. to advance the money and 
go ahead with the project. However, a final understanding is yet to be reached since the 
matter is under consideration of HZ Ltd. Thus, the Department will have to meet the entire 
expenditure of HZ Ltd. subject to the ceilings for which EFC approval exists. The activities 
proposed to be undertaken during the current year are part of the long-term activities 
planned under the programme fot which the tot ·1l financial outlay is Rs.14.05 crore. 
24. The Committee was apprised that Polymetallic Nodule Programme is still in 
experimental stage. Therefore, commercial exploitation of polymetallic nodules may not be 
feasible for some more time. However , the technology for exploration and exploitation has 
been demonstrated. Thus, development of technologies for nodule mining purposes for the 
deep sea may be viewed as contribution to a long term objective . 
25. The Committee observes that the long gestation period, rapidly changing technology, 
economic priorities of the countries and economic importance of the material likely to be 
extracted as also the cost of extraction are some of the factors which are liable to affect the 
viability of the programme. A critical assessment of all these factors was necessary before w 
planning the programme. At this stage, the Committee feels that the programme having · 
commenced, it should not be allowed to suffer because of the reduction in the budgetary 
support for such a reduction would disrupt continuity, may render some of the assets idle and 
thus, in turn, push up the cost of the . project. 
COASTAL OCEAN MONITORING AND PREDICTION SYSTEM (COMAPS) 
26. In view of multipurpose use of the coastal zone such as shipping, fishing, tourism, 
industrialisation and disposal of wastes, the stress on the coastal areas is growing rapidly 
with developments taking place often in an un;Jlanned f&shion and unmindful of long term 
consequences. The programme aims to assess the status and likely trends in coastal marine 

for prediction of tropical cyclones and associated surges (Ocean Dynamics & Modelling) 
would be undertak en. 
40. The Commi ttee is not happy with the claim of usefulness of data generated for 
weather forecas ting to the extent that our weather forecasts often go awry . At times they lack 
precision . Somethi ng i s w ron g s omewhere and needs to be looked into. 
SHORE TO FISHING VESSEL COMMUNICATIO N SYSTEM 
41. The Department of Ocean Developm ent has taken up the Programme 'Shore to 
Fishing Vessel Comr~mnication System' in t wo p hases as a coasta l community activity. The 
Programme is being executed by the State governments. The First Phase covers four States 
i.e ., Andhra Pradesh, Tami l Nadu, Kera la, Karna taka and a part o f Goa. In the Secon d 
Phase, 10 shore stations have been planned to be estab lished i.e., two eac h in the States of 
Maharashtra, West Bengal and Orissa and one each in Pondicherry, Lakshadweep and 
Andaman & Nicbbar Islands. Equipments were made available to the concerned coastal 
State governments. In pursuance of its earlier recommendation the Committee was informed 
that during 1998-99 the Government of Gujarat did not want to partic toate in the 
programm e. As regards Daman & Diu its administration has agreed to prov ide t he requisite 
logistic and other support required for sett ing up the Shore to Fishing Vessel 
Communication System, the Gujarat Government is yet to confi rm the provision of logistic 
and other support. 
42. Besides, 10 shore stations set up dur ing Phase-II of the programme wo..1ld be 
operated during the year and maintained and an MoU would be signed between DOD and 
the concerned 10 stations .for taking over of the communication system in the si:es for 
continuing operation and maintenance beyond 1999-2000. 
43. The Committee notes the position. 
ISLAND DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMME 
44. ln the Ninth Five Year Plan, the Island Development Programme envisages to give 
impetus for achieving various charters oi the Department of Ocean Development in the fielj 
of demonstration of technology having a bear ing on the socio-economic aspects of the Island 
community. Accordingly, the set object ives of the programme are to demonstrate the 
technology of enhancement of marine living resources; demonstration of the technology for 
fattening, sea ranching and sea farming of lobster; and introduction of technology 
development programmes for sea farming of sea bass, ornamental fish, mud crab, etc. 
45. With the commissioning of a sea-front laboratory at Neelankarai, Chennai, and with 
the availability of strengthened infrastructure fa<;ilities at NIOT and AN COD, all three 
components of the Enhancement of Marine Living Resources project, under the Island 
Development Programme, namely breeding and rearing of lobsters, fattening studies and 
sea-farming and sea-reaching would be accelerated. Besides, it is also envisaged to take up 
new programmes on Ocean Env ironment and Conservation of Living Resources including 
coral reefs. 
46. The Comm ittee feels that a new awakening needs to be infused in the islao~s through 
the techno logy such as the Ocean technology and other employment oriented programmes so 
that they do not carry a feeling of neglect by the mainland. 

MARINE RESEARCH AND CAPACITY BUILDING 
47. The Department has been implementing the Marine Research and Manpower 
Development Programme with the active participation of educational institutions, National 
R&D Laboratories, etc. The objectives of the programme are to encourage research on 
physical and chemical processes, which govern the seas of India; impact of natural 
anthropogenic sources on global climate change; to strengthen the infrastructure facilities in 
selected universitiesltnstitutes to carry out basic research in Marine Sciences; to create 
centres of excellence on ocean sciences at selected institutes/universities; to create a code of 
high class ocean scientists and trained personnel/users; and to create awiireness among the 
school children, public and coastal community on the usefulness of ocean resources and 
create scientific temper among the people on ocean science. 
48. The ongoing projects would be integrated for generation of a national project under 
Marine Living Resources Programme. Besides, funding of about 10 socially beneficial 
projects proposed to be taken up with a view to develop suitable technologies. Also, action 
wouid be initiated to bring uniformity in course curriculum for offering courses on Ocean 
Science & Technology in Colleges/Universities and to evolve a mechanism for upgrading and 
bringing uniformity in academic standards in all marine related course, including 
introduction of Ocean Science & Technology at secondary school level. 
49. The Committee observes the need to induct Ocean Science related courses at various 
levels of studies to mak~ the students more conversant with the developments taking place in 
the field of Ocean Sciences. 
50. After considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Ocean 
Development and after reviewing some of the programmes and projects administered by it, 
the Committee recommends that the Demand for Grants of Rs.110.88 crore, as sought by 
tht Department of Ocean Development, for the year 1999-2000, under Demand No. 92, may 
be approved .
