INTRODUCTION 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and 
Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, 
present this Sixty-sixth Report of the Committee. This Report deals with the detailed 
Demands for Grants (1999-2000) of the Department of Biotechnology (Demand No. 75) . 
2. Ln the meeting of the Committee held on the 24th March, 1999 the Secretary and 
other Officers of the Department of Biotechnology gave an overview of the various activities 
of· the Department and the Committee sought clarifications on various aspects of the 
performance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants. 
3. The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Department replying to 
the clarifications sought . by the Members and placing before it the required material to 
enable the ·committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Department of 
13 iotechilOlogy. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on 
April 20, 1999. 
NEw DELHI; 
April, 20, 1999 
S.R. BOMMAI 
Committee on Science & Technology, 
Environment & Forests 

REPORT 
The field of bio-technology has made significant impact in the last decade on the growth 
of agricultural, industrial, plwrmaceutical and medical sectors. The scientific understanding 
at the cellular and molecular levels of biological systems and development of technologies 
based on these hus led to increase in the agricultural productivity, development of vaccines, 
diagnostics, drugs, improved animal husbandry practices, env ironment friendly technologies 
and ~evcral tools for conservation of biological diversity. 
2. In pursuan~:e of these goals, the Department of Bio-technology has provided 
sustained suppo rt to the research, application and commercialising of Bio-technology. The 
Department has made efforts for transferring of some innovations/Research leads to 
indu stry for comme rcia lizutio n and thus serves as a link between research institutions, 
academia and indu stry. Besides supporting basic research, the department has launched a 
number of projects for weaker section of the society. The mandate of the Department 
extends to providing support to R&D, setting up of centres of excellence, promotion of 
large-scal e use of biotechnology, human resource developm ent and manufacturing of 
biologicals. The Department also cremes infrastructural facilities to support Research and 
Production activities; it serves as a nodal point for the collection and dissemination of 
information reluting to biotechnology and evolves bio-safety guidelines. Manufacture and 
application of cell-based vaccines is also one of the major activity of the Department. 
3. It has been stated that during the year 1999-2000, basic research and product and 
process development would be major thrusts through identification of leads from ongoing 
R&D projects . Multi -institutional and multi-disciplinary projects having national impact 
would be pri01·tised and implemented in the areas of agriculture, phyto-pharmaceuticals, 
microbial products, animal biotechnology, infectious diseases and neuro-sciences. 
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
4. Based on the recommendation of the Working Group and the proposal submitted for 
Ninth Plan to the Planning Commission, the Department of Biotechnology proposed as 
outlay of Rs. 1026 crore for a period of five years (1997-2002) against which only an amount 
of Rs. 675 crore was sanctioned. Thus the final anrlllal budget was Rs. 85 crore during the 
first year of the 9th Plan (1997-98) against the allocated B.E. of Rs. 107.00 crore & 
projected plan demand of Rs. 129.50 crore (Annexur~-1). During 1998-99, the department 
proposed an outlay of Rs. 125.00 crore, but · the B.E. was kept at the level of last year i.e. 
107.00 crore and the revised estimates were pegged at Rs. 100.81 crore (Annexure-H). 
During the year 1999-2000 the Department has demanded a plan outlay of Rs. 139.00 crore 
while an outlay of Rs. 110.00 crore only has been sanctioned (Annexure-III). 
5. As regards the reasons for the yawning gap of 25% between what was demanded and 
what was actually spent, the Secretary, Department of Biotechnology, informed the 
Committee that every year the Department has been projecting demands based on the 
recom mendations of various Task Forces and Apex Committee on the projects and 
programmes to be planned for each financial year and also keeping in view the priorities of 
the nation and changing trends in the international scenario. The recommended budgetary 
support being released by the Planning Commission has been in the order of 10-15% over 
the R.E. level of previous year. 

6. The Committee has been given to understand that the Department has proposed a 
budgetary outlay of Rs. 1026 crore based on the recommendations of the work group 
constituted by the Planning Commission for preparing the 9th Plan proposals of the 
Department of Biotechnology. As against this amount Planning Commission has committeed a 
budgetary support of Rs. 675 crore. 
7. The Committee observes that the investments made in the area of biotechnology by the 
department for promoting research and development, human resource, establishment of 
infrastructure and autonomous research institutions, have given rich dividends in the form of 
new technologies, patents and publications, academic excellenced and large pool of expertise. 
It is therefore necessary to mount a major effort for bio-industrial development of the 
country . A priority agenda for the next millennium would be to ensure judicious utilisation 
and conservation of biological resources and to undertake mission mode programmes in the 
areas such as vaccines and diagnostics for communicable diseases, genomic anal ysis and to 
develop friendly technologies including transgenic plant research . This would bring about food 
security, nutritional security also diversification of our bread basket. The original proposal for 
9th Plan had more than 50% of the budgetary provision for basic and product oriented 
research with a view to developing products and processes. With the reduced allocation of Rs. 
675 crore, it may not be possible to complete many activities. Therefore, the additional 
allocation of Rs. 75 crore would be necessary to restore several of these important 
programmes for being taken up during the remaining three year (1999-2000). This amount 
would also facilitate conversion of many important R&D leads into products that enhance 
productivity and efficiency of the concerned sectors, provide easy to use, low cost, 
environmentally sound technologies specially for the health care system, for soil fertility, for 
environmental conservation and protection, aimed at sustainable development particularly for 
rural areas. 
8. The Committee is also of the view that Department should draw up its plans 
sufficiently in advance in order to ensure utilisation of allocated funds during a particular 
financial year. This would have an impact on the allocations made during the next financial 
year also. In case of scientific departments, assessment formula for suggesting mandatory cuts 
need not be based on the trend of expenditure during the first six months of the financial year 
as expenditure on programmes and proje~ts generally picks up after the first half of financial 
year. 
BASIC AND PRODUCT ORIENTED R&D 
9. Department of Bio-Technology supports research and development. Some of the 
institutions under the Depurtment e.g . the National Institute of Immunology and the Centre 
for Finger Printing have made some earnings from transfer of technology. The Department 
has earned royalties for its technology for development of monochronal anti-body. But the 
earnings are ploughed back for research , for the benefit of the animals, animal feed, clean 
conditions etc. The earnings have helped create e.g. animal house facility which is serving 
the entire community . 
lO.Thus the projects aim at creation of a strong R&D base and product development. 
These R&D proje cts mainly fall under (i) Basic research; (ii) Crop bio-technoogy; 
(iii) Medicinal and Aromatic Plants ; (iv) Tree and Woody Species, Tissue Culture; 
(v) Seribiote chnology; (vi) Biopro specting of biological wealth; (vii) Medical Bio-technology; 
(viii) Human Genetics and Gcnoms Analysis; (ix) Animal Bio-technology; (x) Aquaculture 
and Marine Bio-technology; (xi) Biodiversity Conservation and Environment. 

11. The allocation for Basic and Product Oriented R&D activities has been restricted to 
Rs. 45.35 crore against the demanded allocation of Rs. 53.50 crore in the current financial 
year as against Rs. 43.40 crore provided for in B.E. and later-on reduced to Rs. 40.63 crore 
at R.E. stage during the last financial year. In reply to a query as to how many projects! 
programmes evolved through Task Forces and Expert Committee for implementation during 
the last financial year were finally taken up for research, the Committee was informed that 
the Department as per its mandate, generates research projects in the priority areas 
identified by the respective Task Forces and Expert Committees and receives projects and 
programmes from individual scientists and team for support. Out of a total of 517 projects 
received during the year 1998-99 the Department has approved and implemented about 205 
projects based on scientific merit and techno-economic feasibility covering 20 different areas 
of specialisation including both basic and applied research. 
12. The Committee is of view that the projects and programmes designed for the benefit 
of farmers, persons belonging to weaker and back ward sections of the Society and the ones 
relating to bio-technologiclll innovations may be given wide publicity through the electronic 
media so that the sections of the sodety for "hich the programmes are intended can benefit. 
Besides, a mechanism should be evolved, for continuous evaluation and monitoring of the 
projects undertaken. 
13. The Department was aske~ whether Government were cosidering any proposal to 
ensure that the Research/non-earning ac~1demic type and other institute consider 
commercialising a part of their activities with a veiw to reduce dependence on budgetary 
support. The Committee was informed that the Department of Bio-technology has not only 
been advocating but ~llso promoting the reseurch orgunisations to consider commercialising a 
part of their activities with a view to reduce dependence on budgetary support. However, 
the Department would like such earnings to be used for improving the basic infrastructure, 
and giving incentives to young scientists. The programmes supported such as Repositories, 
Animal Facilities, Bioinformatic Centres, Pilot Plant to Tissue Culture and Bio-pesticides in 
various institutions have ulready been generating income through sale-proceeds for their 
service and materials. Industries have been involved in serveral R&D projects from the 
beginning to explore commercialisation of the leads during the course of the project. The 
Department also facilitates TechnologyTransfer in close co-ordination with NRDC and BCIL 
for commercialising the R&D leads: 
14. The Committee is happy to note that certain projects undertaken by the Department 
are already generating income. This would reduce their dependence on budgetary support. 
The Departments should ensure that earnings from the projects are commensurate with the 
inputs and are used for reinforcing the projects, by improving the basic infrastructure and for 
providing incentives to young scientists. 
AGRICULTURAL BIO-TECHNOLOGY 
(i) Biological Control of Plant Pests, Diseases and Weeds 
15. The Committee was informed that the projects undertaken by the Department for 
production of bio-pesticides and bio-fertilizers induded four new bio-pesticide technologies 
which are under feasibility studies for commercialisation mass production technologies of 
some of the bio-control agents like-Trichograma (developed by IARI), Trichoderma 
(developed by RRL, Jammu) and Beaveria bassiana and Verticillium lecam (developed by 
AAU, Assam) are being patented. Successful field demonstrations of the some of the bio­
control agents resulted in the recommendation for their use in various States. 

16. In case of Bio-fertilizers the Committee was informe d that a number of projects on 
crop specific bio-fertilizers have been supported. High nitrogen fixing stra ins of rhizobium 
and blue gree algae suitable for diffe rent agrodimatic regions were isolated and 
demonstrated in field conditions Technology for the mass production of mycorrhiza is being 
transferred to industry. Besides, a number of technologies have been developed by the 
department for large scale production of high quality bio-fe rtilize rs specially for rice, pulses, 
fodder, legumes and importa nt forests trees. These tech nologies have been demonstrated 
and are under transfer to field. The department has initiat ed a network programme i.e. 
Integrat ed Nutr ient and pest M anagement to develop a package of practices involving 
various bio-fertilizers for spec ific cropping systems and bio-pesticides. 
17. The Committee commends the work done by the Department in the field of bio­
control agents and bio-fertilizers. The Committee recommends that techniques de,•eloped be 
upgraded and transferred to industry for pilot level production. Besides, the achievements in

mulberry silkworms: Attempts are being made to isolate and characterize the silk 
genes of non-mulberry silkworms for the purpose of introducing the same into the

67th Report on Demands for Grants of Department of Electronics
 
The Department of Electronics (DOE)  is responsible for the development of the electronics industry formulation,
 promoting application  of electronics and informative technology,  implementation and review of various programmes/schemes
 in the field of electronics.  These schemes are implemented both in-house as well as through PSUs /Societies  under DOE and
 also through various sponsored programmes being funded under R&D.
2.         The Department is a medium not only to provide a focal point of Government’s attention to electronics sector and also to
 function as a coordinator within and outside the Government, but is also responsible for bringing the benefits of electronics to
 every walk of life, and play a catalytic role to make the Indian Electronics Industry a global player  in the light of the new
 Industrial and Trade Policy.
3.         With delicensing of the entire electronics industry (except aerospace and defence electronics), liberalisation in foreign
 investment and Export-Import policies, the country is witnessing new investments, restructuring of existing activities,
 diversification of the product range and an intensely  competitive environment.  All the renowned global brands have either
 established production facilities in the country or are present in the market through technical/financial collaborations, thus
 giving consumer a wider choice in terms of product features, technology quality and competitive prices.
4.         The thrust , according to  DOE, during the Ninth Plan, would be on Export, Employment and productivity-led growth of
 Electronics and Information Technology.  The electronics and Information Technology sector has the propensity to increase the
 overall growth rate to higher level.
5.            Electronics is the fast growing sector of the Indian industry.  During the Eighth Plan, the electronics industry had a
 cumulative annual growth of 20 per cent in production and over 40 per cent in exports.  The electronics industry achieved a
 production level of Rs. 32,070 crores and an export performance of Rs. 9, 500 crores during the year 1997-98 and is likely to
 achieve a production level of Rs. 41,000 crores during the year 1998-99 registering a growth of over 28% and export
 performance of Rs.12800/- showing a net increase of 70 per cent.  A goal of annual electronics production of Rs. 1,38,350
 crores and exports of about Rs. 49,000 crores has been set for the terminal year of the Ninth Plan (2001-02), representing a
 growth rate of 39% and 52% respectively.
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
6.         The Department was given an allocation of Rs. 791.78 for the entire 8
th Five Year Plan, out of which budgetary support
 was to the tune of Rs.  679.38 crores .  An allocation of Rs. 897.37 crores has been made available for the 9 th Five Year Plan
 (1997-2002) and Gross Budgetary support would be pegged at Rs. 542.37 crores.  .  During the first three years of plan Rs.
 769.57 crores  have been spent and left over allocation  is only Rs. 127.8 crores and the share of Budgetary support spent so far
 is Rs. 405.6 crores leaving a balance of Rs. 136.77 cores (Appendix –I).
 
 
7.            Budgetary support for the Department of Electronics for the current financial  year  is Rs. 208 crores (Rs. 180 crores
 Plan and Rs. 28 crores Non-Plan) against the revised estimate 1998-99 of Rs. 156.57 crores (Rs. 135 crores Plan and Rs. 21.57
 crores Non-Plan)(See Appendix –II).  The allocation for the year is thus Rs. 51.43 crores more than RE 1998-99.
8.         As regards the justification for  enhanced allocation the Committee was informed an enhanced outlay of Rs. 20 crores
 has been provided  for setting up of  an  IT Venture Capital Fund .  Besides, an amount of  Rs. 5.00 crores are likely to be spent
 for Electronic Governance. A sum of Rs. 5.09 crores has been provided towards  reimbursement of Central Sales Tax to
 STPs/EHTPs in accordance with the Exim Policy.    This scheme was being handled by Ministry of Commerce till 1996-97 and
 has subsequently been transferred to the Department of  Electronics.  TDC projects, STQC Labs/centre and Ernet India would
 require an additional outlay of Rs. 5.50 crores, 4.00 crores , 5.50 crores and 10.00 crores respectively for their plan expenditure
 and the additional allocation has been proposed  to give thrust to the technology development in the electronic sector  and to
 meet requirements of the approved projects
9.         The Committee finds that the Planning Commission has sanctioned a budget support of Rs. 300 crore for
 Information Technology to be spent during the Ninth Five Year (1997-2002) period.  The allocation has not been
 earmarked against any of the Ministry/Department of Government of India.  The Department is working on so many

REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/67report.htm[29-08-2018 16:12:10]
 programmes/projects concerning Information Technology such as ERNET, NII, TDIL, Electronics Commerce,
 Electronics Governance, Venture Capital for Software etc. and the Planning Commission have not allocated sufficient
 funds for the said programmes/projects .  As DOE is responsible for promotion of Information Technology in the
 country   the Committee is strongly of the view that the amount of Rs. 300.00 crore provided by the Planning
 Commission to be spent during the Ninth Plan may be allocated under the administrative control of Department of
 Electronics and the Department may be designated  as  a  nodal agency in the field of information technology.
NATIONAL INFORMATION INFRASTRUCTURE FOR NATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
10.        It has been stated  that during 1998-99 Department of Electronics had initiated a national focus on National Information
 Infrastructure with the aim of promoting use and proliferation of Information Technology.  Some of the sectors proposed to be
 covered  included – literacy, education and life-long learning leading to increase in employment opportunities, better health
 care, environment friendliness, opportunities for rural populace for acquiring new skills, etc.
11.        A multi-institutional National Resources Centre for low cost multimedia content creation has been set up and projects
 for ‘Object oriented toolkit’ for developing Multimedia and Virtual Reality applications and development of an ‘ATM test-bed’
 have been initiated.  In association with the Government of Andhra Pradesh, the Department has supported development of two
 test-beds in the area of Electronic Governance, namely, ‘Development and deployment of multi-purpose, multi-lingual,
 multimedia, scaleable information warehouse for state level governance of Andhra Pradesh’ and ‘Community Information
 Network for Vijaywada Municipal Corporation (VMC)’. 
12.        While the Committee appreciates the efforts made by DOE in initiating a focussed attention on National
 Information Infrastructure in Andhra Pradesh, it would like the Department to continue its efforts in spreading the
 same culture to other states.
 
 
 
 
NATIONAL TASK FORCE ON INFORMATION TECHNOLOY & SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT
13.          The Government has announced promotion of Information technology as one of the five top priorities of the country
 and constituted a National Task Force on Information Technology and Software Development .  Information Technology
 provides an opportunity to achieve the goal of becoming a strong, prosperous and  self-confident nation.   The Task Force
 submitted  108 point Action Plan  which seeks to accomplish inter-alia
(i)            Infrastructure Drive,
(ii)            Target of IT Exports of $ 50 ,
(iii)            IT for all by 2008,
(iv)            opening of Internet Gateway access,
(v)            encouragement to private STPs,
(vi)            zero customs and excise duty on IT software,
(vii)    income tax exemptions to software and service exports,
(viii)            decision to set up a Venture Capital Fund ,
(ix)            A separate fund to handle the Y2K problem,
(x)            gift tax exemption on computers,
(xi)            1-3% of budget of every Ministry/Department for IT applications,
(xii)            networking of all Universities and research institutions,
(xiii)      Dollar linked Stock Option to employees of Indian Software Companies, Sweat Equity,and
(xiv)     new schemes proposed for students which include attractive financial package for buying computer etc.
                                                        
14.        The Committee was informed that the Government is taking all necessary steps to make India, a Global Information

REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/67report.htm[29-08-2018 16:12:10]
 Technology Superpower and a front-runner in the age of Information Revolution.  Government have accepted the Task Force
 recommendations and have gone ahead in implementing these recommendations by announcing major fiscal benefits to the
 Information Technology sector.
15.        The Government have also recommended that each Ministry/ Department must allocate 2-3 per cent of its Budget on IT
 promotion.  This is a  step for development of domestic software industry and a move towards Electronic Governance.  The
 software industry has emerged as one of the fastest growing sectors in the economy with a CAGR exceeding 50% and with a
 likely turnover of US $ 4 billion and exports of US $ 2.6 billion during 1998-99 which are  expected to go up to US  $ 15
 billion by the Year 2002.   In order to maintain  comparative advantage in skilled manpower required for software development,
 a number of development programmes for manpower, quality up-gradation, stimulation of software engineering and research
 have been started.
 
 
 
16.       The Committee favours the spread of information technology including, of course, the computer culture in the
 country in order to bridge the gap that exists at present between the developed and developing countries.  The
 Committee, however, observes that the computers are at times affected by certain kind of virus, problems like Y2K and
 the systems being rendered non-functional on certain dates – these events indicate that the Nature has not yet opened all
 its mysteries to scientists and thus our efforts to spread IT may be hampered to some extent.  This should not render us
 complacent in switching over to traditional methods of work should the situation so demand.
TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPMENT COUNCIL PROJECTS
17.        The TDCP programme aims to promote and support research, design, development and engineering in the areas of
 computer and computer communications, control and instrumentation, Consumer Electronics , Telecommunication and
 broadcasting.
18.        Asked about the grounds on which the allocation for the Technology Development Council Projects has been increased
 to Rs. 6.80 crores from Rs. 2.50 crores allocated in the Budget Estimate of 1998-99,  the Committee was informed that the
 enhancement of the budget allocation for the Technology Development Council has been sought in view of the recent emphasis
 on developing technologies relevant to the industry.  This would entail funding the projects above the critical level.  Further,
 DOE have recently identified thrust areas of R&D in order to meet  the needs of the industry/users.  In the next year, projects
 would be developed for filling up the technology gaps.
19.        The Committee notes the initiative taken  by the Department of Electronics  in 1998-99 in organising an
 exhibition-cum-seminar for the products and technologies developed under the umbrella of DOE and the interest
 evinced by the industry/users in the exhibition.  The Committee would like the Department to continue such exhibitions 
 from time to time in the overall interests of the consumers  as well as to promote trade.
INDUSTRIAL ELECTRONICS PROMOTION PROGRAMME
20.        The Industrial Electronics Promotion Programme (IEPP) was launched by the Department to promote system
 engineering culture in the country through training, project development and introduction of new technologies.  It also aims at
 introduction of microprocessor application in industrial and service sector of economy, such as, Steel, Fertilizer, Cement,
 Power, Jute, Textile, Pulp and Paper and Food Processing Industry for modernisation and technology advancement.
21.        The financial allocation for the Industrial Electronics Promotion Programme was Rs. 3.90 crores in BE of 1998-99,
 which was raised to Rs. 4.71 crores in the RE of the same year but has been reduced to Rs. 2.90 crores in the current year.    
22.        Asked about the reasons for variations in the financial allocation for the programme  the Committee  was informed that
 the  Programme, during the  current financial year  will  concentrate in the area of Plant Wide-Networking, Total Plant
 Solutions - System Engineering, Integration and Services and IT Solutions for the Process Control Sector.  As regards  the
 specific projects envisaged in the above focussed areas the Department  will  endeavored to bring in supplementary financial
 contributions from users/manufacturers to be  tied up as development partners.  Accordingly they have sought reduced
 allocation  in the B.E. of 1999-2000 .
23.        The Committee notes the position.

SOFTWARE EXPORT PROMOTION PROGRAMME (SEPP)
 24.            Besides, the DOE is spending some amount on creation of basic facilities for development and export of software to
 data links and contribute towards achieving export targets both for software and hardware and for this purpose had to incur an
 expenditure of Rs.2.34 crores during the year 1997-98.
25.        It has been stated that the Software Exports have grown to Rs. 65.00 crores during 1997-98.  The future programme
 involves the following:
(1) Expansion of STPI infrastructure and setting up of new STPs at Pune, Mysore, Chennai, Guwahati.
            (2) Hold Software India Seminars and participate in COMDEX and CeBIT exhibitions.
            (3) Identification and launching of new R&D projects in Software.
            (4) Continue support for Y2K Programme.
26.        Asked about the reasons for reduced allocation for 1999-2000 for the said Programme, of  Rs. 5.00 crores as against Rs,
 7.00 crores allocated in the RE in the previous year  the Committee  was informed that a new scheme viz. IT Venture Capital
 orginally  conceptualised under Software Export Promotion Programme (SEPP) during 1998-99 has been budgeted out
 separately in 1999-2000 to give direct visibility.  For Y2K initiative of DOE, which was earlier supported under SEPP,
 additional funding may be necessary out of a Rs. 700 crore corpus fund being created for the purpose.
27.        The Committee is of the view that  the Department should continue its efforts to promote the integrated
 development and exports, it should at the same time push up development  and export of hardware also.
NATIONAL SOFTWARE CAPABILITY ENHANCEMENT PROGRAMME
28.            National Centre for Software Technology (NCST) Campus located at Navi Mumbai is R&D institution for excellence
 in software technology .  The centre has continued its major R&D activities and also expand its software education actitivites. 
 These activities are carried out through the fiveresearch and developmentdivisions of the centre namely (i) Computer Networks
 and Internet Engineering (ii) Data and Knowledge Engineering (iii) Graphics and Computer Aided Design (iv) Knowledge
 based computer System and (v) Software Engineering .  It has been stated that the Centre would be expanded during the Year
 1999-2000 by taking integrated view of excellence in research and higher end human resource development in three identified
 areas of technologies, namely, Networking and Internet, Visual computing and Intelligent Computing and also NCST,
 Bangalore would entail expansion to focus on similar lines on Software Engineering and Software Development.
29.        A mission on “Moving up the Value Chain in Software Development” is under formulation for initiation during the
 current year.
30.        NCST operates with a small number of staff members and  efforts are being made by the Department  to alleviate the
 staff shortage.  As soon as the staff shortage problem is alleviated, NCST would be able to consider expansion .   Besides, 
 NCST is seriously considering whether the on-line Distance education mode could be used for the PGDST Diploma Course to
 reach other cities.  NCST is also examining the possibilities of extending the PGDST Diploma to a few more important cities
 subject to availability of infrastructure support.
 
31.        The Committee had the occasion to visit the Centre in January, 1999 to see for itself the work being carried out
 by NCST.  The Committee appreciates the work being done by the Centre in the identified areas of technology, namely, 
 Networking and Internet, Visual  Computing and Intelligent Computing.
ELECTRONICS FOR RURAL /SOCIAL/AGRICULTURE/WATER SECTOR
32.        The primary objective of this programme is  to promote the  applications of electronics in the areas of agriculture, rural
 development, watershed development, etc. A large number of projects have been initiated during the last 2-3 years.  The
 Projects are usually executed by National Research Institutions, Agricultural Universities as well as NGOs.  The outputs from
 these projects are disseminated and popularised through a variety of means, for example, working models were displayed on the
 “Swarn Jayanti Express” run by the Railways to display the achievement of the country in the S&T Section during the 50 years
 of independence.  Likewise, outputs from a number of projects were displayed at the “ELITEX –99”, organised on 2
nd and 3rd
 February, 1999 by DOE.  The exhibits elicited a large amount of interest from the visitors and many have shown interest for
 technology transfer.  A good number of projects are also being implemented by NGOs.
33.        In the current year, an amount of Rs. 2.00 crores has been  allocated.  The same amount was allocated  in the BE of 
 1998-99, which was reduced to   Rs. 1.00 crore at  the RE stage  whereas during the Year 1997-98 Department of Electronics
 spent Rs. 1.46 crores on this programme.  The Committee feels that dissemination of information is an important aspect.

 34.            Department of Electronics has initiated an Employment Generation Training Scheme for SCs, STs, Backward
 Regions and the North East.  The objective of the Scheme is to generate  employment opportunities for the educated
 unemployed youth by harnessing the potential of Electronics and Information Technology.  Under the Scheme, free courses are
 offered to SC, ST and OBC candidates.
35.        The Committee was informed the Department of Electronics has identified  certain computer hardware and software
 training courses as well as Electronics related repair and maintenance courses for the educated unemployed youth under its
 Employment Generation Training Scheme.   Efforts are beinginitiated to spread theEmployment Generation Training Scheme
 in deep regions of the North-East, and for this purpose North-eastern Universities have been directed to shortlist the names of
 the affiliated colleges which are conducting B.Sc (Computer Science) and B.Sc.(Electronics) courses.  These colleges would be
 conducting DoE –ACC ‘O’ and ‘A’ Level courses apart from Repair and Maintenance courses in the Electronics area.  Besides,
 a number of new institutions in the North-East have also been short-listed to conduct  training programmes under the DoE’s
 Scheme for Employment Generation.
36.            Department of Electronics is also initiating steps to start non-English language computer training programme in the
 Backward regions and Hindi Heartland States like Rajasthan, UP, Bihar, Orissa and Madhya Pradesh and a number of
 Government educational institutions apart from reputed NGO’s, which are working for the benefit of weaker sections of the
 Society would be included in the Scheme.
37.        The Committee notes with satisfaction the courses proposed to be  started for Physically Handicapped and
 Educated Unemployed women.  The Committee recommends that this programme should be continued with much more
 vigour for these and other deprived sections of the society.

38.        The Electronics Trade and Technology Development Corporation Ltd. (ET&T) was established in 1974 with twin
 objectives of import/export trade and technology development in the field of electronics .  Its initial thrust was to build up
 bilateral rupee trade with the then USSR and other East European countries and to serve as a nodal agency for inter-
governmental electronic trade agreements.  Keeping in view the globalisation of Indian economy and the ideological social and
 economic changes taken place in the East European countries, the company redefined its mission as follows:
            “To provide product and services in the field of electronics, telecommunication and information technology support to
 the end-user sectors with contemporary technology, material and training inputs”.                
39.        ET&T has also successfully completed three months’ full time computer course for 26 foreign students from 14
 developing countries under ITECH SCAAP programme sponsored by Ministry of External Affairs.  Under the aegis of
 Employment Generation Training Scheme of  ET&T started 7 different training programme for Scheduled Castes/Tribes
 candidates free of cost and the scheme is being funded by the Department of Electronics.
40.          ET&T is also conducting various training programmes under “Computer Literacy and Studies in School” (CLASS) at
 more than 200  schools in the States of Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala and schools of Kendriya Vidyalaya
 Sangthan at various locations.
41.        ET&T entered the field of Computer Education & Training during the Year 1994-95 by setting up a modern centre and
 is offering courses in hardware and software.  During early 1996, a new dimension was given to the programme by introducing
 the concept of countrywide setting up of “Licencee Training Centres’.  Currently, the computer education and training activities
 of the Company comprises of:
*            Own Training Centres
*            Country-wide licencee training centres
*          Implementation of Government schemes like CLASS, employment generation schemes, development of North-
East Region etc.
42.        As on 31st March, 1999 , ET&T is having 150  training centres  spread throughout the country.  Currently the computer
 education and training programmes of ET&T are aimed at providing skills in the field of computerisation at the induction level
 and the manpower trained under various programmes are capable of undertaking employment .  ET&T has a Placement Cell for
 providing with the information regarding the employment opportunities, guidance for suitable placement, etc.

45.        In order to promote use and proliferation of Information Technology the Department has initiated a national focus on

 acquiring new skills, etc.

 aimed at facilitating greater use of IT as an enabling tool:-

(2)            Formulation of comprehensive policy of Electronic Governance (EG);

 processes of electronic delivery of public services; and
(6)            Comprehensive synergic collaboration of concepts and implementation mechanisms/methodologies are being

49.        These efforts are expected to lay the ground work for sustained appropriate and workable models of Electronic
 Governance.  Efforts are also being made  to coordinate initiatives taken by other committees like the High Powered Committee

 the National Task Force on IT and Software Development.

 the Department should aim at full utilisation of the budgetary provisions.

 important programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the Demands for Grants of

Sixty-Eighth   Report on Demands for Grants (1999-2000)
of the Department of Space
 
            India’s Space Programme, since its inception in the early sixties, has been guided by a vision which laid emphasis on the
 application of space technology for finding solution to the problems of man and society thereby establishing a viable & self
 reliant space programme.  From the very beginning, long-range plans have been drawn up to steer the programme effectively
 ensuring appropriate linkages among the application needs, satellite missions, launch vehicle capabilities and technology
 development.  Over the last three-and-half decades, significant progress has been made  in  space technology for building
 world-class satellites for communications and remote sensing; for launching the remote sensing satellites from India with
 indigenous launch vehicle; and providing the benefits of space technology to improve the quality of life at the grass root level,
 thus contributing to several areas of national development.
2.         In tune with the goal of self reliant use of space technology for national development, the thrust areas of the Indian
 Space Programme include:-
(a)        satellite  based communication for various applications.
(b)        satellite based remote sensing for resources survey, management and environmental monitoring;
(c)        meteorological applications; and
(d)        development and operationalisation of indigenous and launch vehicles for providing these space services.
3.         The Department of Space (DOS) is responsible for implementing the policies framed by the Space Commission.  The
 policies are carried out through the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the three Grant in aid institutions, viz. the
 National Remote Sensing Agency (NRSA), the Physical Research Laboratory (PRL) and the National Mesosphere-
Stratosphere-Troposphere Radar Facility (NMRF).
4.         The cumulative expenditure on space research till the end of Eighth Plan period i.e. from the inception in 1962-63 to
 1996-97, is Rs.7431.67 crore.  During the Eighth Plan, most of the programmatic targets and missions planned have been
 achieved. The total expenditure incurred is Rs.3928.53 crore (Plan Rs.3155.74 crore and Non-Plan Rs.772.79 crore). The major
 missions achieved are INSAT-2B, INSAT-2C, INSAT-2D, IRS-1E, IRS-P2, IRS-1C, IRS-P3, SROSS-C1 and SROSS-C2.
 Besides, considerable progress in the areas like development of indigenous cryogenic engine and stage for the GSLV
 programme, technological development for indigenisation of strategic and critical sub-systems & components and setting up of
 facilities for realisation of inertial systems and electro-optical systems have been achieved. 
5.         The Committee was informed that the Planning Commission has allocated a Plan outlay of Rs.6511.72 crore, against
 their earlier communication of Rs.7100.00 crore and the Non-Plan outlay of Rs.1200 crore for the Ninth Plan period. Thus, the
 total outlay for the Ninth Plan is Rs.7711.72 crore. However, the actual Plan budgetary allocation would be decided annually
 based on the programmatic requirements.
6.         The programme directions and the programmatic targets for the Ninth Plan have been formulated after extensive
 interactions and consultations with user Ministries. The major missions planned for the Ninth Plan to realise the programmatic
 targets have been indicated in Annexure-I. While the basic vision would continue to be the large scale application of space
 technology for finding solutions to the problems of man and society, the programme would respond effectively to the dynamic
 and complex problems of the coming years. The   major programmes planned include (i) operationalisation of Geosynchronous
 Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) towards achievement of self-reliance in launching communication satellites;  (ii) providing
 additional and newer operational communication satellite services to meet the increasing national needs;  (iii) building earth
 observation systems for wide range of applications related to land, water and ocean resources as well as atmospheric
 observations; (iv) establishing the GRAMSAT programme for integrating the potentials of satellite communication and remote
 sensing for rural development including the tele-education and tele-health; (v) establishing new communication services for
 Digital Audio and Data Broadcasting and Direct to Home TV services; (vi) establishing a viable system for Disaster
 Management through Earth observation, satellite-based communications, conventional survey information and local networks;
 (vii) research and development as well as technology development; and (viii) enhanced interface between Indian industry and
 academia to give boost to the national space effort.

INDIAN NATIONAL SATELLITE SYSTEM (INSAT)
13.        The  system (INSAT), which became operational with INSAT-1B, is a multi-agency, multi-purpose operational satellite
 system which provides domestic long distance telecommunications, meteorological earth observation and data relay, nation
 wide direct satellite TV broadcasting to augmented TV receivers, nation wide radio networking, TV programme distribution
 and re-broadcasting to terrestrial transmitters, etc. The system has enabled communication to and fro any part of India leading
 to training and awareness among rural masses on better agricultural practices, land and water resources management, family
 planning, health care and hygiene, disaster warning and rescue operations, etc.
13.1      The INSAT space segment, which is one of the largest domestic satellites in Asia, at present consists of five satellites
 namely NSAT-ID, INSAT-2A, INSAT-2B, INSAT-2C and INSAT-2DT acquired from ARABSAT Organisation, after INSAT-
2D became inoperable on October 4, 1997.
13.2      Secretary, Department of Space took the opportunity to inform the Committee that the indigenously designed,
 developed and tested INSAT-2E, was launched on 3
rd April, 1999 by the Ariane launch Vehicle of the European Space
 Agency. INSAT-2 is carrying 17 C-Band and lower extended C-Band transponders, a Very High Resolution Radiometer
 (VHRR), similar to that of INSAT-2A and INSAT-2B. It has an additional water vapour channel and a Charged Coupled
 Device (CCD) camera operating in visible, near infrared and short wave infrared bands with 1 km. resolution. Once INSAT-2E
 is operational it would beam television signals not only over India but also over other regions right from Australia on the

SATELLITE NAVIGATION
14.        Satellite navigation is a service  which is expected to become operational in many advanced countries like United
 States, Japan, Europe, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. The International Civil Aviation Organisation has made Satellite
 navigation equipment mandatory on all civilian aircraft. To upgrade the existing Communications Navigation and Surveillance
 (CNS) and Air-Traffic Management (ATM) system in India, the Airports authority of India (AAI) is planning to make them
 adaptable to the Future Air Navigation System (FANS) through the introduction of Indian Wide Area Differential GPS
 (WADGPS) system. Therefore, as a plan AAI would phase out the existing navigational aids and would increasingly depend on
 satellite navigation by the year 2010.
14.1      The Secretary, DOS, informed the Committee that the Department has prepared and sent a preliminary project report on
 satellite based navigation system to the Airports Authority of India (AAI). The AAI has sought certain technical clarifications 
 which are being studied by the Department. Accordingly, a revised proposal would be sent to AAI shortly. The national
 Steering Committee on communications, navigation and surveillance Air Traffic Management (CNS/ATM) is expected to
 review this proposal with the Department of Space for formalising the plan of action.
INDIAN REMOTE SENSING SATELLITE (IRS)
15.        The Indian Remote Sensing (IRS), started with the launching of IRS-1A in March 1988, is the mainstay of National
 Natural Resources Management System (NNRMS) providing continuously space-based data for the optimal utilisation of
 natural resources. At present the IRS system comprises IRS-1B, 1C, 1D and IRS-P3.
15.1      The  Department has undertaken initiatives in the use of IRS data in the country for drought monitoring and assessment,
 water resources management, forest, environment and the resources sector, geology and mineral prospecting, agriculture
 applications, integrated land and water resources management, wasteland mapping, rural and urban development and coastal
 and ocean-related applications.
15.2      The Remote Sensing applications are carried out under the broad umbrella of National Natural Management System
 (NNRMS). The nine NNRMS Standing Committees encompassing major natural resources and developmental areas like
 agriculture, bio-resources and environment, urban development, etc. periodically review the status of utilisation of remote
 sensing in their respective fields and provide guidance for promoting remote sensing based activities.
15.3      Currently the National (Natural) Resources Information System (NRIS) programme has been undertaken on a pilot scale
 in 30 districts spread over 17 states on 1:50,000 scale and in 4 states (Andhra Pradesh, Orissa, Maharastra and Gujarat) on
 1:250,000 scale with active participation from the concerned state governments. The progress made in these states/districts has
 been satisfactory and the systems would be operationalised in these districts and states in the current year.
15.4      The effective utilisation of IRS database on an operational basis is possible only when the states themselves establish
 appropriate mechanism to integrate the database with their developmental planning. In order to realise this objective, the

WATER RESOURCES MANAGEMENT
17.        The Committee was informed about the application of remote sensing data in finding out water resources and its use in
 providing water to villages. The National Drinking Water Mission and the remote sensing based maps and inputs were
 generated and used to locate ground water resources for drilling bore wells in villages.
17.1      As regards the ground water survey, the Committee was informed that recently that the Ministry of Water Resources
 had requested the Department of Space to undertake the second phase of the Rajiv Gandhi Drinking Water Mission. Under this
 mission 4.5 lakhs habitats in the country would be covered. In the first phase, it has been decided to undertake this programme
 in five states i.e. Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa and Maharashtra covering 1.5 lakhs habitats where the
 drinking water resources have to be identified.  At present,  the Department is engaged in developing the hydro-geo-
morphological maps for these 1.5 lakhs habitats. In Tamil Nadu  382 blocks have been identified by the Department with the
 help of this hydro-geo-morphological mapping. In the next three years  a total of 4.5 lakhs habitats are to be covered by the
 mapping.
18.        The Committee observes that amidst high exploitation and fast depleting  ground water table in the country is a
 matter of serious concern.  Therefore, there has to be a balance between the drawl of water from the surface and
 creation of water harvesting structures.  It is therefore necessary to pursue vigorously the project in Tamil Nadu for
 identifying sites for water harvesting structures.  If the exercise proves successful, the Committee would like the similar
 projects to be drawn up for other parts of the country.
WEATHER FORECASTING
19.        The Committee was informed that a vast array of space based meteorological data exists but what was lacking was
 accurate weather prediction system. Modelling in the tropical region is more complex than modeling in the temperate region
 due to complexities in atmospheric circulation for which it is difficult for us to predict even two or three days before. Therefore,
 accuracy in predicting weather conditions is an urgent need of the agricultural sector. Presently a small Committee has been
 constituted consisting of people from the DOS, DST and the India Meteorology Department (IMD). The Director-General of
 the IMD is the Chairman of the Committee to look into these specific issues relating to the weather forecasting.
19.1      In response to a query raised by the Members on the quality of weather forecasting on Doordarshan, the Committee was
 informed that the matter has been discussed with the Department of Science and Technology (DST),  Secretary, DST has
 formed a Committee with Director General, IMD as the Convenor and Members from DST, Doordarshan, DOS and Ministry of
 Information & Broadcasting to review and recommend innovative weather news on Doordarshan.  The Committee would
 specifically recommend measures to enhance the quality of Doordarshan weather news bulletins to international standards,
 suggest mechanism to monitor the news bulletin and ensure standards, recommend necessary software development, and
 maintain regularity of telecast.  Accordingly, necessary action would be initiated based on the recommendations of the
 Committee.        
19.2      The Committee expresses its concern over the lack of precision in  weather forecasts which have an adverse effect
 on agriculture. Besides, our inability to predict cyclones and other natural calamities plays havoc with human life. It is
 therefore necessary to improve our system of forecasting.

INTEGRATED MISSION FOR SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT (IMSD)
22.        Integrated Mission for Sustainable Development (IMSD), which was initiated in 1992, aimed at generating local
 specific action plans for sustainable development of natural resources.  Local specific prescriptions have been  generated using
 data from IRS satellites and collateral socio-economic data.  Presently IMSD covers specific problem areas selected from 175
 districts. Out of which 34 districts are covered in full and in other districts specific blocks or watersheds or parts of the districts
 are being covered, thus covering a geographical area of 84 million hectares.
22.1      Towards institutionalising the use of IMSD action plans in the watershed development planning process of the
 districts/states, 45 demonstrative model districts have been chosen where intense interactions at the state/district/watershed
 levels are going on. Efforts are also on to get appropriate modifications in the guidelines of Ministry of Rural Areas &
 Employment (MoRAE), Ministry of Agriculture (MoA) etc., through interaction with the user Ministries to institutionalise the
 use of IMSD action plan.
22.2      IMSD is mainly carried out in the problem districts of the country and the scope of IMSD would   be enlarged in a
 phased manner after detailed review of the progress made so far. In this regard, consultations with various states have already
 been initiated. Necessary technical details and strategies are being jointly worked out with active participation from the State
 Remote Sensing Centres (SRSC) of various States for taking up the Phase III of the project.
23         The Committee feels that the progress under the project is slow as only 34 districts out of 175 districts have been
 fully covered. The Committee observes that the work under the project needs to be pushed up so as to cover all the 175
 districts within the minimum span of time.
GEO-SYNCHRONOUS LAUNCH VEICHLE (GSLV) PROJECT

 GSLV employs a three stage configuration of which the third stage employs an imported cryogenic stage from M/s
 Glavkosmos, Russia. The first developmental flight of GSLV (GSLV-D1) is planned with the cryogenic engine and stage

 the total project cost has already been incurred. The project has already achieved substantial progress and the flight systems are
 getting ready. Realisation of CS2 and CS3 stages and solid motor stage, NGC, and TTC flight packages for GSLV-D2 are
 planned during the current year.
25         The Committee notes with satisfaction the extent of utilisation of funds under the project.

DISASTER MANAGEMENT
28.        Disaster Management System can be broadly classified into three phases, viz. (i) pre-disaster planning , consisting of
 steps leading to disaster prevention, disaster mitigation, and disaster preparedness (ii) the response to the disaster comprising
 the disaster warning and the emergency relief aspects, and (iii) the recovery phase consisting of rehabilitation and
 reconstruction. Space-based disaster management system provides valuable inputs in all the three phases, when appropriately
 integrated with the conventional ground based system.
28.1      With a view to ensure quick dissemination of weather warnings of impending disaster from approaching cyclones,
 specially designed receivers i.e.  Cyclone  Warning Dissemination Systems have been installed in the cyclone-prone coastal
 areas to disseminate cyclone warning messages directly to the affected areas. At present 250 CWDS have been deployed in
 various coastal states of India. The India Meteorological Department has planned 100 more CWDS receivers for deployment in
 the Ninth Plan period.
EARTH QUAKE PREDICTION
29.        On prediction of earthquakes with precise information on location and time of incidence, the Secretary, DOS, informed
 that it is extremely difficult and currently there are no proven techniques in this regard.  Satellite remote sensing along with
 collateral data helps in identification and delineation of major structural/tectonically significant zones from the point of view of
 seismic risk.  Such information helps in locating major geo-engineering structures like dams as well as infrastructural facilities
 in relatively safer locations in quake prone regions.  With regard to the disasters per-se, ISRO/DOS, has routinely been
 monitoring all major flood events as well as agricultural drought through INSAT and IRS satellites over the last one decade.

 exploitation. Besides, provision for technological consultancy and technology utilisation  have been promoted. So far, more

The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research which forms a part of the Ministry of Science and Technology
 comprises of activities of Departmental Schemes viz. Research and Development by Industry (RDI), Programme
 Aimed at Technological Self Reliance (PASTER), Scheme to Enhance the Efficacy of Transfer of Technology
 (SEETOT), National Information System for Science and Technology (NISSAT) and management of the public sector
 undertaking, National Research Development Corporation (NRDC) and Central Electronics Limited (CEL). The long
 term objective of the programme on Research by Industry and Technology Transfer is technological self-reliance and
 the short term objectives are promotion of R&D by Industry and enhancing efficacy of technology transfer, both
 domestic and foreign. Issues addressed in these programmes include identification of technological gaps, making
 investment in R&D by Industry attractive and productive, development and commercialisation of domestic
 technologies through. In – house R&D in industry and R&D by public funded laboratories coupled with industry. The
 Department also looks after matters concerning the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) which
 functions as a registered society and has a network of 40 laboratories and 81 field stations/extension centres/regional
 centres located all over the country that undertake R&D in various science and technology areas and disciplines.
2. The Secretary explained the achievements of the National Laboratories under the CSIR, in the fields of Aerospace,
 Biology and Biotechnology, Chemicals, Drugs and Pharmaceuticals, Earth resources and Natural hazards mitigation,
 Ecology and Environment, Food and Food Processing etc. which have tangible impact on the socio-economy sectors,
 during the Eighth Five Year Plan and informed about the new projects which the Department proposes to undertake
 during the year 1999-2000.
3. The Secretary also gave a brief presentation on the recent earthquake having an epicentre in the Chamoli region of
 Uttar Pradesh. The Committee enquired about the efforts made by the Department to arrest the damage and
 rehabilitation plans. The Committee specifically wanted to know whether any lead has been made for scientifically
 predicting earthquake. The Committee was informed that within CSIR a National Geophysical research Institute,
 Hyderabad and Central building Research Institute, Roorke are working for minimising the damage after an earthquake.
 As regards, predicting earthquakes, it was stated that as of today, there is no scientifically accepted method available to
 predict earthquakes accurately enough to be of help in saving human lives as there are no well established precursors
 which precede earthquake. A member pointed out that such an event in China was once preceded by strange behaviour
 of animals which led an elder to forecast that an earthquake was about to come and city was got vacated which helped
 minimise the damage. However, it is possible today to broadly work out the earthquake hazard in terms of accelerations
 that may occur at a given region based on the previous earthquake records. Then, on the basis of local geology and
 several other factors, it is possible to carry out mico zoning which indicates the kind of acceleration that would be
 expected in areas at a scale of a few hectares to a few square kilometres. Thereafter retrofitting of vulnerable structures
 can be done to save non engineered structures.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Committee~ on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised by
 the Committee to present the report on its behalf, present this Seventh Report of the Committee. This Report deals with
 issues contained in the Annual Report of the Department of Ocean Development for the year 1992-93.
2. The Committee held in all four meetings on the 10th, 11th, 28th January and 15th March, 1994 (Appendix). In the
 meeting held on the 10th January, 1994, the representatives of the Department of Ocean Development gave an
 overview of various programmes and activities being undertaken by the Department. On 11th and 28th January, 1994
 the Committee discussed in detail the activities of the Department and Members sought clarifications thereon from the
 representatives of the Department.
3. The Committee expresses its appreciation for. the officials of the Department for their cooperation and making
 available the material whenever required by the Committee.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the report at its meeting held on the 15th March, 1994.
 
 
NEW DELHI;
March 15, 1994
SYED SIBTEY RAZI
 Chairman,
Committee on Science and Technology, Environment
 and Forests
 
REPORT
General Background
The Oceans, the world over, provide not only a chief means of trade transportation and Naval activity, but also have vast
 resources within and underneath them which provide considerable scope for tapping· their potential for wealth of
 nations and of human society. In India, however, until the 1960s, the Ocean was not the focus of attention in a major
 way; and Oceanographic research was confined to just a few programmes of the institutions and universities. There was
 the national institute of Oceanography in Goa of CSIR and India metrological Department through the Inte Indian
 Ocean Expedition apart from the interests of the Indian Navy and the regular activities of the Ministry of Shipping and
 Transport. It was only with the adoption of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (1982) following the Third
 United Nations conference on the Law of the Sea that many developing countries including India got the necessary
 impetus to create new infrastructure and institutions for harnessing the resources of the Oceans. The convention also
 provided a comprehensive framework for the regulation of Ocean spaces. A new dimension to the ocean related
 activities was added by the enactment of the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and other
 Part time Zones Act by Parliament in, 1976 and establishment of a 200 mile Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) in
 January, 1977. An Ocean Science and Technology Agency was set up under the chairmanship of the Prime Minister
 which was serviced by the Department of Science and Technology. The creation of the Department of Ocean
 Development’s in January, 1981 first as part of the Cabinet Secretariat directly under the charge of the Prime Minister
 and later in March, 1982 as a separate Department with a Minister of State was in recognition of the need to give
 necessary fillip to the development of oceans within the territorial jurisdiction of the country and to tap their vast
 mineral wealth. Therefore, as a natural corollary an Ocean Policy was enunciated in November, 1982 by the
 Government and duly approved by both the Houses of Parliament. The highlights of this policy are as follows:-
- Need to map living resources, prepare an inventory of commercially exploitable faune and to map and assess the
 availability of mineral resources from the deep sea.
- Optimum utilisation of living resources and seaweeds, exploitation of non-living resources such as hydrocarban and
 heavy placer deposits, harnessing of renewable resources of ocean energy from waves, temperature difference in water
 column.
- Technological advances geared to the utilisation and preservation of the marine environment.
- Research and development in basic ocean sciences.
, - Development of indigenous technology and setting up of infrastructure facilities and services to operate large sized
 fishing vessels.
- Development of technologies relating to instrumentation diving systems, position fixing, materials development,
 oceanic data collecting devices, submersibles etc.

- Establishment of a centralised data system with appropriate mechanism for collection,
collation and dissemination of ocean related information both from indigenous and foreign sources.
- Training of skilled manpower and creation of self-reliant technological base.
- Establishment of an integrated legal framework and commitment for its enforcement.

Programme of the Department
2. The major programmes of the Department include Scientific research in Antarctica, Deep seabed exploration,
 development of technology for extraction of metals from nodules and development of seabed mining system, surveys
 for assessment of living and non-living resources, coastal zone and islands, marine instrumentation and systems;
 promotion of basic research; development of specialised manpower, infrastructure support; operation of research
 vessels; National Ocean information System; policy and law relating to ocean and Antarctica. For this a budget estimate
 of Rs. 56.4 crores (Rs. 43 crores under plan and 13.4 under non-plan) as against Rs. 48.17 crores (Rs. 39 crores under
 plan and 9.17 under non-plan) for 1992-93 has been approved for the Department for the year 1993-94.
3. The important objective of the Department is to function as a nodal department for organising, co-ordinating and
 promoting ocean developmental activities in the country and to promote institutional capabilities in areas where
 significant work is lacking. The department has been given specific responsibilities in relation to (i) Antarctic Research
 Programme to demonstrate India's scientific potential and capabilities and (ii) development of deep seabed mining for
 polymetallic nodules. Going by the budgetary allocation for the Department, it would appear that the Department is
 very small, with just a complement of 209 out of which the component of technical and scientific personnel is just 50
 but the activities and programmes undertaken by it in conjunction with other concerned agencies belief that
 supposition.
4. India has been allotted a mine site of 1,50,000 sq. kms. in the Central Indian Ocean under the new Ocean regime and
 has been accorded a pioneer status in deep seabed exploration. Development of technologies for generation of
 electricity from sea waves, application of remote sensing for identification of potential fishery zones, monitoring of
 marine pollution are some of the activities taken up by the Department recently.
5. The Department of Ocean Development in association with twelve national institutions has designed a National
 Ocean Information System (NOIS). Under this programme data on various ocean related parameters generated by the
 national institutions, universities and other R&D institutions is centralised, stored and disseminated to various users.
 The data centres established at India Meteorological Department, Pune; National Institute of Oceanography, Goa;
 Central Drug Research Institute, Lucknow; and Geological Survey of India, Calcutta have become operational.
6. A marine pollution Information System within the Department for maintaining information on pollution levels at 70
 locations along the coastline of the country is being developed. The past data on oil spills along the Indian Coast will be
 integrated with this system.
7. A National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT) has been set up in Madras as an autonomous body under the
 Department of Ocean Development. The objective of the institution will be to develop indigenous technologies in the
 ocean sector.
8. In order to assess whether the Department of Ocean Development is fulfilling its mandate effectively, the Committee
 decided to study various aspects of the working of the Department on the basis of its Annual Report for the year 1992-
93, particularly with reference to some of the programmes undertaken by it.
9. The Committee was apprised for the various activities of the Department, its thrust areas etc., by the Secretary and
 other officials of the Department as also those of other agencies/ bodies/institutes in conjunction with whom the
 Department co-ordinates its activities.
Antarctic Research Programme
10. Ever since the creation of the Department of Ocean Development in the year 1981 the Antarctic Research
 programme. has been a focus of attention and annual scientific research expeditions to Antarctica are being launched by
 India, 13 expeditions have uptil now been undertaken and scientists have carried out experiments and research in areas
 as diverse as Geology, Geophysics, Meteorology, Atmospheric Sciences, Geomagnetism, Biology oceanogra ­phy,
 Glaciology and Physiology. The permanent year round station at Maitri and supply base at Dakshin Gangotri constitute
 the requisite infrastructure for carrying out the scientific research in Antarctica which provides a pristine laboratory of
 world-wide significance for researchers to detect and monitor global environmental phenomena such as the depletion of
 atmospheric ozone, global warming and sea level changes. The region offers unique opportunities to study the
 specialised adaptations of organisms with their environment and biological researches provide date essential for
 decision making about marine living resources. Work on Human biology and medicine provides information on the

11. The Committee was informed that India is one of signatories to the protocol on Environment Protection and has
 agreed to phase out the use of CFC gases which are aggravating the ozone depletion problem. The scientists have
 conducted some experiments· called laser heteredyne which are first of their kind in the whole world. This technique
 provides the profile of ozone depletion every five minutes and helps to find out where the depletion is maximum or
 minimum. It also reveals as to how the ozone is being sucked from lower altitudes into the Antarctic region. The
 Committee was informed that the scientists were able to find out that the ozone depletion problem is not very serious in
 the case of India. In response to a query from the Committee as to whether it was possible for the CFCs emitted by the
 advanced countries to produce ozone holes over the Third world countries, it was explained that the ability of the CFCs
 to deplete ozone is enhanced only in the presence of Polar Stratospheric clouds (PSCs) when the temperature goes
 below -85°C and with the present knowledge available with the Department, there is little probability that CFC will be
 able to deplete the ozone zone over our country. However, the slight doubt that exists is that if the ozone is being
 destroyed over Antarctica year after year, then slowly the ozone from other latitudes could be sucked into the hole. The
 present knowledge in any case is not enough to forecast the consequences. Further elaborating on the submission that
 the ozone depletion problem is not very serious in India, it was explained that the laboratory experiments have shown
 that the necessary condition for this ozone destruction by CFCs is a temperature approximately minus 90°C which is
 not produced in the stratosphere at any place except Antarctica and not over Arctic. That is our safety factor. On being
 pointedly asked by the Committee about the extent to which the country stood to gain from the Oceanographic 'research
 in Antarctica, the Secretary of the Department explained that the foremost thing that necessitated India's sending
 expeditions to Antarctica on a continuing basis was India's consultative status and that can be retained only because of
 India's continuous endeavour in that direction. Coming to the net gains of Antarctic research, he said that the effect of
 environment on physiology is part of the information that the scientists gained and the responses of individuals are
 monitored by the expert group of doctors sent every time on the expeditions as part of the team. The Committee was
 further apprised that through the expeditions scientists have gained experience in atmospheric research, though the
 economic gain from the research is very difficult to estimate because of the fact that mining in Antarctica has been
 banned for 50 years under the Antarctica Treaty System. He further added that in the event this ban is lifted, the
 scientists of the country should be able to exploit the resources as Antarctica which is supposed to be a repository of
 minerals such .as gas and oil. This would, according to him, be a long term gain. The other aspect touched upon by the
 Secretary related to the exploitation of seabed in Antarctica which still remained to be attempted. In this context, be
 explained that krill - a kind of fish - available in Antarctica had great potential, keeping in' view its high protein
 content, three countries namely Japan, Russia and Poland' had exploited in some measure this potential. As Krill has to
 be immediately processed on being taken out of the Antarctica sea, it calls for not only the vessels to go there, but also
 onboard processing equipment which entails substantial investment and this is one of the initiatives· that the
 Department now wishes to embark upon. To undertake this ambitious programme a multi-purpose vessel would be
 required which should be able to carry out oceanographic research during the time it is anchored in the country's port
 and not required in Antarctica. In this context, the Committee was apprised that an export Committee to draw the
 specifications of 'the proposed vessel and to go through the tendering had been set up and the estimated cost of the
 'Vessel was between Rs: 70 to Rs. 80 crores) On being asked as to how' the Department proposed to arrange necessary
 funds for making the purchase of the multi-purpose vessel, the Secretary replied that the Department was fully
 concerned that the investment should yield adequate results; and with that in view that Department would make a
 strong case for purchasing the multi-purpose vessel. He conceded that funding would, of course, be a problem. Further
 elaborating upon the benefits derived in consequence of the on-going Antarctic research, the Secretary stated that
 another area which bears some technical connection is the polar structure built by the Defence R&D engineers, Pune
 which is in fact a defence laboratory and also a communication system. The Department in co-ordination with other
 agencies/departments, could also use the expeditions for various projects. The engineers from the defence side had gone
 to Antarctica to do cold research work and are finally able to develop a cold research system which could otherwise not
 be developed in the Siachen where the armed forces of the country are face to face with the enemy and have to fight
 them.
12. A point was raised about the latest information gathered by the scientists in the course of their expeditions to
 Antarctica about global warming as a result of the greenhouse effect and whether there was any threat to the human
 population on this planet. It was explained that Antarctica was the most suitable region for studying the greenhouse
 effect and almost all the existing models show that even 0: 1 degree rise in temperature at the equator will be reflected
 as almost 0.5 degree rise in temperature in Antarctica. In other words, the increase in temperature gets amplified as one
 goes to higher latitudes. What the scientists are doing is to monitor the greenhouse gases such as CO , CH  and N 0

Deep Seabed Polymetallic Nodules Programme Exploration and Extraction of metals
14. India as a registered pioneer investor has been allotted an area of 1,50,000 sq. kms. (mine site) in the Central India
 Ocean basin for exclusive exploration and development. An action plan has been drawn up by the Department for the
 implementation of deep seabed polymetallic nodules programme which covers three main thrust areas, Le., survey and
 exploration, development of mining and extractive metallurgy.
15. The Committee was apprised that the allocation of the mine site of 1,50,000 sq. kms. is on the condition that,50% of
 this site will have to be surrendered. The allocation of 1,50,000 sq. kms. site has been made so that the Department is
 able to conduct a survey of the seabed and find out as to which part is most suitable for exploration activities. The
 survey is a highly technical activity by which it has to be found out as to which regions are most inaccessible on

 available they may be of a low quality. The survey has nevertheless been conducted by the National Institute of
 Oceanography (NIO) and in the first phase the Department will be surrendering 20% of the mine site having regard to
 the fact that 50% of the mine site has to be surrendered over a period of time.
16. The nodules from deep seabed are potentially rich sources of metals like copper, nickel, cobalt and manganese. The
 potential of these metals as conveyed to the Committee is of the order of 73 million tonnes in respect of manganese, 3
 million tonnes each in respect of nickel· and copper and 0.5 million tonnes in respect of cobalt. In other words it is of
 enormous proportions. Both nickel and cobalt are useful in high technology applications for aero-engines. 70,000
 tonnes of copper is imported every year in the country. Therefore, realising the intrinsic value of these metals and their
 commercial viability, it is very important to have the technology for extraction of these metals from nodules. But the
 country, however, has not yet developed the technology for taking the nodules out from the seabed as a result of which
 exploiting the potential of these metals appears to be a distant dream for the present.
17. The Committee was, however, apprised that the Department has taken some initiative in this respect in that with a
 view to focus on potentially successful process routes, it has made an analysis of something like 15 routes out of which
 three were ,chosen and two of them have been \ pursued vigorously. Two laboratories, namely, National Metallurgical
 Laboratory, Jam­shedpur and the Regional Research Laboratory, Bhubaneshwar are assessing the potential of these
 two routes. The Department has conceded that taking the nodules out of the seabed involves deep sea mining
 technology which is a rather difficult technology and while making efforts to achieve and perfect that technology, its
 commercial viability has also to be kept in view.
18. The Committee was also informed that the Department has decided in Phase-II of the mining technology programme
 to reorient the programme so as to deal with placer deposits which are at a depth of 200 to 300 metres. The Department
 is concentrating on developing under water technologies, with greater emphasis on remotely operated vehicle system to
 handle different situations. The Department as at present is involved in ocean mining technologies, but it is still far
 from the ocean bed. A Committee to evaluate the proven resources of placer deposits in the near shore and EEZ area
 was appointed which has submitted its report, and the Department is in the process of examining the recommendations
 contained therein. The Committee was told that it is very difficult to enter into joint programmes/ventures with other
