 countries for 0cean bed technologies as the area was totally considered to be a classified one.
19. The Committee feels that the Polymetallic Nodules programme of the Department lacks direction and perspective as
 no concrete results seem to have been achieved and the acquisition of deep sea bed mining technology still appears to
 be a non starter. The Committee would like the Department to seriously examine the feasibility of involving private
 sector in this programme so that not only the private sector people but also the country as a whole gains from the
 exploitation ,of the vast sea resources. The potential for extraction of metals  from the nodules dug out of the seabed
 could be very great and if the deep seabed mining technology is developed on a commercially viable scale, the gains for
 the country will be enormous. The Committee hopes that the Department would attach due importance to the
 recommendations of the Gopalakrishna and B.K. Rao Committees and take expeditious action towards reorientation of
 the mining prog­rammes.
Exploration and Assessment of living and non-living resources
20. India has abundant natural resources in its oceans with an Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) of .02 million sq. kms.
 The potential of living as well as non-living resources in the vast coastline of the country an be exploited suitably if
 there is systematic exploration and fair assessment on the basis of correct data.
21. The Committee was apprised that the brackish water area is something like 9,00,000 hectares out of which only
 about 60,000 hectares is under culture. Among the living resources, we have fish potential to the tune of 2.2 million
 tonnes, but that has been only exploited marginally, the reason being that the bulk of our exploitation is just in zero to
 50 meter depth. Among the non­living resources are petroleum, potable water, polymetallic nodules and energy
 generation, the Department through two ocean going research vessels namely ORV Sagar Kanya and FORV Sagar
 Sampada has been engaged in scientific exploration since 1983-84; up till now 82 research cruises of Sagar Kanya and
 106 of Sagar Sampada have been devoted to extensive exploration. Both these research vessels have, however, become
 quite aged and the Department needs their replacement with state of the art multi-purpose vessels to pursue more
 vigorously its exploration objectives so that the vast ocean wealth is exploited to the fullest extent\ and tangible benefits
 accrue to the nation at large.
22. About 18% of our population i.e. 150 million people is living along the coast line. The Department has undertaken
 certain programmes to benefit this segment of the population. One of these programmes is to make available to the
 fishermen accurate satellite information for fish catch and this has proved to be quite successful. Co-related with this is
 another programme of the Department for development of technology for communication by the fishermen from the
 shore to the fishing vessels. Similarly, the Department is also focussing attention on Island develop­ment.
23. The Committee was told that, under the Marine Satellite Information Service Programme (MARSIS), the
 Department is trying to generate data relating to sea surface temperatures and other necessary information relating to
 potential fishing zones and coral reef maps using remote sensing satellite. When the programme was started the
 emphasis was on direct contact with the users of this information, namely fisher community and providing them
 requisite information relating to potential fishing zones, the reason being that the fishermen could not usefully use the
 information in terms of temperature gradient and sea surface temperatures. Now, there have been established 60
 centres, and information is communicated to the fishermen by Fax-first the information is given to the fishermen's
 cooperatives and then to the fishermen. To facilitate grasping of the information by the fishermen and putting that to
 optimum use, the information is given in terms of distance, depth and direction. Now, the fishermen are quite
 convinced that the satellite data is a valuable supplement to their already existing traditional knowledge in this sector,
 and the two way communication from the fishing vessels to the shore and vice-versa has made their task easier. The
 Committee was informed that the programme aims at providing 1000 walkie talkie sets in four States namely Andhra
 Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka in Phase-I; and after it is found that the programme has achieved its
 objectives and been quite successful, this will be extended to other States also. It will be up to -the State Governments
 to purchase and supply these sets to the fishermen. To a pointed question from the Committee as to what the
 Department is doing for imparting intensive training to the fishermen directly to exploit fish potential in still greater
 measure on the basis of the information made available by it to them, the reply of the Department was that its role was
 only limited to technology demonstration and much would depend upon the State Governments themselves. The
 Department on its part has been quite successful in developing technology for locating potential fishing zones on the
 basis of sea surface temperatures and this has to be perfected by adding the chlorophyll data. Once this package is
 ready, it can be given to the fishermen for effective use.
24. The Committee was informed that the third programme of the Department was related mainly to Andaman and
 Nicobar Islands and there was a break through in the field of aquaculture there because of acidic nature of the soil. The
 production level under this exercise has touched 2 tonnes per hectare, per crop. On being asked as to whether the
 Department was satisfied with the yield when some of the private companies in India had achieved 8 metric tonnes per

 hectare per year per crop, the reply was that it was just the beginning and the achievement was fairly good. It was
 explained to the Committee that in order to .achieve good results in aquaculture, PH value has to be between 7 and 8
 but in Andaman and Nicobar Islands PH value is low and the basic challenge is to raise the PH value. Nonetheless two
 commercially known species have been selected and the islanders can immediately adopt the technology and market
 their produce.
25. The Committee acknowledges the useful· work being done by the Department of Ocean Development in tapping the
 huge wealth lying within the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ)· of the country, particularly in the area of living
 resources. The technology for identification of potential fishing zones and the network of information and
 communication developed by it has definitely benefited the fisher community. But the Committee feels that the scope
 for exploiting the huge fish potential is still great and the Department must concentrate on developing under-water
 technologies so that the fish catch is extended beyond 50 meter depth. There is no denying the fact that India has a
 tremendously long coastline; and the fish potential, if exploited to the fullest extent, can yield valuable food as also
 foreign exchange. The Department would also be well advised to lay greater emphasis on the training of fishermen with
 a view to motivating them to use the latest technology and derive maximum benefits there from. The Committee is
 happy to note that the Department has through its sustained efforts made a break through in aquaculture in the
 Andaman and Nicobar Islands but there is still greater need to identify more areas for application of this technique and
 to evolve techniques/methods to maximise yield. Export potential should be given greater attention.
Ocean Energy Programme
26. Energy from the sea waves is one of the promising sources of renewable energy. The estimated potential for India is
 about 40,000 MW for the 6000 kms coastline. However, this energy is thinly distributed and as the system has to be
 designed for extreme waves, it is expensive. The Department of Ocean Development has, therefore, thought of a multi-
functional system which is likely to be more viable. It would be a barrier type wave energy system built at some
 distance from the coast which could generate renewable power, create a harbour between barrier and shore, and protect
 the coast against sea erosion. The Wave Energy Project· group at the Indian Institute of Technology, Madras started a
 research programme on wave energy in 1982. Based on the design data developed in the laboratories, a demonstration
 plant of 150 KW capacity for conversion of wave energy into electrical energy has been built at Vizhinjam near
 Trivandrum. It was commissioned in October 1991. This is the first off shore power plant of its kind in the world. It is
 functioning well and has been declared as a national facility for Wave Energy and other Wave Application studies.
27. On the basis of experience gained from wave power plant at Vizhinjam, two new projects relating to construction of
 breakwater integrated Wave Energy system at Thangerssery in Kerala and Mus point in Car Nicobar have been taken
 up by the Department. At Thangerssery the breakwater is under construction. Part of the breakwater is built; and by the
 time the system is installed, it will be an improved version of the system on the basis of the experience gained at
 Vizhinjam and it can also demonstrate its utility as part of the integrated breakwater. At Mus Point in Car Nicobar
 Islands there is a proposal to build a harbour and the project is in advanced stage of acceptance by the Government.
 There also the Department is going to demonstrate Wave Energy Programme, as no other source of power is available
 there. An expert group to work out the technical and financial aspect at Mus Point has been constituted by the Planning
 Commission.
28. The Committee was apprised that there are basically three ways of getting energy from the seas, namely, from the
 waves, from the tides and from the use of temperature gradients. The Secretary of the Department provided to the
 Committee a comprehensive statement of all these three technologies and their perspective potential in the country. As
 regards wave energy the anticipated potential is about 5 KW to 15 KW per metre of coastline; the south west coast and
 Andaman and Nicobar Islands are potential areas. Total estimated theoretical potential is 40,000 MW. As pointed out
 earlier, an experimental plant has been set up at Vizhinjam near Trivandrum in Kerala where technology for generation
 of electricity from sea waves is demonstrated. Further work to achieve stabilised output of power and integration of the
 system with the breakwaters of fishery or commercial harbours is in progress. Britain, Norway, Portugal and Japan are
 also carrying on research but no commercial plant has been established so far. In so far as Ocean Thermal Energy
 Conversion (OTEC) prospects are concerned, theoretically estimated OTEC potential in India is about 40,000 MW.
 Preliminary studies have shown that real sites for establishment of shore based OTEC plants are available at Kavaratti
 and Minicoy islands in Lakshadweep, Nicobar group of islands and for off-shore based plant of Tamilnadu. The
 Government of Tamilnadu in consultation with Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources has in January 1994
 signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Sea Solar Power, USA for designing, construction and operation of a
 100 MW OTEC plant at about 40-50 Kms. off Kulasekarapatnam, if the site is proved to be feasible. As per the MOU,
 the US company will construct the plant in the form of a vessel or floating platform and transmit the power to the shore
 through sub-marine cable at its own cost. The project will cost about US dollars 250 Million (approx. Rs. 800 crores) to

 the US company. It will sell the power to Government of TamilNadu at an agreed cost of US dollars 0.069 per Kilo
 Volt Ampere (Approx. Rs. 2.20) and the" payment has to be made in US dollars. The plant is expected to be operational
 for 20 years.
29. As regards tidal energy, Gulf of Kutch and Gulf of Cambay on the West Coast are considered of high potential; and
 the estimated tidal power potential in the Gulf of Cambay is stated to be about 7300 MW and Kutch about 1000 MW. A
 proposal to establish a 900 MW plant at Gulf of Kutch prepared by Central Electricity Authority through the Ministry
 of Non Conventional Energy Sources is under revision by MNES through National Hydro Electric Power Corporation.
 Canada, France, China, Russia, U.K. etc. have set up tidal experimental plants.
30. The Department of Ocean Development has, however, made modest beginning only in the wave energy sector and
 plant at Vizhinjam has been conceived as a project to' demonstrate the potential of generation of electricity from sea
 waves. It is a totally indigenous effort and several institutions have been involved in this project. The power, module,
 that is, the turbine generator system of the wave plant is proposed to be modified so that it can run continuously for a
 long period of time. The project engineers will make one more turbine generator system on the basis of the data
 generated and will test it thoroughly and completely before going in for a bigger system of 1.5 MW. It was admitted by
 a representative of the Department that power from the waves is not constant as from wave to wave there is a change in
 power. But there are many other spin offs of this project, an important off shoot of which is to build big caissons for
 storing iron ore and exploring the iron ore off the Goa Coast. In other words, wave energy is not going to contribute
 much for the energy scene of India though a potential of 40,000 MW is quoted; and if power in megawatts is to be
 derived from the ocean, it has to be technologically made feasible. The Department has admitted that what they have
 attempted at Trivandrum coast is a maximum power of 150 KW and this has merely to be looked upon as an energy
 resource for local area management. The Department has obviously great constraints as waves do not provide enough
 scope for going in for generation of electricity in a big way. The Department's efforts in examining the prospects of
 generating it with the combination of wind and wave energy in far off places like Nicobar Islands where there are no
 other sources of energy, are quite laudatory. As submitted by the Department, the potential for OTEC is great - as much
 as upto 40,000 MW but this is an area where the responsibility of the Department is somewhat restricted; as it is the
 Ministry of Non Conventional Energy Sources which would be looking after this aspect as well as the area of tidal
 wave energy. The Committee was told that even though OTEC area falls within the purview of the Ministry of Non-
Conventional Energy sources, it is the Indian Institute of Technology, Madras which carried out a survey in regard to
 the potential places where the OTEC plants could be located and the information provided by the Institute as a result of
 this survey has been utilised for the proposed setting up of a power plant in Tamil Nadu based on Ocean Thermal
 Power Technology.
31. The Committee has noted that the effort of the Department of Ocean Development in the field of wave energy is 11
 modest one and is still at an experimental stage. The economic viability of the project seems to be in doubt though
 multi-functional aspects of the projects which the Department has in view would definitely make the going very useful.
 As the potential from OTEC and tidal energy appears to be much more vis-a-vis wave or wind energy, the Department
 should in co-ordination with the Ministry of Non Conventional Energy Sources and other concerned agencies carry out
 detailed surveys and focus on dependable data so that energy requirements of the country could be substantially· met
 from these two vital sources.
32. The Committee is conscious of the fact that OTEC system has yet not been set up on a commercial basis anywhere
 in the world and similarly some of the countries are still busy setting up tidal energy plants, but the very fact that
 Government of Tamil Nadu as entered into an agreement with an American Company for setting up an OTEC Plant in
 the State should alert the Department about the viability of setting up OTEC Plants indigenously.
Coastal Ocean Monitoring & Prediction System (COMAPS)
33. Protection of Marine environment and preservation of the health of the waters is one of the important components of
 the activities of the Department of Ocean Development. Therefore, the Department has sponsored a nation-wide
 programme of marine pollution monitoring with a view to monitoring various marine pollutants in the seas around
 India. Under this programme, data on 25 pollution parameters, including the dissolved oxygen, concentration of heavy
 metals and pesticides like DDT, are being collected at 70 locations, along the coastline of the country through eleven
 centres. Forty hot spots have been identified in consultation with the concerned State Pollution Control Boards. The hot
 spots are areas having an alarming level of pollution parameters. The results obtained from various parameters
 collected reveal that the pollution problems are localised and mostly occur in the sea off metropolitan cities and thickly
 populated coastline areas. However, because of being diluted by sea water the pollutant level has not reached any
 alarming on a general basis stage. The areas found to be polluted have been identified in consultation with the State
 Pollution Control Boards. The Department does not monitor the areas which are beil1g monitored by the State Pollution

 Control Boards, and in respect of the areas which are monitored by it necessary data is passed on to the State Boards.
 There is a Steering Committee of the representatives from the various institutions headed by the Director, NEERI,
 Nagpur to continuously monitor and discuss pollution levels. The data collected under the COMAPS programme has
 been found to be useful in monitoring the level of pollutants along the coastal waters.
34. The Committee was apprised that the Department has paid particular attention to the accuracy and validity of the
 data as also the measurements and taken the initiative to set up a group at Trivandrum to do some monitoring to see
 how these measurements are to be made out. The Department is to ensure that people are trained, technology is
 upgraded which is reliable, and validated, so that the information that is passed on to the Pollution Boards acts as a
 reliable feed. The Department basically complements the work of the States; and once the information is provided to
 the State Pollution Control Boards, it become their responsibility to control the pollution. The Department on its part is
 trying to identify a Member in the Pollution Control Board with whom it can constantly interact. Besides, the
 Department is also very closely maintaining liaison, and constantly interacting with the Ministry of Environment and
 Forests for the reason that the implementation of various laws relating to environmental issues falls within the purview
 of that Ministry.
35. The Committee has come to the conclusion that the Department of Ocean Development's role is limited to just
 identifying pollution prone coastal areas and the level of existing pollutants.
The data and measurements which are prepared by the scientists. of the Department are just passed on to the State
 Pollution Control Boards and it appears that the matter ends with the issue being left to be tackled by the State Pollution
 Control Boards, who in fact are independent of each other. The Committee feels that though there is a Steering
 Committee to monitor pollution levels, but still the measures are not very effective particularly in respect of the steps
 taken by these Boards, to review and remove the causes of the pollution. What is, therefore, necessary is that the
 activities of these Boards in pollution control should be co-ordinated in an effective manner through a centralised
 system, where by the Department itself or the Central Pollution Control Board can play a pivotal role. There is greater
 need for coordinated action on this front to save the marine environment from increasing pollution. The Department has
 no doubt its constraints, particularly of availability of funds, and it appears to be handicapped in dealing with this issue
 as it does not even have requisite number of vessels for carrying out pollution monitoring surveys. The Committee was
 told that for this specific; purpose the Department would require about 4 vessels. Initially investment is proposed to be
 made in 2 vessels, the design work of which has been completed by the National Ship Design Research Centre,
 Visakhapatnam. The Committee would like to emphasise that protection of marine environment and health of sea
 waters is of paramount importance, and accordingly recommends to the Government that Department's endeavours on
 this account should not suffer for want of funds.
Bio-active Substances from Marine organisms
36. Drugs from the sea is a potentially important area for the country, and the Department of Ocean Development has
 embarked upon this multi-institutional programme involving as many as 10 universities. The nodal institute for this
 programme is, the Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI) Lucknow. 134 Marine organisms have up till been screened
 for biological activities, but no major breakthrough has been achieved, and a drug in the real sense is yet to be
 developed. In response to a query from the Committee as to whether ,there was some substance in newspaper reports
 that drugs for cancer could be obtained from the living organisms in the ocean bed, the Secretary of the Department
 informed the Committee that the components which had been identified are for controlling the viral fevers from AIDS.
 Amolifying this point the Director, CDRI, Lucknow stated that what has been observed is that there are four organisms
 which show anti-viral activities but have not tested against AIDS. They are, however, being tested against AIDS not in
 our country, but in a centre in USA with which the Institute is linked. The property would, however, remain with this
 country. What the scientists in this institute are doing is to collect the substances in large quantities and synthesise and
 test them for application for viral infections including AIDS. The other area is to develop compounds from animals or
 plants and test their efficacy in other area. The scientists have identified 4 or 5 organisms in the ocean with necessary
 activity and they are in the actual process of testing their efficacy. He explained that so far no marine organism has
 been identified for production of drugs on commercial basis; and it would take 10 or 12 years for a drug to develop, the
 reason being that out of 20 compounds which are clinically tested only one may become a drug. Touching upon the cost
 factor, it was explained that in the developed countries the expenditure for development of a drug was to the tune of
 200 million dollars (about Rs. 700 crores). On the contrary the picture in the developing countries was that
 development of just one drug cost
            between Rs. 18 to 20 crores.    I
37. The Committee feels that having drugs from the sea has immense potential and more sustained efforts should be
 made in tapping this potential by involving more universities and institutes. The Committee is happy to note that this

 area is seriously engaging the attention of the Department, and quite a substantial number of bio-active
 substances/marine organisms have been screened. The Department has agood track record of identification of such
 substances and with that expertise already available, it is hoped that development of drugs in near future on a

Infrastructure, Research Development and Specialised Manpower etc.
38. Infrastructural support forms an essential pre-requisite for ocean development activities and for providing a
 comprehensive and reliable information system through a network of data centres on marine resources and their
 environment. As pointed out earlier, the two vessels namely ORV Sagar Kanya and FORV Sagar Sampada form the
 core of this infrastructural support for carrying out research and exploration in the country's vast coastline; they have
 done quite useful work. But they seem to have outlived their live and need immediate replacement by multi-purpose
 state-of-the-art vessels. The Department of Ocean Development is seized of the matter. Though it is handicapped by
 funds, it proposes to go in for such type of vessels in a phased manner. There is no doubt that the vast potential of ocean
 wealth within EEZ of our country still remains untapped, and there is need for concerted action on this front which
 cannot materialise unless the infrastructural support is fully geared up to meet this challenge. There are certain institutes
 set up by the Department which are doing pioneering work in the field of ocean research and manpower development.
 In this context, mention may be made of the National Institute of Oceanography (NIO) Goa and the National Institute
 of Ocean Technology (NIOT) Madras. The National Institute of Oceanography is a CSIR laboratory intended for
 surveys, development of technologies and basic sciences in marine science area particularly marine biology.
39. The National Institute of Ocean Technology has been registered as an autonomous body and it is intended to
 function as a nodal agency for the ocean development programme. The specific tasks assigned to NIOT are in the fields
 of wave energy, mining technology, development of marine instruments and evolving mathematical models to solve
 user oriented coastal engineering problems like coastal erosion, accretion etc. A point was raised about the approximate
 annual expenditure of NIOT, to which the Secretary replied that though the amount of Rs. 15 crores was for the entire
 plan for this institute, it had means to generate its own resources. A suggestion was made by the Committee as to
 whether it would not be appropriate for the Department to have public funding of its various projects so that a lot of
 benefit could be derived by a large number of industrial houses and secondly would it not be advisable to give some
 representation to the Private Sector on the government body of the National Institute of Ocean Technology. The
 Secretary assured to look at this suggestion of the Committee constructively.
40. This apart, the Department is  working very closely with Indian Institute of Technology, Madras. This Institute has
 set up facilities which are unique in Asia like multi-directional wave basin which have cost between Rs. 30 to 40 crores.
 The Ocean Engineering Centre and Ocean Energy Centre are the other two premier bodies set up by lIT, Madras to
 cater to the requirements of research in Oceanographic fields and substantial amount of money has been invested in the
 Ocean Centre alone for the reason that the Department has got a collaborative programme with Germany.
41. The Committee has noted the existence of a number of Institutes in the country engaged in high quality R&D in
 ocean science and technology. The Department informed the Committee that it is making use of that 'expertise to the
 maximum possible extent.
42. In the course of detailed examination of the working of the Department of Ocean Development, a valid point was
 made by a Member of the Committee to the effect that since India has a vast coastal area, oceans have special
 importance for the country, but an area of this nature cannot be dealt with just by one Department. The exploitation of
 living and non-living resources, promotion of shipping, pollution free environment on the coast reduction of coastal
 erosion are just a few of many· issues which call for greater coordination among Departments engaged in one way or
 the other with ocean related activities. The Department of Ocean Development has a very small budget, a substantial
 part of which goes into areas which do not relate to production sectors~ The Secretary while conceding in his reply that
 with its present size and budget, the Department of Ocean Development is not in a position to co-ordinate ocean related
 activities with all the departments to the desired extent, pointed out that it certainly has information about what the
 other departments are doing. In this context, he pointed out that they have Ocean Science and Technology Board on
 which representatives are drawn from various Ministries. The Committee feels that in view of the special importance
 which the oceans have for us, the Department of Ocean Development in its present form is not geared up to meet the
 challenges of our times. nor for that matter, it is in a position to co-ordinate ocean related activities with other
 Ministries/Departments, some of which like the Ministry of Agriculture and Ministry of Surface Transport are even
 bigger than the Department of Ocean Development itself. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends to the
 Government to set up an Ocean Agency, under the chairmanship of the Prime Minister for effective co-ordination,
 monitoring and implementation of the ocean related activities.

PRESERVATION OF ENVIRONMENT & CONTROL OF POLLUTION
 
8.         The environment policy framework comprises of the National Forest Policy (1988), the Policy Statement for Abatement of
 Pollution (1992) and the National Conservation Strategy and Policy Statement on Environment & Development (1992).  The National
 Conservation Strategy provides for the integration of environmental considerations in the policies and programmes of different
 sectors.  It emphasises sustainable life styles and the proper management and conservation of resources.  The Pollution Abatement
 Policy stresses the prevention of pollution at source.  It encourages the development and application of the best available practical
 technical solutions.  The policy conforms to the “Polluter pays ” principle.  It underlines the protection of heavily polluted areas and
 river stretches.  The Forest Policy stresses the maintenance of environment through preservation and restoration of ecological
 balance.  The policy seeks to substantially increase the forest cover in the country through afforestation programmes.
9.         The statutory framework for the environment includes the Indian Forest Act, 1927, the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1982, the
 Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 and the Environment (Prevention) Act, 1986.  Other enactments include the
 Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, the National Tribunal Act, 1995 and the National Environment Appellate Authority Act, 1997. 
 Implementation is undertaken by various agencies of the Central and State Governments.
10.        On the question of steps taken to control the vehicular pollution, the Committee was informed that a national programme for
 control of vehicular pollution involves the following measures:-
 (i)        Progressive tightening of emission norms;
            (ii)        Improvement in fuel quality/introduction of cleaner fuels and
(iii)       traffic management, improvements in road network, public transport system and introduction of mass rapid transport
 system.
 
11.        The Government have drawn up a major programme for improvement in the quality of automotive fuels. Low-lead petrol had
 been introduced in the four metro cities of Delhi, Mumbai, Calcutta and Chennai with effect from June 1994.  Unleaded petrol was
 introduced in the four metro-cities from 1
st April, 1995.  Since 1 st  September, 1998 only unleaded petrol is available in the city of
 Delhi.  This has resulted in reduction of about 60% in the ambient levels of lead in Delhi.  Low sulphur diesel was introduced in Agra 
 Since 1st  September, 1996 and in Delhi from 15th August, 1997.
12.        In accordance with a notification issued on 31 st December, 1998, premixed oils are being supplied in the retail fuel outlets in
 Delhi to prevent the sale of low quality oils.  Specifications of 2 stroke engine oil has been notified which is effective from 1 st April,
 1999, with a view to reducing levels of pollution from 2 stroke engine vehicles.  Cleaner automobile fuels such as CNG have also
 been introduced in Delhi and Mumbai.  Unleaded petrol (ULP) has also been introduced in the capitals of all States, UTs and major 
 towns since 1 st June, 1998.  It is planned to make ULP available throughout the country by 31 st March, 2000.  Low sulphur diesel
 (0.25%) will be supplied in other parts of the country progressively.
13.        An inter-sectoral committee has been constituted during 1997 to finalise more stringent emission norms effective from 1 st
 April, 2005 for vehicles at the manufacturing stage.  The said  committee will finalise (i) the emission norms for all categories of
 vehicles at the manufacturing stage, (ii) the fuel quality specifications of automotive commercial fuels required, (iii) the reference fuel
 quality specifications at the test stage and (iv) inspection and maintenance programme required for the effective operation and
 maintenance of the vehicles, meeting such norms, in the in-use stage.
14.        In some urban areas, system of synchronized signals and traffic management has been introduced.  Awareness campaigns have
 been launched to educate the public about the statutory punitive provisions related to vehicular pollution, health hazards and
 maintenance measures for the control of pollution from vehicles.  Service stations and workshops have been authorised for pollution
 checking/tuning of polluting  vehicles and issuance of “Pollution Under Control” certificates. Pollution checking facilities are being
 enhanced.
15.        The Committee was also informed that vehicular pollution is an inter-ministerial issue. The Ministries involved are -- Ministry
 of Petroleum & Natural Gas, Ministry of Surface Transport, Ministry of Urban Development, Ministry of Industry, Ministry of

16.        The Committee was informed that the quality of fuel being produced  in  the refineries  generally meets specifications
 prescribed by the Ministry of Environment & Forests under the Environment (Protection) Act,1986 and the specifications  laid down
 by the Bureau of Indian Standards. BIS standards are formulated by experts which include representatives of oil companies, expert
 organisations like the Indian Institute of Petroleum and vehicle manufacturers. These standards are constantly upgraded. In accordance
 with provisions contained in the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 the Ministry of Environment and Forests has with a view to
 control vehicular pollution notified fuel quality specifications for 1996 and 2000 for emission related parameters. These specifications
 have been recommended by expert committees set up by the Ministry of Environment and Forests. Presently, the Ministry and the
 Central Pollution Control Board are examining issues related to fuel quality norms for the year 2005 under the Auto-Oil Programme. 
 The Indian Institute of Petroleum, Dehradun and the Indian Oil corporation, Research & Development Centre at Faridabad have not
 reported any deviance from stipulated standards.  However, some doubts have been expressed with regard to the quality of fuel at the
 retail outlets. Fuel adulteration is checked by the State Governments.  Besides, two fuel testing laboratories are being set up which will
 be located at Noida and Gurgaon.  These laboratories would be managed by the Indian Institute of Petroleum, Dehradun, Association
 of Indian Automobile Manufacturers and Indian Oil Corporation, Research & Development Centre, Faridabad.

18.        The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) under the National Ambient Air Quality Monitoring (NAAQM) Programme is
 monitoring air quality in 290 stations.   The data indicates that levels of sulphur-dioxide and oxides of nitrogen at most of the locations
 are found to be within prescribed limits.  However, levels of suspended particulate matter (SPM) are high at some places and the

 dusty conditions and the increase of vehicular traffic using diesel as fuel.  It has also been found  that city of Howrah is experiencing a
 critical situation on all the three parameters of SO2, NOx and SPM which may be due to the high density of population and increase in
 the vehicular emission load.
19.        The mitigative measures taken by the Government for prevention and control of urban air pollution include the following:
Emission Standards have been notified under the Environment (Protection) Act for about 40 categories of industries.  Besides,
 standards for ambient air quality have also been notified.  Regular monitoring of the ambient air quality and high polluting industries
 in the urban areas is being carried out by the concerned State Pollution Control Boards/Pollution Control committees.
Gross emission standards for on-road vehicles and mass emission standards for all categories of new vehicles have been notified under
 the Central Motor Vehicles rules, 1989 and are being enforced by the Department of Transport in various urban areas.
For control of pollution from automobiles, stricter emission standards, introduction of unleaded petrol in major cities have been
 undertaken.
For control of pollution from vehicles, emission norms for both petrol and diesel vehicles at the manufacturing stage were introduced
 for the first time in 1990 and made tighter in 1996.  More stringent emission norms have also been notified and will come into effect
 from 1
st April, 2000.
Ban on sale of loose 2-T oil from 31st December, 1998 in Delhi.
An Action Plan for controlling pollution in Delhi has been prepared and is being implemented by the State Government agencies and
 the Environment Pollution (Prevention & Control) Authority for National Capital Region. Similarly,an Action Plan for Mumbai
 metropolitan region has been prepared and an authority is being constituted to implement the Action Plan.
Action Plans have been drawn up for restoration of environmental quality in critically polluted areas located in various urban areas.  
 
20.        The Committee observes that in order to evolve a better monitoring structure for fuel quality control the Ministry
 should chalk out a reform programme which should include technical and medical experts in the field. The Ministry should
 take immediate steps to incorporate Fuel quality Standards for parameters related to emission in the Environment Protection
 Act (EPA) in order to make them mandatory.
 
21.        The committee is strongly of the view that the Central and State Pollution Control Boards should have a more
 systematic approach to measure ambient air-quality, with a source-wise inventory and local concentrations. The information
 should be collected on a regular basis, standardised for Metros and for all urban centres and  should be regularly displayed
 publicly. Besides,  gases like benzene and ground-level ozone levels in Indian cities should also be monitored. The Central and
 State Pollution Control Boards should also monitor the local impact of air pollution on health by commissioning
 epidemiological studies and create a comprehensive database for toxic effects of each of the emission gases.
 
CENTRAL & STATE POLLUTION CONTROL BOARDS
 
22.        Central and State Pollution Control Boards have been constituted under the provisions of the Water (Prevention and Control

24.        The CPCB is also assisting many of the Authorities constituted/being constituted under sub-section (3) of Section 3 of the

 and Control) Authority for the Taj Trapezium Zone, the Environment pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority for Mumbai
 Metropolitan Region etc.
25.        The State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs) are under the administrative control of respective State Governments.  The
 functions of the SPCBs under the Water Act, 1974 relate to planning for abatement of water pollution, advising State Governments,
 information dissemination, investigations and research, inspections, standards setting etc.  The SPCBs have been assigned
 commensurate functions under the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981. Powers to close industries, operations and
 processes have been delegated by the Central Government to the State Governments under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
 The Central Governments has also delegated powers to the SPCBs to close down industrial units handling hazardous waste in
 violation of statutory provisions.
26.        There is a wide variation in the staffing pattern, organisational structure, state budgetary support, cess targets and collection
 efficiency of the SPCBs.  The performance of the SPCBs is reviewed by the concerned State Governments.  Also, the activities of the 
 SPCBs are reviewed during periodical conferences of the Chairman and Member-Secretaries of the CPCB and SPCBs.
27.        The Committee was apprised that there have been a number of studies about the structure and review of the SPCBs.  However,
 these reports have been highly prescriptive without taking into consideration the resource constraints.  At the same time, many
 deficiencies in the SPCBs
 
relating to inadequate infrastructure and lack of resources have been recognised.  Steps taken for Central/State Pollution Control
 Boards include the following:-
(i)         Increasing water cess  rate to augment their financial resources.
 
(ii)        Strengthening of Central/State Pollution Control Boards for    enhancing their monitoring and enforcement abilities in
 terms of acquisition of equipment and refurbishing of laboratory facilities.
 
(iii)       Providing training to the officials of Pollution Control Boards under the World Bank aided Industrial Pollution Control
 and Prevention Project and Environment Management Capacity Building Project.
           
28.        The Committee observes that the Pollution Control Boards are regulatory agencies for enforcement and
 implementation, of various provisions of the environmental statutes.  Enforcement continues to be the main thrust of the
 Boards, though many of the Boards are also  engaged in promoting new technologies and pollution prevention measures, but
 they are plagued by many problems. The Committee is strongly of the view that many of the problems in the SPCBs are due to
 frequent change of personnel particularly their Chairman and Member Secretaries. Sometimes the Chairman of a Pollution
 Control Board is a non-technical person such as MLAs, or from Central Services such as IAS and Forest Service Officers and
 the like have been appointed to these positions.
 29.       Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of Environment & Forests should impress upon the State
 Pollution Control Boards to allocate the post of Chairman/Member Secretaries and other important functionaries of the  State
 Board to a technical expert in the field  and they shouldn’t be subjected to frequent transfers and must have adequate tenure
 of functioning with the Board. The Committee is also  of the view that though there is a need to have organic linkages between
 the Central and State Pollution Control Boards, there is also need to have a select cadre of professionals including experts in
 the field to man them.
30.        At present  the capacities of the Pollution Control Boards are limited in terms of technical manpower and
 infrastructure.  Their capacity has to be  suitably augmented to enable them to address to various pollution related problems. 
 The need for strengthening of the Pollution Control Boards also arises in wake of the expanding areas of work relating to
 environmental protection e.g. hazardous substances, environmental impacts etc. and emerging areas e.g. bio-medical wastes,
 fly-ash etc. At the apex level the Central Pollution Control Board is only an advisory body producing enough technical
 information.  In order  to strengthen SPCBs, it is necessary that CPCB should be empowered  under Section 5 –A of the
 Environment Protection Act (EPA) not only to interact directly  with State PollutionControl Boards, but its instructions
 should become obligatory and act as a directive rather than mere advice as at present.

32.        The National Forest Policy of 1952 had envisaged 20% of plain area and 60% of hill area of the country to be under forest and
 tree cover average of which works out to 33% under forest/tree cover.  The National Forest Policy, 1988 also set a national goal of
 having one-third of the total land area under forest and tree cover.  Though the government has taken up programmes of afforestation
 and regeneration, the inadequate financial resources and demands of ever increasing population of human beings (950 million) and
 cattle (450 million) have been the major constraints in achieving the goal set out in the National Forest Policy.  The financial
 allocation to the forestry and wildlife sectors has never increased beyond 1% of the total Plan allocation of the country whereas
 according to one estimate, average annual withdrawal of forest products (recorded and unrecorded) worth around Rs.30,000 crore. 
 Forestry operations on cost-benefit  ratio of 1:2 requires at least Rs.15000 Crore annually as against around Rs.800 Crore average

 programmes but such areas are generally in small blocks below 25 ha which would not be assessed by the Forest Survey of India (FSI)
 because of its limitations of interpretation of satellite imageries.  However, FSI has taken up the task of assessment of such smaller
 areas under tree cover.  It is estimated that the area under such plantations is around 14 million ha.  Exact figures would come out after
 the total assessment.  Adding this estimated figure, the total area under forest/tree cover becomes 78.33 million ha which is around
 23.8% of the total area of country.
34.       The Committee was informed that to achieve the national goal as envisaged in the National Forest Policy, 1988, the
 financial allocation to the forestry sector has to be raised to minimum 3% of the total Plan outlay.  Besides, Government may
 also consider the formulation of population policy to reduce the total demand of forest. The Committee is constrained to
 observe that the National Forest Policy of 1952 had, on an average, envisaged 33% of the land in the country to be under
 forest cover.  Even after a lapse of a period of 47 years what we have achieved is a little more than half way mark and the total
 area under forest cover merely works out to 19.27%.  The Committee feels that the task of increasing or extending the forest
 cover should be the least expensive project and can afford considerable employment opportunities to rural population.  Going
 by this yardstick, the Committee feels that the budgetary provision spent all these years has been a sheer wastage.  There is
 thus a need to review and recast the forestry programme.  It is all the more necessary to contain effects of global warming.
 This can be done by increasing the forestry cover which would produce better  climatic changes  all over the country.

52.        The Committee was informed by the Secretary, Ministry of Environment & Forests that the Wild life (Protection) Act. 1972 as

 chance of survival through coordinated breeding under ex-situ conditions and raise stocks for rehabilitating them in

 conservation of natural resources and for maintaining the ecological balance.
 
(c)        Provide opportunities for scientific studies useful for conservation in general and creation of database for sharing

53.        In order to achieve the objectives of conservation by zoos, the Act provides for creation of Central Zoo Authority to oversee
 the management of zoos and enforce minimum standards and norms for housing, upkeep and health care of zoo animals.  The
 Authority has also the responsibility for providing financial and technical inputs for improvement of zoos, organize training for zoo
 personnel and encourage research on various aspects related to zoo management.
 
54.        In pursuance of the objectives and functions assigned to the Central zoo Authority, the Authority has carried out creation of the
 Central zoo Authority.  Only four zoos have yet not been formally evaluated , but assessment about these zoos through inspection
 reports of various officers of State Government and NGOs is available. Findings of the evaluation are briefly summarised as below:
 
(i) Housing of animals in most of the zoos is not upto the required standards.  In many cases, space available is inadequate and
 environment that could allow the animals relevant biological stimuli to exhibit their natural behavior is wanting.
 
(ii) Many zoos do not have regular veterinarians, the expertise on health care of zoo animals, particularly the infant care is
 lacking.
 
(iii) The collection for endangered species in most of the zoos are genetically non-viable.  The number of species represented
 by single animals is quite substantial.
 
(iv) Population control measures are wanting and the number of specimen of prolifically breeding species in most of the cases
 exceeds the carrying capacity of the enclosures.  This many times leads to infighting injuries and deaths.  Even otherwise,
 excessive number of animals are a drain on previous resources of zoos.
 
(v) Education potential of zoos is not fully utilised due to lack of appropriate technical skills in most of the zoos is wanting.

National Lake Conservation Plan (NLCP)
 
66.        The Secretary apprised the Committee about the various lakes in the country. In the urban areas, lakes assume special
 importance in providing drinking water, recreation, irrigation and fishing. However, these lakes are often seen as main target for
 development particularly in urban areas due to pressure of human activities like urbanisation, industrialisation etc.  As a result of all
 these activities, most of the urban lakes are getting degraded beyond the point of recovery.  Encroachments, siltation, weed infestation,
 discharge of domestic sewage, industrial effluents, surface run-off carrying pesticides and other chemicals used in agriculture, are the
 main causes for degradation of these lakes.  The overall impact of these activities have resulted in deterioration of water quality,
 sedimentation and shrinkage, decrease in productivity, loss of flora and fauna, loss of aesthetic value and decrease in tourism
 potential.

The Chairman, Rajya Sabha in pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
 Committees, referred* the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Bill, 1999, as introduced in the Rajya
 Sabha on the 20 th December, 1999, and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and Report by the 15 th
 February, 2000.
2. The above reference was considered by the Committee in its meetings held on 8 th February, 2000. After some
 discussion the Committee felt that it would not be possible for it to complete the examination of the provisions of the
 Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout Bill-1999 ** and submit its report within the stipulated time i.e.15th
 February, 2000. Accordingly, Chairman, Rajya Sabha was requested to grant extension of time to the Committee, upto
 the 29th day of February, 2000, for presentation of its report on the Bill. The request for extension of time was granted
 and notified in the Rajya Sabha Bulletin Part II dated the 23rd February,2000.
3. Electronics and Information Technology is one of the fastest growing sectors that has played a significant role in the
 world economy. This was primarily due to the advancement in the filed of electronics, computers and
 telecommunications. Microelectronics has rightly been recognized as a core strategic technology world over, especially
 for the Information Technology (IT) based society. Design of Integrated Circuit (IC) required considerable expertise
 and several hundreds of man-years of effort depending on the complexity. Such efforts culminate into the layouts for
 ICs, which are used for fabricating the ICs in the fabrication plants. In order to encourage continued investment in
 R&D leading to technological advancements in the field of microelectronics, protection of Intellectual Property Rights
 is of utmost importance.
4. The question regarding the type of the protection to be given to the layout design of Integrated Circuits is relatively
 new. Although prefabricated components of electrical circuitry have been used for a long time in the manufacture of
 electrical equipment (for example radios) large scale integration of a multitude of electrical functions in a very small
 component became possible only a few years ago as a result of advances in Semiconductor Technology. Integrated
 Circuits are manufactured in accordance with very detailed plans or "Layout designs".
transistors were fabricated and packaged separately and then connected on a board to realise on electrical circuit. With
 the advances in microelectronics technology, it has become possible to
______________________________________________________________________________
* Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part II, dated the 21st January, 2000.
** Annexure.
integrate several such devices on a small chip of semiconducting material. Such circuits are, therefore, called Integrated
 Circuits (ICs).
5. "Integrated Circuit" means a product in its final form or an intermediate form, in which the elements, at least one of
 which is an active element, and some or all of one of the connections are integrally formed in and which is intended to
 perform on electronic function.
"Layout Design" means the three – dimensional disposition, at least one
of which is an active element and of some or all of the interconnections of an integrated circuit, or such a three
 dimensional disposition prepared for an integrated circuit is intended for manufacture.
6. A layout-design of integrated circuit is a creation of human mind. It is the result of an enormous investment, both in
 terms of time of highly qualified experts and financial investment. There is a continuing need for the creation of new
 layout-designs which reduce the dimensions of existing integrated circuits and simultaneously increase their functions.

REPORT 71
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/71report.htm[29-08-2018 16:14:12]
 The smaller an integrated circuit, the less is the material needed for its manufacture, and smaller is the space needed to
 accommodate it. Integrated Circuits are utilized in a large range of products, including articles of mass consumption,
 such as watches, television sets, washing machines, automobiles, etc., as well as sophisticated data processing
 equipment.
Whereas the creation of a new layout-design for an integrated circuit involves an
important investment, the copying of such a layout design may cost only a fraction of that investment. Copying may be
 done by photographing each layer of an integrated circuit and preparing masks for the protection of the integrated
 circuit on the basis of the photographs obtained. The possibility of such copying is the main reason for the introduction
 of legislation for the protection of layout designs.
7. Protecting the Intellectual Property Rights (IPRs) for layout design ensures not only an equitable reward for the
 creators but also acts as an incentive for creation. This, in turn, would encourage adequate level of investment of
 human, financial and technological resources in order to produce new technological solutions and original products for
 the benefit of the public, the advancement of technological progress, and the dissemination of this progress through
 technology transfer.
8. In the context of the integrated circuits industry, reverse engineering is the use of an existing layout design in order to
 prepare an improved layout design. Since reverse engineering through scientific evaluation and research is permitted
 for such intellectual property, individuals/enterprises have opportunities to put in efforts and create new original
 designs, provided that an improved layout design thereby created is an advanced form of technology, which is in the
 general interest. Also, protection of Intellectual Property Rights encourages voluntary licensing. If the creator can be
 reasonably sure that his creation will be protected, he would be more ready to part with his creation by allowing its re-
production or other uses against payment.
9. Layout designs of integrated circuits are not industrial designs in the sense of the laws
providing for the registration of industrial designs. This is because they do not determine the physical location, within
 the integrated circuit, of each element having an electronic function. Moreover, layout designs of integrated circuits are
 not normally patentable inventions because their creation does not require an inventive step, although it requires a great
 amount of work by an expert. Hence the need for a special kind of protection.
10. Basically, systems for the protection of IPR of layout designs are comparatively new in the domain of intellectual
 property. From the nature of the layout design of Integrated Circuits, it became clear that they could not be immediately
 and obviously accommodated in the existing systems for protection in the field of Copyrights, Industrial Designs or
 Patents. The existing practices of providing protection through the methods of Copyright and Patents do not
 appropriately accommodate the requirements of protection of Intellectual Property Rights for the layout design of
 integrated circuits. This is because in the context of layout design of integrated circuits, the concept of "originality"
 means that the creation has originated from the intellectual efforts of the creator, whether it is "novel or not"; whereas
 as per the Patent Law the idea should be original as well as novel. The copyright law is too general to accommodate the
 original ideas of scientific creation of layout designs of Integrated Circuits. Hence, the need for the Bill. The experience
 world over shows that the creator of the layout design is more confident towards the transfer of technology by allowing
 its reproduction under the environment of guarantee of protection.
11. The majority of countries had attached significance to protection of Intellectual
Property Rights in the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits. While USA has added a chapter to their Copyright Act for
 layout design, many countries e.g. Japan and Germany have provided "sui generis" protection of layout designs of
 integrated circuits which is contained in a separate Act of that country. Several other countries, mainly in Western
 Europe, are engaged in the preparation of specific laws for the protection of the layout designs of integrated circuits.
12. In 1985, World Intellectual Property Organisations (WIPO) commenced its examination of the question of the type
 of legal protection to be given to layout designs of integrated circuits. It became clear that an international multilateral
 treaty was necessary. The treaty would have to be established, as one of its basic rules- the national treatment with

REPORT 71
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/71report.htm[29-08-2018 16:14:12]
 respect to the protection of the layout designs of integrated circuits. Accordingly, each country was obliged to grant to
 nationals and residents of other countries the same kind of protection as it grants to its own nationals.
13. Consequently, a draft treaty was prepared and was considered by the Committee of Experts on Intellectual Property
 in respect of integrated circuits in November, 1985. The draft treaty contains a provision requiring Contracting States to
 grant national treatment. It also contains provisions governing the scope of protection to be given to layout designs of
 integrated circuits, in particular as regards the protected acts. These include the copying of the layout design and the
 distribution of integrated circuits. The draft provisions also cover the duration of the protection and its limitations,
 which include, in particular, reverse engineering, innocent infringement, and the commercial use of articles which have
 already been introduced in the market by the proprietor of the rights or with his consent. The draft provisions also deal
 with the question of how far contracting states may require certain formalities, in particular registration, as a condition
 for protection. Finally, the treaty was concluded under the auspices of the World Intellectual Property Organisations
 (WIPO) on May 26
th , 1989 at Washington.
14. On the domestic front, a high level Expert Group was set up on Trade Related aspects of Intellectual property Rights
 (TRIPS) under the Chairmanship of Secretary, Department of Industrial Development with Secretary, Department of
 Electronics as a member. A sub-group under the Chairmanship of Secretary, Electronics was set up for the area of
 layout design of integrated circuits. The sub group evolved draft legislation following the sui generis approach based on
 inputs provided by WIPO as also the inputs from the experts from the academic institutions, R&D laboratories,
 industry, industry associations and Government departments. Moreover, as one of the signatories of World Trade
 Organisations (WTO), India is also expected to align its law in accordance with the TRIPS Agreement and formulate
 suitable legislation.
15. The Committee observes that the Bill provides for : -
i) Protection of Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Designs by the process of registration.
ii) A mechanism for distinguishing layout-Designs, which can be protected.
iii) Rules to prohibit registration of layout-Designs which are not original and/or which have been
 commercially exploited; a layout design which has been commercially exploited for more than two
 years anywhere in India or in any convention country can not be registered.
iv) A period of ten years as the term of protection for layout Designs.
(v) Power of registered proprietor for assignment and transmission as also measures against
 infringement.
(vi) Payment of royalty for use of registered layout-Design and also has a provision for determination
 or royalty payment for innocent infringement.
(vii) Dealing with willful infringement by way of punishment with imprisonment for a term which
 may extend to three years, or with fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees but will not
 exceed ten lakh rupees or with both.
(viii) Appointment of a Registrar for registering the layout designs.
(ix)The mechanism of an Appellate Board consisting of Chairman, Vice-Chairman and such other
 members as the Central Government may deem fit.
(x) A transition arrangement till the Appellate Board is constituted.
(xi) A country to be notified as a convention country and also provides for reciprocity with
 convention countries.

 designs of Integrated circuits needed to be protected. At the same time it was necessary to remove the feeling of

Government’s response
 The qualifications for the Chairman and the other members of the Appellate Board have been spelt out in the Bill since

 appointed by the Central Government will be spelt out in the rules to be made under proviso to Article 309 of the
 Constitution to regulate his service. It is to be noted in this context that in the case of other Acts also like Patent Act,
 Copyright Act, Trademark Act, qualifications of the Registrar or Controller have been mentioned in the rules made
 under the Constitution. It is, therefore, proposed to follow the same approach in this case as well.
SUGGESTION
(ii) It would be preferable to clearly state in the formulation of Clause 18 that infringement means infringement done
 knowingly and willfully. The following modifications should, therefore, be done:
 In Clause 18(1) "infringed" to be replaced by "willfully infringed". In Clause 18(1) (a) "does any act" to be replaced by
 "Knowingly and willfully does any act".
 In Clause 56 and Clause 57(2) "contravenes" should be replaced by "Knowingly and willfully contravenes".
Government’s response
 We do not agree. Sub-Clause (5) of Clause 18 of the Bill is an exception to Sub-clause (1) of that Clause. The words
 "where such person does not possess any knowledge or has not reasonable ground to know" used in Sub-Clause (5)
 connote that it carves out innocent actions from Sub-Clause 91) (b) from being an infringement. The combines reading
 of Sub-clause (1) (b) and Sub-Clause (5) abundantly clarifies that only willful actions or infringement are included
 under Sub-Clause (1) (b) Such provisions are always read together at the time of interpretation. Therefore, for the
 purpose of nicety of drafting, the words "Knowledge and reasonable ground to know" have been used at only one place
 in Sub-Clause (5) of Clause (18). The same logic applied in the case of Clause 56 and Clauses 57(2).

(v) Why is the terms of protection 10 years?
Government’s response
 The IC designs and the ICs in which these designs are incorporated usually have a short life cycle. From the earlier life
 cycle of typically around 6 to 8 years, the life cycle has come down to 3 to 5 years due to the faster introduction of
 newer products. Article 38 of the TRIPS Agreement, however, states that the terms of protection shall not be less than
 10 years and not more than 15 years. In view of the above, it was thought reasonable to limit the term of protection to
 10 years.
SUGGESTION
(VI) How and who will decide that the design is original?
Government’s response
 As brought out in Clause 7(2), the design would be considered original if it is the result of the creator’s own intellectual
 efforts and not commonly known to the creators of layout-design and manufacturers of semiconductor integrated
 circuits at the time of its creation. The Registrar will determine originality based on the information available with him
 as also through the mechanism of advertisement of the application. If no objection is received to the claim within the
 stipulated period and the design also satisfies the other criteria in Clause 7, it would be determined as original.
SUGGESTION
(VII) Why is the period of 2 years put into Clause 7 in relation to commercial exploitation?
Government’s response
 The philosophy behind enacting the legislation to protect IPR of layout designs is to encourage the creators to register
 their intellectual property as soon as it is created without even waiting for its commercial exploitation. If a design is
 already commercially exploited, two years is considered a reasonable period for the creator to make up his mind
 whether he would like to avail of the protection offered under the legislation. If he chooses not to register his design,
 even two years of commercial exploitation, no protection would be provided.
SUGGESTION
(VIII) Clause 9 of the Bill should be deleted since it gives the powers to Registrar to withdraw acceptance of the
 application.
Government’s response
 This Clause allows for the possibility that the Registrar after accepting the application but before granting registration
 may determine it to be ineligible for registration under clause 7 and hence may decide to withdraw acceptance. In any
 case, a decision of the Registrar can be appeal-able to the Appellate Board. Hence, this Clause should not be deleted.

 The intellectual property relating IC design is a private property. The registered proprietor who is the owner of this

 that the concept of registered user is not mandated by TRIPs but is based on the functioning of the intellectual property
 rights.

 Clause 18(4) relates to the concept of reverse engineering through scientific evaluation and research, which is permitted

(XIX) Instead of layout, why we should not protect the mask?
Government’s response
 Protection of layout-design is in fact the protection of masks of the layout. It may be noted here that most of the
 countries including Japan, Germany, Australia etc. call this as protection of layout (topographies) while in America,
 they call it protection of masks.
SUGGESTION
(XX) Both the circuits and the layouts are the intellectual property of the creator. Which one the circuit or the layout
 should be protected?
Government’s response
 Yes, both the circuit and the layout-design are the intellectual property. In fact, to realise a circuit on silicon, a layout
 design of the circuit or mask of the circuit is required to be protected. Hence, it is necessary to protect the layout. It may
 be noted that the right confirmed by registration of a layout design shall be available to the registered proprietor of that
 layout design irrespective of the fact as to whether the layout design is incorporated in an article or not.

file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/72ndreport.htm[29-08-2018 16:14:14]
 of the Committee.  This Report deals with the detailed Demands for Grants (2000-2001) of the Department of Science and

2.         In the meeting of the Committee held on the 30 th March, 2000 the Secretary and other Officers of the Department of
 Science and Technology gave an overview of the various activities of the Department and the Members sought clarifications
 on various aspects of the performance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants.
 
3.         The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Department for replying to the clarifications sought by the

4.         The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on 18
th April, 2000.
 
NEW DELHI;
April 18, 2000
C. RAMACHANDRAIAH,
Chairman,
Committee on Science & Technology,
Environment & Forests.
 
R E P O R T
 
The Department of Science & Technology (DST) has been set up to act as nodal department for organizing, co-
ordinating and promoting S&T activities in the country.  The responsibilities    of DST include, among others to formulate
 policy statements and guidelines on S&T, and also to promote new areas of scientific research and act as a Co-ordinator of
 inter-departmental S&T efforts. The department is also responsible for providing support for basic and applied research in
 universities and other institutions and high quality research in autonomous bodies, interaction in societal programmes, and
 entrepreneurship development, Science popularisation, communication and S&T Management Information System,
 promotion of commercialisation of home grown technology, support to technology development programmes, technology
 information and assessment are also part of the mandate of the department. 
2.      Besides working in the field of international Science & Technology cooperation, its activities are also oriented in the
 undermentioned fields:
(a)  Surveying & Mapping (SOI & NATMO);
            (b) Meteorology (IMD, NCMRWF); and
(c) Technology Development and Applications (TDB).
3.      In his presentation before the Committee, the Secretary, DST mentioned that in order to promote grass root level
 invention the department has set up Innovation Foundation. Swarna Jayanti Fellowships have been initiated for outstanding
 young scientists. Funds have been earmarked for improvement of S&T Infrastructure (FIST) in universities and related
 institutions. The department is also working for Kishore Vigyanik Protsahan and Technopreneur Promotion Program (TePP)
 apart from Indian Climate Research work.  The department has also established high performance computing network
 facilities for research purposes and is in the process of strengthening Seismicity Programme.  The department is trying hard to
 modernise autonomous research institutions and to set up a National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration
 (NABL).  The department also proposes to set up a Patent Facilitating Cell to provide support to scientists and technologists
 on all aspects of patenting .The department also serves as a nodal agency in the field of International S&T Co-operation.
4.      As regard the objectives and achievements of the Department, the Committee was informed that during the 9th Plan the
 Department would lay emphasis on building and sustaining a strong science & technology base in the country, developing
 centres of excellence in the frontline areas of science & technology, and modernising the infrastructure of its autonomous
 research institutions. Under the SERC scheme new initiatives would be launched to further strengthen the S&T base in the
 country in selected areas of technological importance.  The overall approach would be to promote basic research around
 outstanding scientific groups and to a large extent in the academic sector.  The SERC would be provided more autonomy and
 flexibility for better management of R&D schemes and their proper monitoring and evaluation.  Some of the important
 initiatives under the SERC include promotion of research in less endowed universities; setting up Engineering Research
 Centres in the areas of Concurrent Engineering, Bio-Engineering, Technical Acoustics etc; providing industrial research
 fellowships to work in the industry; encouraging some of the frontier areas like biodiversity, noise control, plasma chemistry,
 micro robotics, chemical engineering sciences, modern classical optics, stress biology and immunology, boundary layer
 modelling, study of atmospheric chemistry etc.  The research areas for the engineering sciences, would be in the disciplines
 like Chemical Engineering; Materials, Mining and Mineral Engineering; Robotics; Computer Engineering; etc.  Under the

72nd Report of Committee on Science & Technology
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/72ndreport.htm[29-08-2018 16:14:14]
 programme of Intensification of Research in High Priority Areas (IRHPA), the focus would be on setting up a few major
 sophisticated facilities and Centres in the country to pursue frontline R&D, such as electron spray mass spectrometer,
 radioactive ion beam, multi-GeV Hadron heavy ion accelerator, low energy accelerator, confocal microscopy facility etc.
5.      The National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories (NABL) would be strengthened to meet the
 demands. The assessors’ training programme and the laboratory awareness programme would be intensified.  The NABL
 would be enrolled as a member of the International Laboratory Accreditation Cooperation as well as the Asia Pacific
 Laboratory Accreditation Cooperation for achieving the Mutual Recognition Agreement.
6.      National Science and Technology Manpower Information System (NSTMIS), has now proposed to set up  under the
 National Science Manpower Information System, and it is proposed to be integrated with the ongoing National Technical
 Manpower Information System of the Ministry of Human Resource Development.  An on-line access to international
 databases on S&T statistics would also be established.  In the area of technology development, a more holistic and user-
friendly approach would be adopted towards making the high technologies and products available to the society with thrust on
 technology missions, technology promotion and special technology projects through critical technology promotion, high
 technology intervention in selected export areas and promotion of NGO/society/organisation.  In respect of the Instrument
 Development Programme, it is proposed to support new projects for the development of instruments in some new areas like
 energy monitoring and management, sensors etc. besides conducting training programmes and transfer of know-how of
 instruments to industries.
7.      The new initiatives under drugs and pharmaceutical research include: drug development based on traditional systems of
 medicine like Ayurveda, Unani, and Sidha besides Homoeopathy and support to joint projects leading to drug development
 for infectious diseases.  For undertaking technology projects on a mission mode, the new areas include agro food processing,
 waterways, road transportation, electric power, telecommunication, aviation, sensors, IPR and future technology forecast for
 India for 2020.  The thrust of the S&T Entrepreneurship Development activities is on strengthening and expansion of the
 entrepreneurship development cells and the S&T Entrepreneurship Parks.  Efforts were being made to initiate rural enterprise
 development through innovative S&T based micro-enterprises in rural areas.
8.      The department under the Science communication and popularisation programme propose to impart training in S&T
 communication through short-term courses for voluntary organisations, teachers; support to popular science magazines in
 regional languages; production and screening of science films on Doordarshan; development of low-cost toys, dissemination
 of software for S&T communication/popularisation etc.  The National Resources Data Management System (NRDMS) would
 concentrate on building specialised problem oriented databases and operationalising them for real-life planning and
 administrative decision making.
9.      The Committee was informed that the activities of the State S&T Councils/Departments would be intensified so as to 
 enable them to take up major projects and its impact could be seen during the Ninth Plan.  Under the international S&T co-
operation programme, efforts would be made to strengthen bilateral and multi-lateral joint venture programmes and to expand
 and accelerate the pace of S&T co-operation with research institutions in a number of countries.  The 13 autonomous research
 institutions, being supported by the DST were to be upgraded with state-of-the-art research facilities in a phased manner.  In
 addition, funds would be provided for improvement of S&T infrastructure in universities and related institutions.
10.    The India Meteorological Department (IMD) would further intensify its high technology efforts in improving the
 accuracy of predicting severe weather, its timely warning and dissemination of its long range predictions of the monsoon. 
 The major activities proposed during the Ninth Plan include: modernisation of the observational and telecommunication
 systems, use of contemporary radar and satellite technology for better understanding of weather systems, satellite-based
 dissemination of timely warning of tropical cyclones, monitoring of seismic activities, exploitation of remote sensing data for
 agro-meteorological advisories, etc.

 also be undertaken.  The support under this programme would be to the tune of Rs.50 lakhs to Rs.1 crore for 5 years.
