 conforming to GLP norms for conducting internationally competitive research.  At this level, the support would be in the
 range of Rs. 1-2 crores.
33.    In recent years concern has been expressed about the lack of infrastructural facilities for imparting good quality higher
 education and conducting advanced research.  As a result of the ongoing efforts, Departments in the universities and related
 institutions have made some impact on the development of teaching and research.  These University departments are now in a
 stage where they would be identified for selective strengthening of their infrastructure for post-graduate education and
 research.  It is necessary to extend such infrastructural support to other higher technical educational institutions and medical
 education institutions.  Considering all these factors, a major new programme named Fund for improvement of S&T
 infrastructure in universities and related institutions (FIST) has been initiated.  This would involve providing basic
 infrastructure and the enabling facilities and environment for promoting R&D in new and emerging areas and attract fresh
 talent.

DRUGS AND PHARMACEUTICALS RESEARCH
37.    Research for new drugs is a challenging area of research due to complexity of the biological system and disease process. 
 The scheme on Drugs and Pharmaceuticals Research was initiated in 1994-95 for promoting R&D in the drugs and
 pharmaceuticals’ sectors, development of new molecules leading to commercialisable technology towards new drug
 development, giving special thrust to the development of drugs for treatment of diseases prevalent in the Indian climatic zone
 and promoting R&D in all systems of medicines bringing together the scientific expertise existing in the country in research
 institutions and industry on a joint platform in a project mode and establishment of mechanisms and linkages so as to
 facilitate the development of new drugs by the Indian Industry and the Research Institutes.
38.    The committee was informed that the Department would continue efforts to support joint research projects for the drug
 development in the area of diseases which are of importance to our country i.e. Tuberculosis, Cancer, Gastrointestinal
 disorders like Diarrhoea, Diabetes, Hypertension, Cardio-Vascular disorders and other prevalent infectious diseases in
 particular acute respiratory infections, and food & water borne diseases etc.  Special emphasis is planned to be given towards
 development of novel drug delivery systems and "Diagnostics" for various diseases of national importance.
39.    With regard to development of " Herbal Drugs  ", the Committee was further informed that the programmes included
 standardisation of traditional medicines so far are expected to be concluded successfully. In one of the research programmes
 the active compounds in Ashwagandha, Shatavari and Amtili have been identified while in another project Proposal, a novel
 method has been standardized for the preparation of certain Asavas and Arishtas, which is more innovative and less time
 consuming.  Keeping in view the progress made in the above two projects, emphasis was also being given to development of
 " Herbal Drugs ", using traditional Indian Systems of Medicine (ISM) (Ayurvedic, Unani  & Siddha), which is widely
 practiced in India.
40.    The Committee is constrained to observe that the progress made in the field of drugs is rather slow.  It therefore
 recommends that  the Department should  speed up the pace of work in this area.  Emphasis should also be on use of our rich
 heritage of traditional system and herbal medicines.

 as a part of Government’s endeavour to create conditions for our scientists, technologists, academicians and industrialists to
 work in close collaboration in order to achieve integrated excellence.  In  its endeavour to strengthen basic research in frontier
 areas Government have awarded 11 Swarna Jayanthi Fellowships last year to scholars (in the age group 30-40 years) in

 700 applicants in the year 1998 and 6 scientists were selected in the year 1999.  The scheme covers all the requirements for

 provision of liberal grant for the projects including amount for purchase of equipment, research and administrative support,

 accuracy of predicting severe weather, its timely warning and dissemination of its long range predictions of the monsoon.

 telecommunication systems, use of contemporary radar and satellite technology for better understanding of weather systems,
 satellite-based dissemination of timely warning of tropical cyclones, monitoring of seismic activities, exploitation of remote
 sensing data for agro-meteorological advisories, etc.

2.         In the meeting of the Committee held on the 31st March, 2000 the Secretary and other Officers of the Department of Scientific and
 Industrial Research gave an overview of the various activities of the Department and the Members sought clarifications on various
 aspects of the performance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants.
 
3.     The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Department for replying to the clarifications sought by the Members and
 placing before it the required material to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Department of Scientific and
 Industrial Research.
 
4.         The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on 18
th April, 2000.

R E P O R T
 
Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) which forms part of the Ministry of Science and Technology, provides
 financial support for industrial R&D projects and promotion of industrial research in industry.

2.   The DSIR comprises of the activities of the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), Departmental Schemes viz.
 Research and Development by Industry (RDI), Programme Aimed at Technological Self Reliance (PATSER), Scheme to Enhance the
 Efficacy of Transfer of Technology (SEETOT) and National Information System for Science and Technology (NISSAT) and two public
 enterprises viz. National Research Development Corporation (NRDC) and Central Electronics Limited (CEL). 
3.   CSIR is the National R&D organisation providing scientific and industrial research for India’s economic growth and human welfare. 
 It has a country-wide network of forty laboratories and eighty field centres covering fundamental and applied R&D in all areas of science
 and technology barring atomic research, developing and nurturing S&T human resource for the country through extra mural support and
 promoting scientific talent through awards, fellowships etc. Its mission is to provide Scientific Industrial R&D that maximises the
 economic, environmental & societal benefit for the people the country.  Some of the thrust areas under the consideration of CSIR are
 catalysing civilian aircraft industry, greening of leather industry, new drug discovery through symbiosis of biodiversity, heritage of
 therapeutic knowledge and modern S&T, enhancing hydrocarbons resource base: gas hydrates, promoting National IPR movement,
 spearheading global technology leadership by industry, pioneering knowledge base exports, nurturing budding talent for science.
4.   As regards the performance and achievements of CSIR, the Committee has been informed that the impact and imprint of CSIR is
 manifested in diverse ways namely: industrial production worth more than Rs.1300 crores, productivity savings worth Rs.800 crores and
 rural employment generation of 80 lakh mandays were realised during Plan period.  Besides, 800 technology licence agreements were
 executed; 250 new technologies made available for licensing; 1140 patents filed in India and 194 abroad; 10,000 papers contributed of
 which more than 65% are in SCI journals; technical assistance rendered to about 4000 entrepreneurs, external cash-flow generated
 through sponsored/contract work of Rs.670 crores.
BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS
5.   The financial allocation for the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research for the year 2000-2001 is Rs. 970.38 crores as
 against Rs.820.46 crores in the B.E. and Rs.823.71 crores in the R.E. of 1999-2000.

6.   The details of budgetary projections for the programmes of the DSIR during the year 2000-2001 is given at Annexure.
7.   The allocation on the plan side has been kept at Rs.355 crores, which represents an increase of about Rs.83 crores (including
 provision of Rs.30.50 crores for North-Eastern Region & Sikkim), over the R.E. and about Rs.66 crores over the B.E. of 1999-2000.  On
 this aspect of enhanced allocation, the Committee has been informed that out of the increase of Rs.66 crores over the B.E. of 1999-2000,
 Rs.1.6 crores is for DSIR, Rs.1.4 crores for PSEs and Rs.63 crores for CSIR. 
8.   The Department proposes to undertake a new scheme namely New Millenium Indian Technology Leadership Initiative (NMITLI) for
 which an allocation of Rs.50 crores has been sanctioned.  Its objective is to focus on a few areas which would fulfil the National
 objective of a global leadership in the technology.  The Committee has been further informed that the emphasis of this new initiative
 would be to identify four to five such areas, build a true ‘Team India’ effort inviting both the public institutions and private sector.  It has
 also been given to understand that the funds will be made available through a competitive bidding process for the individual elements of
 the programme.
9.   The Committee observes that the Department has already begun the process of putting in place a system of identifying and nurturing a
 few niche technology areas where the country could attain an undisputed global leadership position in coming decade.  However, it
 recommends that this new initiative may be accomplished by judiciously selecting technology areas where the country has a potential of
 emerging as a global leader.  While making selection of projects, it may also be ensured that these projects are directed towards the
 public good and demands of society at large, so that benefits of the scientific advances could percolate to the most deserving sections of
 the society. 
RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT BY INDUSTRY (RDI)
10.Recognising the need for developing an indigenous technological base for technology absorption and indigenous technology
 development for achieving technological self reliance, the Government has initiated several measures to encourage industry carry out
 R&D for meeting their needs and also for establishing close links between the national laboratory system and industry.  In house R&D
 units in industry provide a desirable and essential interface between
efforts within the national laboratories and the educational sector as well as production in industry.  At present there are around 1200 in
 house R&D units duly recognised by DSIR.  They employ over 50,000 R&D personnel. The R&D expenditure incurred by these units

 was around Rs.2000 crores in 1998-99.  The objectives of the scheme is to bring R&D in and by Industry to sharp focus, strengthen
 linkages among in house R&D system, National Laboratory system and educational system and strengthen R&D infrastructure in
 industry and promote and support R&D initiatives of the industry.
11.The Committee  has been given to understand that the investment in R&D by the industry is about 0.8 percent of the GNP.  The
 Committee is of the view that the quantum of investments for R&D by the Industry is far from satisfactory and recommends that steps be
 taken to promote and strengthen R&D infrastructure in the industry and if necessary by giving incentives.  The Department should
 endeavour to develop  better interface with industry and strive to bring it at par with the rest of world.
SCHEME TO ENHANCE THE EFFICACY TRANSFER OF TECHNOLOGY (SEETOT)
12.An effective technology transfer process is crucial for industrial development, be it related to acquisition and management of
 technologies or export of technologies directly or indirectly.  The scheme essentially aims to facilitate acquisition and management of
 technologies, accelerate export of technologies and services, enhance the consultancy capabilities and increase awareness about the
 usefulness of consultancy services among its customers.  Development and commrecialisation of indigenous technologies is encouraged
 and international organizations concerned with technology transfer such as Asian and Pacific Centres for Transfer of Technology
 (APCTT) are supported.  The main objectives of the scheme are to provide technical and technological inputs for acquisition and
 management of technologies; accelerate technology intensive export including export of technologies, projects and service; enhance
 consultancy capabilities; and support mechanisms for technology transfer.
13.While the Committee agrees that an effective technology transfer process is crucial for industrial development, it is of the view that the
 transfer of technology being a complex and continuous process, there is a need to develop human resource to achieve desired goals.  It
 therefore recommends that the technology should be introduced to the potential user in a manner that he can understand easily and the
 successful demonstrations should be repeated for the sake of user to avoid conflicting results, which may lead to retardation in the
 process of transfer of technology.  The Committee therefore recommends the need for strong linkages between the research extension
 centres and client system.
PROGRAMME AIMED AT TECHNOLOGICAL SELF RELIANCE (PATSER)
14.Programme Aimed at Technological Self-Reliance (PATSER) covers the activities relating to technology absorption, adaptation and
 demonstration and also capital goods development.  The objectives of the Programme are to catalyse industry’s efforts in absorption and
 upgradation of imported technology and promote indigenous development of capital goods.  While DSIR support has been catalytic and
 partial, the bulk of the financial contribution in any project has been from the industry.
15.The Committee is of the view that a separate budget may be provided for the marketing of the successful  technologies and whatever
 research and technological innovations have been made they should be thrown open to potential buyers for commercial exploitation.  The
 Committee recommends that the department should focus its research activities according to the requirements of the industry.
 
16.The Committee would appreciate if it is apprised of the results of the newly launched Technopreneur Promotion Programme (TePP)
 being funded through PATSER.
NATIONAL LABORATORIES
17.CSIR today has a network of 40 Laboratories and 80 Field Stations/Extension Centres/Regional Centres located all over the country. 
 The synergy of CSIR’s competence is sought to be optimised by aligning its R&D programmes/activities more directly with socio-
economic objectives of the country focussing sharply on areas where investment can produce maximum returns.  The R&D programmes
 of National Laboratories have been broadly categorised to various socio-economic sectors.
18.While examining financial allocation for National Laboratories, the Committee observes that the planned expenditure has been
 declining whereas non-plan expenditure has been on the rise at least at B.E. and R.E. stages of last year and budgetary allocation in the
 year under review.  The Department has informed that the financial allocation of Rs.574.75 crore (which includes the NE component)
 under National Laboratories consists of Rs.182.75 crore under Plan and Rs.392.00 crore under Non-Plan.  The increase of Rs.1.75 crore
 under Plan and an increase of Rs.43.75 crore under the Non-Plan allocation is mainly due to increase in the salaries.  It has further been
 informed that as some of the plan projects, initiated in the Ninth Plan, are nearing completion (Light Transport Aircraft (LTA), Bioactive
 molecules etc.), their allocation is tapering off, thus reflecting on the near constant plan allocation for National labs.  The Non-Plan
 expenditure has been mainly increasing due to the committed liabilities on salaries and linked.  allowances to the staff arising from the
 implementation of recommendations of the Fifth Pay Commission.
19.The Committee hopes that the Department would be able to fulfil its non-plan commitments with the allocations made and would not
 resort to diversion of funds from the plan to non-plan sector.  The Committee also recommends that Department should endeavour to
 raise the funds from industry by successful transfer of technologies.  The money thus earned can be ploughed back to R&D activities.
20.The Committee is constrained to find that a large amount of technology intended to benefit the villages has not found its way to the
 villages for want of publicity.  There is thus a need for wider dissemination of information preferably through mass media.
MODERNISATION OF CSIR LABORATORIES
21.An allocation of Rs.60 crores has been made for modernisation of laboratories for the year 2000-2001 as against Rs.58 crores in B.E.
 and R.E. of last year. On being asked about the status of upgradation of equipment and R&D facilities in the CSIR’s laboratories, the
 Committee was informed that modernisation of equipment and R&D facilities in CSIR is being done on the actual minimum year to year
 requirement for up-gradation and modernisation of equipment and R&D facilities and the same is proceeding as per the approved
 schedule and the desired objectives in the form of enhanced efficiency, productivity, quality have been achieved.
22.The Committee expects that the modernisation of laboratories and equipments used therein for providing various facilities should keep
 pace with the prevalent global standards and requirements of trade and industry.  The National Laboratories should be fully 
 computerised and endeavour to create better communication facilities.
INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY & TECHNOLOGY  MANAGEMENT

23.CSIR has been a pioneer in spearheading stray Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) in the country.  It has set for itself a formidable goal
 of holding a valuable portfolio of at least 1000 Indian patents and 500 foreign patents by 2001.  The Department would use them for
 forging strategic alliances with some of the global technological leaders in specific areas and generate at least 1% of its R&D budget
 from IP licensing/alliances.  CSIR would also endeavour to be a national resource and an international reference Centre on IP matters. 
 Major programmes envisaged include: comprehensive protection of intellectual property generated and safeguarding against
 infringement; patent information services etc.
24.The Committee commends the efforts made by the Council in emerging as a pioneer in spreading patent literacy in the country and as
 one of the largest patent holder.  The Committee hopes that the Department could achieve the targets set for itself of achieving at least a
 valuable portfolio of 1000 Indian patents and 500 foreign patents by 2001.  The Committee therefore recommends that the Department
 should gear up to that end for pooling of traditional knowledge of excellence to check the runaway theft of country’s genetic wealth and
 ensure protection of Intellectual Property Rights for validated traditional knowledge systems such as Ayurveda.
25.Asked about the steps taken by the Department to counter the patent on Basmati rice obtained by an American company, the
 Committee has been informed that the Ministry of Agriculture is coordinating the national effort to challenge the Basmati patent and
 CSIR is assisting it by providing its know-how and IPR expertise.
26.The Committee notes with satisfaction the initiative taken in this direction.
DRUGS AND PHARMACEUTICALS
27.The Committee has been informed that the Department through its Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI) is engaged in developing
 new drugs and immunodiagnostics, technology for drugs, intermediates and products, contraceptive agents and devices and conducts
 basic biomedical studies to understand disease process and reproductive physiology and conducts systematic evaluation of natural
 resources for lead identification. Under new drug development a new molecule Centchroman has been discovered and developed by
 CDRI in the first instance as a new non-steroidal once a week female oral contraceptive, which has been introduced in the National
 Family Welfare Programme.  Also a Piperine isolated from an indigenous plant, has been developed by Regional Research Laboratory
 (Jammu) a novel bioenhancer that enables the dosages of the common anti-TB drugs, particularly Rifampicin, to be reduced by at least
 50% resulting not only in the reduction of cost of medication but more importantly in the reduced side effects such as hepatotoxicity and
 neurotoxicity.  The know how has been transferred to the industry.  Its use with other modern drugs is being pursued.  Besides, CSIR has
 developed novel and cost-effective processes for over 30 drugs as well as four drug intermediates which have been licensed and most of
 them viz; Anti-AIDS, Anti-viral, Anti-cancer, Anti-bacterials, Anti-malarial, Cardio-Vascular, Analgesics & Anti-inflammatory, Anti-
allergic, Anti-ulcer, Anti-glaucoma, Anti-inflammatory, Antihypertensive have also been commercialised.
28.The Committee recommends that Department should endeavour to develop cost effective indigenous technologies in the field of drugs
 and pharmaceuticals  keeping in view the ample biodiversity in herbal products available in our country.  At the same time effort should
 be made to develop medicines which help eliminate the sufferings and are not merely an addition to the ones already existing in the
 market.
 
FOOD PROCESSING TECHNOLOGIES AND MODIFIED ATMOSPHERE STORAGE PACKING
29.CSIR is playing a vital role in the Food Processing sector.  The R&D programmes being pursued by the Council are related to
 development of pre and post harvest technologies for a wide range of fruit with an objective to minimise wastage and increase the shelf
 life of the produce with desirable and acceptable ripening characteristics.
30.Asked whether any research was being conducted in the entire gamut of export worthy cost-effective packing to help exporters.  The
 Committee was informed that the cost-effective packaging is an integral part of technology development at Central Food Technology
 Research Institute (CFTRI), Mysore for both fresh and processed fruit and vegetables for the purpose of exports.  CFTRI has carried out
 R&D work on development of technologies based on Modified Atmosphere Packaging (MAP) for the extension of storage life of fresh
 fruit and vegetables and demonstrated extension of storage life of banana, mango, capsicum and tomato to 6,4,3 and 3 weeks
 respectively.  Also CFTRI, in collaboration with Agricultural and Processed Food products Export Development Authority (APEDA),
 had successfully carried out trial export shipments of mango variety Alphonso, Banganpalli and Kesar in Modified Temperature
 containers to UK.  However large scale adoption of these techniques for export of fruit and vegetables would need proper infrastructural
 facilities such as packaging houses, cold storage etc. at different centres and ports.
31.The Committee recommends that Department should take all the necessary steps for commercial exploitation of
 techniques/technologies developed in the MAP.  The Committee is also of the view that for successful demonstration and transfer of
 technology there is a need for strong linkage within and between the research extension and client system.  Moreover, emphasis should
 be given on production of farm literature in all local languages and with the help of print & electronic media so that the farmers can
 understand the message clearly.
RURAL DEVELOPMENT
32.The Committee was apprised of the various development schemes initiated by the National Laboratories of CSIR with a view to
 developing vast majority of rural masses.  It was informed that Industrial Toxicology Research Centre (ITRC), Lucknow has developed a
 low cost online water purification system that quickly makes water free from bacteria as well as removes toxic metals like iron,
 chromium, lead, zinc and nickel to safe levels.  National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI), Nagpur has developed
 a sturdy, aesthetic and easily portable kit for detecting arsenic concentration as low as 0.01 mg/L, the WHO guideline limit for drinking
 water.  A superior and fast growing mint variety called Kosi that can produce three crops instead of two each year has been developed by
 Central Institute of Medicinal & Aromatic Plants (CIMAP), Lucknow.  It has also developed an environment friendly menthol based pest
 repellent to protect stored grains. Under  Technology Mission on Oil Seeds and Pulses  funded project, ten sets of appropriate low cost
 apricot seed oil extraction machines comprising, apricot decorticator, kernel sorter, meal grinder and mechanical oil extractor has been

 filter “Terafil” made from pottery red clay, sand and saw dust mixture.  The filter brings down the turbidity of water from 100 NTU to
 0.5 to 2.0 NTU.  The know-how has been transferred to Orissa Renewable Energy Development Agency (OREDA) for propagation

R E P O R T
 
 
      Biotechnology is a fascinating field of science.  Mankind has used biotechnology since ancient times for wine making
 and baking.  The modern science has uncovered the scientific truth behind these processes.  It has also multiplied the
 applications of biotechnology manifold in several areas of human welfare.      Biotechnology has emerged as the
 technology, which is set to shape the future by promising food security for the world, disease resistance and control,
 sustainable environmental options and thus a more healthier world scenario and ensure optimum utilisation of the scarce
 resources such as land.  The term “Biotechnology” was first described in 1920, although the origin of biotechnology could
 be traced beyond 6000 B.C. Biotechnology involves methods employed to living systems to produce/design or modify
 certain products for selective applications.  It has since made significant advances  and has come out with products that are
 of immense use in the most important areas of health, agriculture and industry. 
2.   The challenges in the modern biology and biotechnology in the next millenium are enormous in terms of research,
 product and process development and commercial exploitation thereof.  Adequate skilled human resources are also crucial. 
 The field of biotechnology in India has already opened opportunities for commercial exploitation in high value Biologicals,
 new generation vaccines, diagnostics in human and animal health care, value addition to agricultural crops through
 nutritional improvements, pests and disease resistance. Water and salinity stress resistance are the agenda for the coming
 years towards food and nutritional security.  Solutions for environmental protection through phytoremediation,
 bioremediation and microbial technologies may be available for treatment of degraded soils, enhanced oil recovery and
 pollution remediation and monitoring.  Therefore, Biotechnology provides a tremendous scope in the form of modern tools
 and techniques for improvement of human life through poverty alleviation, upgradation of skills and self-employment to
 large sections of society  in the rural areas to provide hem sense of social security.
3.   The Committee was informed that during the year 2000-2001 a consolidated effort would be made for application of
 biotechnology for the uplift through skill development of rural population especially women and weaker sections of the
 society and that, these  initiatives would be  pursued.  The efforts made in the first three years of 9
th plan have culminated
 into transfer of about 27 applications of biotechnology, filing of 41 Indian patents and granting of 7 Indian patents and 6
 U.S. patents.
4.   The Department   envisages consolidation of many activities during the third year of the current five year plan,
 operationalisation and speedy implementation of various programmes and supporting new initiatives.  The department is
 consciously moving towards product development in addition to basic research, as is evident from  technology transfers that
 have taken place in  the previous year.  A few  more diagnostics are expected to be taken up by the industry next year.

AGRICULTURAL BIOTECHNOLOGY
8.   The Committee was informed that drought and salinity are two major problems  which tend to limit plant growth and
 make soils unproductive.  A novel gene p5cs (phyroline-5-carboxylate synthase) has been reported to be a functional gene
 and over expression of this gene in transgenic tobacco results in an increased production of proline. Consequently, the
 transgenic plants produced were found to be tolerant to drought and salinity. A programme to develop transgenic indica rice
 (cv.Rasi) with p5cs gene was initiated two years ago at Madurai Kamaraj University (MKU), Madurai.
9.   A protocol for high frequency plant regeneration from embyogenic calli has been confirmed by PCR analysis.  The
 transgenic plants with desired traits would be generated in coming two years and  subjected to field evaluation.
10.The concept of organic farming is capable of  ensuring good soil health, food security and  reduce  environmental 
 pollution.  The  Committee  was  informed  that  the  department  had  started
 
national network programme on integrated nutrient management for sustainable maintenance of soil health through organic
 farming.  The efforts were being made to consolidate use of various biofertilisers and biopesticide technologies in the
 farmers’ field or specific cropping system.  This would ensure optimum use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides.  The
 technologies would help in maintenance of soil health as well as ensure environmental protection.  Various programmes on
 organic farming, specially using vermi compost have also been started in farmers’ field, demonstration to SC/ST, weaker
 sections, rural and women population.
11.The Committee feels that with the rising  costs of chemical fertilisers and the accompanying  risks of degradation of soil
 fertility because of increasing resource of the fertilisers, the role of biofertilisers and biopesticides is becoming significant. 
 The Committee recommends that the Department should encourage  the use of biofertilisers and biopesticides by educating
 the farmers though print & electronic media and field demonstrations, so as to achieve higher consumption levels of the
 bioproducts and with a view to increase their yields.

MEDICAL BIOTECHNOLOGY
15.In the area of medical biotechnology, the Department proposes to lay  emphasis on the development of diagnostics,
 vaccines for prophylactic and therapeutic use, drug delivery systems, production of important biological/biomolecules and
 creation of infrastructures in hitech biomedical areas in order to undertake further research.  During the year 1999-2000 the
 Department  has considered 42 new projects besides monitoring 55 ongoing projects and the National Jai Vigyan
 
Science and Technology Mission on development of New Generation technologies for Vaccines were initiated..
16.The department has been funding research for the development of indigenous diagnostics for major communicable and
 non-communicable diseases.  The basic purpose has been to develop easy to use, affordable and accurate test systems for
 Indian strains which could be converted into appropriate kits with the help of industries for large scale use.  The Committee
 was informed that after reaching  the level of prototype systems, the department is endeavouring  to upscale these
 technologies. The Committee was apprised of the achievements made in the area of major communicable and non-
communicable diseases which include HIV/AIDS, Japanese Encepalitis, Hepatitis, Tuberculosis, Cholera, Shipella, 
 Rotavirus,  Helicobacter pylori, Leishmaniasis Malaria etc
17.The Committee recommends that besides supporting and developing indigenous diagnostics for major communicable and
 non-communicable diseases, the department should simultaneously endeavour to find market for indigenous products, and
 strive for better qualities to ensure priority for indigenous products over the imported ones.
HUMAN GENETICS AND GENOME ANALYSIS
18.The “Human Genetics & Genome Analysis” programme was initiated during 1994 with the objective to identify, map
 and characterise genes related to genetic disorders prevalent in India for diagnosis, prevention and management of genetic
 disorders and to develop new methods of the analysis and interpretations of genomic DNA sequences. Genetic diagnosis-
cum-counselling units established by the department have been providing molecular diagnosis and counselling for the
 common genetic disorders such as betathalassemia, Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD), haemoglobinopathies and
 neurogenetic disorders prevalent in the country, to the affected families.
19.The Committee was informed that since the inception of 14 genetic diagnosis cum counselling units, about 11,000
 affected families have benefitted from prenatal diagnosis and counselling for major genetic disorders an a population of
 1,700 tribals screened for these disorders.
20.While the Committee commends the efforts made by the Department in providing counselling and diagnostics services
 for the common genetic disorders prevalent in the country to the affected families, the question remains how many people
 are aware of such facilities.  Such programmes and facilities should be named in a language which people can understand. 
 The symptoms of such disorders should be publicised as also the programmes and facilities.   The Committee therefore
 recommends that the Department may provide wide publicity to the programme by involving print as well as electronic
 media so that the benefits of these activities of the Department could percolate to the underprivileged and weaker sections
 of the society.

23.DBT has started a new scheme, for the  last two years, for the empowerment and skill development of women and rural
 poor for their economic upliftment.  The Department is extending support in the areas of food technology, sericulture,

NATIONAL JAI VIGYAN MISSION ON DEVELOPMENT OF NEW GENERATION VACCINES
25.The Committee was informed that the Department has initiated the programme based on several leads obtained from the
 R&D projects funded by the department earlier.  The objectives of the programme include generating candidate vaccine(s)
 for diseases like cholera, rabies, Japanese encephalitis, tuberculosis, malaria and HIV.  The programme has been grouped
 under three categories.  Category (A) includes those ‘candidate vaccines’ where potential research leads are available and
 which now require clinical trials or generating pre-clinical data.  Under this category, vaccines for cholera and rabies are
 being attempted.  The programmes under category (B) are related to available leads on candidate vaccines where efficacy
 and immunogenicity need to be worked out.  The target vaccines are tissue culture-based Japanese encephalitis, DNA
 vaccines, epitope vaccinogenes of Japanese encephalitis and synthetic candidate malaria vaccine.  Under category (C),
 programmes requiring sustained R&D efforts with the possibility for development of candidate vaccine(s).  Under this
 category, efforts would be made to produce candidate prophylactic anti-HIV and DNA vaccines for tuberculosis.  It is
 expected that at the end of the programme at least 2-3 vaccines will be available for upscaling and use to control/contain the
 infections while others would reach the stage of the clinical trials.
26.As regards the activities of the vaccine production unit, namely, Bharat Immunologicals & Biologicals Coprn. Ltd.
 (BIBCOL) set up by the Department for the production of viral vaccines, the Committee was informed that BIBCOL is
 formulating Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) from imported bulk since January 1996 and is supplying it to the National
 Immunisation Programme.  During the year, the company has formulated 175 million doses of OPV, a part of which was
 supplied to UNICEF.  When enquired about the proposed diversification plan for production of BCG, Measles and Tetanus
 toxoid vaccines as submitted by BIBCOL, the Committee was informed that the proposed plan has been finalised from
 BIBCOL side and the same is being submitted to the operating agency namely BIFR.
 
 
BIOTECHNOLOGY INFORMATION SYSTEM
27.The Secretary, Department of Biotechnology informed the Committee that recognising the importance of the information
 technology for pursuing advanced research in modern biology and biotechnology, a bioinformatics programme, envisaged
 as a distributed database and network organisation, was launched during 1986-87.  The programme has become  very
 successful vehicle for transfer and exchange of knowledge, information, technology packages and references in the country
 involving 8-10 thousand scientists.  Ten Distributed Information Centres and 38 Sub-Distributed Information Centres
 located in universities and research institutions are fully engaged in this task, five national facilities have been set up for
 interactive graphics based molecular modeling and other biocomputational needs.  The entire network has emerged as a
 very sophisticated scientific infrastructure for bioinformatics involving state-of-the art computational and communication
 facilities.  The computer communication network, linking all the bioinformatics centres, is playing a vital role in the success
 of the bioinformatics programme.  Database development, R&D activities in bioinformatics, human resource development

(ii)        to provide a computer-based information storage and retrieval system of database that collects structured

 continually update the databank and make the information available to the users;
(iii)       an active network mode, in which the scientists get access to the biotechnology community in the identified
 areas, answer requests for information in an interactive and discussive  mode and actively initiate dialogue
 among groups with common interest;
(iv)       to provide  retrieval service either online or offline in their specialised areas and to give overall information

(v)        to provide communication link with international databases for selective bibliographic information for the
 user scientists;
(vi)            to develop software packages and databases specific to user needs; and

 facility among bio-scientists and information scientists.

AUTONOMOUS INSTITUTIONS
30.Department of Biotechnology supports research activities in the autonomous institutions; viz; National Brain Research
 Centre, National Centre for Plant Genome Research, National Institute of Immunology, National Centre for Cell Science
 and Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics.
NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF IMMUNOLOGY
31.The Committee was informed that the Institute has excelled in the pursuit of rigorous fundamental research and emerged
 as a centre of excellence in basic immunology, infectious diseases and molecular design.  As regards the most recent
 achievements of the Institute, the Committee was informed that a major fundamental discovery concerning pathogenesis,
 which concerns survival of bacteria in phagocytes, has been reported in the Journal of Cell Biology. The complete genome
 of an Indian isolate of JEV(GP78) has been sequenced revealing its evolutionary closeness to the Chinese SA14 isolate.  A
 novel immunomodulatory use of an Indian medicinal plant product (NII-60) to prevent septic shock received a US patent
 and was transferred to an Indian Pharmaceutical industry for commercialisation.  A transgenic mice expressing the hepatitis
 B virus X  gene has been generated.  In a novel strategy, genes for different stages of plasmodium falciparum have been
 stitched and expressed in baculovirus system.  The resultant proteins elicit good immune response in experimental animals.
32.The allocation for the National Institute of Immunology has been kept at Rs.14.00 crores for the year 2000-2001 as
 against Rs.13.00 crores as was in B.E. and R.E. for the  1999-2000.  The Committee wanted to know whether the increase
 of Rs.1 crore would be sufficient to carry on the initiatives the Department  propose to take up during the year under
 review.  In response the Department has  informed that the allocation for the Institute has been increased by Rs. 1 crore,
 which is essential to augment the infrastructure of P-3 laboratory which is  to handle infectious materials as well as
 pathogenic microbes and would be sufficient to augment P-3 laboratory facilities.
33.In reply to a question as to how many of the technologies related to diagnosis of AIDS virus, anti leprosy vaccine etc.
 which were under trial, have yielded desired results and have been transferred to industry for pilot level production, the
 Committee was informed that three diagnostic technologies developed under DBT supported programme on HIV/AIDS
 have been transferred to three industries for further refinement/pilot level production.  The technology of anti-leprosy
 vaccine has been transferred to M/s Cadila Pharmaceuticals Ltd. after obtaining regulatory clearances.  The anti-leprosy
 vaccine as immunomodulator is being marketed by this concern as Leprovac.  The contraceptive candidate vaccine,  Beta

NATIONAL CENTRE FOR PLANT GENOME RESEARCH (NCPGR)
36.The Committee was informed that NCPGR, an autonomous research institution is presently carrying out its research
 activities from the  Centre of Plant Molecular Biology of Jawaharlal Nehru University.  The Centre has initiated the work
 for analysing chickpea genome, identifying genes, develop suitable regeneration protocols for improving the nutritional
 quality and resistance against various diseases and a biotic stresses.  More than 100 ESTs have been sequenced from
 chickpea.  
37.The Committee is of the view that Agriculture is not really sustainable anywhere on account of loss of top soil and
 excessive use of pesticides and fertilizers besides growth of population at a rapid pace.  Hence the need for higher
 productivity and for nutritious food. The object can be achieved by changing the plant characteristics by genetic
 modification.  The Committee impresses upon the Department to work with full vigour in this area and efforts should be
 made to cover  value based crops under its ambit which may solve the problem of under nourishment  at the glassroot levels
 of the society.

 progress of various important programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the Demands
 for Grants of Rs.136.08 crores as sought by the Department of Biotechnology for the current financial year, under Demand
 No.75 may be approved.

 are expected to yield multidimensional results in variety of areas.  The Committee, however, recommends that the
 Department should make all out efforts to ensure that biological data created in agricultural and other sectors be
 disseminated in a way that it also reaches the persons working at grassroots levels and desiring to make use of it, so as to
 ensure optimum use of the data created
(Para 29)
9.   The Committee is satisfied with the work being done by the National institute of Immunology.  However it observes that
 there are  certain unexplored areas in the field of  Immunodiagnostics and other diseases, where the institute can focus its
 research activities.  The Committee has been made to understand that 80% of all the R&D and scientific research is
 supported by the Government, and a smaller portion is funded by the Research Institutes/Industry. The Committee
 recommends that  Department should strive to raise funds  by directly collaborating with the Industry for providing
 additional support to Research activities.
(Para 34)
10.The Committee is of the view that Agriculture is not really sustainable anywhere on account of loss of top soil and
 excessive use of pesticides and fertilizers besides growth of population at a rapid pace.  Hence the need for higher
 productivity and for nutritious food. The object can be achieved by changing the plant characteristics by genetic
 modification.  The Committee impresses upon the Department to work with full vigour in this area and efforts should be
 made to cover  value based crops under its ambit which may solve the problem of under nourishment  at the glassroot levels
 of the society.
(Para 37)

R E P O R T
           
      Information Technology (IT) has tremendous potential to become an engine of growth and productivity improvement for
 all sectors of the economy and for the country.  With the continued thrust on liberalization, in order to make IT products
 cost effective and  price competitive, the  use and penetration of computers in the society is fast expanding with special
 emphasis on multi-lingual technologies.
2.   Ministry of Information Technology was set up on 15 th October, 1999 to be the nodal institutional mechanism for
 facilitating all the initiative in the Central Government, the State Government, Academia, the Indian private sector and
 successful Indian IT professionals abroad.  With a view to accelerate the Internet revolution in India, emphasizing the
 creation of useful contents in Indian languages, IT-enabled services, IT education, electronics and computer hardware
 manufacturing and exports, silicon facility, e-Commerce and Internet based enterprises, the Ministry has been entrusted the
 task of implementation of a comprehensive action plan to make India an IT Superpower in the early part of the next century
 and achieve a target of $ 50 billion in software exports by 2008.
      The Ministry has been entrusted with the following responsibilities:-
(i)            Policy matters relating to IT;
(ii)        Promotion of knowledge based enterprises, Internet, e-commerce, IT education and IT based education;
(iii)            Development of Electronics;
(iv)            Development of Microelectronics and Silicon facility;
(v)            Promotion of Information Technology and Standardization;
(vi)            National Informatics Centre (NIC); and
(vii)            Electronics and Computer Software Export Promotion Council (ESC)
In order to make India an IT Super Power by the Year 2008, the vision translates into a mission-‘Move works to India’. 
 The Vision objective are:
(i)            Creation of Wealth
(ii)            Employment Generation
(iii)            IT led Economic Growth
The role of the Ministry of IT will be of a
(i)            Pro-active facilitator
(ii)            Pro-active motivator
(iii)            Pro-active promoter
(iv)            Spread of IT to masses speedily and

3.   Investment in knowledge based industries will determine a country’s dominance in the next century.  The software
 industry  has  emerged  as  one of  the fastest  growing  sectors  in  the economy with Cumulative Annual Growth Rate
 (CAGR) exceeding 50% over the last five years and with a likely turnover of US$ 6 billion and exports of US$ 4 billion
 during 1999-2000.  The Government has targeted an export of US$ 50 billion by the year 2008 for the Indian software
 industry.
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
4.   The Ministry has been provided budgetary support of Rs.392.20 crores (Rs.365.20 crores plan and Rs.27.00 crores Non-
Plan) for the financial year 2000-2001 against the revised estimate of Rs.195.00 crores (Rs.170.00 crores Plan and Rs.25.00
 crores Non-Plan) for 1999-2000.  The allocation for the year 2000-2001 is thus Rs.197.20 crores more than R.E. of 1999-
2000.
4.1As regards the justification for enhanced allocation, the Committee was informed that in the 2000-01 B.E., an enhanced
 outlay of Rs.2.25 crores and Rs.10.00 crores has been provided for initiating Information Technology Certification and
 Information Technology Brand Equity Fund (IBEF) respectively.  IBEF is proposed to be set up with the objective to make
 ‘Made in India’ label a symbol of quality, competitive price, reliability and service to the customers.  In addition, a
 provision of Rs.142.17 crores and Rs.2.00 crores has been made for National Informatics Centre (NIC) and Electronics and
 Computer Software Export Promotion Council (ESC) respectively.  These organizations have now been brought under the
 administrative control of the Ministry since October, 1999.

NATIONAL INFORMATICS CENTRE (NIC)
5.   National Informatics Centre (NIC) which was set up in 1977, is a premier S&T organization of the Government of India
 in the field of Informatics Services and Information Technology (IT) applications in India. NIC was a constituent unit under
 the erstwhile Department of Electronics and then brought under the Planning Commission in 1988. It is now a part of the
 Ministry of Information Technology.  Its main objective is to provide computer support to Central Government
 Departments, State Government Departments, District Administration and new districts being created by the State
 Governments.  NIC has set up a satellite based computer communication network for providing E-mail, INTERNET, File
 Transfer access to  National & International databases etc.  NIC has set up a Local Area Networks(LAN) in Central
 Government Departments and State Government Secretariats.  NIC has been training the Government employees on a
 regular basis to enable them to use MIS databases.  Training is provided upto district level.  It is the only Government
 Organization in India, at present, offering network services over C-band and Ku-band VSATs, Wireless Metropolitan Area
 Networks and Local Area Networks (LANs) with NICNET gateway for Internet resources, so as to promote  social,
 economic, scientific and technological activities, and also for “macro-economic adjustment programme” of the
 Government.
5.1Since its inception, NIC has been propagating “IT-led Development” facilitating rapid economic growth and social
 transformation in India, by setting up a countrywide satellite based VSAT network (NICNET), first of its kind among the
 developing countries, linking about 540 District Administrations, 25 State Secretariats, and 7 NCT/UT Administrations. 
 NICNET links extend to Andaman Islands, Lakshadweep & Minicoy Island , Ladhakh Region, Indian High  Commission
 (Mauritius), and B.P. Koirala Institute of Medical Sciences in Kathmandu (Nepal).  NIC provides the state-of-the-art IT
 solutions to information management, information dissemination, and decision support requirements of the Central as well

5.3In some of the offices there is a large accumulation of hardware such as computer terminals, keyboards and related
 material such as transformers etc. which contained software, which is not in use now because of the upgradation of

 steps are taken for the disposal of the hardware, which appears to have been rendered obsolete, it may pose an
 environmental hazard, more so because of the rapid advances being made in this field.  When asked about removal of this
 material lying in the Government offices, the Committee was informed that the NIC has set up a Obsolete Declaration
 Committee to identify obsolete equipments and outdated software and recommend their disposal.  It has also set up an
 Auction Committee to expedite the auction of the items recommended as obsolete by the Obsolete Declaration Committee.

 will catch up with rapid advances being made in this field as a result of technical innovations.  The Committee therefore
 observes that the Ministry should review its priorities and, if necessary, come out with additional financial projections at
 R.E. stage.  The Committee feels that financial constraints should not be allowed to stay in the way of IT culture being
 spread in the country or in the matter of gaining supremacy in the field.

NATIONAL INFORMATION INFRASTRUCTURE(NII)
8.   Information Infrastructure is vital for the country and has a tremendous potential for bringing rapid transformation in our
 work culture and thus  the development of the country.   Therefore,  the Ministry  has initiated a focused attention on
 National Information Infrastructure (NII) with the aim of promoting use and proliferation of  Information Technology. 
 Thus, the objective of  the programme is to demonstrate the use of contemporary tools in Information Technology,
 enhancing overall efficiency in work, reduce delays in decision making, promote optimal utilization of manpower resources
 by improving access to information and Information Technology tools and  demonstrate the concept in action to other
 users.  Some of the sectors proposed to be covered under the programme include, literacy, education and life-long learning
 leading to increase in employment opportunities, better health care, environment friendliness, opportunities for rural
 populace to acquire new skills etc.  A number of initiatives have also been taken in the area of multi-media promotion,
 electronic governance and ATM test bed.
8.1The allocation for NII during 2000-2001 has been kept at Rs.11.00 crores as against Rs.10.00 crores in B.E. and Rs.6.00
 crores in the R.E. of the year 1999-2000.  The Committee was informed that the enhanced allocation for the NII programme
 during 2000-2001 is because of the requirement of the network security and also towards new test-beds/applications
 projects and promotional measures  towards e-commerce implementation, online learning amongst others.  Three new 
 projects are also in progress for development of e-commerce technology, tourism information system and creation of
 information infrastructure for Sikkim Government.  Certain new projects in the field of telephony overy internet, networks
 security, e-commerce applications and web enabled database management are being initiated. 
8.2The Committee notes that an allocation of Rs.10 crores was made for NII at B. E. stage of the year 1999-2000 which was
 reduced to Rs.6 crores at the R.E. of that year and it has again been increased to Rs.11 crores in 2000-01.  In view of  the
 variations in the allocation, it appears that either the Ministry is not following realistic approach towards the programme or
 there has been   utilization of funds due to  other reasons.  The Committee therefore reiterates its earlier observation made in
 its 67
th Report and would like to emphasize that having once drawn up the programmes, the Ministry should aim at full
 utilization of the budgetary provisions.

 the North-eastern region is next to impossible in view of poor telecom infrastructure.  A decision was taken by VSNL to set
 up an International gateway at Guwahati and it was to be commissioned in 1999.  Till date, the element of uncertainly hangs
 about the project and there appears no physical progress.  The Committee therefore recommends that the International
 gateway should be commissioned within a definite time frame.   Efforts should also be made to improve accessibility to the
 internet through telephone network as an individual subscriber may not have the advantage of LAN.

11.The programme aims at the creation of basic facilities for development and export of software to data links and promote
 integrated development of software/hardware in the country for domestic as well as export market.  Computer software

 Software industry is likely to go up to Rs.7,300 crores during 1999-2000 from Rs.4,900 crores  during  1998-99.  The

 (STPI) infrastructure and setting up of some of the new Software Technology Parks  (STPs) as well as towards launching of
 some new projects.

 therefore observes that the Ministry should review its priorities and, if necessary, come out with additional financial
 projections at R.E. stage.  The Committee feels that financial constraints should not be allowed to stay in the way of IT
 culture being spread in the country or in the matter of gaining supremacy in the field.
(Para 5.4)
2.         The Committee is not happy with the reply given by the Secretary on the allocation of Rs.300 crores being placed
 under its administrative control. The Ministry had informed the Committee through the Action Taken Report “that the
 Planning Commission has been approached again to place funds under the Ministry of IT”.  It is not clear from the
 Secretary’s reply whether the Ministry received any formal reply on the subject from the Planning Commission.  The
 Committee would therefore like the Ministry to look into the matter again, obtain a suitable reply from the Planning
 Commission and appearing the Committee on its part, the Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation (67 th Report)
 that the amount of Rs.300 crores has been sanctioned by the Planning Commission for IT to be spent during the Ninth Five
 Year (1997-2002) period.  The allocation has not been earmarked against any of the Ministry/Department of Government of
 India.  The Department is working on so many programmes/projects concerning Information Technology such as
 ERNET,NII, TDIL, Electronic Commerce, Electronic Governance, Venture Capital for Software etc. and the Planning
 Commission have not allocated sufficient funds for the said programmes/projects.  As DOE is responsible for promotion of
 Information Technology in the country, the Committee is strongly of the view that the amount of Rs.300 crores provided by
 the Planning Commission to be spent during the Ninth Plan may be allocated under the administrative control of
 Department of Electronics and the Department may be designated as a  nodal agency in the field of Information
 Technology.
(Para 5.9)
3.         The Committee observes that it is necessary to ensure perfect co-ordination among the    project implementing
 agencies supported under TDC programme.  This could be reflected only when allocation made during the period under
 review is utilized fully.
(Para 6.2)

 and would like to emphasize that having once drawn up the programmes, the Ministry should aim at full utilization of the

 in the Northeastern region is next to impossible in view of poor telecom infrastructure.  A decision was taken by VSNL to

 hangs about the project and there appears no physical progress.  The Committee therefore recommends that the
 International gateway should be commissioned within a definite time frame.   Efforts should also be made to improve
 accessibility to the internet through telephone network as an individual subscriber may not have the advantage of LAN.

R E P O R T
      The Department of Ocean Development was created in July, 1981 within the Cabinet Secretariat directly under the
 charge of the Prime Minister. In March, 1982 it became a separate Department and has since been functioning as a nodal
 Department for organising, coordinating and promoting ocean development activities in the country, in line with the Ocean
 Policy Statement of 1982. The programmes pursued by the Department over the years have also kept pace with
 developments World over and addressed National needs and issues.
      The programmes of the Department are directed towards:
(i)         Technology Development Programmes for future applications with strategic, industrial and economic
 significance.
(ii)        Societal Programmes with direct/indirect benefit for the community by technology applications and pilot
 project demonstration with the participation of the community for their socio-economic prosperity, and for
 coastal area development.
(iii)       Marine Resources Programmes for exploration of marine living and non-living resources, techno-economic
 studies to evolve strategies for sustainable exploration and utilisation, and resource enhancement.
(iv)       Multi-institutional and multi-disciplinary Polar Science Programmes and Antarctic Expeditions with
 scientific and geo-political significance.
(v)        Capacity Building Programme towards self-reliance through basic scientific research in ocean sector, human
 resource development and establishing Centres of Excellence in academic institutions.
(vi)
              Creation of public awareness on the potential and uses of ocean.

POLAR SCIENCES
Antarctic Expedition:
15.The Secretary informed the Committee that the 19
th Indian Scientific expedition to Antarctica was launched from Cape
 Town, South Africa, on 9 th December 1999, keeping in view the likely scientific and economic benefits and future
 international cooperation in the field of polar science between India and other countries. The 19 th Expedition to Antarctica
 consisted of a 47 member team including 30 scientists and 17 logistic personnel, under the leadership of Mr. Arun
 Chaturvedi a scientist of Geological Survey of India, including a two member lady team – one medical Doctor from India
 and a Geologist from Peru.  This included a contingent of 25 members who would winter-over in Antarctica for 16 months
 duration in pursuit of science.  The logistic support for the Expedition had been provided by a contingent of Army
 personnel, which is headed by Maj. Ravi Sangwan.
16.In addition to the ongoing programmes several new experiments have been initiated during the course of this expedition,
 which includes:
(i)                 Study of earth-air current systems to give an insight to the deep space processes.
(ii)        Experiments on crack propagation of the ice-shelf in order to understand the dynamics and processes of
 Iceberg generation.
(iii)       Installation of a number of automatic weather stations to measure energy balance and albedo factors of the
 ice, as a part of global change studies.
(iv)       Reconstruction of the past climatic and vegetative history through the study of organo-debris present in the
 fresh water lake sediments of Antarctica.
(v)        Establishment of an environment monitoring laboratory for the first time at Maitri in order to carry out an 
 assessment of the status of air, noise, water biological and land environment of Antarctica, throughout the
 year.
17.The summer team of the XIX expedition returned to India via Cape Town on 6 th March, 2000 along with the winter team
 members of the XVIII expedition.
18  The Committee observes that this heralds another scientific feat in the realms of polar science at the end of this
 millennium and demonstrates the capabilities and interest of the country to pursue a well-focussed scientific campaign from
 a pristine scientific platform provided by Antarctica.
18.1  The Committee recommends that  the National Centre for Antarctic and Ocean Research(NCAOR) Goa, should be
 designated as the nodal  agency of the Department in planning, coordinating and executing the XX Indian Scientific
 Expedition to Antarctica for continuation of the scientific/research programmes initiated during the XIX expedition. The
 Committee hopes that the scientific and logistics co-operation gained  with the  launching of the XIX Expedition from Cape
 Town would lead to the initiation of state-of-the-art research programmes in Polar Sciences and should be carried forward in
 initiating and executing Southern Ocean Oceanography & Paleoclimatology, and Antarctic Global Change.

COASTAL COMMUNITY PROGRAMMES
Marine Instrumentation (Shore to Fishing Vessel Communication System)
52.For demonstrating the usefulness of communication system to the fisherfolk who are at sea, shore stations were set up in
 seven places viz. Shankarpur and Frassergunj in West Bengal, Paradeep and Chandipur in Orissa, Salegeo in Noth Goa  and
 Periya Veereampattinam in Pondicherry.  Out of these, four centres in West Bengal and Orissa were operationalised. 
 Construction of shore stations and erection of towers/mast for fixing antenna in Andaman & Nicobar Islands is in progress.
53.The Committee recommends that the Department should develop the shore to vessel communication system  and 
 commission the system in A&N and Lakshdweep  Islands which would be helpful for fishermen going for fishing in high seas.
 The technology should  be handed over  to the State Governments for continuous operation and maintenance.
 
ISLAND DEVELOPMENT
54.NIOT has taken up new initiatives towards helping island communities in their needs relating to Ocan Science and
 Technology as well as marine resource enhancement. The first activity taken up by NIOT is a programme on lobster resource
 enhancement for islands under the DOD project on Living Marine Resources Enhancement (LMRE).
55.In a study conducted on lobster fattening using gray clam as live feed, a remarkable increment in body weight (i.e. around 35
 g/month) has been achieved. Another experiment was conducted using green mussel as a feed source in place of clam. The
 various biochemical analysis such as protein, free amino acids, carbohydrates, free & bound sugars, protease, a-amylase and
 chitinase indicate the suitability of mussel meat as a better alternative to the clam as feed source for lobsters.
56.During the fattening of lobsters, various hydrobiological parameters such as temperature, pH, salinity, dissolved oxygen,
 nitrite, nitrate, silicate, ammonia and phosphate in the source water as well as the experimental tanks were estimated. The
 phytoplankton species present in the source water were also identified in order to utilize them as feed for larvae. The occurrence
 of various protozoans, total heterotrophic bacterial population and Vibrios load was observed in the body surface of lobster, live
 feeds and water (both from tanks and source). The animals with tail rot syndrome were successfully treated with appropriate
 concentration of malachite green and 100% recovery was observed in 20-22 days.
57.At the new campus of NIOT,  R&D laboratories, which will cater to all the analytical requirements of the LMRE project,
 have been organised. All major and minor equipment were commissioned and the laboratory is fully operational.
58.A survey on landing of lobsters at various sites in Gulf of Mannar and Andaman islands has been completed by December
 1999. It indicates a decline in landings at various sites, a trend which was in evidence from previous surveys of lobster
 resources during the last few years.
59.The activities of erstwhile Andaman Nicobar Centre for Ocean Development (ANCOD) of Department of Ocean
 Development has been integrated with NIOT as Andaman and Nicobar Centre for Ocean Science and Technology (ANCOST)
 in order to implement the various core activities previously initiated under the LMRE programme. For this purpose, already
 existing facilities like boats and sea water pumps have been repaired and commissioned. A layout of new laboratory building
 has been finalised and the building is expected to be functional very soon. Using the farm facility in Minnie Bay, the problems

DELINEATION OF OUTER LIMITS OF CONTINENTAL SHELF
61.Traditionally the Coastal States had been claiming few nautical miles into the sea.  In accordance with the UN Convention on
 Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), now the States can establish 12 nautical miles of territorial sea and 200 nautical miles of Exclusive
 Economic Zone (EEZ) from baselines and there are no major technical difficulties in establishing the limits.  The States are also
 entitled for the
rights over the continental shelf, slope and rise extending beyond the EEZ.  The continental shelf comprises the seabed and
 subsoil of the submarine areas that extend beyond the territorial sea throughout the natural prolongation of the land territory. 
 The continental shelf is rich in non-living resources and the minerals, including hydrocarbon resources.
62.The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea stipulates that where the coastal state intends to establish the outer limits of the
 continental shelf beyond 200 nautical miles, it shall submit particulars of such limits to the Commission on the Limits of
 Continental Shelf (CLCS), along with the supporting scientific and technical data as soon as possible, but in any case within 10
 years of entry into force of the Convention for that State.  The Convention came into force on 16.11.1994 and India ratified the
 same in June 1995.  India thus must submit all the necessary data to the CLCS by June 2005.  If delineation is done properly
 India would be in a position to claim more than 1 million sq.km beyond the EEZ.  India is represented as an elected member on
 the Commission on the Limits of Continental Shelf (CLCS).
63.The Committee observes that with the ratification of the UN Convention on Law of the Sea, a new international order has
 been established for the oceans and  India being represented in almost all the important bodies on oceans will stand to benefit
 enormously by provisions of the convention, only if we can build an integrated approach for scientific planning, formulation,
 implementation and overall management of the programmes with a comprehensive organisational and institutional back up.
64.After considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Ocean Development and assessing the progress of
 various programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the Demands for Grants of Rs. 158.00
 Crores as sought by the Department of Ocean Development for the year 2000-2001, under Demand No.92  may be
 approved.

R E P O R T
 
 
The Indian Space Programme, since its inception in the early sixties, is geared to achieve the goal of self-reliant use
 of Space Technology to ensure rapid progress in diversified fields of the country including social, economic, cultural and
 scientific for finding solutions to the problems of man and society. Even as India entered the new millennium, the space
 programme in the country has matured to a status where space has become an important element of the national
 infrastructure, especially in the areas of communication, broadcasting, meteorology, disaster management and resources
 monitoring. India is recognized the world over for its unique application driven space programme. Further, industry
 participation in the space programme  has been expanding, bringing economic benefits. The plan to further enhance and
 improve the space services by launching follow-on satellites in the INSAT and IRS series in coming years and to enhance
 the launch capability to place INSAT class of satellites in orbit through GSLV, the Indian Space Programme is well poised
 to play a stronger role in the country's march towards progress in the new millennium.
2.     Whereas the efforts of the Indian Space Programme in the early sixties were confined to getting familiar with space
 technologies and developing technical and organisational infrastructure in order to develop satellite launch vehicles, during
 the eighties, the space programme moved closer to realising the goal of self-reliant use of space technology for national
 development. The country entered the nineties with the launch of more ASLVs and PSLVs. With the launch of IRS-IB and
 INSAT 2A and 2B, the Indian Space Programme becomes fully operational through its own communication and remote
 sensing satellites. The Indian Space Programme is broad-based and it has an impressive array of achievements in putting to
 use space technology for vital applications - for telecommunications, TV broadcasting, weather watching, forecasting
 agricultural crop and forests wealth assessment, water resources management, flood mapping, drought forecasting,
 identification of marine resources, protection of the environment and rural literacy campaign etc.
3.     Self-reliance in space technology has been an important target of the programme from the very beginning.  Long-range
 plans have been drawn up, from the very beginning, for each decade, to steer the programme effectively, ensuring
 appropriate linkages among the application needs, satellite missions, launch vehicle capabilities and technology
 development. Over the last three-and-half decades, significant achievements have been made in country in the area of space
 technology (i) for building world-class satellites for communications and remote sensing, (ii) for launching the remote
 sensing satellites from India with our own launch vehicle and (iii) in reaching  the benefits of space technology to improve
 the quality of life at the grass root level, thus contributing to several areas of national development.  Necessary
 organizational and institutional mechanisms with users, industries and academia have also been established. In tune with the
 goal of self-reliant use of space technology for national development, the thrust areas of the Indian Space Programme are:-
(a)    Satellite-based communication for various applications;
(b)    Satellite-based resources survey and management and environmental monitoring;
(c)    Meteorological applications; and
(d)   Development and operationalisation of indigenous satellites and launch vehicles for
         providing these space services.

4.     The Department of Space, which was set up in 1972 to promote unified development and application of Space Science
 Technology for identified national objectives, is entrusted with the task of implementing the policies framed by the Space
 Commission.   The policies are carried out through the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the three Grant-in-
aid institutions viz., the National Remote Sensing Agency (NRSA), the Physical Research Laboratory (PRL) and the
 National Mesosphere-Stratosphere-Troposphere Radar facility (NMRF).
5.     Today, the space  sector world over, is poised for a transformation towards a matured, scientific and industrial sector,
 with multiple players and changing roles. Besides, it needs to adapt itself to the implications of a market driven economy
 and the formidable challenges arising out of increased societal needs, technological limitations, resource constraints and
 geo-political scenarios.   In India, while integrating the programmes with the international scenario, the national needs are to
 be addressed; the gains achieved so far have to be consolidated; new and potential areas of space technology utilization are
 to be identified and developed; organisational as well as managerial support have to be ensured to surge forward, harnessing
 national capability and capacity, ensuring synergy amongst the partners as well as space systems.
6.    The Committee observes India is one of the six countries with homemade satellites in orbit. Despite being a new entrant
 to the competitive global space club, which hitherto was an exclusive preserve of a handful of countries, India's overall
 track record both in the field of rocketry and satellites has been impressive. This, of course, does not overlook the fact that it
 had its share of failures too, which needless to say can be expected in any hi-tech project. To cite a few, one can recall the
 failure of the ASLV and of the PSLV.   But these failed missions only proved to be another step on the ladder to success.
 The subsequent flights were a resounding success. This endorsed India's claim to be growing space power. The Committee,
 however, would like the Department to keep the analysis of each failed mission in view so that corrective measures can be
 taken while executing future programmes.
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
7.     The Committee was informed that the total expenditure on Space research till the end of Eight Plan Period i.e. from the
 inception in 1962-63 to 1996-97 was Rs.7431.67 crores. During the Eight Plan Period most of the programmatic targets and
 missions have been achieved and the total expenditure incurred on these programmes was Rs.3928.53 crores (Plan
 Rs.3155.74 crores and non-plan Rs.772.79 crores).
8.     It has been stated that the Department of Space had asked for an allocation of Rs.11,000 crores for the Ninth Plan
 period to meet the programmatic requirements of the Department, but the allocation was restricted to Rs.6511.72 crores for
 the entire plan period from 1997 to 2002. This is however subject to review on annual basis by the Planning Commission. In
 the first three years of the 9
th plan, the Department has expended Rs.4,164 crores which is 54% of the total plan outlay.
9.     Analysing the performance of the Department on the basis of the information made available, the Committee found that
 during 1997-98, the Department had utilised the funds to the extent of 99.13 percent. In 1998-99, the fund utilization level
 was about 99.9 per cent. The provisional expenditure for 1999-2000 indicates utilization of funds by the Department. The
 Committee notes with satisfaction that the Department has made optimum utilization of the funds allocated to it during
 1997-98, 1998-99 and 1999-2000.
10.    The programme directions and proposals for Ninth Plan (1997-2002) have been formulated after extensive interactions
 and consultations with user Ministries. The guidelines provided by the Space Commission have been adopted in the process
 of formulation. The Committee was informed that consistent with the programme directions and targets envisaged for the
 Ninth Plan period, the specific activities/projects to be undertaken during the year 2000-2001 have been carefully prioritised
 while working out the B.E. for 2000-2001 which are in pursuance of the Zero Base Budgeting Methodology of the
 Department in formulating the process of annual budgets. The financial allocation for 2000-2001 works out to Rs.2019.22
 crores as against Rs.l725.86crores in the R.E. of 1999-2000 and Rs.1755.00 crores in the B.E. of 1999-2000, which is
 higher by Rs.293.36 crores over the revised estimates and Rs.264.22 crores over the B.E. of 1999-2000 (Annexure).
11.    The major landmark achieved by the Department during the year 1999-2000 is the successful launch of the Indian
 Remote Sensing Satellite, IRS-P4 (Oceansat) alongwith two foreign satellites, one belonging to South Korea and other to
 Germany. The successful mission has not only given the ISRO enough confidence to market its launchers abroad but also
 enhanced the space services to the nation in the areas of telecommunication, television broadcasting, meteorology, disaster
 management and resources survey.
11.1  The Committee observes that these achievements are a feather in the cap of the Department as the launch of three
 satellites in a single flight is a technological achievement and it marks India's entry in the commercial launch market.
INDIAN NATIONAL SATELLITE SYSTEM (INSAT)
12.    The Indian National Satellite System, which was established in 1983 with the commissioning of INSAT-IB, is one of
 the largest domestic communication satellite systems in the world today which is entrusted with the task of providing
 services in the areas of telecommunications, television broadcasting, radio networking and meteorology including disaster
