INTRODUCTION
 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment
 & Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Ninty-first Report
 of the Committee.  This Report deals with  the detailed Demands for Grants (2001-2002) of the Department of Space
 (Demand No.90). 
2.         In the meeting of the Committee held on the 10 th April, 2001 the Secretary and other Officers of the Department of Space
 gave an overview of the various activities of the Department and the Members sought clarifications on various aspects of the
 performance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants. 
3.     The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Department for replying to the clarifications sought by the
 Members and placing before it the required material to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the
 Department of Space. 
4.         The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on 19th April, 2001.

R E P O R T
 
 
Department of Space (DOS) and the Space Communication were set up in June, 1972 with the primary objective of promoting
 the development and application of Space Science & Technology for the socio-economic benefit of the nation through
 establishment of operational space services in a self-reliant manner.  The thrust areas of the programme are as follows: -
 
·
                     Satellite based communication for various applications.
·                     Satellite-based resources survey and management and environmental monitoring.
·                     Meteorological applications.
·                     Development and operationalisation of indigenous satellites, launch vehicles and associated ground segment for providing these space based
 services.
2.   The Secretariat of DOS and the Head quarters of ISRO are located in Bangalore.  The Policies of the Indian Space Programme are formulated by the Space
 Commission and implemented by DOS through the Indian Space Research Organisations (ISRO), the National Remote Sensing Agency (NRSA), the Physical
 Research Laboratory (PRL), the National Mesosphere-Stratosphere-Troposphere Radar Facility (NMRF) and other  agencies.  The North Eastern-Space Applications
 Centre (NE-SAC) was set up during the year jointly with the North Eastern Council.  The Antrix Corporation established in 1992, is a wholly owned Government
 company for commercial marketing of space products and services.  A close coordination between DOS and other Departments is maintained in the establishment
 of space                 systems - INSAT system is coordinated and managed by the Secretary-level INSAT Coordination Committee (ICC) while the Planning
 Committee of NNRMS (PC-NNRMS) coordinates National Natural Resources Management System (NNRMS). NNRMS Standing Committees (NNRMS-SC), set up
 with user ministries and departments, ensure an efficient and coordinated functioning of different NNRMS elements.  An Advisory Committee on Space Sciences
 (ADCOS) guides the research in space science.

GEO-SYNCHRONOUS SATELLITE LAUNCH VEHICLE (GSLV)
24.The Geo-Synchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle(GSLV) launch was the most technologically challenging mission of the ISRO as its success would herald a
 significant milestone in establishing India’s  capability to launch communication satellites.  The 3-stage GSLV, India’s first satellite launch vehicle using cryogenic
 engines, was the culmination of a 10-year long project which cost the national exchequer Rs. 1,400 crore. The  successful launch of GSLV has enabled India  to
 enter the elite space bazaar and join the US, European Union, Russia, Japan and China which have already crossed the geostationary launch milestone.
25.The GSLV was designed to place a communication satellite into a geo-synchronous transfer orbit (GTO). The 49-metre tall GSLV, which weighs 401 tonnes,
 would place the Geo-synchronous Satellite (GSAT) weighing 1,540 kg in a highly elliptical GTO with a perigee of 185 km and an apogee of 36,000 km.  GSLV
 mission was a step after the PSLV in terms of enhancing the capabilities of  DOS in launch vehicles and orbiting heavier class of satellites. The GSLV mission
 was primarily to realise the launch capability with INSAT class of satellites that weigh between 2,000 kg and 2,500 kg.
26.   The Committee applauds the achievement of the Country’s most ambitious space project, the GSLV, launched successfully  on 18
th April, 2001.   The successful
 launch of GSLV would not only enable the country to launch its own satellites but also the satellites of other   countries.  The  Committee  hopes  that  the  GSLV  will 
 take  India a  step  closer to
realizing the dream of being a genuine space power which so far has been the exclusive preserve of a handful of advanced countries.

27.Remote Sensing is a technology for sampling radiation and force fields to acquire and interpret geospatial data to develop information about features, objects, and
 classes on Earth’s land surface, oceans, and atmosphere.  Thus this activity includes  the detecting and measuring of electromagnetic energy emanating from
 distant objects made of various materials, to identify and categorize these objects by class of type, substance and spatial distribution.
28.The Indian Remote Sensing Satellite (IRS) System, which is the world’s largest constellation of remote sensing satellites comprising five satellites, IRS-IB, IRS-IC,
 IRS-ID, IRS-P3 and OCEANSAT-1 (IRS-P4), continued to provide  valuable data for application in agriculture, forestry, surface and ground water harnessing,
 geology, urban planning, land use and land cover mapping, flood mapping and ocean resources surveys, IRS-ID, which was launched by India’s PSLV in
 September 1997 has successfully completed its design life of three years and continues to function satisfactorily.  Data from OCEANSAT-1 was being used for
 retrieval of several important oceanic parameters.  Many institutions have been associated in the evaluation of data from this satellite and to explore new fields of
 application.  Development, fabrication and testing of follow-on satellites in the IRS series, namely, RESORCESAT and CARTOSAT-1 were progressing well.  
 Significant progress has been made in the development of a Technology Experiment Satellite TES that aims at testing and validating advanced spacecraft bus and
 payload technologies.  Work on the advanced cartographic satellite, CARTOSAT-2, has also been initiated. 
29.The remote sensing applications in the entire country were carried out under the broad umbrella of National Natural Resources Management System (NNRMS). 
 NNRMS continuously provided space based data related to land, water and ocean resources as well as atmospheric observations.  As the effective utilization of IRS
 database on an operational basis was possible with the involvement of the states in setting up appropriate mechanism to integrate the database for effective
 management of natural resources in the states, the idea of State Natural Resources Management System (SNRMS) was conceptualized,  on the pattern of existing
 NNRMS.  The nine NNRMS Standing Committees encompassing major natural resources and developmental areas like agriculture, bio-resources and environment,
 urban development, etc. periodically review the status of utilization of remote sensing in their respective fields and provide guidance for promoting remote sensing
 based activities.
30.The Committee was informed that after completion of first phase of the National (Natural) Resources Information System (NRIS) programme, a national review of
 the NRIS programme was held and it was recommended that the NRIS must be expanded to cover at least one district in each state and also cover the whole
 country in phased manner.   As a precursor to establishing NRIS for the whole country, initially  states of Orissa and NE states were identified for taking up the
 NRIS programme.  The enhanced provision sought in RE 2000-2001 was mainly towards establishment of NRIS in Orissa State and North-Eastern region.
31.     The Committee is of the view that in addition to providing data about country’s natural resources, the programme should emphasize on locating new
 resources in view of the requirements of country’s rising population.  The Department should also address all the State Governments to effectively manage and
 ensure optimum utilisation of the natural resources.
32.     The Committee would also like to impress on the DOS about the need to make an extra effort on mapping natural resources in the North-Eastern region.  It
 is because the region holds a vast potential of natural resources which do not appear to have been explored fully. On the other hand our inability to map these
 resources and ensure gainful utilisation could be one reason for the law and order problems being faced by that region.   Besides, such initiatives might help in
 improving socio-economic development of the region.

 consciousness and time targeted activities, the benefit of which could be tremendous.   DOS should, therefore, consolidate its partnership with Industry with a view
 to achieve optimum utilization of the industrial capability, of the private as well as public sector 
INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION
60.DOS has emphasised international cooperation and partnerships.  In the present scenario of increasing costs and commercial competition, international cooperation
 could accomplish more than what can be achieved by individual countries .

 on India’s satellite communication programme; use of the US LANDSAT and French SPOT spacecraft data on Indian remote sensing programme; availability of the
 US NOAA data for satellite meteorological programme; launch support from erstwhile USSR for India’s satellite programme, etc. are examples to show the benefits
 of international cooperation.   India has not only been able to work jointly with advanced space-faring nations, but also able to market its space hardware and
 services.  Besides, it has been contributing its space resources for the benefit of international community in addition to meeting its own requirements.
62.One of the recent examples of cooperation was the incorporation of the Modular        Opto-electronic  Scanner (MOS) instrument from the German Aerospace
 Centre (DLR) on board the Indian Remote Sensing satellite, IRS-P3, along with ISRO’s Wide Field Sensor (WiFS).    Data from this satellite was  being received
 and analysed not only by Indian and German scientists but also in USA and other parts of Europe.  ISRO and the French National Space Agency (CNES) were
 working together for a joint satellite  mission called Megha Tropiques that aims to study the atmosphere and climate.
63.DOS has also entered into agreements/memoranda of understanding with several countries and space agencies, namely, Australia, Brunei Darusslam, Canada,
 China, European Space Agency, France, Germany, Hungary, Indonesia, Italy, Mauritius, Norway, Peru, Russia, Sweden, Syria, Netherlands, Ukraine, United Kingdom
 and United States of America.  India has an active role in several international bodies such as the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space
 (UN-COPUOS), United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UN-ESCAP), the International Astronautical Federation (IAF), the
 Committee on Earth Observation Satellites (CEOS), the Committee on Space Research (COSPAR), the Inter Agency Debris Coordination Committee (IADC), the
 Space Frequency Coordination Group (SFCG), the Committee on Geostationary Metorological Satellites (CGMS), the International Space University (ISU), the Asian
 Association for Remote Sensing (AARS), the International Society for Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing (ISPRS), etc.
64.DOS  under a scheme called Sharing of Experience in Space (SHARES)  was providing   training in different applications of space technology    to scientists
 from other developing countries.  DOS supported selected candidates with living expenditure and allowances, while the international travel was borne by the country
 sponsoring the  candidates.
65.   The Committee recommends that the DOS should forge international cooperation to explore the areas, which have hitherto remained unexplored.
PUBLICITY OF SPACE PROGRAMME
66.Space programme encompasses a variety of activity in space science, technology and applications, which are of interest not only to the scientific community but
 students and the general public.  Wide publicity is necessary on achievements  of Space programmes. DOS has made efforts to disseminate information of space
 programme.  Information in respect of all major events under the space programme was being provided to the public  through print and visual media, exhibitions,
 public lectures and publications.  General information on the space programme was also available on the internet.
67.Department of Post has by now issued four postage stamps to commemorate the achievements under the Indian space programme.   Of these, two stamps are
 on OCEANSAT-1 and INSAT-3B satellites and the other stamps were on the theme ‘India in Space-2025’.
68.   The Committee is happy to note the efforts being made by the DOS in publicising its programmes and achievements.  The Committee feels that it is necessary to
 provide greater focus on dissemination of the current as well as future programmes with the help of print as well as electronic media.
ANTRIX CORPORATION
69.Antrix Corporation Ltd., the commercial  wing of ISRO, was marketing India’s space products and services.  The objective is to gain entry into  the highly
 competitive international market. Antrix markets subsystems and components for satellites, undertakes order for satellites to user specifications, provides  launch
 services and  tracking facilities and also organizes training of manpower and software development.  Some important achievements of the Corporation include
 marketing of IRS data, satellite launch contracts with Germany, Korea and Belgium, sale of a sounding rocket to Norway and supply  of  satellite hardware to major
 space companies in the world.  Antrix Corporation and Arianspace of France had also signed an agreement to enlarge the launch opportunities for small satellites. 
 The Corporation was also engaged in providing commercial aspects for transfer of ISRO’s spin-off technologies to Indian industries.
70.
     The Committee observes that with the clearance of Direct-to-Home (DTH) Policy in India, the market for telecommunication satellites and related products and
 services holds vast potential.  The Committee, therefore, feels that the Corporation should  explore the possibilities of production and supply of telecommunication
 satellites, facilitating augmentation of transponder capacity under the INSAT system and should also offer consultancy services for procuring, launching, operating and
 maintenance of communication satellites and  evolve its strategy accordingly.
DISASTER MANAGEMENT
71.The Disaster Management System (DMS) was visualised to provide  support for management of disasters in near-real time and also for disaster zonation studies
 and effective initation strategies.  Space-based disaster management system provides valuable inputs when appropriately integrated with the conventional ground-
based  systems.  In the Ninth plan period, the efforts were made to complete a system definition study of the DMS and also conduct pilot experiments for
 establishing a prototype DMS.  Plot project on DMS has been initiated in some flood-prone districts of Assam.
72.About 250 Cyclone Warning Dissemination System (CWDS) receivers have been installed in the cyclone-prone coastal areas of Andhra Pradesh, north Tamil
 Nadu, Orissa, West Bengal and Gujarat.
73.The Secretary  informed that  in pursuance of the earlier recommendation of the Committee, an advanced Cyclone Warning Dissemination system with digital
 version was under development.  This has several new features such as high quality digital transmission, variable duration of siren/audio message and confirmation
 of the receipt of the warning message.  The design and functional specifications have been completed.   The proto-type of the instrument has been fabricated by
 the Industries and the testing was in progress.  These proto units would be deployed in the field for trial runs.  After successfully completing  trial runs, Indian
 Meteorological Department would procure the system from Industries and deploy them in the coastal districts.

INSAT
75.The Indian National Satellite (INSAT) System was one of the largest domestic satellite systems in Asia today.  A joint venture of the Department of Space, the
 Department of Telecommunication, the India Meteorological Department, All India Radio and Doordarshan, INSAT provides long distance telecommunications,
 meteorological earth observation and data relay, nationwide radio networking, TV programme distribution and rebroadcasting to terrestrial transmitters, etc.  DOS was
 responsible for establishment and operation of INSAT space segment.  The overall management of the INSAT system rests with the Secretary-level INSAT
 Coordination Committee (ICC).
76.The INSAT system which became operational with INSAT-1B, is a multi-agency, multi-purpose operational satellite system which provides domestic long distance
 telecommunications, meteorological earth observation and data relay, nation wide direct satellite TV broadcasting to augment TV receivers, nation wide radio
 networking, TV programme distribution and re-broadcasting to terrestrial transmitters, etc.  The system has enabled communication to and fro any part of India
 leading to training and awareness among rural masses on better agricultural practices, land and water resources management, family planning health care and
 hygiene, disaster warning and rescue operations, etc. 
77.The INSAT system has four satellites in operation at present – INSAT-2C, INSAT-2DT, INSAT-2E and INSAT-3B.  Besides, ten transponders have been leased
 from Thailand to augment the system capacity.
78.
     The Committee observes that the unprecedented growth of communication and TV and the projected requirements for the future, require an adequate expansion
 of INSAT services in order to cope with regional as well as national requirements.  Accordingly, any  planning of our future national space programme should take into
 account these requirements.
 
DIRECT-TO-HOME (DTH) TV MISSION
79.The basic concept of a Direct-to Home (DTH) TV Broadcasting Satellite System was a high power satellite operating in the Ku-band for direct telecast of TV
 programmes to homes.
80.Asked  about the current status of DTH mission, the Committee has been informed that during the formulation of 9th five year plan, the Planning Commission had
 given guidelines that the Department has to depend on user funding support for DTH mission. The Department would undertake DTH mission only  if there was a
 requirement and funding support forthcoming from DTH users. A token provision of Rs. 10 lakhs has been kept in the BE of the year 2001-2002 to enable
 configuration studies and preliminary development.
81.   The Committee notes the position and observes that instead of depending on  budgetary support, the Department should explore the possibilities of generating
 revenues from the user community or by inviting investment from private sector. This would  help the Department to execute the mission in right earnest, without  taking
 recourse to the budgetary support.
LONG TERM PLANS
82.The Committee has been informed that the Department has drawn up “Vision and Programme Directions: 2000-2010”  identifying the goals and technology
 requirements of the space programme during the coming decade.  This has been reviewed by the Space commission as well as the Planning Commission.
83.It has further been informed that the Department has planned several activities during     2001-02 in tune with the programme directions identified for 2000-
2010.  These include advanced GSLV MK III with the development of large solid booster (S-200), higher thrust cryogenic engine (C-20) and large liquid strapon (L-
100), developmental efforts towards air breathing propulsion systems, space recovery capsule experiments for micro gravity applications, missions on advanced
 cartography with improved resolution, national systems for satellite based navigation, pilot experiments  in disaster management support, establishment of GRAMSAT
 network for developmental applications, newer communication services for digital audio, tele medicine, mobile communication and a wide range of remote sensing
 applications related to land and water.
84.The Department has also taken up several study  initiatives of Long term plan to identify the thrust areas of the space programme beyond 2010.   A special task
 force was working on “Earth Observation: 2025 strategy”.  In order to elicit views and perspectives of younger generation, a team of young  scientists/engineers of
 the Department was working to generate inputs on “Long term plan: 2000-2025”.  A long term road map was also under finalization in the launch vehicle area.  A
 decade plan for the space science had also been drawn after extensive interactions with the scientific community in various institutions of the country.  Several
 other studies were also in progress in this direction.  These studies provide valuable input for the formulation of 10
th five year plan.

 coverage over large areas from the vantage point in space, enabling the country to monitor and manage its national resources and environment.  Developing
 countries like India, which are burdened with large population density, low agricultural yield, unchecked deforestation, increasing wastelands, large scale illiteracy,
 recurrent natural disasters and poor communication and transportation infrastructure, could only leap-frog with the help of space technology to provide a better life
 style to its citizens in the shortest possible time.

 are carried out at various levels in  the organization in order to arrive at the minimum essential cash flow for each Project, Programme and Centre/Unit, based on
 the programmatic priorities, total cost, scheduled targets, progress achieved and the milestones planned for the budgeting period. Consistent with the programme
 directions and targets envisaged for the 9 th Five Year Plan period, the specific activities/projects to be undertaken and the performance milestones to be achieved
 have been carefully prioritized while arriving at the Budget Estimates for 2001-2002.

th April, 2001.

NEW DELHI;                                                                                       C. RAMACHANDRAIAH
November 28, 2001                                                                                                   Chairman,
   Parliamentary Standing Committee on
 Science & Technology ,Environment & Forests.        
 
 
 
R E P O R T
 
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Biotechnology on the
 recommendations contained in the Eighty-Seventh Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee
 on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants (2001-2002) of the Department of
 Biotechnology which was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 18th April, 2001 and laid on the Lok Sabha on the 18 th April,
 2001.  There are sixteen recommendations contained in the eighty-Seventh Report of the Committee. Action Taken notes
 on the recommendations of the Committee were received from the Department on 23rd July, 2001.
 
The Committee’s recommendations, action taken thereon and comments of the Committee on the action taken by
 the Department of Biotechnology are set out in the succeeding paragraphs: -
 
Recommendation
 
The Committee observes that it is not opposed to enhanced allocations to the Department. While it is necessary
 that the Department keeps itself posted with the developments abroad in the field of biotechnology, it should
 choose projects with utmost caution with a view to ensure that they are in the best interests of the country.
                 
(Para 10)
 
Action Taken by the Department

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/93rd.htm[29-08-2018 16:20:29]
 
The Department has been from the very beginning interacting with all the concerned scientific agencies, user
 Ministries/Departments, national laboratories, universities, state level institutions and NGOs to identify and prioritize
 programmes considering needs and interests of the country. The department is advised by a Scientific Advisory
 Committee. There is also a Standing Advisory Committee (Overseas), a novel feature of this department with non-resident
 Indian scientists as its members to give advice and inputs on the developments abroad in the field of biotechnology. The
 Biotechnology Research and Promotion Committee (BRPC), a High Powered Committee of inter-disciplinary experts and
 16 subject specific Task Forces are also operational to identify, recommend, review and monitor projects in the best
 interest of the country. Every effort has been made to keep itself abreast with latest development world over.
 
Comments
 
The Committee notes the reply and commends the efforts being made by the Department in
 involving non-resident Indians in its programmes.
 
Recommendation
 
As regards the programmes under the forest trees the same need to be developed extensively with a view to
 increase the forest cover. This, in turn, would help in arresting ecological imbalances. Besides, the technology be
 made available for social forestry programmes.                 
       
(Para 17)
Action Taken by the Department
 
The Department has a major programme on forest tree improvement. Tissue culture regeneration protocols have been
 standardized for a large number of economically important tree species and these are now being adopted for large scale
 multiplication. The tissue culture pilot plants set up by the Department at Tata Energy Research Institute, New Delhi and
 National Chemical Laboratory, Pune which were later converted to Micro propagation Technology Parks are producing
 large quantities of elite planting material of forest trees. Approx. 70 lakhs plants have been produced so far and field
 planted over an area of 8000 ha. at multi- locations in 17 states across the country.
 
Comments
 
The Committee notes the reply. However, it would like the Department to focus on the States facing problems of
 deforestation or environmental degradation in any other form.
 
Recommendation
 
The Committee is constrained to observe that the leprosy vaccine developed by the National Institute of
 Immunology is yet to be included by the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare in its leprosy control programme.
 The Committee has been given to understand that voluntary agencies have made use of 24 lakhs doses of the
 vaccines whereas the Ministry of Health continues to import the vaccines instead of making use of the one
 developed by the National Institute of Immunology. If it is really so, the Committee observes that it constitutes
 draining out of the precious foreign exchange from the national exchequer. This needs to be pursued with the
 Ministry of Health on priority basis.
 
                                                                                                                        (Para 19)
 
Action Taken by the Department
 
The Department has already approached Ministry of Health & Family Welfare at the highest level with the request
 to make use of, LAPROVAC in the National Leprosy Eradication Programme, as a therapeutic immunomodulator.
 

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA

Comments
 
            The Committee notes with concern that the outcome of the efforts made at the highest level with the
 Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to make use of LAPROVAC in the National Leprosy Eradication
 Programme has not been indicated.  The Committee apprehends that the Department has either not succeeded in
 persuading the Ministry of Health to make use of LAPROVAC or something is amiss that Ministry of Health finds
 it difficult to make use of indigenous supplies of LAPROVAC.  The Committee would like the Department to take
 up the matter again with the Ministry of Health again and, if necessary, approach the Cabinet Secretariat for
 advice or for placing the matter before the Cabinet.  The Committee would like to be apprised of the outcome.
 
Recommendation
 
The Committee commends the work done by the Department in the field of rice genome sequencing and observes that more
 such programmes need to be undertaken especially in crops like pulses which are in short supply in the country, maize, oilseeds,
 and other dry farming crops keeping in view the extremely varied climate, cropping patterns, variety of crops available in the
 country.
                                                                                                 (Para 22)  
 
Action Taken by the Department
 
The Rice Genome is the smallest of the most economically important cereals like wheat, barley, maize and
 sorghum. There is considerable conservation of gene order among these genomes and hence the information gained from
 rice will be helpful in understanding other cereal genomes. The outcome of sequencing  programme would be
 identification of many genes of interest particularly yield component, plant architecture, resistance to stresses and pests,
 diseases, drought, salinity etc.
 
So far as legumes are concerned, functional genomics of chickpea has received high priority at National Centre for
 Plant Genome Research (NCPGR), New Delhi. The EST, sequences, characterization of putative chickpea disease
 resistant gene and cloning of molecular markers associated with plant differentiation are the ongoing activities. The
 Department at the moment does not have any programme on genomics of maize. However' it is intended to have a
 collaborative programme with CIMMYT, Mexico - the applied Biotechnological Centre which is working on molecular
 markers, genetic engineering and apomixis of maize.
 
In the area of wheat genomics, one of the Department supported Centres has recently become a member of
 International Wheat Microsatellite Consortium (IWMC). This initiative has received positive response from the other
 members of IWMC.
 
Comments
 
The Committee commends the efforts made by the Department in the field of Rice and wheat genomics.  The
 Committee observes that the Department should continue to explore more areas of Genetic Engineering in
 furthering the research.
 
Recommendation
 
The Committee has perused the information available in respect of Patent Cell over the internet. While all the
 institutions etc. can be accessed and through them the homepage of the Department, the home page is not directly
 accessible for some reason of confidentiality attached to it or because of some technical reasons. This needs to be
 looked into. The Committee is also of the view that the efforts be made to make the scientists aware of the need for
 taking patents and procedures for applying a patent must be simplified and displayed over the Internet along with
 facility for downloading of forms as far as possible. The information about the patents applied must also be made
 available which is perhaps not available at present.
                                                                                                                                            (Para 25)

The Department has easily and directly accessible website over the internet. Apart from all the relevant information
 about Department, it contains the format of the application for patent filing both in pdf and html. formats. The hard copy
 of the format is circulated to interested organizations, as and when they require and for reference in their libraries. To
 encourage scientists to patent their innovations and create awareness on the procedures four National Roving seminars

The Committee observes that efforts be made for developing cheaper technologies in waste treatment to enable

 dumps, starch factory waste water treatment, dye industry effluent treatment, desulphurisation of biogas have been
 developed and demonstrated to user industries.

INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment &
 Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Ninety-fourth Report on the
 Action Taken by the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research on the recommendations/observations contained in the
 Eighty-sixth Report of the Committee on Demands for Grants (2001-2002) of the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research.
 
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research Scientific
 & Industrial Research on the recommendations/observations contained in the Eighty-sixth Report of the Department-related
 Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants (2001-2002) of
 the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research  which was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 18
th April, 2001.
 
There are twenty-two recommendations contained in the Eighty-sixth Report of the Committee.  Action Taken Notes on
 the recommendations of the Committee were received from the Department on 31st July, 2001.
 
In the meeting held on 28 th November, 2001 the Committee considered the draft Action Taken Report and adopted the
 same.
 
 
 
NEW DELHI;                                                                                       C. RAMACHANDRAIAH,
November 28, 2001                                                                                                   Chairman,
   Parliamentary Standing Committee on
 Science & Technology ,Environment & Forests.        
 
R E P O R T
  
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research
 on the recommendations contained in the Eighty-sixth Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
 Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants (2001-2002) of the Department
 of Scientific & Industrial Research which was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 18 th April, 2001.  There are twenty-two
 recommendations contained in the Eighty-sixth Report of the Committee. Action Taken notes on the recommendations of
 the Committee were received from the Department    on 31st July, 2001.
The Committee’s recommendations, action taken thereon and comments of the Committee on the action taken by
 the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research are set out in the succeeding paragraphs: -
 
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
 
Recommendation
      The Committee commends the steps being taken by the Department in augmenting its scientific and industrial
 capabilities towards the economic and social development of the Country.  The Committee however recommends that
 besides the on-going research projects, the Department should also support employment generating research such as
 research on Bamboo from which millions of people earn their livelihood worldwide.  This would help in generating
 employment among rural people.
(Para 10)
Action Taken by the Department
      The Steering Committee for formulation of Tenth Five Year Plan on S&T has assigned to the Department of Science &
 Technology the formulation of the mission on Bamboo.  CSIR would provide the requisite inputs for the mission.
Comments
            While the Committee notes the reply with satisfaction, it would like the Department to identify more of such
 projects which can generate employment without any investment on the part of the rural folk and thus help them

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/94th.htm[29-08-2018 16:20:30]
 to eke out their living.
Recommendation
      The Committee feels that on the one hand efforts should continue to be made for securing more and more research
 projects and test-work from the industry, at the same time endeavour should continue by reducing work force by not
 filling vacancies caused by resignations, retirement etc.  This would help ensure optimum utilization of the human
 resources and bring about some reduction in non-plan expenditure.
(Para 11)
Action Taken by the Department
            CSIR is endeavoring to enhance its contract R&D work and rendering of S&T services to industry. CSIR is
 continuously assessing its manpower needs.  As against the sanctioned strength of manpower of 27,000 (in 1995) the
 present strength is around 21,000 only. CSIR would further endeavour to reduce this strength to 20,000 by the end of
 Tenth Five Year Plan.
Comments
            The Committee notes the reply.
 STAFF STRENGTH
Recommendation
            The Committee conveys its appreciation for the efforts made to bring about reduction in the staff strength. 
 The Committee hopes that the Department would keep its word in reducing the staff strength to 20,000 by the end
 of 10th plan.
(Para 13)
Action Taken by the Department
      Noted for periodic review to ensure compliance of the suggestion.
Comments
            The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation
      The Committee feels that in order to make available best talent it is necessary that at least the minimum needs of
 employees are taken care of in this fast changing world.  It is all the more necessary because the monetary benefits given
 by the Fifth Pay Commission have to a large extent been neutralised by high cost of services and rising costs of living.  The
 employees, be they of Central Government or elsewhere are again on subsistence wage level with high component of
 personal taxation whereas according to Taylor’s concept of scientific management, a satisfied worker is an asset to an
 organisation.  The Committee therefore feels that every possible effort including adequate budgetary support should be
 provided for amenities like housing.
(Para 16)
Action Taken by the Department
            CSIR express its gratefulness to the Committee for its recognition and adequate budgetary support for Housing. 
 Government are also seized of the need to provide housing facilities to scientific and other staff.  Thus it has been making
 budgetary allocation to CSIR as per its requirements.  CSIR is making all possible efforts to raise the level of satisfaction
 at the metros and other towns where the housing conditions are difficult.
Comments
            The Committee notes the reply.
 
NATIONAL LABORATORIES
Recommendation
            While the Committee is aware that the year 2001-2002 being the terminal year of the Ninth Five Year Plan,
 the emphasis has to be given on completion of on-going schemes, the Committee would however like the DSIR to
 endeavour to bring about diversification in R&D work.  While the user services for the industry may continue to
 be provided, prioritization and diversification of research may help decrease the dependence on non-plan
 expenditure.  Efforts should also be made to secure research work from abroad to the extent possible.
(Para 18)

Action Taken by the Department
            Over the last decade and especially since 1995, CSIR has renewed its efforts to work closely with the user
 organisations to commercialise its technologies. This was with the view to help industry and users on one hand and
 supplement CSIR’s budgetary resources on other hand to meet the growing expenditures particularly the Non Plan.  CSIR
 today is meeting around 27% of its total expenditure from the contract R&D, Royalty, S&T services and thus lessening
 the dependence on non-plan expenditure.  While CSIR would make all efforts to secure more research work from abroad,
 its primary responsibility is to service and serve Indian industry & users.
Comments
            While the Committee notes the reply, it would like the Department to continue its endeavour to increase its
 earnings from the present level of 27% from Contract R&D, Royalty, S&T services etc.  At the same time, in order
 to bring about equilibrium between the resources available and the work force efforts may be made not to fill the
 vacancies caused by resignations, retirement etc. to the extent possible instead of taking recourse to harsh steps
 such as VRS etc.
 
Recommendation
            The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation made in 73
rd report and observes that there is a need
 to progressively modernise the CSIR Laboratories.  The Committee observes that the process of modernisation
 should be time bound.  The Department should also spell out precisely the areas of modernisation being
 undertaken/ proposed to be undertaken in the laboratories.  The Department should also ensure that the
 modernisation matches the international standards.  Also, the Committee should be apprised about the training
 being imparted/proposed to be imparted to the scientists for handling the upgraded/modernised laboratories.  The
 Committee, however, recommends that CSIR should continue its modernisation in the next plan period.
(Para 22)
Action Taken by the Department
            With the support and recommendations from the Parliamentary Standing Committee, the Modernisation Plan was
 implemented in a time bound manner during the Ninth Plan period.  The phase-wise modernisation plan for upgradation
 of equipment and R&D facilities at all the National Laboratories was approved by the Government and implemented.  By
 the end of the current financial year, this phase is expected to be over.  CSIR is seized with the matter of modernisation to
 continue and as recommended by the Committee, the next phase of modernisation proposed for the Tenth Five Year Plan
 relates to Infrastructure Renovation and Refurbishment.
Comments
            The Committee notes the reply.  It would, however, like to be apprised in brief about the modernisation
 brought about in the laboratories, giving details laboratory-wise so that the Committee could consider visiting any
 of these laboratories during its visit to those areas.  The Committee would also like the modernisation to be made
 an integral part of each of the laboratories notwithstanding the phases of recession like the one through which the
 Indian economy, like many other countries of the world, is passing through.
 
NATIONAL S&T HUMAN RESOURCES DEVELOPMENT
Recommendation
            The Committee observes that the Universities and Institutions will have to play a meaningful role to achieve
 widespread excellence in both teaching quality and high calibre human resources.  Therefore, there is a need for
 reviewing and strengthening/revamping the existing S&T supports systems in the universities and other
 educational institutions, be it in terms of infrastructure or quantum of funding as well as operational structures
 and mechanisms.  The issues related to the institutional mechanisms, policy guidelines, approval and clearance of
 procedures should be looked into with a view to simplify and make them user friendly.
(Para 26)
Action Taken by the Department
            The Scientific Advisory Committee to the Cabinet is seized with the matter of creating suitable mechanisms and
 policy directions to bring in together Universities/Institutions and S&T support systems for developing high calibre
 human resources.  The Steering Committee on Science & Technology for the Tenth Five Year Plan inter alia has also
 dwelt on the issue on interface between industry, R&D institutions and academia for S&T.  The recommendations of the
 Steering Committee are to be submitted to Planning Commission, which in turn, is expected to appropriately reflect the
 issues in its Report on Tenth Five Year Plan.
Comments
            The Committee notes the position.

Recommendation
            The Committee feels that CSIR should also consider introducing Scientific Research Scholarships to school
 leaving students in order to encourage them to pursue a career in S&T related areas.  National Women Scientific
 Research Award could also be introduced to the outstanding women researchers to encourage their partnership in
 the mainstream.  These initiatives would help in accelerating the pace of scientific & technological research for the
 development of a strong knowledge base and its application for the welfare of humankind.
(Para 27)
Action Taken by the Department
CSIR has already initiated a scheme known as CSIR Programme for Youth Leadership in Science (CPYLS)
 wherein top 50 students from each of the State Boards passing the X class exam are encouraged and motivated to take up
 science as a career.  They are invited for two days to nearest CSIR lab along with their teacher/parent, at CSIR cost, to
 experience and see the excitement and adventure of science, those who pursue science are assisted in the project work at
 the CSIR laboratory.  Those students passing XII class exam with 90% marks in science are further encouraged to pursue
 science at degree level by giving them the opportunity to work for 14 weeks/year for three years in any of the CSIR labs
 during vacations.  They are called ‘CSIR Students Associate’ and are given a stipend of Rs.500/- a week.  These Students
 Associates would also be provided support to pursue M.Sc.
The number of women scientists is maximum in life sciences, the Department of Biotechnology has accordingly
 introduced special awards for women scientists.
Comments
            The Committee commends the efforts made by the Department in promoting S&T culture in the Country. 
 It hopes that such measures will sustain the interest of  the young students in pursuing a career in S&T related
 areas.  In order to encourage more & more students, the Committee suggests that the experiences/initial
 observations of the students already availing the benefit of such schemes be obtained in writing/through their
 reactions and be made the basis/background of Newspapers/Electronic media ads with new visuals, pictures
 delivering messages.  This would help attract more students.
 
INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY
Recommendation
            The Committee commends the efforts made by the CSIR in maintaining its standards for Intellectual
 Property Movement by setting a formidable goal of achieving 1000 Patents and 500 foreign Patents by 2001.  The
 Committee, however, feels that the Department should create a Patent Facilitating Cell which should assist in
 writing, and completing of all formalities for filing of patents. Roving seminars should also be conducted at regular
 intervals to create  awareness on intellectual property rights and related issues.
(Para 29)
Action Taken by the Department
            The suggestion of the Committee to conduct roving seminars to create awareness on intellectual property rights and
 related issues are being initiated and it is expected that four such seminars would be conducted during the financial year. 
 It is proposed to prepare a CD based module that could enable an innovator to check the possibility of patenting an
 invention and also guide him step wise on formalities to be completed for filing of a patent application.
Comments
            The Committee notes the reply with satisfaction and hopes that the steps would continue to be taken for
 creating awareness on intellectual property rights and related issues.
 
NEW MILLENNIUM INDIAN TECHNOLOGY LEADERSHIP(NMITLI)
Recommendation
            The Committee notes with satisfaction that a beginning towards technology leadership has been made in
 NMITLI.  However, it is constrained to observe that there has been poor projection of the programme and the
 financial visualization has been unsatisfactory; consequently an amount of Rs.25 crores was surrendered at the RE
 stage of previous year.  The Committee hopes that the Department would take prudent steps to optimise on
 investments and come up with enduring projects.  The Committee also expects that the Department would
 continue its efforts in devising a much more transparent system of implementation and national consultation in
 perfecting the niche opportunity technology areas into project modes.
(Para 33)
Action Taken by the Department
            The Committee’s observations have been noted and CSIR has adopted more widespread national consultations at

 diverse levels, constituencies and sectors to solicit ideas.  Thereafter a four tier open and transparent system of scrutiny,
 project formulation, assessment and brain storming and project approval has now been put in place.  It is only in the first
 year of allocation that there was a surrender of funds as the Scheme had to be conceptualised and widespread national

 consuming.

            The Committee notes the reply and hopes that steps would be taken to avoid such situations in future.

RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT BY INDUSTRY (RDI)
Recommendation
            The Committee observes that the socio-economic advancement of a nation demands a strong relationship
 between Industry and R&D laboratories, which unfortunately is not a reality in India.  Rather the wholesome
 involvement of national R&D with industry, which is a hallmark of the advanced industrial societies, is missing in
 India. The Committee, therefore, recommends that CSIR laboratories should put more emphasis  on  consolidating
its partnership with the industry so that the technologies developed by the laboratories can be commercialised and
 fully exploited.  More the commercialisation of technologies, more would be the confidence in the CSIR
 laboratories, providing further impetus to their R&D activities.
(Para 35)
Action Taken by the Department
            The CSIR is fully cognizant of the Committee’s concerns, however mere responsiveness of the CSIR and R&D is
 not enough.  The state of health and well being of the industry and conducive and enabling environment are needed for
 symbiosis of national R&D with industry.  These aspects of the innovation system are to be developed concurrently,
 which are beyond the ken of CSIR.  Nonetheless CSIR is making vigorous efforts to bring about such a system.
Comments
            The Committee observes that what has been stated by the Department is indeed true.  It is more so in
 periods like the one through which Indian economy is at present passing through with slump in economic activity. 
 But even in present periods competitiveness, cost controls and product innovations could be of help.  The
 laboratories must endeavour to make inroads in the industry with such qualities which help improve quality, cut
 down costs and product innovations.
 
NATIONAL INFORMATION SYSTEM FOR SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY(NISSAT)
Recommendation
            The Committee is of the view that dissemination of information can be facilitated through electronic
 network, as well as physical networks like libraries, booksellers, broadcasting companies and organization selling
 information in electronic form e.g. database available in the form of CD-ROM, DVD etc. Widespread
 dissemination of information depends upon availability of reliable and dependable networks.  Therefore, the
 Department should try to create appropriate delivery mechanisms.  Such delivery mechanisms would provide
 quality education, create a strong knowledge base and provide widespread access to information to the research
 community as well.                                                                
(Para 40)
Action Taken by the Department
            The views expressed by the Committee on the dissemination of information are well taken.  National Information
 System for Science and Technology (NISSAT) has been promoting information facilities on S&T by upgrading the
 existing centres, promoting resource sharing, providing access to international databases and imparting training for skill
 development, etc.
            With the development of internet technology, NISSAT is promoting and supporting developing of web-based
 information resources and information access and dissemination facilities.  NISSAT has established a number of web
 based information access facilities for the dissemination of information on specific sectors such as; iprlawindia.org,
 Indian-ocean.org, vigyan.org.in and calibnet.org. Indigenous database have been developed on various subjects like
 Directory of Indian Scientists and Database of Indian Chemical and Pharmaceuticals Industry.  These are made available
 on CD-ROMS and Vigyan server supported by NISSAT at IISc, Bangalore.  These are continuously being updated and
 efforts will be made to strengthen the delivery systems as recommended by the Committee.  
Comments
            The Committee appreciates the efforts being made by the Department in augmenting its mechanism for

 dissemination of information.
 
PROGRAMME AIMED AT TECHNOLOGICAL SELF-RELIANCE(PATSER)
Recommendation
The Committee notes with satisfaction the support rendered by the DSIR in the field of technology
 absorption and adaptation.  The Department should continue its efforts to interact with other Ministries for wider
 dissemination and utilisation of its technology development projects. This would help in generating new
 technologies.  An integrated and sustained approach would certainly help the Department in realising its projected
 goals.  Besides, it is necessary to create awareness about the Technopreneur Promotion Programme (TePP) so that
 enthused and encouraged individual innovators come out with their creative talents.
(Para 45)
Action Taken by the Department
            The Committee has, inter-alia
, expressed satisfaction about the support rendered by DSIR in the field of
 technology absorption and adaptation.  In pursuance of the Committee’s supportive recommendations, the Department
 will continue its efforts to network and interact with other Ministries for wider dissemination and utilisation of its
 technology development projects.  As advised by the Committee, the Department would continue to adopt and follow an
 integrated and sustained approach towards reaching the projected goals. Likewise, the Department along with Department
 of Science & Technology will continue to create further awareness about Technopreneur Promotion Programme (TePP)
 and disseminate the details and support measures available to individual inventors under TePP, with a view to tap their
 creative talents.
Comments
            The Committee notes the reply with satisfaction.
 
SCHEME TO ENHANCE THE EFFICACY OF TRANSFER OF TECHNOLOGY (SEETOT)
 
Recommendation
            The Committee is of the view that the need for transfer of technology in bringing improvement  in industrial
 productivity can not be underestimated.  The Committee is pained to observe that Transfer of Technology
 programmes have moved at snail’s pace.  It is necessary to identify the prevailing constraints and have insight of
 Industrial sector problems and then devise appropriate technologies to address the problems.  To that end, the
 Committee recommends that a multi-disciplinary team should work on priority basis for identification and
 solution of the problems being faced with regard to the technology.
(Para 48)
Action Taken by the Department
            The thrust of Committee’s observation is that it is necessary to identify & assess industrial sector’s problems and
 devise appropriate technologies to address the problems and evolve solutions through a multi-disciplinary team effort. 
 The Department considers, assesses, supports and reviews projects of industry and/or R&D organization and academic
 institutions, related to their specific problems in technology absorption, adaptation, development and commercialization. 
 This is done through inter-departmental and inter disciplinary Committees such as Technology Advisory Committees and
 Project Review Committees.  The Department through its various plan schemes promotes close linkages between the
 industry and R&D system, so as to encourage formulation and implementation of activities & programmes which are
 mutually relevant and beneficial to industrial units as well as R&D laboratories.  CSIR laboratories have been directly
 involved in conducting industrial research and are therefore, in a position to identify problems of industry in their
 respective areas of operation and work towards finding solutions for the same. 
Comments
            The Committee notes the reply.
 
Recommendation
            The Committee would also like to point out that it is equally necessary to plan the research projects before
 hand, concentrate and conduct research only in those areas where it can gainfully be employed in the interest of
 the economy.  The Committee, therefore, feels that the scientists and all other working for transfer of technology
 should bear in mind all these points.
(Para 49)
Action Taken by the Department
            The thrust of the Committee’s observations is on careful planning and implementation of research projects, keeping
 in view the likely economic gains.  The programmes and activities of CSIR laboratories are assessed and prioritised by the

 there is careful scrutiny of the value and impact of the projects on diverse aspects such as advancement of knowledge,

FOOD AND FOOD PROCESSING
Recommendation
            The Committee visited Central Food Technological Research Institute (CFTRI), Mysore a few years back
 and had the occasion to see some of the machines like large scale dosa making machine.  The Committee doubts
 whether there is demand for machines designed to cater large scale commercial requirement.  The Committee
 would therefore like to impress on all concerned to engage themselves in activities which are either against
 confirmed orders or can otherwise be gainfully exploited.
(Para 55)
Action Taken by the Department
            The Committee’s observations that activities should be taken up only which have either confirmed orders or can
 otherwise be gainfully exploited are well received. CFTRI efforts had always been to generate technologies that can be
 gainfully exploited, sometimes these are market led and sometimes lead the market. In respect of the dosa making
 machine CFTRI estimates the demand of 2000 numbers of dosa making machines, with 400 dosa per hour capacity, from
 large catering fast food establishments and social feeding centers.
Comments
            The Committee is not satisfied with the reply and feels that the recommendation made by the Committee
 was of general nature and was supported by an instance.  In case the recommendation was not based on just
 assumption, the facts in this regard should have been brought forward to clarify whether the instant case was
 against an order instead of giving a vague reply which did not lead the Committee to any conclusion.
 
Recommendation
            The Committee feels that in order to provide impetus to the technologies developed by the CSIR
 laboratories in food processing sector, the Department should take the initiative of interacting with all State
 Governments for providing sales and trade tax exemption, so that interest of the Industry can be sustained in
 extending the benefit of technologies to the larger sections of the society.
(Para 56)
Action Taken by the Department
            With reference to the suggestion of the Committee for taking initiatives with the State Governments for the Sales
 and Trade Tax exemption, a team of CFTRI Scientists have been formed to pursue these issues with the respective State
 Governments and CFTRI is making all efforts to bring in mechanisms for large adaptation of technologies by the State
 development departments/agencies.
 
Comments
            The Committee observes that the Department should continue its endeavours to impress upon the respective
 State Governments to waive Sales & Trade tax so that optimum exploitation of technologies can be ensured.
 
Recommendation
            The Committee suggests that the Department should emphasise on need based R&D activities for cereals,
 pulses and oilseeds to develop marketable products and technology achieving highest recovery and top quality of
 the desired constituents/parts of the raw materials processed with minimum energy spent and no pollution created.
(Para 57)
 
Action Taken by the Department
            CFTRI has always given emphasis to need based R&D activities concerning cereals, pulse and oilseeds to develop
 marketable products.  The technologies developed for primary processing of cereals, pulses and oilseeds give high priority
 to recovery with high efficiency of operation.  Nutritious and comparatively inexpensive foods have been developed
 based on oil seeds and their derived products.

INTRODUCTION
 
      I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment &
 Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Ninety-Fifth Report of the
 Committee, which relates to the Biological Diversity Bill, 2000
 
2.   In the meetings of the Committee held on the 18 th July, 15th & 16th September, 17th & 18th October, 2000 and 10th, 11th, 30th  &
 31st January, 18th & 19 th June, 10th, 11th, 12th , 13th  & 14 th September, 2001 the Secretaries / representatives of the Ministry and
 various other organizations / experts / individuals etc. having knowledge and expertise in the field tendered oral evidence on the
 various aspects related to the Biological Diversity Bill, 2000.
 
3.   The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Ministries / Departments and representatives of the various
 organizations for rendering their valuable views / clarification sought by the Members of the Committee.
 
4.   The Committee considered and adopted the draft Report at its meeting held on    28
th November, 2001.
 
 
NEW DELHI;                                                                                     C. RAMACHANDRAIAH
November 28, 2001                                                                                                    Chairman,
   Parliamentary Standing Committee on
 Science & Technology ,Environment & Forests.     
   
 
 
R E P O R T
 
1.   The Chairman Rajya Sabha in pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee
 referred*the Biological Diversity Bill, 2000**as introduced in the Lok Sabha on 15th May, 2000 and pending therein to the Standing
 Committee on Science & Technology Environment & Forests for examination and report.
2.   At their first meeting held on 18 th July, 2000, the Committee held general discussion on the various provisions of the Bill and
 referred to the importance and urgency of the task before the Committee. The Committee had also the benefit of presentation on the
 subject by the Secretary and other Officers of the Ministry of Environment & Forests on the Bill under reference and the need to
 bring the proposed legislation. The Committee observed that the Bill dealt with an important issue and required a thorough study. 
 The Committee then considered its future course of action and decided that a press Communique might be issued in all the national
 dailies both in English and Hindi versions inviting therein memoranda on the subject matter of the Bill from the interested
 organizations/institutions/individuals having knowledge and expertise in the field or otherwise interested in the subject.  The
 Committee also desired that the contents of the Press Communique be given wide publicity through All India Radio and
 Doordarshan.  The Chairman also requested the Members to suggest the names of organisations, individuals, etc. from whom
 memoranda might be invited. Besides, the Committee directed the Secretariat to request the Ministry of Environment & Forests to
 forward to this Secretariat a list of Organizations/Experts/ Individuals in the field along with their complete addresses.  The
 Committee also desired that they might undertake an on-the-spot study visit to various parts of the country to elicit the views of the
 representatives of various organisations, associations and general public on the subject matter of   the Bill.
Accordingly, a press communiqué inviting memoranda etc.  was issued on 18
th August 2000.
As per decision taken by the Committee letters inviting Memoranda containing comments/suggestions on the provisions of the
 Bill were also issued to Organizations/Experts/ Individuals in the field whose names were furnished by the Ministry of Environment
 & Forests.
3.   In all 35 Memoranda containing comments/suggestions on the various provisions of the Bill were received by the Committee
 from various associations/organizations and individuals etc. which were sent to the Ministry of Environment & Forests for their
 Comments/observations (Annexure-II).
4.   Biodiversity or the variety of living organism is the foundation on which life on earth sustains itself. This variety among living

fdfdfdf
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/95threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:20:33]
 organisms extends to both variety within each species, between different species and ecosystems, which support them. Biodiversity
 is a fundamental necessity of nature to maintain the ecological balance on the planet. No single organism can exist on its own; each
 one depends on numerous others in myriad ways to sustain itself and its kind. This interdependence between organisms, often
 referred to as the web of life, is greatly endangered today as a result of our insensitive tampering with the nature's well-preserved
 checks and balances.
5.   Scientists and conservationists all over the world agree that life on Earth faces enormous risks due to rapid and large-scale loss of
 bio-diversity, unprecedented in the history of humankind.
______________________________________________________________________________
*    Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part II dated the 28th June, 2000.
** Annexure-I
Moreover, diversity has an insurance value, for it widens the range of environmental conditions under which different species can
 perform key ecological and economic functions. India is endowed with a rich biodiversity, as the country is well spread out in a
 wide variety of climatic zones and habitats that range from tropical rainforests to alpine vegetation, and from temperate forests to
 coastal wetlands. Eastern Himalayas and Western Ghats are two of world's 18 biodiversity hotspots, where bulk of Earth's plants
 and animals are found. India is one of the twelve mega-biodiversity areas of the world with over 45,000 wild species of plants and
 77,000 wild species of animals on record.
6.   India's rich biodiversity that exists today is estimated to be the result of over three and half million years of evolution, which
 involved speciation, migration, plate tectonics, natural holocausts, extinction and of late the human influences, interventions and
 disturbances. But during the last century, biodiversity has been drastically falling due to indiscriminate rise in human activities in
 and around forests, wetlands, rivers and oceans.
7.   There are fewer varieties of wild plants and animals today than a few decades before, and the lost varieties are gone forever. A
 high degree of endemism makes the Indian biodiversity particularly vulnerable to extinction. In last few decades, at least 50 percent
 of India’s forests have been cut down, 70 percent of its water bodies have been polluted, its grasslands cultivated and its coasts
 degraded. In addition, hunting, overexploitation, poisoning by pesticides, excessive botanical and zoological collection,
 displacement by exotic varieties and a host of other activities have taken a heavy toll of biodiversity. Already, 23 species, which
 include cheetah, the lesser one-horned rhino, and pink-headed duck, have become extinct in India, and many more species of plants
 and animals might have vanished without anyone noticing them. Nearly 750 species of plants and animals appear to be on the verge
 of extinction and the Gangetic river dolphin, Red Panda, Lion tailed macaque and the Bengal tiger are some of the highly
 endangered animals in the country today.
8.   Indiscriminate and illegal trade in wild plants and animals, combined with ecologically insensitive development projects,
 explosive growth in human population and the resultant pressure on the natural resources, are the main reasons of chronic
 biodiversity loss in India during last few decades. Specific causes have always varied with ecosystems. Even after independence,
 forests continued to be plundered in the country on a large-scale by the industries in construction, furniture making, paper & pulp,
 mining and textiles, until very recently when most of the remaining forest cover in India has come under the protection of national
 parks and wildlife sanctuaries. An important cause of habitat destruction in the Eastern Himalayan states like Sikkim and Arunachal
 Pradesh is jhum, or shifting cultivation, which is practised in 70% of the land in the region. Some experts believe that given
 sufficient area to operate, and long enough fallow periods, jhum cultivation can be sustainable. However, population pressures have
 led to a shortening of the fallow cycle, which has made this form of cultivation totally unsustainable. The Forest Survey of India has
 recently estimated that 57% of the forests have been lost due to shifting cultivation.
9.   Human interference has intensified a natural process like siltation to a degree where it has become a major threat to the wetlands
 in India. The Dal lake receives 80 000 tonnes of silt from Talbal Nalla every year, while the Chilka lake has been shrinking by
 roughly 1.5 square kilometres every year since 1925 because of siltation and the reclamation of marginal areas. Another process
 affecting wetlands is eutrophication the process by which a body of water becomes either naturally or by pollution, rich in dissolved
 nutrients and often shallow with a seasonal deficiency in dissolved oxygen.  Chilika lake in Orissa, for instance, is infested  with the
 weed Potamogeton pectinatus as a result of eutrophication of its water from the fertilizer run-offs regularly flowing in from the
 surrounding farmlands. Further, intensive fishing in rivers, lakes and seas can reduce fish populations to such an extent that they are
 no longer able to regenerate a viable number for their continued survival. The best example of this is the whale shark, which is now
 being mercilessly caught in most coastal regions of India for both eating and its fins, which command a huge price in the
 international markets.
10.  Biodiversity is India's real wealth and its resource base determines and ensures this country's survival and growth. Therefore,
 conserving and protecting this natural endowment is our primary necessity. Historically, our culture and civilization evolved and
 edified around this immense natural wealth. Our present population, with nearly 80% still directly dependent on agriculture and
 forests, cannot afford to be different.
11.  All India Ayurvedic Congress Manufacturers Association, New Delhi in their representation to the Committee submitted that the
 definition of “ commercial utilization” should be added as follows:
“Commercial utilization means end uses of biological researches for commercial utilization such as drug, industrial enzymes,

 food flavours, fragrance, cosmetics, emulsifiers, oleoresins, colours, extracts and genes used from improving crops and livestock
 through breeding or genetic interaction and shall not include traditional practices in use in any agriculture, horticulture, poultry,
 dairy farming or animal husbandry and beekeeping.
They stated that the definition of value added products should also be added as follows:
Value added products/means “Product which may contain portions/extracts of plants in recognizable and physically inseparable

They were of the view that the definition of “Biological researches” should also be incorporated in the Bill as follows, “Bio

12.  Dr. Ranjitsinh of Indian National Trust for Art and Cultural Heritage (INTACH), New Delhi in his presentation on 19 th June
 2001 expressed concern over the provisions of the Bill which were in conflict with  certain existing laws particularly those dealing
 with conservation of Biological Diversity in the field such as, Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, Indian Forest Act, 1927, the Forest
 Conservation Act, 1980 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and   suggested that this Bill instead of overlapping should
 complement the existing laws.  He also expressed his concern over non-inclusion of Biological components from the Agriculture,
 Forestry or Fishery in the Bill.   He was of the view that the Bill did not answer as to who decides as to what was sustainable?  The
 National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) couldn’t decide for every area.  So State Biodiversity Board (SBB) should be empowered to
 decide in consultation with the Biodiversity Management Committee (BMC) created by local bodies i.e. panchayats, municipalities
 etc.  what was sustainable.  The question then arose whether BMCs would be technically qualified to decide what was ecologically
 sustainable use of biodiversity and whether it would be able to enforce that sustainable use and in the process forego revenue and
 also earn the ire of their own people who would be out to exploit the biological resources for not just personal bonafide use but for
 commercial purposes?  If not, what could be the safeguards?  “Sustainable use” means the use of biological resources after
 ascertaining on a scientific basis the harvestable   surplus of   biological   resources  in  a   given  ecosystem  after  ensuring  that  
 the productivity and ecological security of the said ecosystem, biome and biological resources were maintainable at the optimum
 level on a long term basis and also ensure that in the harvesting and removal of such harvestable surplus no adverse impact was
 caused on other biota or the land in terms of Clause 7 of the Bill.  He submitted before the Committee that it should be omitted.  It
 was a totally impracticable and indeed an absurd provision.  As agriculture, fisheries, horticulture, animal husbandry etc. were also
 commercial utilization of biological resources as defined under Clause (2)b, no person who was not a local could cultivate crops,
 grow fruit, do animal husbandry or commercial fishing, establish an atta chakki or do any research in biological sciences without
 giving prior intimation to the concerned State Biodiversity Board.  This section was not simply implementable but would also cause
 hardship and corruption. 
13.  Arya Vaidya Sala, Kottakkal, Kerala made following suggestions for consideration of the Committee that Clauses 7, 8, 17, 18,
 22 and 40 be modified in view of giving sufficient protection to Ayurveda and its practitioners and also by ensuring trouble free
 access and availability of biological resources for activities related to people’s health. They had submitted that the provisions of the
 Bill should earmark financial support from the Consolidated Fund for the development and maintenance of biological resources.
14.  All India Biotech Association, New Delhi made following suggestions for consideration of the Committee:-
(i)         The proposed Bill should concentrate on Sustainable Use of Biological Resources and formulate the policy for
 replenishment of Biological Resources used.  Guidelines for Sustainable Uses of Biological Resources and for
 replenishment of Biological Resources could be administered by the NBA.
(ii)        Reaffirming the ownership of the entire Nation as such over the Biological Resources, Equitable Sharing of Benefits
 should be restricted only to royalty payments for commercialisation of Biological Resources.
(iii)       Proposals for transfer of technology and joint ownership and relocation of production facilities should be dropped.
(iv)       The Biotech industry be granted representation in the NBA and the State Biodiversity Board.
(v)        No prior approvals should be required to be taken for commercialisation of a Biological Resource.  In the present
 competitive scenario confidentiality of research and development should be granted highest priority.
(vi)       NBA should be empowered to sponsor scientists for generating intellectual wealth from the Biological Resources
 and create healthy competition for research and development.
(vii)      While fixing rates of royalties, due consideration should be given to R&D efforts put in by various commercial
 players in developing a commercial product from the Biological Resources.  This would avoid the cascading of
 costs making the end products out of reach of the common man.
(viii)      Companies with minority foreign equity or foreign management should be treated as Indian Companies under the
 Bill.  This is essential to ensure technical advancement of the country, which could then be used for commercial
 good of all.
15.  The Committee undertook study visits to Bangalore, Goa, Pune, Mumbai, Ahmedabad from 15
th to 26 th September,
