Groundwater targeting
 
12.       Remote sensing is an important aspect of space technology which has proved useful in many areas such as flood
 monitoring, mapping forest cover and wastelands, drought assessment, groundwater targetting, fisheries forecast, etc. Several
 remote sensing application projects are being carried out by       the Department of Space and the user Departments as part of
 the Remote Sensing Application Mission (RSAM). The Committee evinced keen interest in application projects in the areas
 of groundwater targetting and fisheries forecast. As regards use of remote sensing in water resource management, the
 Committee was told that use of Space based imageries are of great importance in conservation and optimal use of water in
 India.  These are: predication of snow melt runoff; identification of ground water potential both in terms of quantity and
 quality; assessment of causes of pollution of water; sedimentation, etc.  It was also explained to the Committee that by the
 range of information obtained from Space imageries on types of soil, geomorphology, water, and wasteland. Watershed
 characteristics land use, agricultural, meteorological and forestry information, etc. a long-term strategy for land and water
 conservation can be chalked out to combat drought. The Secretary of the Department also informed  the Committee that under
 the Integrated Mission for Sustainable Development (IMSD), pilot studieson land and water resources in some drought prone
 districts were undertaken. Encouraged by the results,        this study was recommended to be extended to additional districts in
 the country which are perennially affected by drought, floods; as also certain other areas which fall within hill and tribal
 regions. These  districts have to be covered under three phases. In Phase-1, 6 districts have been covered for which data have
 already been generated and implementation taken up.* 15 Districts are proposed to be covered in Phase-II for which Action
 Plans am being finalised.** In Phase III, 136 districts are proposed to be covered for which study has been initiated and
 Action Plans would be finalised within a period of 3-4 years. *** The Committee was also informed that
 hydrogeomorphological maps obtained from remote sensing imagery have been utilised for identification of ground water
 potential zones for all the districts in the country on a mapping scale of 1:250,000 under the National Drinking Water Mission
 and these maps were given to the Ministry of Rural Development. For some of the problem districts, large scale maps have
 also been prepared. This activity of Department has led to a great success in identifying ground water. The Committee was
 told that as against the success rate of 40-45% achieved by the traditional method, borewells drilled on the basis of satellite
 data have led to a success rate of 90-95%. It proves the efficacy and commercial viability of the Space based data in this
 regard.While commending the efforts of the Department initiated under the IMSD which cover at present 45% of the
 geographical area of the country, the Committee feels that the Government should make available more funds through public
 finance institutions like banks, insurance companies etc. so that more area can be covered under this programme in view of
 the efficacy and the cost-effectiveness of the technology.
 
Potential Fisheries Zones (PFZs)
 
13. The Committee was informed that data derived from satellite imageries are also utilized to identify Potential Fisheries
 Zones (PFZs). The PFZs charts are prepared from the sea surface temperature data derived from satellite imageries. The PFZ
 information obtained from satellite imageries is, at present, disseminated through the AIR, in the local language, for the
 benefit of fishermen; and it has been found that generally fishermen who make use of this information are able to increase
 their catches by 2 or 3 times. The Department agreed with the Committee that adopting method for identifying the
 phytoplankton concentration would further improve the accuracy of prediction of PFZs. The Department of Space is
 coordinating its efforts with the Department of Ocean Development to develop an ocean colour monitor payload which can be
 incorporated on board the IRS Satellites. This could help in identifying phytoplankton which is the main source of food for
 many types of fishes. The Committee, while appreciating the efforts of the Department in the area of making available
 satellite based data for identifying PFZs, feels that the Department may also evolve a suitable programme to effectively tap
 the potential of space based information for deep-sea fishing. The Committee recommends that the Department should accord
 priority to the designing and developing the ocean colour monitor payload which could be put on board future IRS satellite as
 this would lead to more accurate predictions about PFZs.
 
Indigenisation
 
14. Space technology being one of the most advanced and useful area ideally calls for self-reliance and a significant effort to
 produce file systems, sub-systems and products indigenously. The Committee wanted to know as to how much of

The Committee is happy tonote that achieving self reliance in Space Technology is one of the vowed aims of the Department,

Linkages with Industries
 
15. Establishing linkages with industries has been one of the major thrusts of the Department of Space. The Department has
 transferred several technologies to Indian industries. The Committee wanted to know as to what specific actions have been
 initiated to strengthen the linkages with industries. The Secretary of the Department informed that, from the very beginning,
 concerted efforts have been made to involve the Indian industry, both in the private and public sector, in the Space
 programme . There are, at present, about 500 industries, most of them in the private sector, contributing to the space
 programme. Flow of funds from space programme to the industry is to the tune of Rs. 2.50 crores annually. Major space
 hardware for PSLV and GSLV, which includes hardware for the Cryogenic segment have been contracted to industry,
 including those in private sector such as L&T, Walchand Industries, Godrej, NOCIL, Andhra Sugar etc. So far, 216
 technologies/processes developed under the space programme have been transferred to industry. The expertise built up, and
 the infrastructure established, in these industries are now being commercially exploited. The Committee was further told that
 the Department had earned Rs. 15 lakhs in 1991-92, Rs 19 lakhs in 1992-93 and Rs. 25 lakhs in 1993-94 from royalties and
 nominal technology fee from recipients of the spin-off technologies. The Committee notes that though the earnings of the
 Department on this score appear to be meagre, this has, however, got a multiplier effect. The Committee is happy to note that
 the money so earned is being ploughed back for R & D and technology development.
 
Linkages, with Universities
 
16.  Space science research under the Indian Space Programme encompasses a wide spectrum of activities including study of
 cosmic rays, astronomical investigations, using space and ground based systems, study of meteorites and lunar samples and
 physical observations of sun. Another major branch of activity relates to the study of the earth's atmospheric system through
 rockets, balloons and orbiting space systems. When Committee asked if there was any programme for starting post-graduate
 courses in atmospheric sciences in Universities, the Secretary, Department of Space told that apart from what is already
 ongoing, post-graduate courses and research in atmospheric sciences have been taken up by the Gujarat University in
 Ahmedabad, Kerala University in Thiruvanthapurarm and SV university Tirupati, which draw support from the Centres of the
 Department of Space located at these places. About 100 universities participated actively in the workshop on atmospheric
 sciences, organised at Tirupati recently, as part of the utilisation programme of MST (Mesosphere-Stratosphere-
Troposlghere) Radar. The Committee was further informed that under the sponsored Research Programme-- (RESPOND) the
 Department of Space has been promoting research projects in space technology/science/applications since 1976. So far, more
 than 250 projects have been funded in 75 Universities from all parts of the country. Three space technology cells have already
 been established at Bangalore, Madras and Bombay for ensuring advanced research in some of the critical areas. Efforts have
 been made to establish space technology cells in IIT, Kharagpur and BIT, Ranchi. Space Science Education Centre has been
 established at Ahmedabad. The Punjab State Remote Sensing Centre has been established as part of the Punjab agricultural
 University. Under the scheme for promoting remote sensing technology in educational curricula, both at college and school
 level, action has been taken jointly with UGC and NCERT. Under the IRO Geosphere-Biosphere programme, Universities are
 being encouraged to work in several related research areas. Jadavpur University has been involved in some Space science and
 technology (including Onboard processor development) areas. The Committee, while appreciating the efforts of the
 Department in promoting academic linkages, emphasises that there is a need to cover more universities at least by starting
 post-graduate courses in space/atmospheric sciences with a view to preparing more and more scientists who could assist in the
 area of space R & D.

GRAMSAT
 
GRAMSAT is a satellite system which intends to provide useful information to the people particularly in the rural
 areas by broadcasting development oriented programmes in the field of education, rural development, health, etc. It is
 envisaged under this programme to provide 6 to 8 TV channels for this purpose. The Committee noted that the department
 could utilize a sum of Rs. 10 lakhs  which was only one-tenth of the total amount provided in the budgetary outlay for this
 programme for the year 1993-94. For the year 1994-95 budget estimates for this programme are kept again at Rs. 1.00 crore.
 The Committee wanted to know as to how the Department proposes to utilise the funds provided for this project.  The
 Secretary, Department of Space informed that since the GRAMSAT project is yet to be defined, and formally sanctioned by
 the Government, the budgetary provision is only notional. While it is possible to define the satellite now, it is to be ensured
 that the user ministries (Rural Development, Human Resources Development, Information & Broadcasting, Health etc.) are
 geared up with facilities and software on the ground for its utilisation. Efforts are under way in this regard. The Committee is
 of the view that the GRAMSAT project can play a meaningful role in the lives of our people, particularly those living in the
 remote and rural areas. The Committee, therefore, would like the Department of Space to give full information about the
 potential of this project to the Ministries/Departments (both at the Centre and the States), which are concerned with
 socio­economic development. Such a contact would enable the Department to develop proper formats for the utilisation of
 the GRAMSAT system, when it is implemented, hopefully soon.
 
Second launch pad
 
18. The committee noted that Rs. 3.00 crores provided for the development of second launch pad and common facilities at
 Sriharikota for PSLV and GSLV launches could not be utilised during the year 1993-94. Budgetary outlay for the purpose for
 the yea
r 1994-95 has been kept at Rs. 2.00 crores. The Committee enquired about the non-utilisation of the amount sanctioned
 during the year 1993-94 for developing a second launch pad. The Committee was informed that to meet the immediate
 requirement of the GSLV, the Department had decided to augment the existing PSLV launch pad by adding the Cryogenic
 fluid handling facility. However, in view of the increasing number of launches per year, the need to have a second launch pad
 cannot be ignored. The Committee, therefore, strongly feels that due priority should be accorded to the development of the
 second launch pad at SHAR.
 
Housing for staff
 
19. The Committee asked the Department as to why the percentage of satisfaction of housing for scientific and technical staff
 was only 29.8% and why the funds provided for this purpose for the year 1993-94 could not be utilised fully. The Secretary,
 Department of Space informed the Committee that the aim of the Department at present is to provide at least 50% satisfaction
 for its staff. The funds provided, however, could not be utilised fully because longer time was taken in planning the activity in
 procuring the necessary statutory clearances. The Committee is of the view that providing accommodation near the work
 place attracts high quality talents and increases the efficiency of personnel working in any organization. The Committee,
 therefore, feels that the Department should make earnest efforts to achieve the target of providing 50% satisfaction for its
 employee within a reasonable period of time.
 
20. After making a detailed Scrutiny of the Demands for Grants of the Department of Space and assessing the progress of
 various important Programmes and projects administered by it the Committee recommends that the Demands for Grants of
 Rs. 755.00 crores, as sought by the Department of Space for the year 1994-95, under demand No. 88, are in order and may be
 approved.
NEW DELHI
April 15, 1994
 
SYED SIBTEY RAZI
Chairman
Committee on Science and Technology , Environment and Forests.

R E P O R T
1.         The Space Commission and Department of Space (DOS) were set up in 1972 to promote the development and application of
 Space science & technology for national development. The DOS is responsible for implementing the policies framed by Space
 Commission.  These are carried out through Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the Grant-in-aid institutions.  ISRO has
 established Nine Centres/Units for carrying out research and development activities as well as for undertaking various projects and
 programmes in the area of Satellites, Launch Vehicles, Space applications and Space science research.
2.         The Indian Space programme is characterized by a vision to use space technology for national development.  The primary
 objective of the Space Programme has been to establish operational space services in a self-reliant manner in the thrust areas of
 satellite communications, satellite based information to assist in Survey/management of natural resources and satellite meteorological
 applications.  The indigenous development of satellites, launch vehicles and associated ground segment for providing these services
 is integral to these objectives.
3.         The Indian space programme has established two indigenously built operational space systems, namely, the Indian Remote
 Sensing Satellites (IRS) and the Indian National Satellite System (INSAT).  The constellation of Indian Remote Sensing Satellites
 comprises of five satellites viz., IRS-1B, IRS-P3, IRS-1C, IRS-1D and India’s first oceanographic satellite (IRS-P4) providing a
 range of spatial resolutions, spectral resolutions and coverage cycle.  The IRS system is among the best in the world for generating
 information useful for natural resources management besides providing data worldwide.  The multi-purpose INSAT satellite system,
 with currently four satellites in orbit viz., INSAT-2C, 2DT, 2E and 3B, is one of the largest domestic communication satellite
 systems in the world and is the mainstay for television broadcasting services, for remote areas and transmission of developmental
 programmes in rural areas, educational training of developmental programmes in rural areas and educational training.  India’s Polar
 Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) is well proven through four successive successful flights and provides launch capability to orbit
 Remote Sensing satellites of 1.2 ton class in polar sun-synchronous orbits.
4.         The first successful test flight of Geo-synchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) from Sriharikota on April 18, 2001 was
 the most significant milestone of the Indian space programme during the year 2001-02.  The launch unequivocally demonstrated
 India’s capability to place satellites into geo-synchronous transfer orbits.  India is among the six nations in the world to achieve such
 a capability.  The launch of GSLV is the culmination of efforts of several DOS centers and other institutions that involved complex
 interfaces between scientific and technological disciplines, industries and research institutions.
5.         Another important milestone during the year was the successful flight of PSLV-C3 on October 22, 2001 from Sriharikota.  In
 this fifth consecutively successful flight, PSLV placed three satellites –– India’s Technology Experiment Satellite, TES, Belgian
 Project for on-Board Autonomy (PROBA) and German Bispectral and Infrared Remote Detection (BIRD) into their intended polar
 sun-synchronous orbit.  The requirement of a higher orbit for the Belgian PROBA compared to other two satellites was successfully
 met by a flight manoeuvre.  Both German and Belgian satellites were launched under commercial agreements.  The flight has clearly
 established the reliability of PSLV for launching not only the Indian remote sensing satellites, but also, multiple  satellites  thus
 making it an attractive  vehicle for the  international  space community to
launch their satellites.  PSLV is also planned to be used for a geo-synchronous transfer orbit mission for launching India’s METSAT
 in 2002-03.
6.         The INSAT system for telecommunication, television broadcasting and meteorology has received further boost during the year
 with the successful launch of INSAT-3C on January 24, 2002.  INSAT-3C will not only augment the present INSAT system but also
 continue the services of some of the satellites that need to be phased out at the end of their mission life.
7.         Besides, the remote sensing applications continue to expand to several new areas; the data has been used to assess damage due
 to floods, earthquakes, etc and for helping in relief operations.  The announcement of Remote Sensing Data Policy (RSDP) during
 the year will help to streamline the availability of remote sensing data from Indian and foreign satellites to users in India.
8.         In the field of space sciences, the cryogenic sampler that had been developed by ISRO for Geosphere-Biosphere Programme,
 has been used to detect micro-organisms in the stratosphere, which could have far reaching implications on the understanding of the
 origin of life on earth.  Detailed analysis of the samples collected were going on in scientific research laboratories in India and
 abroad.
9.         Educational and research institutions in India continue to participate in the space programme taking up projects under the
 Sponsored Research scheme of DOS.  During the year, 22 new projects were initiated under the scheme.  The task team constituted
 to study the feasibility and scientific objectives for undertaking an unmanned mission to the moon has made substantial progress in
 their work.
10.       The Committee  observes that  with sustained efforts of DOS end-to-end capability in space for vital application in
 communications, broadcasting, meteorology and natural resource information which have direct relevance for national development,
 has secured India a unique place in the International Community.  However, the committee is of the view that front ranking scientific
 investigations in the field of astronomy, atmospheric sciences and long term climatic research using satellites, balloons, sounding

GEO STATIONARY SATELLITE SERVICES
17.        The Geo-stationary Satellites which are placed in an orbit, about 36,000 km over the equator are used for telecommunication,
 television broadcasting and meteorological services.  India established the geo-stationary satellite system, namely, Indian National
 Satellite (INSAT) system in 1983.  INSAT is one of the largest domestic communication satellite systems in the Asia Pacific Region
 with five satellites, INSAT-2C, INSAT-2DT, INSAT-2E, INSAT-3B and INSAT-3C in operation.  INSAT system also includes
 eleven transponders that have been leased from other agencies to augment the INSAT capacity. Beside, INSAT-1D which was,
 launched in June 1990, is used for meteorological imaging and a few other services even after eleven years of its operation. INSAT-
2B launched in July 1993 which was decommissioned from regular services during the year, is still used for Satellite Aided Search
 and Rescue and Data Relay Services and two of its transponders are used for scientific experiments.
            One of the major accomplishments during the year was the realisation of INSAT-3C, and its launch on board an Ariane-4

25.        Telemedicine is a recent application of the satellite communications that makes specialized medical facility available to the
 remote areas of the country.  The expert consultancy could be obtained for the patients in remote areas from specialists in speciality 
 hospitals in cities.  Five VSAT terminals have been set up for telemedicine in Chamarajanagar, Kenchanahalli, Bangalore, Kolkata
 and Tripura which are networked with a hub on shared basis.  Port Blair in Andaman Nicobar islands, and Leh in Jammu & Kashmir
 and Lakshadweep are also being provided with telemedicine facilities.  ISRO has already provided its SPACENET terminals to a
 private hospital at Chennai and a rural Hospital at Argonda in Andhra Pradesh for telemedicine network.  The Hospital at ISRO’s
 SHAR Centre, at Sriharikota is also being connected to this spacenet for telemedicine.
26.        A Standard Time and Frequency Signal Dissemination Service (STFSDS), using a Radio Networking (RN) type of CxS
 carrier on INSAT-2B, is being operated by the National Physical Laboratory (NPL).  This service is available round-the-clock in a
 broadcast mode in S-band and it can be received on a system consisting of a 2.4 m diameter antenna, a front-end converter, an FM
 demodulator and a microprocessor controlled signal decoder.  The STFSDS consists of a train of frequency modulated 5 kHz burst
 signal.  The time has a precision better than one micro-second and an accuracy better than 20 micro seconds.
27.        An exclusive 24 hours Educational TV (Gyandarshan) is being operated by Doordarshan.  Curriculum-based programmes are
 produced with active involvement of State educational active involvement of State educational administrators and teachers and
 programmes for school children are produced by the State Institutes of Educational Technology (SIET) –– Marathi at Pune, Gujarati
 at Ahmedabad, Oriya at Bhubaneshwar and Telugu at Hyderabad –– which are relayed by all transmitters in the concerned Sates. 
 Hindi programmes are produced at State Institutes of Educational Technology at Delhi, Lucknow and Patna.  Programmes for
 university students are produced by Education Media Research Centres and Audio Visual Research Centres at different places. 
 These programmes provide quality education, within the reach of students in small towns and villages.  Syllabus-based programmes
 for students enrolled in Indira Gandhi National Open University (IGNOU) are also relayed on this channel.
28.       The Committee is happy to note the introduction of Telemedicine through  application of the satellite communication. 
 However, it recommends that the establishment of a tele-medicine network connecting district health care hospitals to specialized
 health centers in cities supported by INSAT transponders should be a thrust area of the application.

EARTH OBSERVATION SYSTEM
29.        Earth Observations System (EOS) is an important space infrastructure that has been established by the Department of Space
 (DOS).  This system,  which was commissioned in 1988 with the launch of Indian Remote Sensing Satellite, IRS-1A, has the world’s
 largest constellation of five satellites (IRS-1C, IRS-1D, IRS-P3, IRS-P4 and TES) presently in operation.  It provides space-based
 remote sensing data in a variety of spatial resolutions and spectral bands meeting the needs of various applications.
            The EOS definition, development, operation and its application are co-ordinated by the National Natural Resources
 Management System (NNRMS), for which DOS is the nodal agency.  NNRMS is an integrated resource management system aimed
 at optimal utilization of country’s natural resources by a systematic inventory of resource availability using EOS data in conjunction
 with conventional techniques. NNRMS is supported at the national level by the Planning Committee of NNRMS (PC-NNRMS),
 which provides guidelines for implementation of the system and also oversees the progress of remote sensing applications for natural
 resources management in the country. 
30.        The Committee has been informed that the IRS-P4 (Oceansat), successfully launched on May 26, 1999,  is  oriented towards
 oceanographic, land and atmospheric applications.  The data from IRS-P4 also help in conducting specific experiments that are of
 relevance for future developments.
            The IRS-P5 (Cartosat-1) satellite envisages an advanced Space based mission with enhanced spatial resolution for large-scale
 thematic mapping applications and to further stimulate applications in the newer areas of cartography, urban management, disaster
 assessment and relief planning and management, environmental assessment and GIS applications.  The satellite is scheduled for
 launch on-board PSLV in 2003-2004.
            The objective of IRS-P6 (Resourcesat) is to provide continued remote sensing data services on an operational basis for
 integrated land and water resources management at micro-level with enhanced multi spectral / spatial coverage and stereo viewing
 capability.  The satellite is targeted for launch in 2002-2003 on-board PSLV.
The IRS-IIA (Cartosat-2) Project envisages design, development, fabrication, testing and launching of an advanced remote
 sensing satellite carrying on-board a Panchromatic camera capable of providing scene-specific imageries of normal 1 m spatial
 resolution to meet the information requirements for urban and rural planning, micro water shed development, geo-engineering
 applications, etc.  The budgetary allocation in the year 2002-03 for IRS-II (Cartosat-2) satellite has significantly gone up to RS.60.56
 crores as against Rs.40 crores and 38.30 crores last year at both BE and RE stages respectively. When asked to explain the reasons
 for  this significant hike, the Department informed that the IRS-II (Cartosat-2) project was initiated in June 2000. The total approved
 cost of the project is Rs.216.73 crores. The preliminary design has been completed and the procurement action for major items have
 been initiated. The activities  planned for 2002-03 include procurement of major contractual items, parts and materials (substantial
 part) and subsystem development. Accordingly, enhanced budget provision has been sought in BE 2002-03.
31.       The Committee appreciates that the  thrust in the Earth Observations application programmes during 10
th plan would be on the
 Natural Resources Census (NRC)  thus addressing the need for a regular census activity of the nation’s Natural Resources (NR) and
 generation of a “State of the Country’s Environment Report”. The Committee notes that the system would also assess “NR Hot-
Spots” that are cause for concern and lead to identification of environmentally sensitive areas which require urgent conservation /
 management action.  However, the Committee recommends that priority should be given to establishment of the National Spatial
 Data Infrastructure (NSDI) in a phased manner mainly as a spatial data repository with specialized information services on natural
 resources.  The Committee feels that the Department should ensure that  Earth Observations data are used for developmental
 programmes by various user agencies which may include rural roads connectivity analysis, drinking water mission, water shed
 development programme, urban / city master plan preparation, coastal zone regulation and other developmental projects involving
 private sectors.  Perhaps a long-term, multidisciplinary, operational oceanographic database for prediction of the ocean state and
 contributing to climate change and variability studies may be useful.
DISASTER MANAGEMENT    
32.        Landslide Hazard Zonation (LHZ) mapping on 1:25,000 scale is being carried out for all major pilgrim and tourist routes in
 the Himalayan region in Uttaranchal and Himachal Pradesh.  Data base has been created for the entire 2000 km long corridor and
 LHZ maps has been prepared.   The routes covered  include:  Rishikesh-Rudraprayag-Chamoli-Badrinath, Rishikesh – Gaumukh,
 Rudraprayag – Okhimath and Pithroragarh – Malpa, all in Uttaranchal; Shimla – Manali, Shimla-Sumdo and Dalhousie – Brahmaur
 in Himachal Pradesh.  The maps are used by State Public Works Departments (PWD), Border Roads Organisation and some NGOs.
Gujarat Earthquake:  The Space based imagery along with aerial remote sensing provided inputs to the Gujarat State
 Administration during the Earthquake in January 2001 in terms of locating the worst affected towns, to assess the changes in the
 terrain features and damage assessment.  The satellite news gathering terminal was also moved from the Space Applications Centre
 and set up at Bhuj which was the only link till February 2, 2001 to co-ordinate rescue and relief operations.
33.        The Committee observes that the Disaster Management Support (DMS) should be a key area of space applications.

SPACE TRANSPORTATION
34.        Space Transportation system includes the satellite launch vehicles to place satellites like INSAT and IRS and scientific
 satellites in the required orbits as well as the sounding rockets for carrying out short duration scientific experiments.  India made a
 modest beginning in this area with the launch of a 75 mm diameter sounding rocket in 1963 for investigation of ionosphere over the
 geo-magnetic equator over Thumba, near Thiruvananthapuram.  Since then, the country has established a substantial capability in the
 design, development and operationalisation of a series of sounding rockets for scientific investigations, Polar Satellite Launch
 Vehicle (PSLV), for launching Indian remote sensing satellites and Geo-synchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV), for
 launching geo-stationary communication satellites.
            The maiden developmental flight of GSLV-D1 on April 18, 2001 which successfully injected the GSAT-1 satellite in Geo-
synchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO) is a historic milestone for the Indian Space Programme.  This has validated the complex vehicle
 and mission design aspects, soundness of a number  of new vehicle systems such as cryo stage, liquid strap-ons, hot separation of
 first stage,  large diameter payload firing, launch hold release mechanism, launch pad facilities for handling and filling earth storable
 and cryogenic stage has been completed and based on its outcome the preparation for the second developmental flight of GSLV is in
 progress.  The subsequent flights, GSLV-D2 and GSLV-D3, respectively carrying G.SAT-2 and G.SAT-3, are targeted for launch in
 the timeframe 2002-2003.
35.        The objective Cryo Upper Stage (CUS) Project is to realize an indigenous cryogenic stage employing liquid oxygen and
 liquid hydrogen as oxidizer and fuel respectively for upper stage of GSLV.  In this technologically complex area, significant
 developmental efforts have been carried out resulting in the realization of the second cryogenic engine.  A series of ground
 qualification tests are planned to evaluate the engine.  The first flight of indigenous cryo stage is targeted for flight-testing by GSLV
 in 2003-2004.
The budgetary allocation amounting to Rs.16.38 crores for Cryogenic Upper Stage Project (CUSP) in BE 2002-03 are less as
 compared to Rs.21.30 crores and Rs.20.31 crores at BE and RE stages respectively in 2001-02. Asked whether this would affect the
 project adversely the Department informed  that the total budget approved for the Cryogenic Upper Staged Project was  of Rs.335.89
 crores. The cumulative expenditure of the project till March 2002 is Rs.288.48 crores i.e. Rs.85.9%. As substantial part of the total
 project cost has already been incurred, the budget sought in BE 2002-03 is relatively less compared to RE provision of last year. The
 budget provision in 2002-03 is based on the planned progress in engine and stage fabrication activities and hence does not affect the
 project’s progress, though it appears less compared to RE of last year.
36.        The successful launch of PSLV-C3/TES mission on October 22, 2001, was a significant milestone in the operational PSLV
 programme.  The mission met all its objectives by placing into desired orbit the main satellite – Technology Experimental Satellite
 (TES) of India and in addition two auxiliary satellites, Project for on-Board Autonomy (PROBA) of Belgium and Bispectral and
 Infrared Remote Detection (BIRD) of Germany, on a commercial basis.  With  this, PSLV has once again demonstrated the multiple
 satellite launching capability.  One significant feature of this mission was the orbit-raising manoeuvre carried out for PROBA for
 placing it in an elliptical orbit, different from the orbit of the main satellite.  A high-performance composite solid propellant upper
 stage motor for PSLV has been successfully test fired.  The PSLV C4-C6 flights are targeted for completion in 2002-2004.
37.        The Secretary informed the Committee that DOS was working on several critical technologies, which are related to Reusable
 Launch Vehicle System.  This would bring down the cost of space transport.  In this direction the Department is currently working on
 the concepts of the Reusable Transportation Vehicle, including engines, air breathing and so on.  The Secretary further informed that
 the Department has also started working on Space Capsule Recovery Module.  Explaining this he said that the idea was to place a
 Capsule in space and use it for some experiments and then retrieve it back to earth. 
38.        In the area of Launch Vehicle Development, the Committee desires that DOS should strive to complete the development
 flights and operationalise the GSLV (with indigenous cryogenic upper stage) for launching 2T INSAT class of satellites. 
 Considering the trend towards going for bigger and heavier spacecraft for satellite communications, the Department should  initiate
 development of an advanced GSLV Mk III capable of launching 4T INSAT class of satellite.  Besides, in tune with the long-term
 vision of low cost access to space, advanced R & D in Reusable Launch Vehicles (RLV) should be pursued. To this end smaller-scale
 technology demonstrator in the areas of air breathing propulsion technology and space capsule recovery missions could be planned.
LAUNCH VEHICLE INFRASTRUCTURE
39.        The launch infrastructure at SHAR Centre, Sriharikota supported the launch of GSLV-D1 and PSLV-C3 during the year.  The
 first developmental test of GSLV has completely validated the modified mobile service tower along with the propellant service
 facilities including the cryogenic propellants.  In reply to a question about present position with regard to development of Second
 Launch Pad the Department has informed that the project has made significant progress in 2001-02. The order placement for all
 major subsystems has been completed. All the civil works except part of Vehicle Assembly building and Jet Deflector duct were

 process and mechanical equipments has also commenced.

SPACE SCIENCES.
 42.       The Indian space programme encompasses research in space science besides space technology development and its
 application.  Space science research is mainly carried out at Physical Research Laboratory (PSL), at Ahmedabad, Space Physics
 Laboratory (SPL), at Thiruvananthapuram and ISRO Satellite Centre, at Bangalore.  The National Mesosphere – Stratosphere –
 Troposphere Radar Facility (NMRF) near Tirupati, which is an autonomous society established and funded by the DOS, is available
 to scientists from universities and research institutions for atmosphere research.  Space science research institutions through the
 ISRO’s Advisory Committee for Space Science (ADCOS) as well as through Sponsored Research (RESPOND) programme of DOS.
43.       The Committee observes that Space Science & Environment research has been an important component of the Indian Space
 Programme.  The Committee feels that the thrust of the Space Science Programme should be towards investigations in the new,
 emerging and challenging areas of Space Science research including Planetary Science / exploration and Micro gravity Science.  A
 dedicated and state-of-art Indian Multi-wavelength Astronomy satellite could be of immense value for detailed scientific
 investigations on celestial X-ray sources.  The Committee is also of the view that something needs to done for the study of tropical
 weather system for climate research area.
LUNAR MISSION
44.        The Committee has been given to understand that ISRO has constituted a Moon Mission Task Force to study the technical
 feasibility of various scientific proposals and to determine realistic and optimum mission objectives.  The task team comprises
 scientists and engineers from the various centres of ISRO, as well as, those from Physical Research Laboratory and Tata Institute of
 Fundamental Research. Further the task team has held elaborate discussions and was analyzing the various options of the scientific
 objectives and associated instruments to be flown, the spacecraft configuration, the spacecraft trajectory, feasibility of using India’s
 PSLV to launch the spacecraft and aspects related to cost, schedules and technology issues. The report was expected to be received in
 the near future. A decision for undertaking the mission would be taken after the report was received and reviewed. 
45.        Replying to the queries of the Members about the Lunar Mission during the presentation before the Committee the Secretary,
 DOS explained that there were many missions being contemplated to explore the various objects of solar system and this would be an
 era of planetary exploration.  To that end they were required to build up impressive capability in this space and having undertaken
 major missions there was no reason why the Department of Space should not consider the feasibility of being a part of that kind of an
 adventure, which has science in it and technological content in it.  However, he said, it would be very premature to imagine that India
 should undertake a manned mission to the moon. He added that the question of manned mission has its own implications.  A long-
term strategy of doing as a partner of planetary, not exploration, but exploitation, then quite obviously, lunar bases were very
 important.  There was a lot of thinking how to create lunar bases, how the human settlement could take place in lunar regions.   Even
 a rocket take-off would be much easier from the Moon than from the Earth.  Hydrogen is there; many other fuel elements were there. 
 It was possible to have a sustainable space to fly rockets, but Department of Space would go step by step and see where they could
 really meet.

 keep abreast of the developments in the area of IPR.

 formidable goal of achieving more patents in areas of its interest.  Also, the Department should create a Patent Facilitating Cell which

INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION
50.        International co-operation has been an important aspect of India’s Space Programme.  DOS has entered into agreements or
 signed memoranda of understanding with several countries and space agencies.  These include: Australia, Brunei, Canada, European
 Space Agency, France, Germany, Hungary, Indonesia, Peru, Russia, Syria, Sweden, Italy, Norway, U.K., U.S.A, and Ukraine.
 During the year, MOU’s were signed with China and Thailand and the MOU with European Space Agency (ESA), renewed.
            ISRO and the French National Space Agency (CNES) have entered the Phase-B of the joint satellite mission, “Megha
 Tropiques”, which is aimed at the study of the tropical atmosphere and climate.  The mission envisages joint development of
 scientific instruments to be carried on a French satellite platform (Proteus) and the satellite is programmed to  be launched by India’s
 PSLV in 2006.
            The Modular Opto-electronic Scanner (MOS) instrument from the German Aerospace Centre (DLR) which was flown on the
 Indian Remote Sensing Satellite, IRS P3, launched on India’s PSLV continues to provide valuable data.  The data was being received
 and analysed  by scientists in India.
51.          India plays an active role in several international bodies such as the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of
 Outer Space (UN-COPUOS).  United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UN-ESCAP), the
 international COSPAS-SARSAT system for search and rescue operations, the International Astronautical Federation (IAF), the
 Committee on Earth Observation Satellites (CEOS), the Committee on Space Research (COSPAR), the Inter Agency Debris
 Coordination Committee (IADC), the Space Frequency Coordination Group (SFGC), the Coordinating Group on Meteorological
 Satellites (CGMS), the International Global Observing Strategy (IGOS), the International Space University (ISU), the Asian
 Association for Remote Sensing (AARS) and the International Society for Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing (ISPRS).
52.        India has been selected by the United Nations for establishing the Centre for Space Science & Technology Education in Asia
 and the Pacific (CSSTE-AP) which was formally inaugurated on November 1, 1995, at New Delhi.  The centre has been established
 around the facilities of the Indian Institute of Remote Sensing (IIRS), Dehradun, Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad and
 Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), Ahmedabad.  The Centre offers Post-Graduate education courses, leading to award of
 M.Tech/M.Sc(Tech) degrees in Remote Sensing and Geographical Information Systems, Satellite Communications, Satellite
 Meteorology and Space Sciences to students of different countries in the region.

INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment &
 Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this One Hundred-First Report of the
 Committee.  This Report deals with the detailed Demands for Grants (2002-2003) of the Department of Ocean Development
 (Demand No.91).
 
2.         In the meeting of the Committee held on the 9
th April, 2002 the Secretary and other Officers of the Department of Ocean
 Development gave an overview of the various activities of the Department and the Members sought clarifications on various aspects
 of the performance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants.
 
3.         The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Department for replying to the clarifications sought by the Members
 and placing before it the required material to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Department of Ocean
 Development.
 
4.         The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on  2
nd May, 2002.
 
NEW DELHI;                                                                                                   C.RAMACHANDRAIAH,
May 2, 2002                                                                                                                               Chairman,
                                                                            CommitteeonScience&Technology,Environment & Forests.
       
R E P O R T
           
            India has a long maritime history.  The peninsula is surrounded by the Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal and Indian Ocean.  The

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/101streport.htm[29-08-2018 16:20:40]
 vast coastline of the mainland and islands is about 7,500 kms.  It’s territory includes, 1,256 islands.  The area of Exclusive Economic
 Zone (EEZ) of the country is 2.02 million sq. km. the vast coastal and offshore environment support a wide variety of marine
 ecosystem rich in species diversity and multifarious economic development activities.  The sea has tremendous influence on the
 physical and meteorological conditions of the country.  Appreciating the importance of the subject, Government of India established
 Department of Ocean Development in 1981 with an aim to create a deeper understanding of the oceanic regime of the northern and
 central Indian Ocean and also to develop technology and technological aids for harnessing of resources and understanding of various
 physical, chemical and biological processes.  The Ocean policy statement was also enunciated in 1982.
2.The Department of Ocean Development is the nodal Department for organising, coordinating and promoting development activities
 relating to ocean development in the country.  The national level R&D laboratories, educational institutions and industries assist the
 Department in carrying out its multi-disciplinary plans and programmes of national importance.  Further, marine research and
 capacity building is one of the key areas of the Department to promote basic research in marine science for self-reliance. Hence, the
 activities of the Department are targeted towards scientific research and technology development with orientation towards its
 applications and harnessing ocean resources. The Department has also mandate towards international programmes arising out of
 international obligations and bilateral and multilateral cooperative ventures to create a technological capacity building and human
 resource development for self-reliance.
3.The programmes of the Department are directed towards:
Technology Development for future applications with strategic, industrial and economic significance.
Society with direct/indirect benefit for the community by technology applications and pilot project demonstration with the
 participation of the community for their socio-economic prosperity, and for coastal area development.
Marine Resource for exploration of marine living and non-living resources, techno-economic studies to evolve strategies for
 sustainable exploration and utilization, and resource enhancement.
Multi-institutional and multi-disciplinary Polar Science Programmes and Antarctic Expeditions with scientific and geo-political
 significance.
Capacity Building towards self-reliance through basic scientific research in ocean sector, human resource development and
 establishing Centres of Excellence in academic institutions.
Creation of pubic awareness of ocean development, its immense potential and diverse uses.
 
 BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
4.         A sum of Rs.142 crores was allocated as B.E. to the Department of Ocean Development for the year 2001-02.  This was
 reduced to Rs.120 crores at RE stage which forced the Department to scale down most of its activities last year except in the case of
 National Institute of
Ocean Technology (NIOT) where more funds were required to carry out the task of operationalising 1 MW Ocean Thermal Energy
 Conversion (OTEC) plant. However, for the year 2002-03, total budget allocation for the programmes and activities of the
 Department has been placed at Rs.199.28 crores which includes Rs.175.00 crores (Plan) and Rs.24.28 crores (Non-plan). The plan
 outlay is Rs.33 crores more than the plan outlay of the last year. The following areas have been identified to be focussed in the year
 2002-03:-
The approved outlay for the Antarctic Research is placed at Rs.26.50 crores, which  would be given as Grants-in-aid to National
 Centre for Antarctic & Ocean Research (NCAOR) for launching the 22
nd Scientific Expedition to Antarctica, carrying out scientific
 experiments, maintenance of the permanent research station “Maitri” at Antarctica and operation and manning of the NCAOR, Goa.
In the case of Poly Metallic Nodules (PMN) programme, an outlay of Rs.20 crores has been provided.
For the mission mode programmes of National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT) including Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion
 (OTEC), an outlay of Rs.7.80 crores has been provided. The Expenditure Finance Committee has approved an outlay of Rs.35.25
 crore for OTEC programmes which was revised to Rs.61.13 crores. The pilot plant which was scheduled for commissioning in
 March, 2001, could not be done due to an operational mishap in the sea and will now be implemented by December, 2002. The
 activities of OTEC and other programmes on Technology for sea bed mining, coastal engineering and marine instrumentation will be
 continued in this year.
An outlay of Rs.7.10 crores has proposed for Marine Living Resources Programme.  Besides, an amount of Rs.2 crores is proposed to
 be allocated for the ongoing Drugs from Sea programme. During the year 2002-03, a provision of Rs.1.15 crore has been made for
 Marine Non-Living Resources. An outlay of Rs.25.00 crores has been provided for the Ocean Observation & Information Services.
 Out of this, the provision for the Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS) at Hyderabad is Rs.11 crores and
 for the National Data Buoy programme and the other Ocean Observing System programmes, a sum of Rs.10 crores has been
 provided.
An outlay of Rs.2 crores and Rs.5 crores has been made for Coastal Ocean Monitoring and Prediction Systems (COMAPS) and
 Coastal Research Vessel (CRV) respectively during the Annual Plan 2002-03. For the Integrated Coastal and Marine Area
 Management (ICMAM) Programme, an outlay of       Rs.5 crores has been provided for 2002-2003. 
In line with the guidelines provided by the Island Development Authority the Department has made a provision of Rs.0.75 crores for
 Island Development.  This is a coastal community programme implemented through National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT)
 by which viable technologies for enhancement of marine living resources would be developed and disseminated to the island
 community for their benefit.
An allocation of Rs.8.5 crores has been made during 2002-03 for identification of Gas  Hydrates  areas  in  the seas around India.  A
 programme of ComprehensiveSwath Bathymetric Survey with an allocation of Rs.14 crores would be initiated for conducting survey
 in the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) for supporting the activities relating to exploration of non-living resources in this area.
 The          geo-physical study of Laxmi Basin would also be initiated with an allocation of Rs.7 crores in order to understand the
 geology specially the crystal characteristics of the Laxmi Basin in the Arabian Sea. In order to replace the age-old existing ocean
 going research vessels of the Department, an activity for designing a new research vessel would be initiated with an allocation of

During his presentation on Demands for Grants, Secretary, Department of Ocean Development informed the Committee that an outlay
 of Rs.18.00 crores has been provided for the Delineation of Continental Shelf in 2002-03. Since India ratified the UN convention on
 the Law of the Sea in 1995, the claim for extending the outer limits of our continental shelf beyond 200 nautical miles Exclusive
 Economic Zone (EEZ) has to be made before 2005. The time frame for carrying out the bathymetric and seismic surveys and
 preparing necessary documents to submit to the Commission on the Limits of Continental Shelf is 5 years. This activity will have to
 be extended to the 10
th plan period (2002-07). 
5.         The Secretary, Department of Ocean Development, informed the Committee about the details of major disproportionate
 variations during the year 1999-2000 and 2000-2001 as follows:
i)          Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management (ICMAM)
            2000-2001:      B.E. – Rs. 6.7 crores               Actual – Rs. 3.59 crores
            ICMAM programme envisages development of integrated management solutions to solve a variety of coastal problems. 
 ICMAM reflects a new approach and in order to provide training on the subject, institutes abroad were contacted.  It was found that
 the foreign institutes provided only basic training and they were not meeting our specialised requirements.  Therefore, no foreign
 training was undertaken.  This led to non-utilisation of funds.
            Regarding the time taken to finalise the contract to engage the consultants, the World Bank that funded the consultancy had
 made recommendations regarding the award of the contract which was not acceptable to Government of India as these were against
 GOI rules.  It was therefore decided not to avail the loan for this work and instead fund the programme from internal resources.  This
 took considerable time to finalise and the amount earmarked could not be utilised during the year.
            2001-2002:      B.E. – Rs. 6.5crores                Actual – Rs. 5 crores
            As the task relating to collection of data for ICMAM plan in respect of Goa and Gulf of Kuchch could be initiated only at the
 end of the financial year, the entire funds earmarked could not be utilised in the  year. Further, the savings were also on account of
 reduction in the scope of work in the foreign consultancies.
ii)         Polymetallic Nodules Programme
            The variation in the BE & actual expenditure in respect of PMN Programme was mainly on account of inability to initiate the
 project on ‘Unmanned Submersibles’.  The provisions made for the years for 2000-01 (Rs.4.09 crore) and for 2001-02 (Rs.5.00
 crore) could not be utilised for want of necessary approvals from the competent authority.
 
iii)         Delineation of outer limits of Continental Shelf (CLCS)
            There have been variations between the Actuals and the budgetary provision in both 2000-01 and 2001-02.  The Continental
 Shelf Delineation programme was one of geo-political importance. The interpretations of UN Convention of Law of Sea (UNCLOS)
 for the delineation have implications for the claims of other countries in the region.  Due to certain special provisions only for India
 and Sri Lanka with major implications in the quantum of claim, various legal issues came up which involved extensive inter-
ministerial consultations including with the Solicitor General of India.  Further, baselines were to be promulgated by Ministry of
 External Affairs which was also delayed.  It was therefore decided to reduce the allocations at the RE stage itself by Rs.43.00 crores
 in 2000-2001 and hence the reduction.
            Once the legal issues were resolved, the action would be taken to finalize the contract for the marine geo-physical surveys. 
 Before the award of the contract the required security clearances were also to be taken.  These have taken some time.  Further, due to
 budgetary constrains it was decided to restrict expenditure to Rs.25.00 crores as against Rs.43.00 crores in 2001-02.
iv)        National Institute of Oceanography (NIO)
            There was substantial additional requirement of funds for the successful implementation of the OTEC project by NIOT. The
 original estimates of Rs.35.25 crores for the OTEC project were revised to Rs.61.13 crores.  Accordingly, there was an increase of
 Rs.17.00 crores in the allocation to NIOT at the RE stage during 2001-02 and this expenditure has been actually incurred by the
 Department.

POLAR SCIENCE (ANTARCTIC RESEARCH) PROGRAMME
11.       The objectives of Antarctic research programme is to identify and initiate programmes of scientific and economic significance
 besides establishing infrastructure. The Programme, which was initiated in 1981, has culminated into a major national programme
 that has a distinct multi-institutional and multi-disciplinary approach.  The objective of the Antarctic mission is to plan, promote, co-
ordinate and execute the entire gamut of polar science and logistic activities of the country, in order to ensure a perceptible and
 influential presence of India in Antarctica. So far 22 scientific expeditions have been launched on a regular basis including two
 expeditions to the Southern Ocean one to Weddel Sea and another one for assessment of Antarctic Krill, which have carried out
 research work in the thrust areas of polar science.  Till date, more than 55 national institutions have participated in the scientific and
 logistic components of the expedition thereby putting about 1425 Indians to the icy continent. With this year’s allocation of Rs.26.50
 crores, the Department proposes to augment the research facilities at Indian Antarctic Station and also to actively undertake research
 in the Southern Ocean Oceanography area.
12.The Committee was informed that a modern and indigenously build station ‘Maitri’ established in Schirmacher Oasis in 1988 has
 replaced the first Indian station, Dakshin Gangotri that was established on the ice-shelf in 1984.  Maitri is equipped to provide
 comfortable living facilites for 25 persons on a year round basis and has eight permanent observations and several laboratories to
 carry out research in the frontier areas of Antarctic Science.  Since ‘Maitri’ has already withstood 12 years of Antarctic weather and
 gradually a number of shortcomings were being noticed with the station, the Department was planning to establish a new station
 during the Tenth plan, replacing the ‘Maitri’,  with an estimated cost of  Rs.75 crores. 
13.The success of the Antarctic Programme and sustained capabilities in Antarctic science and logistics promoted the Department to
 establish the first polar research lab of the country at Goa namely the National Centre for Antarctic Ocean Research (NCAOR) since
 1998 which is responsible for carrying out all the activities relating to Antarctic expeditions. The research on polar science and
 expeditions to Antarctica was being planned, executed and launched annually on behalf of DOD by the Centre.  The Centre has a
 specific R&D mandate in the realms of polar science and to coordinate and launch Indian Antarctic expeditions.  The Centre has a
 unique laboratory for low-temperature research on ice cores retrieved from Antarctica and the Himalayas.  It would also have the
 facility for the application of remote sensing techniques aimed to understand the sea-ice-atmosphere interaction in the Polar Regions. 
 It would also have an Antarctic museum and a database repository on polar sciences. During 2002-03, the Centre would co-ordinate
 all the activities related to launching of the XXII Indian Antarctic Expedition.
14.During the year 2002-03, NCAOR plans to coordinate and launch the XXII Indian Scientific Expedition to Antarctica through a
 multi-institutional and multi-disciplinary approach. Moreover, efforts would be made to induct state-of-the-art experiments in
 accordance with the long-term science strategy for the Antarctic expeditions.
15.The Secretary, DOD informed the Committee that Scientific research in Antarctica was of  National and global importance. 
 Besides, important research work had been done in the areas of Earth Sciences, Atmospheric Sciences etc.  which were of
 significance to the country,  for example the research in meteorology and atmospheric sciences helped in understanding the
 relationship between Polar weather and the Indian monsoon.  Biotechnology research helped in identification of low temperature
 genes available in Antarctic microorganisms that would be coned to mesophilic bacteria.  The Antarctic programme had also helped
 the Indian Army in acquiring skills and knowledge relating to operations of vehicles and machineries under extreme cold conditions.
16.The Committee is of the view that in addition to on-going programmes in various domains of polar sciences, National Centre for
 Antarctic Ocean Research (NCAOR) should also initiate cutting-edge experiments in such frontier areas as assessment of
 biotechnological potential of Antarctic microbes, biodegradation of organic wastes using microbial consortium and productivity and
 ecosystem dynamics in the Antarctic lakes. It should also envisage initiating meaningful logistics operation with other countries
 which could lead to operational and financial cooperation.
17.The Committee is further of the view that the National Centre for Antarctic Ocean Research (NCAOR), being the nodal
 Department to execute the Antarctic Programmes should strive to further expand its infrastructure facilities for carrying out research
 in the realms of Polar Sciences and Southern Ocean Oceanography. Besides, the Centre should also initiate its activities related to
 establishing the  Country’s first ice-core repository and analytical facilities with focus on high-resolution histories of fact changes in
 climate, atmospheric composition and ice-cover in Antarctica.
18.The Department should pass on the data collected about the impact of cold climate on human body to defence establishments to
 facilitate treatment of soldiers stationed in cold regions or for such other uses as might be required in the national interest.

COASTAL OCEAN MONITORING AND PREDICTION SYSTEM(COMAPS)
25.       Under the Coastal Ocean Monitoring and Prediction System (COMAPS) Programme, the Department of Ocean Development

 has been stated that the recent data has indicated that there was marginal improvement in water quality in Versova and  other Creeks
 of  Mumbai which was due to  treatment of sewage as well as disposal of sewage in the deep sea through out falls.  Similarly, in Puri,

DRUG FROM SEA
29.The major objectives of the programme include:–
Systematic exploration of the entire coastline and collections made from deep sea as well for identification of more flora and fauna
 having potential for extraction of drugs and chemicals.
Collection, extraction and biological evaluation of 150 species, and evaluation of biologically potential organisms, leading to possible
 development of new drug(s).
Isolation of bioactive constituents and development as possible drugs.
Development of suitable models for biological activity in certain priority areas.
Undertaking regulatory pharmacology and toxicology of 2-3 extracts.
Initiation and completion of clinical trials for at least two drugs.
Development of at least 2 herbal drugs from the samples and marketing.
Industrial participation in drug development and marketing.
30.The Committee was informed that drug development takes nearly 8-10 years as there were several phases in drug discovery and
 development that costs about 600 million USD for each drug developed.  The ‘Drugs from Sea’ programme was initiated in 1990,
 while the  developed countries initiated this programme in the early ‘60s.  Even then, so far not even a single drug has been put in the
 market by any country.  6 to 7 products were currently in Phase II clinical trials of drug development but none of these have yet
 entered the Phase III clinical trials i.e., the final development stage. 
31.  Under the programme one lead was taken up for product development in 1996-97, but after two years of intensive research
 activities; it was found that the preparation had an unanticipated toxic effect leading to faecolith formation in the monkeys during
 chronic toxicity studies.  Therefore, efforts were made to detoxify the preparation, which took considerable time.  Finally a
 preparation  was  isolated  which  demonstrated  antidiabetic  activity  and  was  also  found  to be largely safe.  This new preparation
 is free from any side effect and has wide margin of safety.  This antidiabetic preparation was now entering clinical safety-cum-
efficacy in humans.  If found safe and effective in humans, we should be ready with this drug for marketing in next 2-3 years.   CDRI
 might also succeed in coming out with one more drug with cholesterol-lowering properties. Under the programme, so far no antiviral
 preparations have been developed.  Instead, it was only antifungal lead that has been taken up.
32.       The Committee feels there is need to concentrate efforts on the project with a view to develop the drugs as expeditiously as
 possible.

OCEAN OBSERVATIONS AND INFORMATION SERVICES (OOIS) 
51.       During the examination of Demands for Grants (2002-03) the Committee was informed that in order to generate user-oriented
 data products and provide services to cater the needs of the coastal and ocean sectors, an integrated programme called “Ocean
 Observations and Information Services (OOIS)” was being implemented by the Department. The OOIS envisages generation and
 dissemination of reliable coastal and ocean data products such as waves, winds, temperature, current, salinity, upwelling, potential
 fishing zone information, coastal maps, etc. to support coastal and off-shore development activities and for furthering quality
 oceanographic research. Besides, it seeks to provide ocean information services for various applications in the ocean section. 
52.       The programme consists of four major components viz. Ocean Observing Systems, Ocean Information Services, Satellite
 Coastal and Oceanographic Research (SATCORE) and Indian Ocean Dynamics & Modeling (INDOMOD).
53.       The Ocean Observing Systems envisage collection of sea truth data using moored data buoys, drifting buoys, expandable
 bathythermographs (XBT), current meter arrays and tide gauges, and designed particularly for acquisition of real-time sea surfaces,
 meteorological land upper oceanographic parameters from the coastal and deep waters.  Validation of the satellite sensors has also
 been undertaken using the sea truth data generated under this programme.  The Data Buoy Programme was initiated in 1996 with
 partial financial assistance from Norwegian Agency for Development (NORAD) and National Institute of Ocean Technology
 (NIOT).  It has been entrusted with the responsibilities for deployment, operation and maintenance of the data buoys.  A set of 12
 buoys were procured from M/s OCEANOR, Norway out of which, seven were moored in the coastal waters and five in the off-shore
 waters.  The buoys were equipped with state-of-the-art sensors for accurate measurement of winds, waves, currents, atmospheric
 pressure, atmospheric temperature, sea surface temperature, dissolved oxygen, chlorophyll, radioactivity, hydrocarbon and turbidity.
 The data Buoy will continue as Govt. of India (GOI) programme.
54.       The Ocean Information Service envisages generation and dissemination of ocean data/data products on an operational basis. 
 Data products in the form of Sea Surface Temperature maps, Potential Fishing Zone maps, wind vector maps, mixed layer depth-
maps, at least on heat-budget are proposed to be made available.  It is also planned to develop ocean state forecasting system; initially
 on an experimental basis.  Services will be offered in the form of coastal wetland maps, shoreline change maps, and close contour
 coastal area maps etc.  which were needed for coastal zone management activities.  The Indian National Centre for Ocean
 Information and Services (INCOIS) at Hyderabad is working as an autonomous society for efficient development and dissemination
 of Data products.
The Satellite Coastal and Oceanographic Research (SATCORE) component envisages development of regional algorithms, data
 assimilation techniques and operational models which would be transferred to the Ocean Information and Service Centre for
 operational use.  The Ocean Modeling and Dynamics (INDMOD) project addresses basic issues on the ocean dynamic, climate
 variability, ocean state forecast, sea level variations, ocean flux studies etc.  These R&D projects are expected to provide basic
 models that could explain the dynamics of the Indian ocean and form an essential input in designing system for ocean state forecast.
56.       The budgetary allocation of Rs.25 for the year 2002-2003 crores would be utilized for procurement of new buoys,
 maintenance of existing buoys, modeling of oceanic phenomena and setting up of infrastructure at the Indian National Centre for
 Ocean Information Services, Hyderabad.
57.       The Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), being the nodal agency for providing coastal and ocean
 data and value added products to the users, the Department should monitor the performance and work-mechanism of the INCOIS to
 process and disseminate ocean data and data products to user communities like fisheries, weather, climate, ports, shipping etc. on a
 regular basis so that ocean weather forecasting is precise.
MARINE RESEARCH AND CAPACITY BUILDING
58.       The objectives of the programme are to foster the concept of stewardship through education, training and human resource
 development and increasing awareness at all levels. The activities proposed in the programme include promotion of research under
 the basic categories of marine  ecology,  marine biology,  marine  microbiology,  marine benthos,  coastal marine culture systems,
 marine geology/geophysics and ocean engineering & underwater robotics. Besides the ongoing programme of award of fellowships
 to students for pursuing higher studies in academic/educational institutions in various disciplines of ocean science and technology,
 and organizing exhibitions and fairs to create awareness among the public on ocean would continue.

59.       The Committee feels that the Department should focus its efforts in assisting Universities to create infrastructure facilities and
 building up a skilled human resource base in Marine Sciences. Moreover, the Department should also participate and showcase its
 activities in national and international level exposition, exhibition, fairs etc. from time to time. Inter-active computer generated
 information on Ocean Science & Technology could perhaps help educate the public on the ocean and its resources.
ARRAY FOR REAL-TIME GEOTROPIC OCEANOGRAPHY (ARGO) PROGRAMME
60.       The array for Real-time Geotropic Oceanography (ARGO) is an internationally coordinated programme for deployment of an
 array  of 3000 profiling floats at a spatial resolution of 3” X 3” (300km X 300 km) to measure temperature and salinity profiles of the
 upper ocean (up to a depth of 2000 m), periodically.  These temperature and salinity profiles are expected to improve the
 understanding of the oceanic processes and contribute to improved prediction of climate variability.
61.       The ARGO floats, equipped with pressure, temperature and salinity sensors, would drift up to a depth of about 2000 m and
 popup to the surface every 10 days for a short period to transmit the data in near real-time via Satellite to ground stations.  The
 expected life of an ARGO float is four years.
62.       Data from the global array of profiling floats would be put on GTS immediately to enable it use in operational forecasting. 
 Delayed mode data, after detailed quality control checks by the ARGO Data Centres, would be available within a few months via
 internet.  The expected life of each float is about 4 years.
63.       India is participating in the ARGO Programme and plans to deploy 150 floats in the North Indian Ocean (north of 10 S). 
 INCOIS was assigned the overall responsibility for implementation of India ARGO Programme.  A Canadian ARGO float deployed
 successfully by INCOIS onboard FORV Sagar Sampada Vessel in December 2001 is providing good quality data.  Data from 20
 ARGO floats currently deployed in the Indian Ocean by different countries are being archived at INCOIS.  This data would be made
 available to the scientific community through INCOIS ocean portal.  INCOIS participated in the International ARGO Science Team
 meeting.  Study on “Analysis and Synthesis for Indian Ocean ARGO Programme” was initiated jointly by Indian Institute of Science
 and INCOIS.  A Project Report for the Indian ARGO Programme (150 Floats) by INCOIS.
64.       The International Argo programme, endorsed by World meteorological Organisation (WMO) and intergovernmental
 Oceanographic Commission (IOC) is directed by an International Argo Science Team.  The international ocean community plans to
 deploy 3000 ARGO Floats in a phased manner by the year 2002 to give a global coverage at a spacing of 300 km.
65.       The Indian Ocean would be covered by about 450 Argo floats.  Of this, India plans to contribute 150 Floats, Australia,
 Canada, China, France, Germany, Japan, UK and USA have committed to deploy Argo Floats in the Indian Ocean Region.
66.       The Implementation planning meeting for Argo in the Indian Ocean was held in Hyderabad, India in July, 2001 where
 representatives from 17 countries and 6 International Organisations participated.  India was identified as (i) the Regional Coordinator
 and (ii) the Regional Data Centre for the Indian Ocean.
67.       The Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), an autonomous body under the Department of Ocean
 Development (DOD) is the implementing agency for the programme.
68.       After considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Ocean Development and assessing the progress of various
 important programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the budgetary allocation of Rs. 199.28
 crores, as sought by the Department for the year 2002-2003, under Demand No. 91, may be approved.
RECOMMENDATIONS / OBSERVATIONS AT GLANCE
 
1.         The Committee observes that there were major variations in the budgetary allocations and their utilization.  The non-utilisation
 of the allocation meant less or reduced activities of the Department.  The Committee is not happy with the reasons advanced by the
 Department for the non- utilization of funds which includes delay in transfer of foreign consultation, change of priorities, delay in
 initiating discussion with the neighbouring countries, non approval and uncertainty of elements.  The Committee feels that the
 Department should have foreseen these difficulties before asking for budgetary allocation and should have evolved suitable
 mechanism to monitor the budgetary proposal and its allocations.
(Para 7)
2.         The Committee commends the efforts being made by the Department in utilising the services of two vessels. However, in view
 of decommissioning of existing vessels after another 10 years, it is time to plan for acquiring new vessels  which can cater to shallow
 water survey, data buoy maintenance and provide a platform for various coastal and deep ocean activities and other requirements
 which could reasonably be foreseen in the years ahead . The new vessels would not only serve as a platform for the programmes
 envisaged in the Tenth plan but also serve as a utility vessel which might augment the capacity requirements for programmes on the
 marine living and non-living resources.
(Para 10)
3.         The Committee is further of the view that in addition to on-going programmes in various domains of polar sciences, National
 Centre for Antarctic Ocean Research (NCAOR) should also initiate cutting-edge experiments in such frontier areas as assessment of
 biotechnological potential of Antarctic microbes, biodegradation of organic wastes using microbial consortium and productivity and
 ecosystem dynamics in the Antarctic lakes. It should also envisage initiating meaningful logistics operation with other countries
 which could lead to operational and financial cooperation.
(Para 16)
4.         The Committee is of the view that the National Centre for Antarctic Ocean Research (NCAOR), being the nodal Department
 to execute the Antarctic Programmes should strive to further expand its infrastructure facilities for carrying out research in the realms
 of Polar Sciences and Southern Ocean Oceanography. Besides, the Centre should also initiate its activities related to establishing the 
 Country’s first ice-core repository and analytical facilities with focus on high-resolution histories of fact changes in climate,
 atmospheric composition and ice-cover in Antarctica.
(Para 17)
5.         The Department should pass on the data collected about the impact of cold climate on human body to defence establishments
 to facilitate treatment of soldiers stationed in cold regions or for such other uses as might be required in the national interest.

            The Department of Science and Technology (DST) was established with the primary objective of promoting new areas of
 Science and Technology and to play the role of a nodal department for organising, co-coordinating and promoting S&T activities
 in the country.  The mandate given to DST includes, among others:Formulation of policy statements and guidelines on
 S&TPromotion of new areas of scientific researchCo-ordination of inter-departmental S&T effortsSupport basic and applied
 research in universities and other institutionsInternational S&T Co-operationSupport high quality research in autonomous
 bodiesCatalyzing S&T interaction in societal programmes, and entrepreneurship development Science popularisation,
 communication and S&T Management Information SystemPromotion of Commercialisation of home grown technologySupport
 to technology development programmes, technology information andassessmentProviding services in the areas of:Surveying &
 Mapping by Survey of India & National Atlas & Thermatic Mapping Organisation. Meterology by India Meteorological
 Department & National Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasting. Technology Development and Application by
 Technology Development Board. The Committee was apprised of the recent initiatives taken by the Department for Innovation
 Foundation in order to promote grass root level invention, Swarnajayanti Fellowships for outstanding young scientists, Fund for
 Improvement of S&T Infrastructure (FIST) in universities and related Institutions, Kishore Vigyanik Protsahan, Technopreneur
 Promotion Program (TePP), Indian Climate Research, Establishing high performance computing network facilities for research
 purposes Executed Joint Technology Development projects with industry and socio-economic Ministries, Strengthen Seismcity
 programme, Modernizing autonomous research institutions, Setting up of a National Accreditation Board for Testing and
 Calibration (NABL), Setting up a Patent Facilitating Cell in order to provide support to scientists and technologists on all aspects
 of patenting.
