R E P O R T
 
The world over environmental degradation has assumed alarming proportions.  Concerns for preservation of
 environment constitute the defining feature of our age.  Our first Prime Minister Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru while
 remaining a moving force behind the establishment of heavy industrial enterprises and hydroelectric projects had also
 articulated the needs for protection of environment.  In a letter to the Chief Ministers on 15 August, 1957 he observed,
 “I should like to refer to something which I think is rather important and which, perhaps, has not received much
 attention.  We want to exploit as well as conserve our natural resources. Sometimes the desire to exploit them outruns
 discretion and we forget the part of conservation.” He further added, “We have many large scale river valley projects
 which are carefully worked out by our engineers.  I wonder however, how much thought is given before the project is
 launched, to having an ecological survey of the area and to find out what the effect would be on the drainage system or
 to the flora and fauna of that area.  It would be desirable to have such an ecological survey of these areas before the
 project is launched and thus to avoid the imbalance of nature.”  Establishment of the Ministry of Environment and
 Forests in 1985 as the nodal Ministry in the Government for the planning, promotion, coordination and overseeing the
 implementation of various schemes relating to environment and forests remained at the heart of our efforts to
 effectively address the challenges of the deteriorating environmental situation.  While the Ministry is entrusted with the
 responsibilities of conservation and survey of flora, fauna, forests and wildlife, its functions and jurisdiction also
 encompass numerous other activities such as promotion of afforestation, regeneration of degraded areas, prevention and
 control of pollution and overall protection of environment.  By assessing the impact of developmental projects on the
 environment, by extending assistance to organizations engaged in implementing environmental and forestry

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION OF TAJ MAHAL
10.       The Committee was informed that in pursuance of directions of the Apex Court , Ministry of Environment &
 Forests has taken up the    work of Environmental Protection of the Taj Mahal. The work will be implemented through
 State Government of Uttar Pradesh and Ministries concerned.  The work also involves making of a green belt around
 the Taj Mahal. It is proposed that from  Tenth Plan onwards, the scheme would be expanded to cover other important
 Heritage sites.
11.       The Committee was apprised that ten projects under the Taj Protection Mission Programme which aims at
 improving electric supply, water supply, solid waste management, roads of Agra city were approved and are at different
 stages of implementation.  To reduce and contain pollution, construction of a by-pass for diverting the vehicular traffic
 is also being implemented.   Besides these ten projects, seven other priority projects as recommended by the Mission
 Management Board constituted under the Programme, are also being considered. These include a Heritage Corridor in
 the Taj Trapezium Zone, Automatic Air Monitoring Station, Hazardous Waste Secured Land-fill site for Agra &
 Mathura, common treatment facility for treatment of biomedical waste at Agra, creating public awareness in the Taj
 Trapezium, etc.  The EFC Memo of these projects has been circulated and will be finalized soon.  The Mission
 Management Board, Central Pollution Control Board and the Ministry are regularly monitoring the progress of
 implementation of the projects formulated under this scheme.  The annual average level of Sulphur Dioxide has come
 down from 23mg/m3 in 1992 to 4.5 mg/m3 in 2002 and SPM level from 438 in 1992 to 385 in 2002.  The Nitrogen
 Oxide level has increased from 15mg/m3 in 1992 to 21.7 mg/m3 in 2002.   It has been observed that hydrogen sulphide
 which generate from the swamp of river Yamuna is causing more damage to the Taj.
12.       The protection of the Taj Mahal has been a major priority and constant efforts are required to save the
 monument. The Committee feels that concerted effort should be taken for the protection of the Taj which suffered
 substantial damage due to pollution. The Committee recommends that instead of involving multiple agencies for the
 protection of Taj, a constituent body be formed which would be responsible for coordination with all allied agencies,
 supported by a strong legal framework for effective implementation of the policies undertaken. 
NATIONAL RIVER CONSERVATION PLAN INCLUDING GANGA ACTION PLAN
13.       The objective of the National River Conservation Plan is to improve the water quality of the rivers to acceptable 
 standards by preventing pollution load reaching the river by undertaking works like (i) interception & diversion works

14.       Under this scheme, polluted stretches of major rivers have been identified for sewage collection and treatment. 
 At present, 153 towns have been considered under the National River Conservation Plan (NRCP), out of which 74
 towns are located on Ganga, and 21 on Yamuna.  This project was started with 100 per cent funding by the Centre. 
 However, given resource constraints, states have to share 30 per cent of the cost during the Tenth Plan.
15.       The first River Action Plan was taken up in 1985 under the NRCP as the Ganga Action Plan (GAP) to improve
 the water quality of the River Ganga.  An amount of Rs.452 crores has been spent on the GAP Phase-I.  The entire
 funding has been provided by the Central Government.  It was initially expected that programme would be completed
 in 6-7 years.  However, it has been delayed considerably due to land acquisition problems, court litigation and lack of
 experience in implementing a programme of this nature and magnitude. The work under NRCP, including that of GAP
 are expected to cost Rs.3780.00. Till January, 2002, Rs.1,295 crores has been spent on the scheme.  About 45 per cent
 of the cleaning of the Ganga has been completed.  However, overall progress is poor because of delays in land
 acquisition and slow pace of work by municipal corporations.
16.       GAP Phase-I,  launched in 1985,  was completed on 31.3.2000 at  a total cost of Rs.452 crores, although two
 projects of sewage treatment plants in Bihar have not been completed so far due to problems of litigation on the land
 proposed for these facilities.  Under this plan, a sewage treatment capacity of 865 million litres per day (mld) has been
 created which will become 882 mld against the target of 873 mld after the remaining two sewage treatment plants are
 completed in Bihar.  This will account for about 35% of the pollution load presently reaching the Ganga.
17.       The Committee was informed by the Ministry that despite the problems of operation & maintenance (O&M) of
 assets created under GAP Phase-I the water quality of the river has shown improvement over the pre-GAP period water
 quality.  It is seen that in 1986, the Bio-Chemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) which is an indicator of pollution of river
 water quality was ranging from 5.5 to 15.5 mg/I in the critical stretch of Ganga from Kannauj to Varanasi.  As against

37.       In a recent article written jointly by Shri Nitin Desai of the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs; 
 Mark Malloch Brown of UN Development Programme; Klaus Toepffer of UN Environment Programme; Koichiro
 Matsuura of UNESCO, Anna Tribaijuka of UN-Habitat; Carlo Bellamy of UNICEF and Hans Van Ginkel of UN
 University the following has been written which has a bearing on the cleaning of our rivers.
“There are signs of hope.  Up until the middle of the last century many of the rivers on continents like North America
 and Europe and especially those running through big industrial areas were so polluted that they were classed as “dead”. 
 Some were so polluted that the water could be used as ink, and noxious gases, bubbling up from their depths, could be
 ignited by a match.  Today after billions of dollars of investment in water treatment and agreements with industry on
 effluents, fish are again spawning and migrating to their upper reaches through these now relatively clean estuaries and
 tributaries.  The Thames in Britain was officially declared a dead river half a century ago, save for a few mud worms. 
 Today some 120 species including migrating salmon can be found.”

INDUSTRIAL AND HAZARDOUS WASTE
66.       Hazardous waste includes sludge contaminated with heavy metals, wastes from paints, dyes and organic
 chemical units and highly acidic and alkaline wastes.  The major hazardous waste generating industries are petroleum
 and petro-chemicals, pharmaceuticals, pesticides, paint and dyes, fertilizers, inorganic chemicals and general
 engineering industries etc.  The presence of toxic chemicals in solid/liquid effluents from industries and other activities
 leads to ground water contamination. 
67.       The Committee was informed that at present, around 7.2 mt of hazardous waste are generated in the country, out
 of which, according to one estimate, 1.4 mt re recyclable, 0.1 mt to be incinerated and 5.2 mt to be disposed on land. 
 The hazardous waste of 5.3 mt would  require about Rs.1,600 crores a year for treatment and disposal at an estimated
 rate of Rs.3,000 tonne.  In addition, land required for disposal will be around 1km   taking a depth of 4 m and density of
 disposal as 1.2 tonnes/m3.
68.       The Committee was also informed that the Water Act, 1974  and Air Act, 1981 were not sufficient to regulate
 the disposal of hazardous waster and has called for the formulation of the Hazardous Waste Management and Handling
 rules, 1989.  Since then, efforts to make an inventory of hazardous waste were initiated. The initiatives taken in this
 direction are:
Estimate of the hazardous waste inventory in various States and identification of disposal sites based on environment
 impact assessment.
CPCB has prepared a ready reckoner to provide information on the source of the hazardous waste, their characteristics
 and the methods for recycling and disposal.
Training programmes have been organized to deal with hazardous waste management.
Import of hazardous waste containing toxic metals like beryllium, selenium, chromium, thallium, pesticides etc. have
 been restricted on the recommendations of an Expert Committee.
Export and import of waste containing cyanide, mercury and arsenic have been prohibited since December 1996.
The import of waste oil and metals such as brass, zinc and lead for processing to recover resources is fully regulated by
 the Ministry of Environment and Forests.
69.       Though the Committee appreciates the efforts being taken by the Ministry for handling of industrial & hazardous
 waste, it proposes that parameters to assess the impact of measures adopted should be evolved to enable the country to
 know their effect vis-à-vis the money being invested in this highly important programme.  It is hoped that the
 Department shall be able to let the Committee know of the nature and periodicity of such monitoring.
BIO-MEDICAL WASTE MANAGEMENT
70.       Bio-Medical Waste is the waste generated by hospitals, nursing homes and clinical laboratories consisting of
 human tissues, organs, body parts, body fluids, blood and blood products and excreta and other human anatomical
 wastes, swab, soiled cotton and bandage, needles, disposable syringes, scalpels, IV fluid bottles and bags, catheters,
 urobags, amputees, bottles, expired medicines, used gloves etc.  Waste produced by veterinary institutions, slaughter
 houses and microbiology laboratories have also been categorized as Bio-Medical Waste.  These waste materials are
 potential source of dangerous diseases.
71.       The Committee feels that the scientific management of medical waste is being dangerously neglected in the
 country.   The staff charged with the responsibility for sanitation and cleanliness in hospitals and other medical units
 seem to be  ignorant of the regulations for Bio-medical waste (BMW) disposal.  Hoards of broken needles, soiled
 cotton and bandages, laboratory tested blood/urine/stool samples, leftover plaster of Paris coats, abandoned organs,
 used utensils, instruments and containers lying right in the precincts of hospitals have been noticed by people.  Even

ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION, TRAINING AND RESEARCH
72.       The Environmental Education and Training Scheme of the Ministry is precisely meant for creating
 environmental awareness.  Under this scheme, various programmes are conducted every year for creating
 environmental awareness both through non-formal activities as well as through the formal education system.  While the
 programmes like national Environment Awareness Campaign (NEAC), National Green Corps (NGC), use of electronic
 Media etc. fall in the non-formal sector, the Ministry’s initiative of taking up a pilot project for strengthening
 environmental concepts in the school curriculum and the linked Global Learning and Observations to Benefit the
 Environment (GLOBE) programme use the formal education system for creating awareness.  The recent initiatives for
 strengthening Environment Education in Business Schools and development of Environmental Appreciation courses
 also fall in this category.
73.       Environmental Research aims at developing strategies, technologies and methodologies by way of better
 facilities and infrastructure to facilitate research and training of manpower. The Environmental Research Programme
 specially deals with problems related to air, water and soil pollution and development of suitable cost effective
 technology for abatement of pollution load in the environment .  Emphasis is given on development of eco-friendly, 
 biological and other interventions for prevention of pollution and development of strategies/technologies, instruments
 etc.  Many projects have been taken for development of biodegradable plastics. Besides, emphasis has been laid on the
 development of clean technologies.  Many studies have been undertaken to reduce the impact of mining on
 environment. Waste recycling and resource recovery from waste along with development of eco-friendly and cleaner
 technology are given due priority.
74.       To strengthen the system of forestry research in India, the Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education
 (ICFRE) is entrusted to undertake, aid , promote and coordinate forestry research and its application; function as a
 clearing house for research results and information; and disseminate technology.  ICFRE imparts forestry education and
 is developing forestry curricula at various levels to accelerate the pace of research and to provide expertise in different
 fields of forestry research.  Universities providing forestry education are being given grants-in-aid for strengthening
 their infrastructure and technical capabilities.  Opportunities are also being provided for furthering the academic
 advancement of foresters/scientists/academicians in the field of forestry.
75.       During the year 2003-04 a budgetary provision of Rs.17.00 crores in plan side and Rs.0.02 crores in non-plan
 side has been made.
76.       The Committee recommends  that talented persons may be encouraged with remunerative schemes and attractive
 pay scales to do research on environment issues.  Besides, Ministry should also consider introducing research
 scholarships to school leaving students in order to motivate them to join frontier areas of research in the field of
 environment.  These initiatives may help in accelerating the pace of environmental research for the development of a
 strong knowledge base and its application for society at large. Efforts should also be made to include environment as a
 formal subject in the schools / professional management courses.
77.       The Committee observed that the organisations like Botanical Survey of India, Zoological Survey of India and
 other organisation under the control  of Ministry of Environment and Forests should be given more autonomy in
 implementing their plans.

 people about environmental issues and making them conscious about their own roles in protecting nature and

NATIONAL FOREST COMMISSION
79.       The constitution of National Forest Commission has been notified on 7.2.2003 by the Ministry of Environment
 & Forests and Wildlife Sector with the following terms of reference:
Review and assess the existing policy and legal framework and their impact in a holistic manner from the ecological,
 scientific, economic, social and cultural viewpoint.
Examine the current status of forest administration and the forestry institutions both on all India and State level to meet
 the emerging needs of the civil society.
Make recommendations indicating policy options for achieving sustainable forest and wildlife management and
 development, bio-diversity conservation and ecological security.
Suggest ways and means to make forest administration more effective with a view to help to achieve the above policy
 options.
Establish meaningful partnership and interface between forestry management and local communities including tribals.
80.       The Commission will work under the administrative control of the Ministry of Environment & Forests and will
 be given funds from the budget of the Ministry for its smooth functioning.
81.       For effective implementation of the policies and programmes of the Ministry the Committee feels that instead of
 bureaucrats more and more technocrats and scientists should be associated.
82.       An absurd implementation of a rule to conserve the seacoast from pollution was brought to the notice of the
 Committee.  The Construction of toilets along the sea coast is prohibited by rule.  Not even mobile toilets are permitted.
 The result is that people defecate along the beaches thus leading to stink & high pollution on thebeaches.  This rule
 evidently  needs to be reviewed immediately. The objective is to prevent  pollution of beaches and not just enforce the
 rules rigidly thus defeating the very objective.
83.       The Committee was informed about toilets on the Goa beaches.  It was informed that funds have been released
 for the construction of toilets from the MPs funds but permission has not been granted to construct them.  The
 Committee therefore recommends that immediate action may be taken in this regard and construction of toilets should
 be permitted to maintain cleanliness of beaches. Alternatively mobile toilets in sufficient numbers should be placed on
 all beaches of the country where people throng in large numbers.

 of various important programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the budgetary
 allocation of      Rs.1124.59 crores, as sought by the Ministry of Environment & Forests for the year 2003-04, under
 Demand No.  29, may be approved.
SUMMARY OF THE RECOMMENDATIONS
1.         The Committee recommends that at R.E. stage curtailment of funds for the Ministry may be avoided so as to
 enable  the smooth and unhindered implementation of programmes  and policies of the Ministry.  The Committee also
 recommends that the programmes and policies may be effectively and substantially implemented at the ground   level
 so as to get the desired result.
(Para 7)
2.         The protection of the Taj Mahal has been a major priority and constant efforts are required to save the
 monument. The Committee feels that concerted effort should be taken for the protection of the Taj which suffered
 substantial damage due to pollution. The Committee recommends that instead of involving multiple agencies for the
 protection of Taj, a constituent body be formed which would be responsible for coordination with all allied agencies,
 supported by a strong legal framework for effective implementation of the policies undertaken. 
(Para 12)
3.         The Committee observes that for any plan or programme regarding cleaning of rivers of such a magnitude as
 Ganga, to succeed, it is necessary to have a meticulous planning.  Any delay in its execution is bound to result in the
 plan going awry.  More so, because the parameters regarding the size of the population and the extent of urbanization
 etc., which would have been taken into account at the stage of planning, are subject to rapid changes in a country like
 India.  Hence, timely execution is crucial for such programmes or else we would suffer severe consequences of
 contamination of our rivers on the banks of which our civilization began and flourished.
(Para 22)
4.         The Committee is constrained to observe that even after nearly two decades of  Ganga Action Plan (GAP)-I, the
 pollution levels at various places in the River has more or less remained the same. It is seen that every programme
 failed to achieve its stipulated objectives and proved ineffective. The Committee feels that a strong administrative will

availability of funds in the Tenth Plan would become a major constraint to effectively address the problem of cleaning

(Para 24)
 
6.         The Committee is deeply perturbed to note that the Yamuna water at Delhi continues to be stinking and dirty.  It
 notes with concernthat  waste is still dumped in the Yamuna river through drains. The Committee notes with anxiety
 that cleaning of sewerage has become erratic and the functioning of the sewage treatment plants have been stalled due
 to frequent power cuts or some other reason.  These STPs cannot afford to be dysfunctional  for even a minute and the
 Committee would like to knowthe arrangements for captive power gensets.  It also noted with concern about the lack of
 public awareness and public participation in the cleaning of rivers. The Committee is, therefore, of the view that the
 cleansing of Yamuna has to go beyond cosmetic measures like removal of slums along the banks and greening of
 banks. Perhaps the more concrete solution is to prevent the drainage wastes from entering  the river and to ensure the
 increase of the flow of  fresh water. The Committee would also like to know if the Delhi Government/Central
 Government have obtained an extension of time from the Supreme Court  for compliance of its order which was to be
 implemented by 31.3.2003 or are the Governments responsible for non-compliance, therefore, committing  contempt of
 the Supreme Court. 
(Para 34)
7.         The Committee is also of the view that the Ministry in coordination with the State Government of Uttar Pradesh,
 Haryana and Delhi should plan a strategy for augmentation of water resources in the upper stretches of the Yamuna and
 for conserving water both for domestic and irrigational purposes. 
(Para 35)
8.         The Committee is of the view that the present status of the river cleansing programme is not satisfactory and
 under these circumstances it would not be possible to achieve the target of clearing all the rivers by 2007.  All the
 phase-wise programmes need to be monitored and the Measure of Performance (MOP) should be introduced to review
 the cleaning activities.
(Para 36)
9.         The Committee therefore feels that efforts at the government and community levels must be redoubled to clean
 our rivers.
(Para 38)
10.       Our rivers have been revered throughout ages. Our tradition invested divinity with our rivers.  Pages of our
 mythologies show as to how norms were prescribed to keep the water of the Ganges clean.  The Committee observed
 that the Bramhanda Purna prohibited thirteen actions to maintain the purity of the Ganges. Some of these are (i)
 defecations (ii) ablutions (iii) discharge of waste water (iv) throwing of used floral offerings (v) rubbing of filth (vi)
 body shampooing (vii) frolicking                (viii) acceptance of donations into the rivers (ix) obscenity (x) discarding or
 cleaning of garments (xi) beating and swimming across.  The Committee recommends that many of these can be
 incorporated by the Ministry in their norms for prohibiting activities to keep the Ganges clean.   
  (Para 39)

 that the active and willing participation of local communities is necessary for the success of any forest regeneration

(Para 53)
14.       The Committee recommends that the rural people, particularly, women and the tribal community have an
 intimate knowledge of forest products, their species, their growth characteristics, utility, medicinal value, etc.  They are

 fodder, timber, and other non-wood forest products.  This knowledge should be utilized under the JFM for the larger
 cause of environmental protection and benefit of the community.  The progress made in measurable terms should be
 reported to Parliament in the Department’s Annual Report on the successof JFM scheme on these specific points. This
 will be an important step for empowerment of these people. There is also need to give thrust to it during the Tenth
 Plan.  However, its strengths and weaknesses need to be identified.
(Para 54)
15.       The Committee was given to understand that one of the goals of the Ministry is to increase the forest cover of the
 country upto 25% by 2007 and 33% by 2012. The Committee appreciates the goal set out by the Ministry but is of the
 view that a blanket approach should not be adopted in this regard. Some States already have a forest cover in excess of
 33% and complain about hampering of development activities due to thick forest cover. Therefore, the policy of
 increasing forest cover should be implemented only in those states which are short of the stipulated target so that a
 balanced proportion of forest cover can be maintained in all parts of the country. 
(Para 55)
16.       The Committee has noted that there was a programme in the 1980s when women used to do social forestry and
 grow and supply seedlings for which they were paid. The Ministry has withdrawn this scheme and given it to forest
 contractors. The Committee recommends that it should be restored to woman Self Help groups.
 (Para 56)
17.       The Committee notes that active involvement of people in the development of the forestry sector has to be
 further strengthened.  The destruction and depletion of forests will not only lead to loss of our vegetation but will also
 result in widespread deterioration of environment with fatal consequences to the very existence of all forms of life. 
 There is, however, much to be done in this area as the phenomenon of cutting of trees, removal of precious timber and
 forest fires continues unabated.  The problem cannot be overcome unless a consciousness is built among the people that
 the forests belong to them and they belong to the forests and the feeling of alienation among the tribals and local
 population goes.  The Committee feels that the local population (including tribals) residing in the forest areas should be
 actively associated with the management of forests and allowed to share the its products,
 without in any way
 compromising the preservation of our national forests.  If this happens, many of the ills currently afflicting our forests
 will disappear.  The Ministry should devise steps to inculcate among them a sense of belonging and commitment to
 forests.  People performing outstanding work in their area should be suitably rewarded and honoured at an appropriate
 forum.
(Para 60)
18.       The Committee also recommends that the vacancies of forest guards needs to be filled immediately in order to
 strengthen the manpower requirements of the forest Department to enforce forest protection at the ground level.
(Para 61)

th Report pertaining to Demands for Grants (2003-2004) of the
 Ministry of Environment & Forests.   A Member of the Committee, Shri B.P. Singhal, has suggested some amendments
 in the report.  While discussing the recommendations on Ganga Action Plan in the report, some members raised the
 issue of proper monitoring system of the Action Plan.  Accordingly, the Committee constituted a Two-member Core

            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology,

 of Scientific & Industrial Research gave an overview of the various activities of the Department and the Members sought
 clarifications on various aspects of the performance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants.

R E P O R T
            Long years back while fighting for freedom Mahatma Gandhi, the father of our nation had conjured up a vision of
 India studded with research laboratories for the service of her people.  Establishment of the Council for Scientific and
 Industrial Research in 1942 was a landmark event in our quest for using science and technology, for national
 reconstruction.  During sixty years of its existence it has emerged as one of the largest R&D organizations in the world for
 scientific and industrial research.  In spite of budgetary constraints and many other bottlenecks the CSIR has striven to
 achieve excellence in promoting and applying science for nation building.  Responding to the new challenges of our
 society, economy and international environment it has now remained in the forefront of forging science-business
 partnerships.  It is now awake to the new norms of competition and innovation and is moving towards the path of self-
financing by generation of its own funds.  After the formation of a separate   Ministry of Science and Technology on
 January 4, 1985 the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research became part of this Ministry.  Business allocated to
 this Department under the Notification is: All matters concerning the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research
 (CSIR), National Research Development Corporation (NRDC), Central Electronics Limited (CEL), National Information
 System on Science and Technology (NISSAT), Registration and Recognition of R&D Units, Matters relating to
 UNCTAD and WIPO, National register for foreign collaborations, the Creation of a pool for temporary placement of
 Indian Scientists and Technologists and  National register of Scientific Manpower.
2.         The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research deals with the Technology Promotion, Development &

 Utilisation (TPDU) programmes (other than supporting the two public sector enterprises namely National Research
 Development Corporation and Central Electronics Limited.
            The scheme on “Technology Promotion, Development and Utilization (TPDU) Programmes” has been formulated
 by merging the following schemes:
      i      Research and Development by Industry (RDI)
      ii.      Programme Aimed at Technological Self Reliance (PATSER)
      iii.   Scheme to Enhance the Efficacy of Transfer of Technology (SEETOT)
            Besides the above, the Department carries out the following activities;
      i.    Matters relating to International R&D collaboration involving industrial companies, and industrial R&D centres.
      ii.            International Cooperation/Collaboration agreements with other countries relating to industrial R&D with the
 concurrence of the Ministry of External Affairs.
      iii.   Matters concerning domestic technology, particularly the promotion of ventures involving the commercialisation
 of such technologies other than those under the Department of Science and Technology.
      iv.   Matters relating to Technology Trade including exports of Technology and Consultancy Services, in close
 cooperation with the Ministry of Commerce.
      v.   Matters relating to technical, engineering and management consultancy organisations and services.
 
COUNCIL OF SCIENTIFIC & INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH
4.         The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), an autonomous organization with its 38 laboratories and
 fifty outreach, centers has recently completed sixty years of their existence. CSIR has emerged as a scientific institution
 which has been highly acclaimed inside and outside India.  It aims at achieving global excellence with local relevance; it
 symbolizes a culture that links science with society through technology , industrial manufacture, and dissemination of
 scientific temper among people.
5.         The Committee was informed that during the Ninth Five Year Plan, CSIR had effected wide spread changes to
 meet the challenges of economic reform, introduction of new industrial and trade policies and liberalization of economy.
 It also effected a reorientation of its programmes with the aim to make CSIR more responsive and move towards a self
 sustaining R&D institution. The cardinal feature of the Ninth Five Year Plan was the White Paper on CSIR focusing on its
 Vision and Strategy. Some of the reform process effected relate to re-engineering of the organizational structure; linking
 research to market place; mobilizing and optimizing the resources base; creating conducive and workable infrastructure
 and investing in high quality science that would be a harbinger of future technologies.
6.         As a result, CSIR stands today amongst the finest publicly funded scientific industrial research establishments of
 the whole world. As the nation’s strongest holder of intellectual property rights (IPR), it leads the way in protecting
 traditional knowledge strength while adding to the new IPR capital.   CSIR today ranks second amongst the major PCT
 applicants from developing countries at USPTO.
7.         CSIR has also promoted excellence in science and is the only S&T organization which had nurtured and supported
 human-tech from 16 to 65 years of age through numerous schemes on human resource for scientific research.  CSIR’s
 mission is to provide scientific industrial R&D that maximizes the economic, environmental & societal benefits for the
 people of India.
8.         The detailed functions assigned to the Council are:
      i.            Promotion, guidance and coordination of scientific and industrial research in India, including the institution
 and financing of specific researches;
      ii.            Establishment or development and assistance to special institutions or departments of existing institutions for
 scientific study of problems affecting particular industries and trade;
      iii.      Establishment and award of research studentships and fellowships;
      iv.            Utilization of the results of the researches conducted under the auspices of the Council towards the
 development of industries in the country and the payment of a share of royalties arising out of the development of

      v.            Establishment, maintenance and management of laboratories, workshops, institutes and organizations to
 further scientific and industrial research and to utilize and exploit for purposes of experiment or otherwise any
 discovery or invention likely to be of use to Indian industries;
     
            vi.            Collection and dissemination of information in regard not only to research but also to industrial matters
 generally;
      vii.      Publication of scientific papers and journals; and
      viii.Any other activity or activities to promote generally the objects of the resolution.
9.         The Committee was informed that the guiding principle for CSIR during the Tenth Five Year Plan would be to
 provide scientific industrial R&D that maximizes the economic, environmental and societal benefits for the people of
 India and accordingly, the Tenth Five Year Plan of CSIR and the Annual Plans have been formulated keeping in mind 8%
 growth rate envisaged by the Planning Commission and Government policy to invest 2% of GDP on Science &
 Technology. 
10.       CSIR seeks to foster the organizational values of: Excellence in science; Global competitiveness in technology
 based on high science; Local relevance in tune with socio-cultural and economic ethos of the people; and Innovation
 ranging in all the spheres of activities from science to technology and from management to financing.  These principles
 coupled with detailed analysis on strength, weakness, opportunities and threats carried out by CSIR laboratories were
 taken into consideration in deriving the opportunities for CSIR in the market place as well as for socio-economic
 development.
11.       The other factors which has bearing on CSIR programmes for the Annual Plans are: Responsibilities on CSIR
 arising out of International Intellectual Property Rights arena; continuous training and re-training of CSIR staff;
 advancement of knowledge through enlarging the scope of fellowships to trans-disciplinary areas and supporting basic
 research that dovetails with its own requirement and expansion of S&T to proliferate CSIR technologies to the masses.

 to promote its activities, it informed that the enhanced allocation of Rs.95.48 crores (Rs.80 crores plan and Rs.15.48
 crores under Non-Plan) would be helpful in meeting the demands of higher expenditure as successful concepts move
 towards commercialization/field implementation stage.  In the Tenth Plan, CSIR has focused attention on programmes of
 National Laboratories under the three categories viz. (i) continuously building & refurbishing competence at globally
 competitive level, skills and competency, in all scientific areas; (ii) taking up in house projects with well defined
 objectives, deliverables, time frame; and (iii) performing contract R&D for industry and other users to deal with problem
 through expertise gained over the years.  Accordingly, some well focused programmes/projects were identified and
 formulated with a view to synergising the competencies developed in laboratories and getting them implemented in a
 network mode.
15.            Explaining the reasons for reduction on allocation in R.E stage last year the Department informed that the
 projects, after formulation, were sent to the Planning Commission for “in-principle” approval.  This procedure took time
 as apart from coordination within CSIR laboratories, formal letters of approvals were also needed from participating
 concerned ministries before the “in principle” approval of Planning Commission could be obtained.  Thus, due to resource
 constraints and the delays in obtaining the “in principle” approval from the Planning Commission, the progress of
 expenditure was not commensurate with allocations. Finance ministry effected a cut of Rs.65 crores under the plan
 scheme at RE stage.
NATIONAL LABORATORIES
16.       CSIR today has a network of 38 Laboratories and 50 field stations/extension centres/regional centres located all
 over the country that undertake R&D in various S&T areas and disciplines. The extension and regional centres have been
 established to reach  out to the diverse users and disseminate knowledge and information on R&D capabilities, techniques
 and technologies developed by the National laboratories of CSIR.
17.       The Committee was informed that CSIR in the Tenth Five Year Plan (TFYP) would seek to further broaden and
 strengthen this trend and undertake more of its activities in the project mode by networking and alliancing on a Team
 India basis. The programmes of National Laboratories have been further categorized sectorally under the following
 sectors: Aerospace; Biology and Biotechnology; Chemical; Earth Resources and Natural Hazards Assessment; Ecology &
 Environment; Electronics and Instrumentation; Energy; Food & Food processing; Health Care, Drugs & Pharmaceuticals;
 Housing & Construction; Information Dissemination and Products; Leather; Materials, Metals, Minerals and
 Manufacturing and Rural Development so as to enable and facilitate an easy alignment with the overall ‘National
 Planning process’. The areas of thrust in these categories have been identified through interactions with various national
 agencies, government departments, industry associations and potential clients keeping in view the strengths and
 capabilities in the CSIR laboratories and the external opportunities. 
18.            Projects of the Tenth Five Year Plan have been evolved, over a period of one year, through interactive and
 repetitive consultations with the Steering Committee on S&T, Working Group for Tenth Five Year Plan, Sectoral
 Subgroup of the Working Group, Research Councils of the respective National Laboratories.  The evolution of the
 Projects, thus, has gone through a great deal of churning of vast S&T expertise available in the country and also in the
 concerned departments/agencies of the Government.
19.       When the Committee asked the Department whether they have identified any core areas for research activities for
 which an increased allocation for national laboratories have been sought the Committee was informed that CSIR has
 formulated programmes to be implemented in Network and Mission mode during the Tenth Plan.  The emphasis is on
 synergising the core competencies available at various laboratories.  The core areas identified include genomics &
 proteomics, integrative biology, herbal preparations for global positioning, bioinformatics, green technologies,
 nutraceuticals & nutragenomics, new approach to drug development, specialty materials, waster minimization through
 new routes, advanced manufacturing technologies, nano technology etc.
20.       The Committee was informed by the Department that during the Tenth Plan CSIR laboratories would synergise

23.       It will establish fellowships in trans-disciplinary areas.  In a calculated manner it will support researchers to come
 out of the areas where there are limited opportunities and challenges and enable them to rise to the new problems and
 opportunities offered by ever widening of scope of science and technology.   Since research scholars hardly seek
 opportunities for self employment and entrepreneurship they end up looking for employment opportunities in government

 establish their own R&D enterprise through appropriate motivation, skills development and venture financing.  It also
 aims at enlarging CPYLS to attract bright school leaving children.
24.       The Committee was informed that CSIR would continue to upgrade extra mural human resources in diverse

27.       CSIR has been on the forefront of filing & managing IPR since its inception.  However a massive programme of

 commencement of the Ninth Plan Period only. As a result most of the CSIR scientists are now IPR and R&D business
 savvy and literate.   The earlier operating slogan of CSIR 'patent, publish and prosper has since been enlarged to 'patent,

 Patent. This demonstrated CSIR's capabilities to understand the complex techno-legal-issues of IPR both defensively and

POLLUTION MONITORING MITIGATION SYSTEMS AND DEVICES
59.       The Committee was informed that as a result of rapid urbanization and industrialization most Indian cities have
 higher levels of gases, particulate matter and chemical pollutants in air than is permissible.  Mortality and morbidity
 statistics also indicate that respiratory infections and chronic illness are becoming wide spread among the urban
 population.  The quality of water in most water bodies has considerably degraded and in most cases cannot be used for
 any human purposes unless adequately treated. Solid wastes abound   in    cities and their hinterland.  In fact human
 beings have emerged as  the greatest waste makers among all the species inhabiting this planet.  This imposes a high cost
 on the economy in terms of loss of life, mandays, productivity and production. Thus the department felt there is an urgent
 need to undertake networked & coordinated mission programme to better understand pollution and its impact on human
 health so as to devise systems and mechanisms for its mitigation. Keeping this as an objective the Department plans for
 development of analytical tools and devices for monitoring selected pollutants in small quantities in water, air and food
 materials, Development of new instruments/methods for analysis and monitoring of the pollutants including biosensors
 and cleaner technologies for reduction of waste generation have received attention.  Waste disposal of industries such as
 bakeries, brick kilns, refractoriness etc, which adversely affect the environment of metropolitan and industrial
 conglomerates has to be addressed.  Vehicular Pollution Monitoring and Management has to be accorded priority.  An
 Integrated Approach to Wastewater Management Systems and Appropriate Effluent Treatment Technologies and the
 Study of Structural and Functional Characteristics of Organic Compounds of Environmental Significance have to be done
 with a sense of urgency.
60.            Keeping in view the objectives to be achieved the Department plans to undertake the study of impact of
 discharge of waste water at elevated temperature from a thermal power station on surrounding ecosystem and developing
 of quantitative structure actively relationship (QSAR) model for prediction of biodegradability of organic compounds.
61.       The Committee feels that all pollution monitoring devises should be site specific as the causative agents in different
 areas are diverse and every anti-pollution process must have measurable parameters to monitor its efficacy. The

 come up with new scientific tools to monitor and review the existing health based ambient quality standards. The
 Committee observes that the department should coordinate with Pollution Control Boards in various states so that
 effective action is taken to sharply curb & finally prevent pollution in the country.

INFECTIOUS DISEASES HANDLING STORAGE AND RESEARCH FACILITIES
76.       The Committee was informed that diseases like tuberculosis, cholera, leprosy and filaria are serious health
 problems to our people. India has no option but to take the lead to develop therapeutics and vaccines against such
 infectious diseases.  There are apocalyptic predictions that in the twenty first century infectious diseases might return
 back. In India the situation is presently alarming. We are in no position to work on these virulent strains due to lack of
 safe and proper preservation facilities. More so because as most of the developed countries have banned or severely
 restricted the access to their reference strains owing to the potential use of these materials as biological weapons. There is
 also increased global pressure to adopt and implement the international guidelines on handling of dangerous pathogens.
77.       In order to encourage and undertake basic research on pathological microbes of interest to tropical countries, CSIR
 seeks to create facilities for storage, handling, cultivation of virulent pathogen strains and invitro and invivo screening
 facility caused by these strains to develop therapeutics against parasitic and infectious diseases. Also such facilities may
 be utilised for conducting tests on disease specific transgenic animals that will be increasingly used in the future for new
 drug discoveries. Thus there is a need to create one each of biosafety level BSL-3 and BSL-4 facility in select CSIR
 laboratories.
78.            Apprising the Committee of the objectives of the programme, the Department stated that Construction of bio-
safety level 3 (BSL-3) facilities in selected CSIR labs and a BSL-4 facility at CCMB with Formulation and
 implementation of appropriate safety guidelines would be undertaken.  The Committee was also informed that
 Networking and accelerating the ongoing research work on infectious microorganisms at these facilities would be
 undertaken.
79.       The Committee feels that the new storage and handling facilities should be of world-class standard.  The
 Committee hopes that this facility would conduct basic research for controlling infectious diseases to reduce the risk of
 morbidity. The Committee hopes that the Department would conduct periodic review of such facilities to properly
 maintain their standards.  The Committee emphasizes the need for adopting measurable parameters for effective
 monitoring of the progress being made in this direction.
 
NEW AND IMPROVED ROAD TECHNOLOGIES
80.      Connecting different parts of India particularly the rural areas through a network of all-weather roads remained an
 immense challenge and goal for our nationalist leaders right from the days of our struggle for independence. While
 fighting for freedom Mahatma Gandhi, the father of our nation was once asked a question as to what he would do if he
 had power to wield.  In his characteristic way he replied, “I would build good and fine roads which would be useful both
 for man and beast”.  That was a remarkable statement of a great visionary of the world to have sustainable roads for the
 use of human beings and animals.  During 1950’s the Brooking Institute, a major think tank of USA made a study on the
 roads of India and commented that India needs good quality roads for ending stagnation of her people and different
 regions caused by distance and isolation.  Successive plans emphasized on the building up of all weather roads.  The
 present condition of roads in our country particularly the quality of its surface deserves serious attention.  It is heartening
 to know that the CSIR is according priority to build roads by using improved and cost effective technology and material. 
 It is also satisfying to know that the CSIR is focusing attention to develop region specific technologies so as to cater to the
 special requirements of different parts of our country.  In the background note for Demands for Grants the Department of
 Scientific & Industrial research has set the target of developing appropriate cold mix technologies for construction of
 roads in North East and urban areas.  It is also stated in the note that technology would be developed to use fly ash for
 road construction purposes.

 through the National Highway Development programme and Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana respectively.  Mobility
 of people is an important indicator and determinant of the overall progress registered by our country.  Roads, which
 constitute the artery of a nation, thus remain central to its forward advancement.  The vision of making India a developed
 nation by the year 2020 will remain only a dream without appropriate connectivity though a network of roads.

ESTABLISHMENT OF GENETICALLY MODIFIED FOODS REFERRAL FACILITY (GMFRF)
83.       The advancement in modern agricultural biotechnological R&D has led to development of diverse novel food
 crops.  These have been designed to possess unique nutritional characteristics.  Such crops are being increasingly used in
 food processing without proper labeling. The market is flooded with imported processed foods without specifying their
 content of GM component. At present there is no referral facility in the country for detection and analysis of GM foods
 and their safety as well as nutritional aspects. Hence they propose to establish such a facility in CFTRI, which will also
 network with ITRC and CCMB under the CSIR umbrella.  In the market many irradiated foods and food products are
 available. They are erroneously confused with GM foods by consumers. It is also believed that radiation brings about
 changes at molecular levels in the food. It is very important to distinguish irradiated food from GM food because
 irradiation constitutes the cheapest method of food preservation. Therefore the proposed facility will also develop
 methods for distinguishing irradiated foods from GM foods.  The facility will be a referral centre for the nation and will
 boost export of foods and food products based on their declared absence or presence of the GM component.
84.       The new Centre has a short term as well as long-term objectives. The short-term objectives include: to develop and
 standardize appropriate detection procedures for identification of GMOs in raw, processed and complex foods using DNA
 and protein based methods;  to establish a single robust method for accurate quantification of GMOs in raw and processed
 foods; to Validate  methods with Certified Reference Materials (CRM) for suitability and certainty; to  develop sampling
 plans to ensure adequacy of testing; to document time  tested procedures, practices on a sound scientific basis so as to
 ensure their replicability in other testing laboratories; to develop database containing data on GM foods worldwide; to 
 evaluate safety of GM food in the light of  Allergenicity, physico chemical stability toxicity,  to establish  a GMO
 germplasm preservation centre and maintain a culture collection of microorganisms used in Indian traditional foods.
 Long-term Objective would be to evolve the GMFRF as the reference centre for the South East Asia.
85.       The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Department has taken an important step by establishing this unique
 centre, which would monitor the quality and content of G.M. food.  The Committee feels that such a referral centre is
 necessary for checking the activities of those who flout laws related to the import of G.M. food and target those who trade
 in such foods without proper trials and approvals.

 need for publicity about the quality testing facility so that people at large avail of it.

91.            Evolution of human civilization from steam age to the age of biotechnology is indeed fascinating and exciting. 
 While human capability is expanding through science and technology, the attitude and outlook of people do not change
 correspondingly.  Enormous technological strength without a scientific and humane approach would create imbalances in
 as well human personality and society at large.  To enable our scientists to file their patents we teach them patent literacy. 
 It is important for their success in the age of competition and innovation.  Even more important is to promote scientific
 temper among our people.  The Committee has been focussing  its attention on this issue.  Swami Vivekananda regarded
 modern science as a manifestation of the real religious spirit, for it sought to understand truth by sincere effort.  Pandit

 promote scientific humanism among our people.

R E P O R T
 
INTRODUCTION
One of the most exciting and spectacular developments in the recorded history of mankind is the exploration of
 space and application of space technology for solving the complex social, economic and environmental problems
 confronted by mankind.  Since ancient times infinite space fired the imagination of Indians and their minds soared high to
 unravel its mysteries.  In more modern times pioneers of India's space programme considered space research and space
 technology as essential and indispensable for national reconstruction. While space technology has emerged as a proven
 means of successfully transforming society in a cost effective and limited time frame, the investment involved has
 prompted skeptics to question its relevance. Dr. Vikram Sarabhai the founder of our space programme when asked about
 the necessity of India venturing into such high profile scientific quest against the background of our resource crunch and
 social and economic backwardness had said,
There are some who question the relevance of space activities in a developing nation... we are
 convinced that if we are to play a meaningful role nationally and in the community of nations, we must
 be second to none, in the application of advanced technologies to the real problems of man and society
 which we find in our country. 
2.         One of the first astronauts of the USA John Glenn who subsequently  became a Senator justified the huge
 expenditure on space programmes by saying "Every dollar we put into the space programme gives us seven dollars worth
 of new technology".  In 1995 while delivering the annual K. R. Narayanan Oration, established by the Australian National
 University, Professor U. R. Rao, former Chairman of the Space Commission focused on the theme “Space Technology
 for  Sustainable Development in Asia” and stated that space technology could transform stagnant societies within less
 time and money.
3.         Today India is nothing short of a role model in space research and application  of space technology for

ONE HUNDRED-FOURTEENTH REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/114threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:24:49]
 transforming and improving our social, economic and environmental conditions and for reaching the "the high peaks of
 development in the fields of science and technology". 
4.         During four decades of India's space programme which commenced with the formation of the Indian National
 Committee for Space Research in 1962 our country has reached many milestones and scaled unprecedented heights in
 applying space technology for nation building.  Beginning with the launch of the first sounding rocket from Thumba
 Equatorial Rocket Launching Station in November 1963 the Indian Space Programme has progressed with many restraints
 imposed on it and is rightly described as "Success under Embargoes".
5.         The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) was established in 1969 under the Department of Atomic Energy. 
 The Government of India gave a fillip to the space activities by formally setting up the Space Commission and the
 Department of Space (DOS) in June 1972, and bringing ISRO under DOS.  The primary objective of DOS is to promote
 the development and application of space science and technology for the socio-economic benefit of the nation.  The
 programme is executed through ISRO, National Remote Sensing Agency (NRSA), Physical Research Laboratory (PRL),
 National Mesosphere-Stratosphere-Troposphere Radar Facility (NMRF), North Eastern-Space Applications Centre (NE-
SAC) and other agencies.  The Antrix Corporation, a wholly owned Government  company,  which was established in
 1992, is  engaged
in commercial marketing of space products and services.  The establishment of space systems and their utilization are
 coordinated by national level committees, namely, the INSAT Coordination Committee (ICC), Planning Committee of
 National Natural Resources Management System (PC-NNMS) and Advisory Committee on Space Sciences (ADCOS). 
 Five Regional Remote Sensing Service Centres (RRSSC) help in undertaking remote sensing application projects relevant
 to the region.
6.         The Secretariat of DOS and the Headquarters of ISRO are located at Antariksh Bhavan in Bangalore.  Programme
 offices at ISRO Headquarters coordinate the overall programmes like satellite communication, earth observation, launch
 vehicle, space science, space-industry coordination, disaster management   support, international cooperation, publications
 and public relations, budget and economic analysis and human resources development.
7.         The Indian space programme was initially directed towards demonstrating the efficacy of space systems for
 national development through development of experimental satellites, launch vehicles and conduct of application
 experiments.  While the Satellite Instructional Television Experiment (SITE), was conducted during 1975-76, the Satellite
 Telecommunication Experimental Project(STEP), was conducted during 1977-79. These were the two important steps
 undertaken in this direction to gain experience in the use of satellite for developmental communications and domestic
 telecommunications.
8.            Simultaneously, space hardware was developed for experimental missions which would ultimately lead to
 indigenous operational space systems.  Aryabhata, the first  Indian satellite launched in April 1975, provided experience
 in design, fabrication and operation in space of a satellite system.  It was followed by two experimental remote sensing
 satellites, Bhaskara-1 and Bhaskara-2, launched in June 1979 and November 1981, respectively.  The Bhaskara satellites
 gave hands-on experience in building and operating space-based remote sensing system.  APPLE (Ariane Passenger
 Payload Experiment), an experimental communication satellite launched in June 1981, besides, enabling continuation of
 telecommunication experiments that had earlier been conducted under STE provided inputs in orbit raising and in-orbit
 maintenance of a geo-stationary satellite.  India’s first satellite launch vehicle, SLV-3, was launched successfully on July
 18, 1980.
9.         The experiments and demonstrations of the 70’s were consolidated to evolve operational space systems.  In this
 direction, over the years, India has established two operational space systems – the Indian National Satellite (INSAT)
 System providing services for telecommunications, TV broadcasting and meteorology including disaster warning support
 and the Indian Remote Sensing Satellite (IRS) System for resource monitoring and management.  The Polar Satellite
 Launch Vehicle (PSLV) is well proven through six successive successful flights. The successful launch of the first
 developmental flight of Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle, GSLV-D1, in 2001 was a major land mark in the
 Indian space programme making India the sixth country in the world to demonstrate capabilities for launch of geo-
stationary satellites of INSAT type.
10.       The constellation of Indian Remote Sensing Satellites comprises of five satellites including India’s first
 oceanographic satellite (IRS-P4).  They, besides, provide data worldwide, through a network of international ground
 stations serve as  a  main  stay of the  National Natural Resources Management System (NNRMS).  The Vital applications
 such as identifying zones which could yield ground water, suitable locations for recharging water, monitoring command
 areas estimating crop areas and yields, assessing deforestation, mapping urban areas for planning
purposes, delineating ocean areas with higher fish catch potential and monitoring of environment are being pursued

 actively by users with the space based data.  In the field of space communication and meteorology, the INSAT system,
 currently consisting of four satellites, viz, 2DT, 2E, 3B and 3C, is one of the largest domestic communication satellite
 systems in the world.  METSAT, a satellite exclusively for meteorology, was launched in September 2002.  It has been
 renamed after Kalpana Chawla, the Indian born space scientist, who lost her life after the space shuttle Columbia
 disintegrated during its return journey to earth.    INSAT contributes significantly to a variety of services in
 telecommunications and television broadcasting including meteorological observations, disaster communications, distance
 education, telemedicine and training.  The Department of Space has taken initiatives to pilot a Satellite Communication
 Policy in 1997 paving the way for the use of INSAT capacity by private users.  The new Satellite Communication
 (Satcom) Policy has also opened the possibilities for private Indian Satellite Systems in India.  A comprehensive Remote
 Sensing Data Policy on acquisition and distribution of satellite remote sensing data from Indian and foreign satellites for
 civilian users in India has been formulated and approved by the Government which ensures that users are not denied
 access to valuable satellite data for developmental purposes.
11.            Significant  scientific investigations are being carried out in the fields of astronomy, atmospheric sciences and
 long term climatic research using satellites, balloons, sounding rockets & ground instruments.  The Indian space
 programme has played a critical role for our industrial sector for augmenting their capabilities.  A strong bond with
 academic institutions exists through extensive research partnerships.  Unique organizational systems have been evolved in
 the national space programme for fulfilling diverse functions like development, operations and applications of complex
 space systems.  The space programme has enabled significant technology growth in multiple disciplines as spin-off
 benefits.
12.       Indian capabilities in space thus represent a wide spectrum of expertise ranging from the conceptual design to
 building and operating a variety of space systems, which are matched only by a few nations in the world.  In view of these
 multiple dimensions and capabilities, India is recognised as a leader in application  of space technologies.  The end-to-end

INSAT
18.       INSATis a multipurpose satellite system for telecommunications, broadcasting, meteorology and search & rescue
 services.  Commissioned in 1983, INSAT is the largest domestic communication system in the Asia-Pacific Region.  It
 now comprises of five satellites – INSAT-2DT, INSAT-2E, INSAT-3B, INSAT-3C and METSAT – with a total capacity
 of over
hundred transponders in C, Extended C and Ku-bands. Besides it has got meteorological instruments.
19.       It carried twenty four transponders – twelve operating in the normal C-band frequency, six in Extended C-band and
 six in Ku-band.  Nine of the twelve normal C-band transponders provide expanded coverage and the remaining three have
 India coverage beam.  All the extended C-bands as well as the Ku-band transponders have India coverage beam.  INSAT-
3A also carried a Ku-band beacon.
20.       For meteorological observation, INSAT-3A carried a three channel Very High Resolution Radiometer (VHRR)
 with 2 km resolution in the visible band and short wave infrared bands providing a spatial resolution of 1 km.  A data
 Relay Transponder (DRT) operating in UHF band is incorporated for real-time hydro meteorological data collection from
 unattended platforms located on land and river basins.  The data is then relayed in extended C-band to a central location.
21.            INSAT-3A also carried another transponder for Satellite Aided Search and Rescue (SAS & R) as part of India’s
 contribution to the international Satellite Aided Search and Rescue programme.
22.            INSAT-3A is launched by European Ariane-5 Launch Vehicle into a Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO)
 with a perigee of 200 km and an apogee of 35,980 km.  The satellite is manoeuvered to its final orbit by firing the
 satellite’s apogee motor.  Subsequently, the deployment of solar array, antennae and the solar sail is carried out and the
 satellite is commissioned after in-orbit checkout.
23.            INSAT-3A is the third satellite in the INSAT-3 series. INSAT-3B and ISNAT-3C were launched in March 2000
 and January 2002 respectively by the Ariane launch vehicle and both the satellites are now providing regular service. 
 INSAT-3A is to be located at 93.5 deg east longitude in the geostationary orbit and was launched by Ariane-5 launch
 vehicle of Arianespace in the early hours of April 10, 2003 (as per IST), from Kourou in French Guyana.
24.       The Committee congratulates the Department for the successful launch of the INSAT-3A and records its
 appreciation for the abilities and talents of our scientists who have further enhanced the glory of our nation through this
 splendid performance.  The Committee hopes that the other satellites in the INSAT series would be launched as planned
 without any cost escalation.  Proven abilities of our scientists have now to be used to develop the cryogenic technology
 which has been subjected to many experiments.  The Committee feels that the indigenous development of cryogenic
 engines is critical to the development of our own geostationary satellite launch vehicles.  It expresses full faith on our
 space scientists and hopes that they will accomplish the mission.

25.       In its maiden test flight on April 18, 2001, GSLV successfully placed a 1540 kg experimental satellite, GSAT-1,

 the improvement of GSLV capability was the successful testing of the up-rated version of the liquid propellant Vikas
 engine.  The up-rated version develops higher chamber pressure than in the current version.  This new engine uses UH25
 (a mixture of unsymmetrical Di-methyl Hydrazine and hydrazine hydrate) as fuel and nitrogen tetroxide as
oxidizer.  The new engine has the potential to increase the payload capability of GSLV by about 150 kg in the Geo-
synchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO) and the GSLV-D2 can carry a mass of 1,800 kg in GTO.

GSLV Mk-III Project
28.       The development of an advanced version of ISRO’s Geo-synchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle, known as GSLV
 Mk-III, which will have a capability to launch four tonne satellites into GTO, was approved during the year.  The
 development is expected to take about six years.  GSLV Mk-III will be a three-stage vehicle with a 110 tonne core liquid
 propellant stage and strap-on stage with two solid propellant motors, each, with 200 tonne propellant.  The upper stage
 will be a cryogenic stage with a propellant loading of 25tonne and will be 42.4 m tall.  The payload fairing will have a
 diameter of 5 metre and a payload volume of 100 cubic metre.

 cryogenic propellant storage and servicing facility and range instrumentation systems for GSLV Mk-III have been

 plan and schedules have also been prepared.

 satellites in to GTO. The GSLV Mk–III project was approved in May 2002 at an estimated cost of Rs.2498.00 crores, and
 envisages development of a number of technologies which include 200 tonne solid stage booster, 25 tonne cryogenic
 engines, cluster of two vikas engines as core booster, vehicle characterization, etc. Realisation of the vehicle is targeted in

METSAT (KALPANA-1)
32.            KALPNA-1 is the first in the series of exclusive meteorological satellites built by ISRO. Earlier, meteorological
 services were combined with telecommunication and television services in the INSAT system.  This meteorological
 satellites are named after the Indian born American astronaut Dr. Kalpana Chawla, who died on February 1, 2003 in the
 US Space Shuttle Columbia.  KALPANA-1 is a precursor to the future INSAT system that will have separate satellites for
 meteorology and telecommunication & broadcasting services.  This will enable large capacity to be built into INSAT
 satellites, both in terms of transponders and their radiated power, without the design constraints imposed by
 meteorological instruments, which are also expected to become heavier with advanced features.
33.       For meteorological observation, KALPANA-1 carries a Very High Resolution Radiometer (VHRR) capable of
 imaging the Earth in the visible, thermal infra-red and water vapour bands.  It also carries a Data Relay Transponder
 (DRT) for collecting data from unattended meteorological platforms. KALPANA-1 will relay the data sent by these
 platforms to the meteorological Data Utilisation Centre at New Delhi.  Such platforms have been installed all over the
 country.
34.       At the time of launch, KALPANA-1 weighed 1060 kg, which included about 560 kg of propellant.  The propellant
 carried by Kalpana-1 was mainly required to raise the satellite from the Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit to its final
 Geostationary Orbit.  KALPANA-1 is located at 74 deg. East longitude. 
35.       The main objective of METSAT is to support the India Meteorological Department (IMD) in ensuring
 meteorological data and weather imageries on a continuous basis.  The sanctioned cost of the project is Rs.75.00 crores.

 satellite is satisfactory.

 studies would be better and this would improve the quality of prediction for accurate weather forecasts.

ISRO-GEO SPHERE BIOSPHERE PROGRAMME
44.       Global climate change is of great concern to the world scientific community UN and many others.  Realising the
 importance of scientific studies to arrive at specific migration strategies for the Indian sub-continent, the Department
 initiated the ISRO Geosphere-Biosphere Programme 10 years back which has contributed significantly in understanding
 various issues related to climate change using space-based and convention systems.  This programme encompasses the
 study of land-air-ocean interaction, past climate, changes in atmospheric composition, aerosols, carbon cycle, bio-mass
 estimation, bio-diversity and other related areas of scientific investigation.  The ISRO-GBP is aimed at using maximum
 data from ISRO’s own satellites.  Data from balloon-borne experiments are also used for studying the climate change
 processes.
45.       ISRO-GBP contributed significantly to Indian Ocean experiments (INDOEX-I) during 1998-1999.  Investigation
 on the aerosol distribution and spatial variability of AOD using the network of observations is continuing.  Satellite
 observations of the regional aerosol loading, aerosol transport and the clear sky aerosol rediative forcing over the oceanic
 areas around the Indian subcontinent are being carried out.  The studies  are being made on the impact of El Nino related
 south Asian forest fires on the regional aerosol distribution over the Indian Ocean.
46.       The Committee hopes that the ISRO-GEO sphere programme would be helpful in predicting, the arrival of
 monsoon with greater precision. It also hopes that the programme would be useful to study the recent phenomenon like
 Asian Brown cloud. 
LUNAR MISSION
47.       In order to promote space exploration, discussions had been held under the auspices of Indian Academy of
 Sciences and Astronautical Society of India to study the feasibility of undertaking an unmanned Lunar Mission.  These
 studies were primarily related to definition of possible scientific objectives, conceptualization of mission including the
 spacecraft and the feasibility of using Indian launch vehicles to place a spacecraft into lunar orbit.  Based on the inputs
 from discussions, ISRO has set up a Lunar Mission Task Force, to study the various possibilities for undertaking a
 scientific mission to the moon.  The National Task Force has submitted its report.  After considering various options, the
 team has recommended that it is feasible to launch a lunar polar orbiter at an altitude of 100 km using the existing
 PSLV/GSLV capabilities of ISRO.  The main objective of such a mission would be to realize the technological goal for
 planetary missions.  In addition, the first lunar mission may have the following scientific objectives:
(i)
                 Preparing a 3-dimensional atlas (with a high spatial and altitude resolution of 5-10m) of regions of
 scientific interest on the moon.
(ii)                Chemical mapping of the entire lunar surface for exploring elemental abundance of Mg. Al, Si, Ca, Fe and
 Ti with a spatial resolution of abut 10km and distribution of high Z elements such as 222Rn, U, Th, etc,
 with a spatial resolution of about 20 km on the lunar surface. At present, the report of the Task Force
 (Study Group) is being examined for further action.
48.       In reply to the Committee Question whether the Department has any plans to send the man to the moon in the near
 future the Committee was informed that the Department of Space has no immediate plan for sending a manned expedition
 to the Moon. However some studies are being carried out to explore the possibility for launching an unmanned lunar
 probe in the near future.
49.       ISRO had constituted a Lunar Mission Study Task Force for considering and making an assessment of the possible
 configuration and feasibility of taking up such a mission. The task force has submitted its report identifying the potential
 scientific objectives of the mission, the payload options, the spacecraft configuration, the launch vehicle requirements and
 the mission related aspects.
50.       In order to review and formulate the recommendations on the Indian Mission to Moon programme based on the
 study group report, Chairman, ISRO/Secretary, DOS has convened a peer review meeting in the first week of April 2003.

TELEMEDICINE
75.       The Committee was informed that  telemedicine is an emerging area where there is a lot of scope to successfully
 apply space technology.  Most of the States are interested to adopt telemedicine practices to extend medical facilities to
 people inhabiting remote and inaccessible areas.  Doctors are showing keen interest to offer their services to patients
 through telemedicine. Tele-medicine mainly consists of customized medical software integrated with computer hardware,
 along with medical diagnostic instruments connected to the commercial VSAT (Very Small Aperture Terminal) at each
 location, which is turn, is linked to a super specialty hospital through satellite.  The medical records of the patient like
 medical images and outputs from medical devices are sent to the specialist, who in-turn study them, diagnose and advice
 on the course of treatment through videoconference with the doctor or a paramedic at patient’s end.  The
specialist could even guide the junior doctor at the patient’s end during a surgery.  Thus the patients in distant and rural
 areas can avail timely consultations of specialists without the ordeal of travelling long distances and spending a large
 amount of money.
76.       DOS undertook tele-medicine demonstrations with the involvement of selected super specialty hospitals located in
 major cities and smaller health centres in remote areas during the year.  They include Tele-medicine links between Port 
 Blair and Car Nicobar and Chennai benefiting the inhabitants of Andaman & Nicobar Islands,  Kavaratti in Laksha
 Dweep linked to Cochin and Karnataka tele-medicine project connecting a specialty hospital for heart care in Banagalore
 with District Hospital at Chamrajanagar and a rural hospital at Sargur in H D Kote taluk.  Apart from these, telemedicine
 facilities were set up in remote areas like Tripura, Assam and Leh. 
77.       The Committee commends the Department for bringing high quality medical care to patients transcending the
 barriers of geography, distance, time and costs.  It believes that this can be a boon for countries like India where the
 majority population lives in remote areas without access to even basic health care.   The Committee however hopes that
 the poor quality of internet/telephone services will not come in the way of effective functioning of telemedicine services.
78.       The Committee also hopes that in the next few years there will be telemedicine kiosks throughout the length and
 breadth of suburban and rural India. It is hoped that the government scheme to provide such kiosks will go hand in hand
 with the spread of telemedicine facility.
DISASTER MANAGEMENT SUPPORT (DMS)
79.       As part of the continuing support to Disaster Management in the country, DOS has initiated several actions towards
 operational use of space data.  The disaster management support programme encompasses following aspects:
Flood Monitoring: Near real-time monitoring of major floods is being continued using data from IRS and RADARSAT. 
 The information generated is being disseminated to State administrations.  They propose to use the digital database for
 generating village level information on flood inundation and affected population.
80.       During the year, recent flood waves of Bihar and Assam were monitored and inundation maps prepared.  These
 maps were disseminated in near real-time (by e-mail) to the Control Room on disaster Management, of the Ministry of
 Home Affairs, Central Water Commission and Relief Commissioners of Bihar and Assam States.  14 States in the country
 (AP, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Haryana, Jharkhand, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Rajasthan,
