5.         Today, critiques often describe “Dal Lake”, as “Dull Lake” and even accuse concerned authorities of preparing for its
 funeral.   They sadly compare it with ‘Anchar Lake’ which is already finished and to ‘Wular Lake’ which was recently
 shown as only knee deep due to extensive silting and area of the lake has drastically reduced by over 60% from original 200
 sq. kms. The vistas have become a sewage canal. Srinagar city’s drains are clogged with human waste. The city has created
 satellite slums around it. Population is increasing at an alarming rate putting pressure for housing them in the land locked
 valley. As a result, mountains are losing their forests, rivers and lakes their limpidity, valley its chinars that stood as
 sentinels of time and living witnesses of the rise and fall of many a kingdom, roads their poplar and willow avenues, Mughal
 gardens the great variety of their flowers.
PHYSICAL FEATURES OF THE LAKE
6.         The Dal Lake is a postglacial lake of shallow depth and is believed by some geologists that it is the remnant of a
 Pleistocene oligotrophic Lake that once covered the entire valley of Kashmir. There are other geologists who opine that it
 was a flood plain lake. The Dal Lake is at an altitude of  1600 m above sea level and lies between 34
o 5’ and  34o 10’ North
 Latitude and 74o 8’ and 79o 7’ East Longitude. With a catchment area of about 300 sq., km the lake is fed by several small
 streams around the shoreline, by springs under the lakebed and by one large stream, Telbal Nalla on the northern end of the
 lake.  Outflow from the lake is though a weir and lock system, Dal Gate at the south-western corner into Chinar Bagh which
 is a loop channel of Jhelum River and through Amir Khan Nalla into the Anchar Lake.
7.         The Dal Lake is multibasined with Hazratbal, the Bod-Dal, and the Gagribal and the Nagin as its four basins. The
 Hazratbal basin is situated between the Telbal and the Nishat.  On the eastern side of the basin is situated Nagin Bagh, while
 on its western side two famous Mughal gardens are located. The area of the Bod-Dal extends from Kotarkhana to Nishat
 Bund.  A small island, Ropa Lank, in its centre is the conspicuous feature of this part of the lake.   The Gagribal basin
 extends from Kotarkhana to Nehru Park.  This part of the lake touched the outer fringes of Shankaracharya hill before 1930
 when the present Boulevard Road was constructed.   The Nagin basin, which is separated from the main lake by a narrow
 strip of marshy land, is connected with the Hazratbal basin on the northwest.
8.         Morphometrically, these basins differ markedly in regard to their area, volume, maximum depth and indices of
 shoreline development, etc. Among different lake basins of Dal Lake the largest in area is the Hazratbal (3.54km
2) and the
 smallest the Nagin (0.89km2), but the Nagin is the deepest (6.0 m) and the Gagribal the shallowest (2.5 m).  The lake basin
 walls are essentially convex towards the water as the volume index figures are less than unity. The ratio between and mean
 and the maximum depth ranges between 0.20 and 0.25, indicating the gentle slope of the lakebed. The total water surface of
 the Dal Lake is 11.45 sq. km and total volume estimated at 9.83 X 10 6  m 3.  Floating gardens covers a sizeable portion
 (approx.0.3 km.) of the lake extending from the Hazratblal basin to the Gagribal, on the western side.  The lake has been
 extensively manipulated in this part to form man-made islands separated by canals and areas of water covered by floating
 gardens. Natural deposition of silt from the Telbal Nalla has also created extensive marshes around the northern end of the
 lake.   Many dwellings have been built on these islands and reclamations, apart from the areas used for agriculture, are
 extensively covered by willow and poplar trees.
9.         The catchment area of Dal Lake can be broadly divided into five subcatchments: (i) Dachigam, (ii) Telbal, (iii) Lake
 Hillside, (iv) Srinagar North, and (v) Srinagar City.   Among these subcatchments, Dachigam is the largest in area (145 x
 106 m2) and comprises mainly the Dachigam Game Reserve and south-facing slopes.  The Dachigam Game Reserve is a
 restricted area and has good forest and ground cover but the south-facing slopes have been denuded of forest cover due to
 overgrazing of cattle and in the past by burning off.  It is evident that denudation of this area is resulting in significant
 contribution of silt to the Dachigam Nalla which drains this catchment area.  At the outlet of the catchment, the flow of the
 Dachigam Nalla is diverted to the irrigation canals in Telbal catchment, the Harwan.  The balance continues to flow through
 Telbal Nalla into Dal Lake. The Telbal catchment, which begins at the foothills of the south-facing hills, has been denuded
 by overgrazing.  The gentle slopes in lower reaches of this area are, however, extensively used for paddy cultivation. The
 Lake Hill side catchment drains into Dal Lake via a number of small streams around the east and south sides of the lake.  
 Around the lake shore, the lower land slopes of this catchment have been utilized for rice cultivation, orchards and gardens. 
 Beyond this, the land rises very steeply to 1000 m above the lake.   The steep expose slopes do not support any vegetation,

SOURCES OF POLLUTANTS
10.       One of the main factors contributing to the environmental deterioration of the lake comes from the pressure of human
 settlements along its shores and within the lake itself. With the growth in population, the pressure on the lake and it’s
 surrounding as potential settlement areas has increased.   Agricultural activities within floating gardens and reclaimed land
 have also contributed to the pollution of the lake. A serious issue of contention is that islands have been formed and
 residences built on them, when the title to the water surface in fact restricts the use to water only.  Similarly some areas
 have been converted into solid horticulture land.  Despite increased vigilance on the part of the authorities and restrictive
 legislation and ordinances, a small number of people are continuing to develop and extend their illegal encroachments.
11.       Apart from 250 houseboats a number of villages have come up in the floating gardens i.e Tang Bagh and Chowdri
 Bagh. Treated water is available only in some areas at present.  Most of the houseboats use the lake water, which is elevated
 into a bolding tank in the roof with a hand pump.  Sewage and sullage waste is discharged directly into the lake.   Solid
 wastes such as vegetable scraps and paper are dumped into the lake.  Toilets used by the local residents have been
 constructed over water.  The Dal Lake receives pollutants from these point sources as well as non-point or diffuse sources. 
 The point sources include (i) sewage and other human wastes from the houseboats and residential huts within the lake area
 (ii) sewage outfalls from the adjoining settlements including some tourist spots. The non-point source, which cannot be
 exactly pinpointed, includes the run-off from agriculture fields and erosion from the catchment area.
POINT- SOURCES
12.       Continuing pressure of human settlements along the shores and within the lake itself could be singularly identified as
 one of the major causes of pollution in respect of organic load.  Over the years, a number of settlements have come up in the
 floating gardens from Tang Bagh to Chowdri Bagh.  It has been estimated that about 10,500 people live within the house
 boat area and almost the same number of people live outside this area on islands, boats etc.   The total population living
 within the other catchments of the Dal Lake is about Rs.2.5 lakhs.  As per the records of the State Town and Country
 Planning Department, there has been an increase of 25,040 people within the catchment area during 1971-77 (the population
 increased from 1,66,040 to 1,91,000) and since then about 50,000 persons have been added to this area over the passage of
 time.
13.       There are several hundreds of houseboats in the area adjacent to Boulevard Road from Dal Gate to Kotal Khana. It is
 said that houseboats represent a long tradition and basic infrastructure of tourism. The number of houseboats has
 considerably increased in recent years without significant improvement in commensurate facilities of sanitary waste
 disposal.  As a result, sewage, human wastes and sullage waste including solid wastes are directly discharged into the lake. 
NON-POINT SOURCES
14.       Run-off from the agricultural fields and erosion of hillsides in the catchment area are the major non-point sources of
 pollution causing silting and loading of nutrients. It has been mentioned in the proceeding pages that the catchment area of
 the lake can be broadly sub-divided into five sections viz. (i) Dachigam-Telbal area (ii) Lake Hill side (iii) Srinagar North,
 (iv) Srinagar City and (v) littoral area of the Dal Lake.  Among  these, Dachigam is the largest in area (145 X  10
6 m2) and it
 comprises mainly   Dachigam Game Reserve and south facing slopes with Telbal area at its foothills. Dachigam Game
 Reserve has a reasonably good forest and ground cover but its south facing slopes have been denuded due to overgrazing
 and fire.  It has resulted in increasing movement of silt to Dachigam Nalla, which drains this catchment area.  A major
 portion of the flow from this catchment area is diverted to the Harwan Reservoir and the water treatment plant at Harwan. 
 However, considerable quantities of flow laden with silt and nutrients are also led through the Telbal Nalla into the Dal
 Lake.  The gentle sloping lower reaches of the Telbal area are extensively used for paddy cultivation and as such the run-
off-from these fields significantly contribute to the concentration of soluble phosphorus.
15.       The ‘Lake Hillside’ catchment drains into the Dal Lake through a number of small streams in the east and south sides
 of the lake.  Around the lake shore, the land slopes of this catchment have been utilized for paddy cultivation, orchards and
 gardens.  Beyond this, there is steep gradient in land slope about 1000 m above the lake level, which is heavily grazed and
 denuded.
16.       The  ‘Srinagar North’ comprises mainly outer suburbs of Srinagar city that is extensively used for paddy cultivation.  
 The topography is very flat and it drains through slow flowing canals and open drains which, in parts, are grossly polluted
 with sewage and rubbish.

17.       The ‘Srinagar City’ sub-catchment is highly urbanized and in most areas it drains through Brari-Nambal, a large
 swampy area that is also polluted with sewage and rubbish.
18.       The Lake itself forms the ‘Dal Lake’ sub-catchment and it includes floating gardens, marshes and land areas within
 the lake.  This sub-catchment is being extensively utilised for cultivation of vegetables etc.   In fact, the vegetables in the
 Srinagar City are mostly provided from the area.
LOADING OF POLLUTANTS
19.       Dr. C.L. Trisal who obtained his doctorate from Kashmir University on “Dal Lake”, has stated that the problem of
 pollution is mainly due to the addition of nutrients particularly phosphorus and nitrogen at an accelerated rate.   These
 nutrients have been chiefly responsible for recurrence of dense macrophytic growth and deterioration of water quality.  
 "Eutrophication", is a scientific process in which the lake changes colour due to the blossoming of an algae called
 Euglenineae, which only happens when the lake is sufficiently rich in organophosphates i.e nitrates, phosphates, and
 potassium found in raw sewage and agricultural effluents. As the water becomes overloaded with nutrients, the algae
 spreads and oxygen levels falls consequently resulting in the death of plant and animal life. Man-made eutrophication as
 opposed to natural eutrophication is linked to the addition of major plant nutrients viz. phosphorus and nitrogen derived
 from human wastes, detergents, fertilizers, agricultural activities, etc. which thrives as a result of the floating population on
 the lake.
20.       According to a research study, carried out by ENEX- a group of consultants from New Zealand who prepared a report
 for the Commonwealth Fund for Technical Cooperation in 1978, among the non-point sources, the Dachigam Telbal
 subcatchment contributes significant amount of nutrient input to the lake  (5.3 tonnes P/year and 228 tonnes N/year) and a
 comparison of the nutrient input from both point and non-point sources reveals that Srinagar city and Dachingam-Telbal
 sub-catchments are mainly responsible for heavy load of nutrients going into to the lake system.
21.       Prof. (Dr.) Helmut Kroiss of the Vienna University of Technology submitted a report entitled Dal Lake Conservation
 Project in 1998’, in which he has also observed that “Dal Lake: The beauty of Kashmir is in a critical state since waste
 water, solid waste and fertilizer discharge to the lake have caused increased eutrophication with excessive growth of weed
 and algae in most of the areas”.
22.       However, the picture is slightly different when nutrient outflow pattern of the Lake is taken into consideration.   The
 two principal outflows that carry water out of the Dal Lake are Amir Khan Nalla    and the Dal Gate.  The Amir Khan Nalla
 carries water from the southern end of the lake into the River Jhelum.  Together, these represent an average outflow of
 47.3x  106  m3/year. It has been calculated that these outflows carry 1.7 tonnes of phosphorus and 42.4 tonnes of nitrogen
 out of the lake each year.  Besides, the nutrient inputs from Srinagar North are directly discharged through the Dal Gate and
 Nalla Amir Khan and as such do not enter the Dal Lake.  Thus, Dachigam-Telbal area, and the houseboat area of Dal Lake,
 are chiefly responsible from nutrient loading into the Lake.
23.       Based on the data collected for preparation of a report for the Commonwealth Fund for Technical Cooperation by
 ENEX of New Zealand Inc., the nutrient balance of the lake indicates that there is a net positive inflow of 15.5 tonnes of
 phosphate and 322 tonnes of nitrogen per year. The total outflow of nutrients from the lake ecosystem has been estimated to
 be 10 tonnes of phosphorus and 275.6 tonnes of nitrogen per year.  Thus, there is a net build up of 5.5 tonnes of phosphorus
 and 88.9 tonnes of nitrogen annually into the lake. 
24.       The Committee is of firm belief that Conservation of Dal Lake is a national issue.  It forms the axis of life for the
 Kashmir valley and therefore it is not only important from the point of view of ecology, but also from the point of
 augmenting economy of the people and ensuring peace in the region.  The Committee is therefore deeply worried about the
 deterioration of water quality and other associated problems arising out of development of eutrophic conditions, which have
 reduced the environmental, recreational and aesthetic value of this lake. The Committee therefore is strongly of the view
 that in order to formulate a plan of action to control pollution, the principal sources of these nutrients have to be identified
 and the rate of accumulation of these nutrients in the lake basin should be precisely known.
25.       The Committee was informed by the Vice Chairperson of the Jammu and Kashmir Lakes and Waterways
 Development Authority that the threat to the Dal Lake is not only posed by the encroachment problem but also by the silt
 within the nutrients which becomes a land mass over a period of years. 
26.       Hence, the Committee strongly recommends the following of these procedures and suggests acquiring a precise
 knowledge about the rate of accumulation of these nutrients at the lake basin:

MEASURES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF THE LAKE
37.       The Committee understands that the lake has reached a critical stage as the nutrients are deposited in the sediments
 rather than in the lake water.  Since macrophytes have an adaptive advantage to derive nutrients from lake sediments, the
 recurring growth of these weeds is obvious in the lake ecosystem.   The macrophytes provide a biological sink to the
 nutrients, and thus play a very important role in suppressing the plankton population.   Continual expansion of macrophytes,
 have accelerated the process of eutrophication, as they have the capacity to translocate nutrients from the sediments into
 water thereby increasing nutrients available to the plankton and floating plants such as “Sylvinia-Lemna” complex.  With
 the subsequent release of nutrients from sediments, growth of plankton will be accelerated.   In conjunction with floating
 plants, such growth might cause anaerobic conditions which would make the lake unsuitable as a source of drinking water.
38.       The Committee therefore, recommends that any management programme to be adopted for the conservation of the
 lake ecosystem should primarily aim at minimizing the inflow of nutrients into the lake. Some of the measures which the
 Committee strongly feels would be helpful in diversion of pollution and would reduce the inflow of pollutants to a great

(f)     Immediate arrests of deforestation, quarrying, increased land use for unabated urbanization.  
39.       The Committee is strongly of the view that provision of proper sewage disposal facilities will reduce the organic
 loading in the lake to a great extent.  The Committee therefore recommends, that it is necessary to look into the possibilities
 such as a common sewerage system for a cluster of house boats, sanitary systems in individual units and devices for removal
 of the wastes in containers.   The Committee notes with satisfaction that some NGOs are engaged in collecting the solid
 waste on a day-to-day basis from inside the lake.   It will also be desirable to rearrange the mooring areas of the house-boats
 so as to have them in an orderly manner instead of being located in an unplanned and random manner, as these are now.  It
 will help in ensuring common service facilities including sewage disposal systems.
40.       The Committee recommends that following specific measures be adopted for restoring the health of the lake.
(i)
      Selective harvesting of macrophytes, particularly, emergent and submerged at the time of peak growth can
 substantially help removal of nutrients from the lake sediments;
(ii)    Increasing water circulation is also an effective method of diverting nutrients along with out-flowing water; 
(iii)   Sediment removal, in-situ manipulation of the bottom sediment and manipulation of the biological components
 in the lake ecosystem are among the various other measures which need to be considered for reducing the
 detrimental symptoms of the eutrophication;
·                    Afforestation of degraded forest land though plantations, contour, hedgerows and in situ moisture  
 conservation;
·                    Fuel, wood and fodder plantation of indigenous exotic species;
·                    Drainage line treatment through properly design structures such as check dams, RCC drop structures,
 stone walls, trenching, fencing, water tanks and troughs and wetting;
·                    Forage production through silvi-pasture development and on farm fodder development;
 
(iv)  Although the Ministry has apprised the Committee that infestation of the ‘Euglena rubra’ in the lake water has

 menace:-
a)
      Skimming, agitation of water, removal of scum; and
b)      Aeration of stagnant pockets with anoxic sediments and oxygen depleted underwater and the
 construction of ring bounds to check ingress of solid waste/organic matter.
(v)        The Committee is happy to note that in pursuance of its recommendation made in its 112 th Report at para 64

 northern shore. Although the project is still in progress, the Committee, however, feels that general tempo of
 activities is essentially sluggish and hence again suggests for enlisting the assistance of Army Engineering

41.       Working with French engineers in 1992, Clean-Flo restored the ‘Minuere River’ in Fourmies, France, for which the
 city won two prestigious environmental awards from the French Government.  The key to the process is a special
 formulation, termed C-FLO by the company. Equipment is set up on the shore and at the bottom of the water body. The
 entire lake is artificially filled with oxygen starting from the bottom. Oxygenation kills anaerobic bacteria which live in the
 absence of oxygen, and are the source of toxic hydrogen sulphide, sulphuric acid and ammonia gas. The sulphate in
 sulphuric acid already in the lake is absorbed by microbes, plants and aquatic animals. Low-oxygen microbes convert nitric
 acid to inert nitrogen gas. Carbon in the sediment is used as an energy source, so carbon dioxide is another end-product.
42.       Generally when the Lake runs out of oxygen at the bottom, there is a massive release of phosphorus and nitrogen that
 breed weeds and algae, from the bottom sediment. Exposure to sunlight and oxygen in the atmosphere kills disease bacteria
 and toxic gases accumulated at the bottom are released. Putting oxygenated surface water on the bottom of lakes binds
 phosphorus and nitrogen to inorganic sediments like clay. This reduces the content of these two compounds in water by up
 to 97 percent and neutralizes acids so that the lake can begin its recovery.
43.       A characteristic feature of this mechanism is that no human intervention is required to operate the equipment. Once
 started, they run all day. In five to six years, a few parts in the air compressor, and in 7-10 years, bearings may wear out.
 Turning off the equipment for five days results in an algal bloom. It requires minimal maintenance - annual maintenance
 costs typically range between 10 and 20 percent of the equipment cost. The cost is not at all high, according to ‘Clean-Flo
 Laboratories, Inc.’, U.S.A., and the larger the water body, the cheaper it is. The cost is one-tenth the cost incurred in
 dredging or nutrient diversion. In India, the Kachrali Lake cleaning project in 'Inane, Maharashtra, and a few lagoons for the
 Leela Group of Hotels in Goa, have adopted Clean-Flo systems and have shown a marked improvement in the clarity of
 water as well as adequate oxygen levels even though “water- hyacinth seeds”, are present in the four-hectare Kachrali Lake.
44.       The Committee also recommends that the Ministry of Environment & Forests may examine such mechanisms/
 processes developed by ‘Clean-Flo Laboratories, Inc.’, U.S.A. which was started in 1970 and operates with a special
 formulation, termed “C-FLO” by the company. Beneficial microbes, which feed on organic sediment, ooze and peat at the
 bottom, are introduced. These microbes convert the pollutants into carbon dioxide and water. ‘C-FLO’ also adds organisms
 that are natural food for aquatic insects. 
45.       The Committee notes that certain variety of exotic fishes introduced in some water bodies in West Bengal have been
 found to be acting as cleaning agents by eating the away pollutants.  The Committee suggests that such fishes may also be
 tried in Dal Lake so that pollution and contamination levels could be brought down in a natural way.  Besides, the
 Committee suggests that both the Ministry of Environment & Forests and the J&K Government may explore the
 biotechnological options to address the issue of conservation of the lake.   Further, the Committee feels that “polluter must
 pay” principle may be applied to make the polluters responsible for their actions in spoiling the lake.
REHABILITATION & RESETTLEMENT PROGRAMME OF LAKE DWELLERS
46.       Some of the dwellers who have settled in the Dal Lake areas form part of the history of the Lake.  They have been
 doing cultivation on floating gardens and demb lands since late 19
th century and had property rights on the marsh land and
 related water channels. The Lake water is being used for irrigating vegetable fields, which have grown in number during
 recent years. The present maximum depth of the lake (Nagin basin) is 6 m. Many aquatic plants growing in the lake are used
 as food, fodder and compost by people whose main occupation has been to collect wild products of Dal Lake and grow
 vegetables for the city consumption. They were registered as tenants and revenue was collected daily from them by the state
 administration. The cultivators of the Dal Lake were called Mir Behris. In due course, the number of dwellers has been
 continuously growing and the families have got extended and the occupations have diversified. The lake dwellers claim to
 be part and parcel of the lake ecosystem.  But ironically the lake ecosystem has come under severe pressure due to their
 activities.
47.       Relocation and rehabilitation of population living inside the lake constitutes one of the most important measures to
 conserve it.  All other efforts to clean the lake may not effectively address the conservation issue without dealing with the
 problems caused by the people who are settled inside it.  The Report of Prof.(Dr.) Helmut Kroiss, which has been mentioned
 earlier, observed that “all actions within the lake such as deweeding, local aeration and skimming of algae help to fight the
 symptoms of the degradation process but will not be able to restore the desired water quality and sustainable, ecological
 development for the future”.  The same Kroiss report had also observed, “the actual population of about 50,000 people
 living in the lake area without proper sanitation will not allow sustainable development.   It has to be doubted that there
 exists an economically feasible technical solution to restore the lake and to provide adequate social development of the
 people living in this area at the same time.  It is therefore recommended to carefully consider the relocation of the majority
 of the population actually living within the lake to an area outside the lake”.

 the report however acknowledged that, “transfer of this population to new housing areas is a complex and sensitive process

ASPECTS RELATED TO GENERATING PUBLIC AWARENESS FOR CONSERVING THE DAL LAKE
51.       Public awareness, education and information programmes are essential to spread consciousness among people about
 the fundamental necessity of conserving the lake and the ways and means of doing it.  People’s understanding of
 preservation of fresh water lakes and their consciousness regarding the protection of water resources and such lakes has to
 be further awakened.   Agenda 21 of the Rio Summit of 1991 specifically devoted to the issue of public awareness to
 preserve sources of water, which are getting increasingly depleted.   Prof. (Dr.)  Kroiss in his important Report observed,
 “the whole process of lake restoration is linked to a common understanding of water protection.   It needs a new behaviour
 towards waste and waste handling”.
52.       Stating that “…education does not interfere with any decision on the technical measures to be taken” he
 recommended that “educational part of the project should be started without any delay” and schools and media must be
 involved in the whole process”.
53.       The Committee welcomes the efforts to integrate public awareness programme with DPR (Detailed Project Report)
 for the Dal Lake for educating people about the benefits of the lake.   The Committee is happy to note that the State
 Government has been following a programme in this direction by developing films to educate regarding pollution and
 conservation of the lake.   It is also happy to note that a separate public awareness cell is functioning in the J&K LAWDA.
 By awakening people’s consciousness and sensitizing them about the importance of the lake for protecting ecology,
 economy and peace of the region we can enlist their willing support in restoring the lake to its lost glory, beauty and purity.

 effectively managing the solid waste.

R E P O R T
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Ocean Development on the
 recommendations contained in the One Hundred-fifteenth Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee
 on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants (2003-2004) of the Department of Ocean
 Development which was presented/laid to both Houses of Parliament on 2
nd May, 2003.  There are twenty one
 recommendations contained in One Hundred- fifteenth Report of the Committee. Action Taken notes on the recommendations
 of the Committee were received from the Department on 31st July,2003.
The Committee’s recommendations, action taken thereon and comments of the Committee on the action taken by the
 Department of Ocean Development are set out in the succeeding paragraphs: -
BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR 2003-04
Recommendation
The Committee feels that the Department during 2002-03 had to scale down its activities due to reduction in its B.E.
 from Rs.175 crores to Rs. 150 crores.  The Committee is constrained to note that in many cases   major  disproportionate
 variations is due to delay in getting the necessary Government approvals.  The Committee feels that these kind of hassles should
 be removed and strongly recommends higher allocations for activities of the Department which is doing a commendable job. 
 The Committee also feels that there is an urgent need to review the whole planning and budgeting process in the Department so
 that realistic physical and financial targets are projected in the Budget and planned projects are not hampered due to drastic cuts
 at R.E. stage.  It is equally important to prioritise the projects in the light of their potential benefit to the Nation.
                                                                                                                      (Para 8)
Action Taken by the Department
            The budget projection for various Plan and Non-Plan Schemes is made on the basis of inputs received from the
 Programme officers controlling the Schemes.  The Ministry of Finance following  exhaustive  discussions  between  the 
 Department  and the Planning Commission makes final Budget allocation for the Plan Scheme available.  The Budget allocation
 and actual expenditure for the year 2002-03 was;
Scheme
                        B.E                              R.E.                             Actual Expenditure
Plan Schemes:              Rs.175.00 Crore          Rs.150.00 Crore          Rs.139.58 Crore
Non-Plan Schemes       Rs. 24.28 Crore           Rs. 24.28 Crore           Rs. 27.42 Crore
Comments
While the Committee notes the reply, it reiterates that Department should review the whole planning and budgetary
 process by keeping in mind the long term policy perspective so that any reduction during R.E. stage can be avoided.
 
POLAR SCIENCE (ANTARCTIC RESEARCH ) PROGRAMME
Recommendation
Commencement of the Antarctic Programme in the eighties and its evolution and growth represent the excellence of our
 scientific and technological capabilities beyond the frontiers of our country.  The study and research undertaken during
 Antarctic expeditions have produced a repository of data and  information  which are of immense importance not only for India
 but for the entire world.  Pursuing this mission as part of the mainstream of the international endeavour to explore the icy
 continent has made invaluable contribution to promote international understanding.  The Committee, therefore, feels that the
 Antarctic programme should not be allowed to suffer for want of funds.  Besides, with a view to strengthening our scientific
 base in Antarctica, there is a need for expanding the area of activities by installing many more research stations in different
 regions of Antarctica.

The  Indian Antarctic Programme was reviewed on recommendation of the Union Cabinet by National Council for

nd  expedition team and the research activity  will shortly start in this

COASTAL OCEAN MONITORING AND PREDICTION SYSTEM (COMAPS)       
Recommendation
The Committee recommends that the Department may augment its ongoing Coastal Ocean Monitoring and Prediction
 System to regularly monitor the condition of the coastal waters and adjoining areas.       
(Para 31)
Action Taken by the Department
The Department monitors the health of our seas on a long-term basis to facilitate the Pollution Control Authorities for
 management of marine pollution related issues, like prescription of appropriate disposal standards, as per the assimilation
 capacity of the receiving water bodies, water quality criteria etc.  During the X Plan period, the Department has augmented the
 programme with following additional activities: (1) Pesticide residues analysis in organisms at selected stations along the
 coastline; (2) Physical oceanographic studies leading to determination of Waste assimilation capacity; (3) Development of GIS
 based data base for source of pollutants; and (4) Establishment of a Microbial reference Centre.
Comments  
The Committee observes that there is a need for greater co-ordination between the Department and respective State
 Pollution Control Boards for a continued monitoring of marine pollution levels and data generated through Geographical
 Information System (GIS) must be utilized to the fullest extent to achieve desired results.
MARINE RESEACH AND  CAPACITY BUILDING
Recommendation
For strengthening ocean research centers in coastal universities, the Department is emphasizing on quantum jump in our
 approach towards the ocean.  To achieve that purpose the Committee recommends that the Department should formulate an
 integrated approach and explore the possibilities of bringing all maritime educational institutions under one body such as a
 Maritime University.  Since ocean sciences are multi-disciplinary sciences such an integrated approach, the Committee feels,
 will be of vital significance.  The Committee recommends that the Department should establish Oceanariums in different parts

Action Taken by the Department
The   Department through nine Ocean Science and Technology Cells (OSTCs), which have been established to act as
 nodal coordinating agencies in various universities/institutes, has been providing funding support to research projects in selected
 disciplines of marine science and technology.  This is being done in addition to the marine science courses that these and other

 (Chennai), the     National Centre for Antarctic and Ocean Research (Goa) and the Indian National Centre for Ocean
 Information Services (Hyderabad) and two attached offices – Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management (ICMAM)
 Project Directorate (Chennai) and the Centre for Marine Living Resources and Ecology (Kochi) to conduct research, training
 and provide specialized facilities in marine science & technology sector.  However, as suggested, the possibility of bringing
 organizations/institutes set up in the marine sciences & technology field under one umbrella agency for better coordination, will
 be actively explored.
Department has taken initiative by developing exhibits and through national and state level expositions it is promoting
 awareness about oceans and their resources amongst people and students.  Development of Oceanariums, which are very
 specialized permanent exhibits containing live specimens under artificial conditions, will be taken up in consultation with State
 Governments and technical institutes such as NIOT, CMFRI and NIO, considering the high level of capital investment and
 technical skills required for establishing and maintaining such Oceanariums.
Comments  
The Committee commends the efforts being made by the Department in achieving programme objectives and hopes that
 desired results would be achieved.

Recommendation
The Committee observes that the Coastal research Vessels (CRVs), with the participation of scientists of other related

Both the vessels are being fitted with small A-Frame and handling systems in the AFT of the vessel, so that the vessel

 to West Coast circumventing Sri Lanka to increase the frequency of cruising.  The vessel have been able to achieve more that
 70% of sea time.   
Comments  
The Committee notes the reply and recommends the Department to try to cover maximum number of islands spread over
 Indian Coastline in near future. Besides, the cruises should also observe critically the habitats including flora and fauna
 specially sea turtles in Lakshdweep Islands and coastal areas of Orissa.
INTERNATIONAL   CO-OPERATION
Recommendation
The Committee notes that India is a signatory to the Ocean Charter which is not a legal entity, but which stipulates that
 all nations shall act in unison to protect the oceans.  India being a major maritime country in the Indian Ocean rim, it has a
 greater responsibility to take initiatives for bringing together all littoral countries for the development, protection and
 conservation of oceans.  The Committee notes with trepidation the observation of Dr. R. Sengupta, renowned oceanographer,
 “Of the three greatest water bodies, the Atlantic, the pacific and the Indian ocean, the latter was the cleanest.  But that is history
 now”.  The Committee therefore recommends that India must take a lead to protect its own interests and the interests of
 developing countries vis-a-vis their oceanic resources.
(Para 47)
Action Taken by the Department
Noted.  It may be mentioned that Inter governmental Oceanographic Commission(IOC), UNESCO has established
 Global Ocean Observing System(GOOS).  GOOS did not exist so far for Indian Ocean.  India has taken lead in establishing
 IOGOOS, involvingh several Indian Ocean Rim  Countries.  India has also taken lead in establishing Argo floats in Indian
 Ocean.  It may be mentioned that Indian is pioneering the cause of developing Indian Ocean Rim countries.
Comments  
The Committee notes the reply and appreciates the efforts of the Department.
OCEAN OBSERVATION & INFORMATION SERVICES (OOIS)
Recommendation
The Committee recommends that in order to improve Oceanography services, the Department should strengthen the
 observation platforms.  The moored buoy network should also be augmented to improve generation of data useful for the
 Coastal and off shore developmental activities.  The Department should also process the data collected from Array for Real-
time Geotropic Oceanography (ARGO) Floats for obtaining temperature and salinity profiles from the Indian Ocean to study the
 long-term climate and Monsoon variability.
(Para 52)
Action Taken by the Department
In order to strengthen the observation platforms to cater to the needs of coastal and off shore developmental activities,
 the Department has proposed to augment from the 12-buoy network established during 9
th Plan to the 40-buoy network during
 the X Plan period.  Besides, about 150 ARGO Floats would be deployed in the Indian Ocean region for acquiring temperature &
 salinity data profiles, to understand the upper ocean processes for studying the long-term climate and Monsoon variability.  The
 temperature salinity profiling data being collected under ARGO project would be utilized for studying the large scale
 oceanographic process to address issues relating to climate variability and monsoon with active participation of reputed
 institutes like, Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore, NIO, Goa etc.
Comments
            While the Committee appreciates the Department’s efforts for undertaking programmes aimed at developing Ocean
 Observation Information Service for different states, it is of the view that the data collected must be timely disseminated so that
 the same can be utilized to predict cyclones and prevent loss of life and property.

I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised
 by the Committee to submit the report on its behalf, present the Twelfth Report on the Demands for Grants pertaining
 to the Department of Science and Technology (Ministry of Science and Technology) for the year 1994-95 (Demand No.
 71).

 Science and Technology on the basis of the documents made available to it and the submission made before it by the
 Secretary and the other representatives of the Department.
 
3. The Committee expresses its thanks to the officers of the Department for replying to the clarifications sought by the
 Hon'ble Members and for placing before it the required material to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for
 Grants of the Department of Science and Technology.

REPORT
 
The Department of Science and Technology (DST) has a broad mandate of promoting science and technology on
 an overall basis in the country. This Department, inter alia, deals with the formulation of policy statements and

12th Report of Committee on S&T
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/12threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:09:54]
 guidelines on science and technology and also looks after their implementation. Promoting new areas of science is one
 of the major activities of the Department. Since the Department  of Science and Technology is the nodal Department in
 so far as promoting scientific activity in the country is concerned, it has to coordinate its endeavors with a host of
 scientific organisations, institutions and autonomous bodies which operate in the country. It also runs science and
 technology related programmes under schemes of bilateral and multilateral cooperation with other countries and foreign
 agencies. The Department deals with the promotion of ventures, which involve commercialisation of technologies
 developed indigenously. Through India Metrological Department (IMD), Survey of India (SOI) and National Atlas
 Thematic Mapping Organisation (NATMO), the Department provides scientific services.
 
2. The Secretary of the Department of Science and Technology, in his presentation, informed the Committee about the
 thrust areas of the Department and gave an account of the activities of the Department ,undertaken during the year
 1993-94. The Committee was particularly informed about the society related programmes, expansion of seismological
 network, strengthening linkages with other scientific organisations, establishing coordination with other Ministries and
 Departments including the socio-economic Ministries/Departments, promotion of home-grown technologies and
 supporting new R&D projects. The Committee was told that two Mission Mode projects - one on ‘Sugar Production
 Technologies' and the other on 'Advanced Composites' are being implemented by the Department. The Committee was
 also given to understand that for the year 1994-95, the Department intends to derive its guiding principles from the
 Sixth Report of the Committee on Science & Technology, Environment and Forests. These guiding principles would be
 to vigorously sustain support to scientific research, enuciate programmes which are of societal relevance and establish
 greater linkages with various Ministries/Departments including the socio-economic Ministries/Departments. The
 Department would also promote effective coordination. The Secretary of the Department especially made a reference to
 the new fund which would be created by transferring the 5 per cent cess on payment of royalty for imported
 technologies which is presently collected under the Research & Development Cess Act and would be administered by
 the Department of Science and Technology to help the indigenously developed technologies to reach the stage of
 commercial application. This new fund would be termed as the' Fund for Technology Development and Application'.
 
3. After listening to the presentation made by the Secretary of the Department of Science and Technology, the
 Committee examined the budgetary allocations of the Department for the year 1994-95. * While considering the
 Demands for Grants of the Department, the Committee got an opportunity to review the working of various projects
 and programmes which fall within the mandate of the Department of Science and Technology.
* For summary of the Demands for Grants, see Schedule.
4.     The Committee expressed its happiness that  Government  had  decided  to  set up a Fund for Technology
 Development and Application' into which the cess collected under the Research and Development Cess Act, 1986
 would be put. This Fund would be administered by the Department of Science and Technology and utilised to help
 indigenously developed technologies to reach the stage of commercial application. The Committee wanted to know as
 to how much money is likely to accrue to the Department through this new Fundduring the year 1994-95 and how the
 Department proposes to utlise it. The Committee was informed  that the Government is considering the proposal to
 amend the Research and Development Cess Act, 1986 so as to enable it to reappropriate the cess collected. The Fund
 would be utilised to meet the expenditure incurred in providing equity capital and/or any other form of financial
 assistance to research and development institutions and industrial concerns which would attempt commercial
 application of indigenous technology or adapting imported technology to wider commercial application. The
 Committee was told that the amount collected initially may not be very large, but if more and more technologies are
 imported which is a possibility under the liberalised economic policies, naturally the amount collected for this Fund
 would also increase. In a period of  five years ending March, 1993, the total collection of cess has been about Rs. 150
 crores. The Committee is of the view that the proposed new Fund would certainly act as a catalyst in promoting
 indigenously developed technologies reach the stage of commercial application and would result in a greater interface
 between scientific institutions and industry. The Committee would, however, like the Department to do proper analysis
 about the use of this Fund and the manner in which it would utilise the proposed Fund for Technology Development
 and Application. The Committee feels that the  Department would not treat this Fund just as an additional resource and,
 therefore, proper thrust and direction would be provided to the utilization of this Fund. A proper institutional
 mechanism to ensure this is called for.
 
5. The Committee wanted to know about the total Eight Plan outlay made for the Department under different heads and

 total allocation made to the Department was to the tune of Rs. 351 crores(B.E.). This included Rs. 10.2 crores which
 were transferred to Ministry of Urban Development for civil works of IMD, SOI and NATMO. Taking into account the

 352.6 crores, and on the basis of the expenditure incurred, the Committee was told that the Department could almost
 fully utilise the total allocation. While taking note of this explanation furnished by the Department, what was observed

 the funds and there is excess utilisation in the non-plan component which normally reflects the running cost of the

92, as there had been slippage in delivery of certain radars which were subsequently received in 1992-93. The reason for
 under utilisation in 1992-93 was due to delay in the receipt of the new computer for the Northern Hemisphere Analysis
 Centre, which had since been received in 1993-94. It was clarified to the Committee that savings by NCMRWF in
 1993-94 were mainly due to revision of the cost estimates of the proposed NCMRWF building and residential quarters,
 as it was felt by the Expenditure Finance Committee that there was scope for reduction in the area of construction and
 construction cost. It took some time to re-examine the proposal and revise the costs through an export committee. The
 Committee was informed that the Expenditure Finance Committee has not approved the proposal and the Department
 would be able to show some progress in this matter. As regards anxiety expressed by the Committee about the
 installation and upkeep of the Cray computer, the Committee was told that it continues to operate from the IMD
 complex at Lodhi Road and the absence of the new building has not hampered the working of the NCMRWF centres.
 The Committee hopes that during the year 1994-95, IMD, SOI and NCMRWF would be able to utilise fully the plan
 component of the budget estimates earmarked for these organisations for the year 1994-95.
9. Mass Employment Generation through S&T (MEGSAT) can be an important programme under which training is
 imparted to various identified trades with the help of S&T experts and institutions for creating technical manpower. The
 programme also aims at generating jobs on a sustainable basis. In the year 1993-94 a sum of Rs. 3.50 crores was
 provided for this programme but in the budget estimates for the year 1994-95 the allocation has been reduced to only
 Rs. 50 lakhs. The Committee wanted to know the reasons for this drastic reduction in the allocation for this programme.
 The Committee was informed that the MEGSAT programme was discussed by the Department of Science and
 Technology with the Planning Commission and it was decided that any new employment generation programme like
 MEGSAT needs to be integrated with the existing employment generation programmes like TRYSEM, IRDP, JRY, run
 by the Ministry of Rural Development. Recognising the fact that by the application of science and technology skills can
 be improved, the Department of Science and Technology should co- ordinate its activities with the Ministry of Rural
 Development and other Departments so as to explore the possibilities of employment generation particularly for the
 rural youth, women and weaker sections of society by providing greater S&T inputs into the existing employment
 generation programmes.
              
10.Under the head 'Drugs an Pharmaceuticals Research' in the budget estimates for the year 1994-95, a provision of Rs.
 10 crores has been made, but the Committee found that there         was no allocation made under this head last year. The
 Committee, therefore, wanted to know why this allocation has been made in the budget estimates for this year. The
 Committee was informed that the Department of Science and Technology is giving emphasis on the support of        
 Life Science activities along with the Department of Biotechnology and the Council of Scientific           and Industrial
 Research. According to the Department, due to the emerging global scenario, it would be necessary for the country to
 prepare itself in a big way by stepping up capabilities for indigenous drug design and development. For achieving this
 purpose, a provision for Rs. 10 crores has been made in the budget estimates for this year. The Committee was also
 informed that a committee consisting of Secretary, Department of Science and Technology, Secretary, Department of
 Biotechnology and Director-General, CSIR would guide the activities in this area. One or more of the important
 national institutions like the laboratories of CSIR and industries would also be involved in this programme. The
 Committee is concerned that when major institutions and infrastructure in this area exists in CSIR, DBT and ICMR
 why Department of Science and Technology should get involved. Any capabilities under DST which are marginal at
 present should be made available to these agencies. DST should concentrate on areas where serious gaps exist on the
 S&T scene. The Department may also made efforts to attract industry to work in developing drugs and pharmaceuticals
 from basic research to product.
 
11. The Committee observed that in the budget estimates for the year 1994-95 for the Technology Information
 Forecasting and Assessment Council (TIFAC), a sum of Rs. 7.16 crores has been allocated while in the revised

 estimates for the year 1993-94, this Council got Rs. 3.99 crores. In view of this increased allocation for TIFAC, the
 Committee wanted to know whether the Department has some special programmes to be undertaken by the TIFAC
 during the current year. The Committee was informed that TIFAC was set up to undertake technology forecasting,
 technology, and assessment and to disseminate technology information. The Department has initiated Mission Mode

 have been formulated in the form of multi-institutional projects. Further, at the instance of Planning Commission,

 project management role of TIFAC in the project on advanced composites. The Committee is of the view that TIFAC
 can make a great impact in promoting science if it clearly follows its original objectives. The Committee feels that,
 being the nodal agency for promoting S&T, the Department of Science and Technology should bring about flexibility
 in the operation of the scientific departments and that there should be transparency in t operation of TIFAC. The
 Committee noted that funds allocated for TIFAC were far great than support provided to many major aided institutions.
 
12.  Societal programmes of the Department of Science and Technology aim at providing
the benefit of science and technologies directly to the people. The Committee has, however observed that in regard to
 some of the society-related programmes there are other institution which too are looking after similar types of
 programmes. In order to avoid duplication  supporting such programmes the Committee is of the view that the
 Department of Science and Technology may consider transferring some of the programmes to the specialise      
 institutions or concerned bodies, and the money thus saved can be utilized for promoting other thrust areas of the
 Department. The Committee strongly supports the S&T programme       undertaken by the Department because it is
 interested in having a very strong S&T base for the country but it would like to point out that the Department should
 regroup its activities or shed some of its load so as to concentrate on thrust areas that are not being dealt with by    
 other agencies.
 
13. The Department should also promote indigenous technologies which exist in the country which are highly useful
 and very cheap. By strengthening this area the Department would not only create Societal impact but would also be
 able to generate employment. The Department of Science and Technology should make efforts to create a strong
 technological base in the country relying on its technological traditions. The Department should investigate areas where
 India had a strong technological base and replace and upgrade some of the old technologies so that with less investment
 India can gain competitive technological edge over other countries.
 
14. Through science and society programme, the Department of Science and Technology makes the use of S&T for
 societal development, which particularly aims at influencing the lives        of weaker sections, tribals and women. The
 other component of this programme relates to the popularisation of science and entrepreneurship development .   
 through the intervention of S&T. The Committee was given an account of the activity undertaken by the Department
 during the last year and a recent successful experiment conducted by the department in this area was the Children’s
 Science Congress which was every popular among children.  The Department is also thinking of setting up of a
 National Children’s Science Academy. The Committee feels that
many of the ills which beset Indian society today are largely due to the unscientific attitude. Creating scientific temper
 among masses is, therefore, a great responsibility of the Department of Science and Technology. This is an area of great
 importance.

5. The Committee noticed that for the Mission Mode on Cyclone Warning  and Seismic Observation in the budget
 estimates for the year 1994-95, there is only a marginal increase of Rs.  15 lakh over the last year's budget estimates.
 The Committee, therefore, wanted to know whether with this meager increase the Department would be able to run this
 programme in Mission Mode, particularly when the Department intends of re-orient its approach after the earthquake in
 the Marathwada region. The Committee was told that under the Mission Mode Project, a sum of Rs. 2 crores has been
 provided in this years budget against Rs. 1.85 crores provided last year. While this Mission Mode Project will be with a
 specific intention of enhancing the capabilities of seismic observations, there is also a provision of Rs. I crore under
 seismicity. Thus total provision under seismology for the year 1994-95 comes to Rs. 3 crores. IMD also incurs some
 expenditure on seismology in maintaining its national network. The Committee was informed that as a post-budgetary
 development, a World Bank loan of 7.5 million US dollars for improving the seismic monitoring set-up in peninsular
 India has been approved. The Department also intends to strengthen its seismic network in the Himalayas and the
 North-Eastern Region. It intends to initiate the programme of micro-zoning of selected cities and locations in the
 country as this would lead to reduction of loss of life and damage to property. The Committee observes that the whole
 area of seismicity has two aspects: one relates to seismology and the other to the disaster mitigation efforts. In the area
 of seismology, the Department should upgrade - its technology. The instruments which are awfilable to the Department
 for observing seismological activities have to be upgraded as also the manner in which the data is processed and
 analysis made. The Department should also spend a part of its funds in imparting knowledge to the people as to how
 they can cope with the disaster and how the loss of life and damage to property can be minimized. The Committee feels
 that some major efforts are required to be made by the Department in the area of earthquake prediction like the
 Department has done in the case of Cyclone warnings and there is tremendous need for software development. The
 Committee is of the view that the Department needs to evolve an  integrated disaster prediction and mitigation
 programme for the entire country.
 
16. The Committee was informed that under the instrument development programme, the Department aims at planning,
 co-ordinating and implementing programmes leading to indigenous development and production of instruments. The
 allocation made for the instruments development in the budget estimates for the year 1994-95 is Rs. 2 crores. The
 Department is also making an attempt to get some part of the funding from industry. The Committee agrees with the
 Department that it is a very vital area for modernising the industry in the country and needs adequate financial support.
 
  17.       The Committee wanted to know the reasons for increase from the revised estimates of Rs. 45 lakhs for the year
 1993-94 to Rs. 1.20 crores in the budget estimates for the year 1994-95 in the area of National Coordination of Testing
 and Calibration Facilities (NCTCF). It was explained to the Committee that the increase in the provision has been made
 with a view to developing and establishing a national accreditation and wants to initiate new system of accreditation in
 order to promote our exports. The Committee felt that there was need for an integrated look at the areas of standards
 quality control, reliability evaluation, accreditation of facilities, national testing capabilities, etc. There were widely
 disparate investments in different areas, for example, Department of Electronics, Department of Science and
 Technology, etc. These need to be reviewed. A strong programme in this area is called for with the thrust on exports
 and global competitiveness.
 
18. The Committee is of the view that Science and Society programmes, Seismicity, Instrument Development and the
 National Coordination of Testing and Calibration Facilities are vital areas which require to be strengthened and,
 therefore, recommends that at the time of doing mid-term appraisal of the Eighth Five Year Plan, the Government may
 consider enhancing the allocation for these four programmes suitably.
 
19. The Committee noted the vital role that the Department of Science and Technology plays in the matter of bilateral
 and multilateral international cooperation and in particular, successful programmes that have been embarked upon with
 the former Soviet Union (now Russia and the new initiatives with the other Republics), Germany and the USA.
 
20. The Committee noticed that in the area of policy formulation anti related aspects for the science sector much
 headway has not been made but the Committee noted that the Government has recently constituted the Cabinet

 setting up of Science Advisory Council to the Cabinet Committee on Science and Technology, Statement of
 Technology policy or a science and technology approach to the post GATT period would receive its prompt attention as
 these measures are vital from the viewpoint of our national development.

 Recommendations contained in the One Hundred-thirteenth Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
 Science & Technology, Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants (2003-2004) of the Department of Scientific and
 Industrial Research which was presented/laid to both Houses of Parliament on 2 nd May, 2003.  There were twenty-one
 Recommendations contained in One Hundred- thirteenth Report of the Committee. Action Taken notes on the Recommendations of
 the Committee were received from the Department on 30th July, 2003.
The Committee’s Recommendation, action taken thereon and comments of the Committee on the action taken by the
 Department of Scientific and Industrial Research are set out in the succeeding paragraphs: -
NATIONAL LABORATORIES
Recommendation
The Committee appreciates the Department for carrying out research in many frontier areas of science and technology.  It
 notes with satisfaction the laudable claim of the CSIR that science is one of the areas, which can bring leadership and meet the kind
 of objectives that India has set for itself.  However, it is of opinion that the Department should make efforts to raise funds from
 Industry by successful transfer of technologies.  There is also a need for wider dissemination of technologies so that there is a greater
 interface between Industry & R&D laboratories
(Para 21)
Action Taken by the Department
Department at the outset is thankful for the encourging remarks and appreciation received from the Parliamentary Standing
 Committee.  The Committee is informed that CSIR laboratories periodically organises lab-industry get together. Department also
 shares the concern of the Committee as how to raise further funds from industry through transfer of technologies. CSIR would like to
 apprise the Committee that in order to address the issue, CSIR Society, had constituted a Committee under the Chairmanship of Shri
 H.S. Singhania an eminent industrialist for suggesting further measures for enhancing CSIR – industry interface. Several suggestions
 to deepen CSIR-industry interaction now has been made by the Committee. The Recommendation interalia include stronger customer
 orientation, customisation of products and services, shifting to relationship models of business, exchange of business management
 personnel from laboratory to industry and vice-versa etc. The Recommendation of the Committee is being processed for their
 acceptance and these would be implemented.
In addition to above the department through its Public Sector Enterprise, National Research Development Corporation
 (NRDC) generates revenues by transferring/licensing technologies to industry assigned to it by R&D laboratories and other sources.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply and hopes that the Recommendation of the Committee constituted by CSIR Society would be
 accepted and implemented for augmenting CSIR- Industry interface.
 
NATIONAL S&T HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT
Recommendation
The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation made in 86
th Report that there is a need for reviewing and
 strengthening/revamping the existing S&T support systems in the universities and other educational institutions.  The Committee is
 of the view that an agreement be reached with various financial institutions for providing loans to those research scholars for setting
 up their own enterprises.
 (Para 25)
Action Taken by the Department
During the Tenth Plan, CSIR has initiated a new activity titled as Entrepreneurship support to Research Scholars, under HRD
 scheme.  The basic aim of initiation of this activity is to inculcate the spirit of entrepreneuriship into young talented scholars.  Its
 implementation would not only enable scholars to complete doctoral programme but also help them in making use of this knowledge
 by establishing linkages with those industry which requires technological knowledge as a base and thus realise value through such
 joint efforts.  The success gained by them could encourage them to setup their own enterprises. The proposal is being processed for
 consideration by the Government during the year.
The Department of Science and Technology has been implementing a programme called ‘Fund Improvement of S&T
 Infrastructure in Universities and higher Educational Institutions (FIST) for the past few years. A total of 459 science departments in
 various universities and other higher educational institutions have been given funds for strengthening the infrastructure in their
 teaching and research laboratories.
A high-level Committee has been constituted to draft an action plan for implementing the Recommendation contained in
 Science and Technology Policy 2003 in key areas like human resource development and basic research which would also include the
 existing S&T support system in the universities and other educational institutions.
Comments

POLLUTION MONITORING MITIGATION SYSTEMS & DEVICES
Recommendation
The Committee feels that all pollution monitoring devices should be site specific as the causative agents in different areas are
 diverse and every anti pollution process must have measurable parameters to monitor its efficacy.  The Committee observes that
 pollution in the country has become acute and it is being seen as a challenge to the scientists to come up with new scientific tools to
 monitor and review the existing health based ambient quality standards.  The Committee observes that the department should
 coordinate with Pollution Control Boards in various states so that effective action is taken to sharply curb & finally prevent pollution
 in the country.
As far as the presence of arsenic content in water is concerned the Committee was informed that Bangladesh has developed
 some technology to rectify it.  The Committee recommends that CSIR may study that technology with a view to adopting it for our
 country’s benefit.
( Para 61)
Action Taken by the Department
The Central Pollution Control Board has the nodal responsibility to monitor and control pollution. They have informed that the
 present monitoring system does include assessment of water and ambient air quality.
For monitoring of water quality, 784 locations on rivers, lakes and ground water have been identified. In respect of ambient air
 quality monitoring, 290 locations in 94 cities/towns have been identified. The parameters being monitored for assessing the quality of
 water and ambient air are based on sources identified discharging waste into recipient environment. The devices used for monitoring
 are general and site specific as well. For example, for ambient air quality monitoring, high/low volume samplers are used for carrying
 out monitoring of criteria pollutants such as RSPM, SO
2 and NOx.
Special devices are used to monitor critical pollutants like VOC, PAH and BTX. To monitor the source emissions, from
 stationary sources (industries), stack monitoring devices and on-line monitors are used. However, devices used in the country for
 monitoring purposes are not completely indigenous and still number of devices are being imported. Efforts would be made to
 promote indigenous firms and institutions to manufacture equipment as per Indian conditions considering sites where monitoring are
 to be carried out and pollutants to be measured.
As far as CSIR is concerned, at NEERI all pollution monitoring devices are site specific & are being used substantially &
 extensively to identify and quantify pollution parameters of sources which are specific to sites: Antipollution process has certain
 measureable parameters which are determined by the regulatory authorities to monitor its efficacy. Pollution Control Boards are
 consulted in any pollution prevention and control assignment in the country taken by NEERI. It is true that the pollution levels in the
 country are increased and, NEERI is determining both ecotoxicity as well as genotoxicity of relevant pollutants in order to evolve
 health risk based ambient quality standards.
ITRC will coordiante with CPCB for manning use of bioremediation technologies developed as these have measurable
 parameters for monitoring their efficacy. CSIR has given a major thrust on the environmental health issues and ITRC has initiated a
 programme to develop new scientific tools for assessment of the genotoxicity. As observed by the Committee, it will intensify its
 efforts in this direction. As far as review of the health based ambient quality standards is concerned, information generated in this

Recommendation
The Committee feels that intensive efforts should be made for acceptance of herbal medicines as complementary to modern
 mainstream medicines.  Besides, the committee feels that a regular watch has to be kept on those agencies who patent our traditional
 formulations and claim them as their own.  The Committee appreciates the observation of the Director General of CSIR who while

 India has an abundant reserve.  The Committee entirely endorses the point that if our scientists apply themselves with dedication to
 harness these reserves twenty first century would be an Indian century. In fact Eric Hobsbwam in his book A New Century has
 written that India might surpass many other countries in the world and emerge as a  great country primarily because of the originality
 of her scientific and technological traditions which date back thousands and thousands of years.  At the same time the Committee
 feels that a check should be exercised on quacks in the healing profession specially those people who pose as doctors after having
 attained a degree in Ayurveda and misuse their positions to prescribe mainstream allopathic medicines or vice-versa.  The graduates
 in Ayurveda should be given the nomenclature of Ayurvedacharya & not doctor.
(Para 68)
Action Taken by the Department
CSIR through NISCAIR is already active in creation of a digital library in traditional knowledge, the project entitled
 Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL). It is a collaborative project between NISCAIR and Department of Indian System of
 Medicine and Homoeopathy, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and has been implemented at NISCAIR. About 36,000
 formulations mentioned in 14 authentic Ayurvedic texts listed out in Indian Drugs and Cosmetics Act have been transcribed in five
 international languages which are English, French, German, Spanish and Japanese. Images of the original Slokas, which have been
 transcribed, will also be included along with the references. The objective of creating TKDL is the defensive protection of traditional
 knowledge or in other words the database shall prevent the bio-piracy of traditional knoweldge. In all likelihood these database
 would act as a bridge between the codified traditional knowledge existing in Sanskrit and Hindi and the patent examiner at global
 level. It will serve as a non-patent online literature for use by the patent examiners. The transcription work on 36,000 formulations
 has been completed. However, the verification and validation work carried out by Eminent Ayurveda Experts is likely to be
 completed by August, 2003. Once validated the database will be available to patent examiners so as to prevent the misappropriation
 of the data use signing of the non-disclosure agareement by the patent offices and to prevent the misappropriation of the data.
The Department of Indian System of Medicine & Health has been requested to look into the concern of the Committee on
 quacks and also on graduates passing in Ayurveda for being given the nomenclature of Ayurvedacharya etc.

 the quality of their formulations. For example, in the budget for 2003-2004 government has given some incentives for Glucometers,
 but the prices of insulin are very high. Diabetes is spreading like an epidemic. India has been described as the future diabetic capital
 of the world. The Committee feels that the Department should make persistent efforts not only to produce insulin in our country by
 recombinant method so that its cost is reduced and it is made affordable for poor people, but also to create Ayurvedic cheaper
 formulations to treat diabetes for curing it and not just controlling it.
(Para 73)
Action Taken by the Department
Established in 1951 and committed to development of new drugs, pharmaceuticals and cost-effective process technologies
 against diseases prevalent in the country, CDRI made real impact in the Indian Health Care by developing a blood schizontocidal
 antimalarial marketed as E-mal; an antirelapse antimalarial as Aablaquin ; a non-steroidal oral contraceptive as Saheli and for use in
 dysfunctional uterine bleeding as Sevista and three economically viable process technologies for I-ephedrine, Dextropropoxyphene
 and a antimalarial Arteemether. Other significant achievements are a strong knowledgebase comprising 8000 research publications,
 more than 500 patents filed in India and abroad and about 1000 Ph.Ds spread over the Academic and Pharmaceutical sector nation-

wide holding prestigious positions in the best multinational pharma companies.
New drug discovery research and development being a multifaceted and multidisciplinary activity, the institute has since been
 actively involved in various research activities ranging from understanding of host-pathogen interactions, identification of new
 targets and designing bioassays rational drug design mechanism of action and admetox profiling of new drug molecules for
 development of safe and effective drugs. This has led the institute to acquire expertise, infrastructure and a strong knowledgebase not
 only to work in areas of current thrust but also take-up challenging problems likely to affect developing countries especially India in

 Lucknow, but have also been incorporated in the on-going R&D programs at the Central Drug Research Institute, Lucknow.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply and hopes that adequate efforts would be made in making cheaper medicines using indigenous
 systems.
DEVELOPING NEW BUILDING CONSTRUCTION MATERIALS
Recommendation
The Committee is of the opinion that new construction materials should be less energy intensive for building economical
 dwelling units for millions of our people. As large parts of our country live in villages, locally available material may be used to
 produce technologies for construction of houses & the technologies need to be region-specific.
(Para 75)
Action Taken by the Department
Building materials and technologies developed by Central Building Research Institute (CBRI) for construction of houses and
 other buildings is based on  use of locally available materials and manpower with low energy consumptions.  These Technologies are
 relevant to different geo-climatic regions of the country depending upon the availability of materials and skills of the region.  As
 desired by the Committee, under a new network programme of CSIR, full cognizance of the energy and use of local materials has
 been taken.  The major objective of the project is the development and application of low alternative/new building construction
 materials from conceptual to commercialisation through use of energy efficient and environment friendly building materials
 processes and construction technologies with emphasis on value addition to agro industrial wastes for sustainable development.  The
 project envisage to provide materials for building economical dwelling units to cater to the masses in difficult regions of the country.
Comments
The Committee observes with satisfaction the fact that building materials and technology developed at CBRI takes into
 account the different geo-climatic regions and different local needs.
INFECTIOUS DISEASED HANDLING STORAGE & RESEARCH FACILITIES
Recommendation
The Committee feels that the new storage and handling facilities should be of world-class standard. The Committee hopes that
 this facility would conduct basic research for controlling infectious diseases to reduce the risk of morbidity. The Committee hopes that
 the Department would conduct periodic review of such facilities to properly maintain their standards. The Committee emphasizes the
 need for adopting measurable parameters for effective monitoring of the progress being made in this direction.
(Para 79)
Action Taken by the Department
CSIR has been at the fore front of finding new diagnostics and therapeutic methods for controlling infectious organism and
 disease caused by them. CSIR is initiating a programme during the Tenth Plan to create adequate infrastructural storage & handling
 facility in number of CSIR laboratories. These facilities once created would enable CSIR for implementation of appropriate safety
 guidelines and enhance the speed of ongoing basic research carried on infectious microorganism at these facilities to be accelerated
 through networking.
Comments
The Committee is satisfied that the methods and techniques devised by the department to control and eliminate various
 infectious diseases are of immense significance and beneficial to the masses.  It further suggests that the Department should take
 utmost care for the maintenance of laboratories and promotion of basic research.
GIVING SPECIAL AWARDS TO THE UNEDUCATED PEOPLE WHO DISPLAY THEIR GENIUS IN SCIENTIFIC FIELD
Recommendation
The Committee observes that innovative ideas on scientific aspects not only come from urban educated people but also from
 persons who are not educated and who hail from rural areas.  Scientific discovery of excellence gives rise to technological innovations
 of excellence.  The Committee therefore recommends that the Department should create special awards for the uneducated people
 who apply their genius in scientific fields and make important discoveries.  There is also need for publicity about the quality testing
 facility so that people at large avail of it.

Recommendation

 resources in the fields of science and technology.

January 23,2004
NEW DELHI
C. RAMACHANDRAIAH,                                                                                                  
 Chairman,
